Nirvana literally means 'blowing out' or 'quenching' — early Buddhist texts pictured it as a flame going out once the fires of craving, hatred, and ignorance have burned themselves to nothing.

Tradition holds that the sage Vyasa — regarded by many Hindus as a partial incarnation of Vishnu — arranged ancient hymns passed down by word of mouth into the four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur, and Atharva.
The Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, is traditionally believed to have been revealed by God to Moses atop Mount Sinai.
Compiled by rabbis over centuries of debate on how to interpret and apply the Torah, the Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.
An acronym for its three sections — Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings) — the Tanakh is the canon of the Hebrew Bible.
Muslims believe the Quran's first verses were revealed to Muhammad by the angel Gabriel in the Cave of Hira, near Mecca, in 610 CE; revelations continued for 23 years.
The Christian Bible unites the Hebrew scriptures as its Old Testament with a New Testament of gospels and letters recounting the life and teachings of Jesus.
Composed predominantly by six Sikh Gurus and compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, the Guru Granth Sahib was declared the Sikhs' eternal, living Guru by Guru Gobind Singh in 1708.
The doctrine that God exists as three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — in one being; the New Testament describes the Holy Spirit descending 'like the blowing of a violent wind' at Pentecost.

The five obligatory acts of Islam: declaring the faith (Shahada), praying five times daily (Salat), giving to charity (Zakat), fasting during Ramadan (Sawm), and, if able, a pilgrimage to Mecca (Hajj).
Hinduism has no single founder; many of its traditions hold that a single Supreme Reality, Brahman, is expressed through gods such as the Trimurti and taught in the ancient Vedas.
Founded on the dharma the Buddha taught after his enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, Buddhism holds that suffering ends by following the Noble Eightfold Path.
The oldest of the Abrahamic religions, built on God's covenant with Abraham and on the Torah, the law revealed to Moses.
Centered on Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians believe to be the Son of God; God is understood as a Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Founded in 7th-century Arabia when Muhammad began receiving revelations later collected as the Quran, Islam teaches submission to the one God, Allah.
Traditionally traced to the sage Laozi, Taoism teaches that harmony comes from living according to the Tao ('the Way') and keeping yin and yang in balance.
Founded by Guru Nanak in 15th-century Punjab, Sikhism's line of living Gurus ended in 1708, when Guru Gobind Singh named the Guru Granth Sahib itself as his eternal successor.
Founded by the prophet Zoroaster in ancient Persia, one of the world's oldest continuously practiced religions; its fire temples keep a sacred flame burning as a symbol of Ahura Mazda.
An ancient Indian religion built on ahimsa, strict non-violence toward all living things, as the path to moksha; its most revered teacher is Mahavira, the tradition's last Tirthankara.
The absence of belief in gods; Charles Darwin's 1859 On the Origin of Species offered a natural explanation for life's diversity that many atheists point to as evidence a creator isn't needed.
The view that God's existence can never be proven or disproven; biologist Thomas Henry Huxley coined the term in 1869, from the Greek for 'not knowable.'
Yin and yang: two complements, neither of which exists or means anything at all without the other.
Considered the primordial sound of the universe, the sacred syllable Om (or Aum) is chanted across Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism alike.
Islam's holiest city, in Saudi Arabia: birthplace of Muhammad and home to the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine built around the sacred Black Stone at the center of the Grand Mosque.
A Jewish house of worship built around an ark that holds its Torah scrolls; full communal prayer traditionally requires a minyan, a quorum of at least ten adults.
An Islamic place of worship with a mihrab, a niche set into the wall to indicate the direction of Mecca, so that everyone can pray facing the same way.
Names both a building used for Christian worship and, more broadly, the entire community of Christian believers gathered around it.

Most everyday Hindu worship happens at home shrines, but grand stone temples such as the Brihadisvara Temple, built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE, host puja, ritual devotional worship, on a monumental scale.
A teacher and spiritual leader qualified to interpret Jewish law; the title comes from the Hebrew for 'my master,' and rabbis are the primary voices behind the Talmud's centuries of legal debate.

Carum carvi is Apiaceae, family to carrot, and unlike its warm-climate lookalike cumin it grows wild as far north as Scandinavia. What is sold as caraway ‘seed’ is the dried fruit of the plant's second year.
Piper cubeba is a climbing pepper vine of humid Sumatran and Javan rainforest; its berries are picked unripe and dried whole, stalk and all — the ‘tail’ that gives tailed pepper its name.

Trigonella foenum-graecum is an annual Fabaceae legume of the Near East, grown for its cuboid amber seed. It has long been used to try to raise milk supply and manage diabetes, but no good evidence confirms either use works.

Glycyrrhiza glabra is a Fabaceae legume harvested in autumn, two to three years after planting, for its sweet root — the source of glycyrrhizin, which can be 7 to 10 percent of the dried root by weight.

Myrtus communis is an evergreen Myrtaceae shrub of the Mediterranean, growing to 5 metres, with white-pink flowers giving way to blue-black berries — the same berries steeped in alcohol to make the Sardinian liqueur Mirto.

Quassia amara is a Simaroubaceae tree of tropical South America; its intensely bitter bark, dried into chips, is named after Graman Quassi, a formerly enslaved man in Suriname credited with discovering its medicinal use in the eighteenth century.

Carthamus tinctorius is an Asteraceae thistle bred for two different oils — one high in monounsaturated oleic acid, one high in polyunsaturated linoleic — and for petals that yield both a yellow and a red dye.

Zanthoxylum peppers are Rutaceae, the citrus and rue family, not related to true pepper or chili despite the name. What is sold as the peppercorn is the dried pericarp — the husk — with the shiny black seed discarded.
Capers are the unopened flower buds of Capparis spinosa, hand-picked in the morning before they can bloom and preserved by pickling in a salt or salt-and-vinegar solution.
Alpinia officinarum is a Chinese ginger-family plant grown for its rhizome, thin and orange-fleshed under a brown skin, dug up and dried for use in curries and Chinese herbal medicine.

Alpinia galanga is the same ginger-family genus as lesser galangal but a far bigger plant, growing to ten feet in Java's tropical warmth; red cultivars are used mainly as medicine, white mainly as a spice.

Ferula assa-foetida is a foul-smelling Apiaceae; harvesters expose the taproot's crown and score it repeatedly over several weeks, and the oleo-gum-resin that oozes out is collected and dried into the lump ground into asafoetida.

Aframomum melegueta is Zingiberaceae, the ginger family that also holds cardamom, native to West African wetlands. Its purple flowers give way to pods holding small, pyramid-shaped reddish-brown seeds.

Capsaicin binds TRPV1, the same heat-sensing nerve channel piperine and gingerol open, which is why an unrelated fruit reads as ‘hot’. A transdermal capsaicin patch, Qutenza, was FDA-approved in 2009 for nerve pain after shingles.

S-(+)-carvone makes up 60 to 70 percent of caraway's essential oil and gives it that rye-bread spiciness. Its mirror-image molecule, R-(−)-carvone, is the main scent of spearmint — same formula, opposite shape, a completely different smell.

Glycyrrhizin, 7 to 10 percent of dried licorice root by weight, is 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar. It also blocks the enzyme that breaks down cortisol, which is why overuse raises blood pressure and drops potassium — a real, dose-dependent risk.

Hydroxy-alpha-sanshool is the compound behind Sichuan pepper's signature sensation — food writer Harold McGee describes it as tingling and buzzing, closer to a carbonated drink than to the burn of chili or black pepper.

Safflower petals hold both a water-soluble yellow dye and an alcohol-soluble red one, carthamin, that needs no mordant to fix to cotton or silk — the same red used for centuries as a natural rouge and lip colour.

About 15 percent of a dried cubeb berry is essential oil. In Victorian England it was distilled out and sold as an antiseptic marketed specifically against gonorrhoea, and 1908 medical literature described it as acting directly on the genitourinary tract.

Nigella seed is about a third oil, and the thymoquinone in it is under active laboratory study rather than settled medicine: it is flagged as a pan-assay interference compound, meaning it binds many proteins nonspecifically and can produce misleading lab results.

Quassin and neo-quassin, the quassinoids that give quassia bark its bitterness, are the compounds behind its historic use flavouring bitters and beer. Modern research has tested quassin alongside artesunate against malaria and classes quassia as a plant-toxin insecticide.

Elecampane root's bitter, camphor-scented resin, historically called helenin, is made largely of the sesquiterpene lactones alantolactone and isoalantolactone. Herbal medicine still uses the root as an expectorant for bronchitis.
The Ganges is worshipped in Hinduism as the goddess Ganga and considered sacred along its entire length, and cattle are honored as sacred, protected from slaughter across most of India.
Buddhism's eight-spoked dharmachakra represents the Noble Eightfold Path taught by the Buddha, while the lotus, rising unstained from muddy water to bloom, symbolizes the purity of enlightenment.
The Star of David is a widely recognized symbol of Jewish identity, and the eight-day festival of Hanukkah is marked by lighting candles on a nine-branched menorah each night.
The ichthys fish was reportedly used by early Christians as a secret sign to identify fellow believers during Roman persecution, alongside the cross, Christianity's principal symbol.
Traced to Laozi, and water is its central image: it yields to everything and wears away what will not yield to it.
Sikhism's central scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, was declared the eternal, living Guru in 1708; initiated Sikhs also carry a kirpan, a small sword of iron or steel, as one of the Five Ks.
Zoroastrians hold fire sacred as a symbol of Ahura Mazda and worship at fire temples, while the winged Faravahar figure is Zoroastrianism's best-known emblem.

Shinto kami are typically tied to a natural feature such as a mountain, waterfall, or tree, and a sacred mirror, the Yata no Kagami, is one of Japan's three Imperial Regalia, associated with the sun goddess Amaterasu.

Confucianism is built on sayings attributed to Confucius, compiled by his followers into the Analects; Confucian temples still hold ceremonies honoring Confucius and ancestors with ritual offerings and incense.
The belief that souls or spirits are in animals, plants, rocks and rivers, and not only in people.
Monotheism, belief in one God, characterizes the Abrahamic religious traditions of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
Hinduism, which reveres deities such as Vishnu, and ancient Greek religion, led by Zeus and the Twelve Olympians, are two of many traditions built around the worship of numerous gods.
Shinbutsu-shūgō, the syncretic blending of Shinto kami worship with Buddhism, was Japan's dominant organized religion from Buddhism's arrival until the Meiji era.

In Buddhism, dharma refers to the Buddha's teachings and to the true nature of reality those teachings point to — one of the "Three Jewels," with the Buddha and the monastic Sangha, in which Buddhists take refuge.

Karma is the Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and Sikh principle that good or bad intent and deeds shape a person's fortune and the quality of their rebirth, turning the "wheel" of samsara that dharma's teaching aims to still.
Nirvana literally means "blowing out" or "quenching" — Buddhism describes it as the extinguishing of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, as a flame is snuffed out and left as ash.
Eggs have served as a symbol of fertility and rebirth since prehistory, while South Asian traditions describe the endless cycle of rebirth itself as a turning "wheel," samsara.
Andrei Rublev's 15th-century icon "The Trinity" depicts the three winged angels who visited Abraham in Genesis 18, an image that came to represent the three persons of the Christian Trinity.
The Five Pillars of Islam are the testimony of faith, prayer, almsgiving, fasting during Ramadan, and pilgrimage (Hajj) to Mecca — the obligatory acts of worship at the center of Muslim life.

The idea of a god taking bodily form links Hinduism's avatars of Vishnu with Christianity's doctrine of the Incarnation, though theologians debate whether "avatar" and "incarnation" truly describe the same thing.

"Messiah" comes from the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed," from a verb meaning "to rub with oil" — originally describing kings and priests ritually anointed before it came to mean an expected deliverer of Israel.
The covenant between God and Israel, given to Moses at Sinai, contains the foundations of the written Torah and lies at the heart of Jewish religious law.

Ancestor veneration — honoring and making offerings to the dead — is central to Chinese folk religion and many African traditions; incense sticks are burned before a household's ancestral spirit tablet, sometimes made of wood.
Filial piety (xiao) — a person's duty to respect, obey, and care for their parents and ancestors — is the cardinal virtue of Confucianism, said by Confucius to be "the root of virtue."
Rooted in animist belief in a spirit world, shamans enter trance states — sometimes through drumming, chanting, or the smoke of burned herbs — to travel between worlds on their community's behalf.

Christianity's Desert Fathers withdrew into the Egyptian desert to live lives of prayer, fasting, and self-denial — a pattern of ascetic renunciation echoed by Hindu sadhus and by Jain and Buddhist monks elsewhere.
A journey to a sacred place, undertaken for devotion, in nearly every major religion.

Sikhism recognizes ten human Gurus beginning with founder Guru Nanak in 1469; in 1708 the tenth Guru passed the title to the Guru Granth Sahib scripture, which Sikhs have treated as their living Guru ever since.
The Guru Granth Sahib is Sikhism's central scripture, compiled from hymns of the Sikh Gurus and other saints; since 1708 Sikhs have honored it as their eternal, living Guru.
Tibetan Buddhist prayer wheels are inscribed with a written mantra, often "Om mani padme hum"; spinning the wheel is believed to carry much the same spiritual benefit as reciting the mantra aloud.
Incense, made by burning aromatic plant materials such as resins and fragrant woods, is used in ceremonies across Hindu, Buddhist, Christian, Jewish, Islamic, and Chinese religious practice.
Trigonella foenum-graecum is a legume grown three ways at once — as a seed spice, a dried herb and a fresh vegetable leaf. Charred seeds have turned up in Tutankhamun's tomb.

Alpinia galanga (greater) and Alpinia officinarum (lesser) are both Zingiberaceae rhizomes, ginger's own family, dug up and used fresh or dried. Each has its own heat and its own flowery, peppery edge.
Carum carvi is an Apiaceae herb; what's sold as a caraway seed is really the dried fruit, an achene about 3mm long. It looks so like cumin that many languages never separated the two.

Physalis philadelphica and P. ixocarpa were domesticated in Mexico before European contact and outranked the tomato in Aztec and Maya cooking. The fruit is picked once it fills out the papery husk formed by its calyx.

Physalis peruviana is a perennial shrub in the tropics but behaves as an annual anywhere frost cuts it back. Its papery calyx keeps expanding after the petals drop, sealing the ripening berry inside its own husk.

Citrus microcarpa is a hybrid of kumquat and mandarin orange, native to the Philippines and nearby islands — standing in here for those two unmodelled parents. It's crushed whole for juice and used as a lemon or lime substitute across Filipino, Malaysian and Indonesian cooking.

Ilex paraguariensis is a species of holly, native to Paraguay, northern Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil, first cultivated by the Guaraní. Harvested branches are dried over a wood fire, which is where the drink's smoky flavour comes from.

Citrus bergamia is a probable hybrid of lemon and bitter orange, standing in here for that unmodelled bitter-orange parent. Its rind is cold-pressed for the oil that flavours Earl Grey tea, and Reggio Calabria in southern Italy supplies nearly the entire world's crop.

Jasminum sambac flowers are harvested as unopened white buds in the early morning, then open at night before closing for good the next day. About 70 percent of the scent is indole — foul in high concentration, floral in trace amounts.

Most plantains are sterile AAB-group triploids, hybrids of Musa acuminata and M. balbisiana. They carry far more starch and far less sugar than dessert bananas, so they're cooked rather than eaten raw, and Musa's poor wind tolerance leaves plantations vulnerable to hurricanes.

Amomum subulatum is Zingiberaceae like green cardamom but a separate species; its pods are dried over open flames, which is where its smoky flavour comes from. Nepal is the largest producer, ahead of India and Bhutan.

Cucurbita moschata; the butternut cultivar was bred in 1944 by Charles Leggett of Stow, Massachusetts, crossing two older squashes. Its orange flesh carries over 4,500 micrograms of beta-carotene per 100g.

Tropaeolum majus, native to the Andes, has flowers, leaves and seed pods that are all edible, with a peppery bite close to watercress. Its leaf is a textbook case of the lotus effect: water gathers into beads and rolls off instead of wetting the surface.

Perilla frutescens is a Lamiaceae annual native to Southeast Asia and the Indian highlands, grown for its aromatic leaves — shiso, in Japanese cooking. In the United States it has escaped into pastures, where cattle grazing on it can develop acute respiratory distress, called panting disease.

Nigella sativa is a Ranunculaceae flowering annual, unrelated to true cumin despite the 'black cumin' name. Its seeds carry thymoquinone alongside p-cymene, carvacrol and thymol, and are dry-roasted before use in blends like Bengali panch phoron.

Artemisia absinthium, the herb that gives absinthe its name and much of its bitterness, is a hardy plant of temperate and cold climates — the Ukrainian city of Chernobyl takes its name from the local word for it. Its thujone can cause convulsions at high doses, but studies have found no evidence it caused the 19th-century 'absinthism' panic.

Boiled, pounded soybeans are shaped into meju bricks and air-dried until a wild mould coats them, then aged in brine inside earthenware jars, sometimes for months. Jars used for doenjang production appear in 4th-century Goguryeo tomb murals.

Traditional gochujang blends red chilli powder with fermented soybean and glutinous rice, aged for years in sun-exposed earthenware jars — simplified here to chilli fermented against an existing fermented-soybean base. Sunchang has been renowned for its gochujang since the Joseon dynasty's founding in the 14th century.

Steam distillation, not crushing, is how geraniol is actually drawn out of lemongrass — a monoterpenoid alcohol and, together with citronellol, one of the two compounds that give lemongrass its lemon scent despite no citrus being involved. It is also a major component of rose and palmarosa oil.

Oxidative cleavage breaks beta-carotene down into beta-ionone, the compound behind the scent of violets and a reason cooked carrots and squash smell more floral than raw ones. It's synthesized industrially from citral and acetone for the fragrance trade.

Ethyl hexanoate is a fruity, pineapple-and-apple-peel ester formed from hexanoic acid and ethanol. Penicillium roqueforti produces it as blue cheese ripens, and food-chemistry surveys list it among the compounds most responsible for the cheese's aroma.

A sulphur compound whose smell is foul at high concentration and pungently savoury in the trace amounts found in food. It has been identified among the volatile sulphur compounds of Tuber melanosporum black truffle, and separately in the aroma profile built by Penicillium roqueforti in blue cheese.

Sufi practitioners cultivate dhikr, the remembrance of God, sometimes visualizing his name as written upon the heart -- an inward path toward union with the divine that complements Islam's outward law.

In 1889, Mirza Ghulam Ahmad founded the Ahmadiyya movement, claiming through revelation that he was the Mahdi ('rightly guided one') and Messiah that Islamic tradition expected to appear at the end times.

Shia Muslims trace legitimate leadership of the Muslim community through Muhammad's bloodline, beginning with his son-in-law Ali, rather than through election -- a hereditary claim to succession that Sunnis reject.

Sunni Islam holds that Muhammad did not appoint a successor; instead the first caliph, Abu Bakr, was chosen by the consensus of the community -- the elected, communally bound model of leadership followed by roughly 85-90 percent of Muslims today.

The word sharia literally means 'path to the watering hole,' a metaphor rooted in the importance of a reliable route to water across the Arabian desert -- sharia is likewise conceived as the path God has laid out to a good life.

Jihad, Arabic for "striving," is traditionally divided into the "greater jihad" — the internal struggle against one's own base desires — and the "lesser jihad" of external effort, guided directly by the Quran's own teaching.

In 1744, the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab formed a pact with the Najdi ruler Muhammad bin Saud, uniting his puritanical desert movement with a ruling dynasty in an alliance that founded the first Saudi state.
Salafi, Arabic for 'predecessors,' names a movement that looks to the salaf -- the first three generations of Muslims, from Muhammad onward -- as the root and purest model of Islamic practice.
The Nation of Islam grew out of and reinterprets Islam in an African-American context; its own flag places a star beside the crescent moon, on a design modeled on the flag of Turkey.

The Druze faith, which took shape in Cairo around 1017 CE, teaches that the soul is eternal and passes through successive reincarnations until it reunites with the Cosmic Mind; the five-pointed star is its principal religious emblem.

The nine-pointed star, the Baha'i Faith's most widely used symbol, reflects the numerical value of 9 that the word 'Baha' -- meaning glory -- carries in the Abjad numeral system used in Baha'i scripture.

Haile Selassie's full imperial title, 'Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah, Elect of God and King of the Kings of Ethiopia,' taken at his 1930 coronation, was seen by Jamaican Rastafarians as fulfilling prophecy and confirming him as their returned savior.

In Santeria, the Yoruba orisha Chango -- god of thunder, lightning, and fire -- was concealed by enslaved worshippers in Cuba behind the image of the Catholic martyr Santa Barbara, since both are depicted wearing red.

In Haitian Vodou, the lwa spirit Papa Legba, who guards the crossroads between the human and spirit worlds, was syncretized with the Catholic Saint Peter, keeper of heaven's gate, since Legba is likewise the 'door' to the spirit realm.

After World War II ended and military cargo deliveries stopped, some Melanesian islanders built life-size replicas of airplanes out of straw and cut new landing strips from the jungle, hoping the ritual would attract more cargo-bearing aircraft.

Scientology grew from L. Ron Hubbard's 1950 book Dianetics; its central practice, auditing, uses a wired device called the E-meter, which the Church describes as a spiritual tool for detecting areas of mental or spiritual trauma.

Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in Seoul in 1954; it became known worldwide for mass 'Blessing' wedding ceremonies, including one in 1982 that joined 2,000 couples at Madison Square Garden.
Wicca, popularized by Gerald Gardner in 1950s England, is typically duotheistic, venerating a goddess and a god traditionally conceived as the Triple Goddess and the Horned God.
Unitarian Universalism, formed in 1961 by the merger of the Unitarian and Universalist churches, uses the flaming chalice as its most widely recognized symbol.
Tenrikyo, founded in 1838 by Nakayama Miki, teaches that eight kinds of mental 'dust' -- including greed, anger, and self-love -- must be swept away through acts of kindness to live the Joyous Life.

Cao Dai, founded in Vietnam in 1926, represents God with the Left Eye of God, or Divine Eye, enshrined at its Tay Ninh Holy See, reminding believers that God witnesses everything, everywhere, constantly.
Jehovah's Witnesses are widely recognized for their door-to-door ministry, distributing literature such as The Watchtower magazine as they visit homes to spread their beliefs.

Joseph Smith said the angel Moroni directed him to a set of golden plates buried near Palmyra, New York, which he translated into the Book of Mormon, published in 1830 alongside the founding of his church.
Quakers, founded by George Fox in mid-17th-century England, traditionally practice waiting worship, gathering mostly in silence and speaking only when moved by the Inner Light.

In 1693, Jakob Ammann led a stricter schism from the Swiss and Alsatian Mennonites, founding the Amish, whose communities remain distinctive today for traveling by horse-drawn buggy rather than motor vehicle.
Mennonites trace their name to the Frisian reformer Menno Simons; the movement's Anabaptist founders baptized one another as adults near Zurich in January 1525, rejecting infant baptism.
The Shakers, founded by Ann Lee around 1747, were originally nicknamed 'Shaking Quakers' for the ecstatic trembling, marching, and dancing that characterized their worship services.

Formally established in 1863 in Battle Creek, Michigan, the Seventh-day Adventist Church has advocated a vegetarian diet since its founding, alongside observing Saturday, the Bible's seventh day, as the Sabbath.

Pentecostalism takes its name from the Christian Pentecost, when the Bible describes the Holy Spirit descending as 'tongues of fire'; the modern movement began at the 1906 Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles.

Mary Baker Eddy founded the Church of Christ, Scientist in Boston in 1879; her textbook Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, alongside the Bible, is regarded by the church as its 'dual impersonal pastor.'
The Salvation Army, founded by William Booth in 1865, is famous for its Christmas-season red kettles, where volunteers ring bells to invite passers-by to drop coins and cash into donation pots.
In 1534, King Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy severed the Church of England from Rome and declared the English crown its supreme head, founding Anglicanism.

Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses, written in 1517, protested the Church's sale of indulgences -- payments believed to reduce punishment for sin -- and are traditionally seen as having sparked the Protestant Reformation and Lutheranism.

John Knox, who studied under John Calvin in Geneva, carried Calvin's Reformed theology back to Scotland, establishing the Presbyterian tradition of church government by elected elders bound together in representative assemblies.

John Wesley, founder of Methodism, described his 1738 conversion experience at a Moravian meeting in Aldersgate, London, saying he felt his 'heart strangely warmed' -- the spark that ignited the Methodist revival within the Church of England.

In 1609, John Smyth baptized adult believers by full immersion in Amsterdam, founding the Baptist tradition on the principle -- laid out in his own tract -- that only professing believers, not infants, should be baptized.
Reform Judaism's 1885 Pittsburgh Platform declared that ceremonial rituals were binding only insofar as they enhanced the religious life of the modern Jew, elevating ethics over ritual observance.

Orthodox Judaism emerged as a self-conscious movement during the 1818-1821 Hamburg Temple dispute, when Rabbi Moses Sofer led rabbis across Europe in defending traditional, unaltered observance of halakha against Reform-influenced changes.

Hasidic Judaism was founded around 1730-1740 by Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov ('Master of the Good Name'), who taught a joyful, mystical path to God centered on ecstatic devotion rather than solely scholarly study.
Conservative Judaism developed as a deliberate middle path between Reform and Orthodox Judaism, institutionalized around the Jewish Theological Seminary of America, founded in New York in 1887.
Kabbalah's foundational text, the Zohar, describes ten sefirot -- emanations through which God sustains the universe -- traditionally diagrammed as a Tree of Life.

The Heliodorus pillar, a stone column erected around 110 BCE by an Indo-Greek envoy who inscribed himself as a devotee of the 'God of gods' Vasudeva, is among the earliest archaeological evidence of organized Vaishnava worship of Vishnu.

Shaktism's oldest scriptural evidence is the Rigveda's Devi Sukta hymn, in which the Goddess proclaims herself 'the Queen, the gatherer-up of treasures' -- the supreme reality later known as Devi or Shakti.

Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875 as a Hindu reform movement; it became the first Hindu organization to actively seek converts, and today runs more than 1,000 colleges and 10,000 schools across India.

Maharishi Mahesh Yogi introduced Transcendental Meditation to the West in 1955; practitioners silently repeat a personal mantra for 15-20 minutes twice a day, a technique popularized in the 1960s by the Beatles and the Beach Boys.

The Pali Canon, scriptural foundation of Theravada Buddhism -- the oldest surviving Buddhist school -- was committed to writing in the 1st century BCE, the most complete Buddhist canon in a classical Indian language.

Mahayana Buddhism, which spread from India to become the dominant tradition in China, Korea, Vietnam, and Japan, emphasizes the bodhisattva vow -- a pledge binding practitioners to postpone their own final liberation to help save all beings.

Zen Buddhism, which developed as Chan in Tang-dynasty China and is traditionally said to have been brought from India by the monk Bodhidharma, centers its practice on zazen -- seated meditation in profound stillness.
In 1578, the Mongol ruler Altan Khan bestowed the title Dalai Lama on the Tibetan Buddhist monk Sonam Gyatso, a title of spiritual authority that has passed by recognized reincarnation ever since.

Pure Land Buddhism teaches that Amitabha Buddha vowed to create a paradise, Sukhavati, described in Buddhist scripture as covered in beryl and gold and free of filth or evil, reached by the faithful through devoted recitation of his name.

Nichiren, a 13th-century Japanese monk, taught that chanting devotion to the Lotus Sutra -- Namu Myoho Renge Kyo -- was Buddhism's sole valid practice for this age, founding the school that bears his name.

In 1930, Japanese educators Tsunesaburo Makiguchi and Josei Toda founded Soka Gakkai as a lay society grounded in Nichiren Buddhism's veneration of the Lotus Sutra; Makiguchi died in prison in 1944 after refusing to recant his beliefs during WWII.
Sumerian scribes pressed a sharpened reed stylus into wet clay tablets, first as pictographs and, by the mid-3rd millennium BCE, as wedge-shaped signs -- faster to make in soft clay.
Hammurabi's roughly 4,130 lines of cuneiform law were cut into a 2.25 m basalt stele, using a layout already old-fashioned by his own reign.

Harappa and Mohenjo-daro rose along the Indus in standardized fired brick, sharing a single measuring system -- the Mohenjo-daro ruler, marked off in 34 mm units -- across a civilization larger than Egypt or Mesopotamia.
Shang diviners scorched turtle plastrons and ox scapulae with a hot rod until thermal stress cracked them, then read the crack pattern as an answer from the ancestors.
The Shang court that commissioned oracle-bone divinations also cast some of the ancient world's most elaborate bronze vessels, reserved for ritual rather than daily use.
By around 2650 BCE, masted Cretan ships -- and bronze that had by then moved from arsenical alloys to tin bronze -- carried Minoan trade beyond the Aegean to Egypt and Syria.
By 1450 BCE the palace of Knossos had passed to a Mycenaean elite, who adapted the Minoans' undeciphered Linear A into Linear B -- the earliest written record of the Greek language.

Within decades around 1200 BCE, Mycenaean palace centers were destroyed, the Hittite Empire collapsed entirely, and Ugarit was sacked, even as ironworking -- which needed no long, vulnerable bronze trade routes -- was spreading in from Bulgaria and Romania.

The Phoenicians' maritime trading culture carried their compact, phonetic script across the Mediterranean to North Africa and southern Europe, where it became the direct ancestor of the Greek alphabet.

The Neo-Assyrian Empire, which began in 911 BCE with the accession of Adad-nirari II, administered its territory in Akkadian cuneiform and conquered Egypt in 671 BCE -- where iron only replaced bronze in the wake of that conquest.

Cyrus the Great's Achaemenid empire, built on cavalry-heavy conquests of Media and Lydia, overran Nebuchadnezzar's Neo-Babylonian empire in 539 BCE, entering Babylon with almost no resistance and freeing its Jewish exiles per the Cyrus Cylinder.

Two generations after Cyrus founded the Achaemenid Empire, his successor Darius I sent it against Greece; Athenian hoplite spearmen, outnumbered roughly two to one, broke the Persian line at Marathon in 490 BCE.
Two centuries after Cyrus founded it, Alexander's ten-year campaign broke Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela, conquering the entire Achaemenid Persian Empire in his father's stead.

China's First Emperor was buried near Xi'an behind an army of thousands of individually crafted, life-sized terracotta soldiers, chariots, and horses -- fired clay meant to guard him in the afterlife.

After the Kalinga War left him remorseful, Ashoka had edicts of Buddhist dharma carved into rock and stone pillars across his empire -- the Dhauli inscription's rock face shaped into a standing elephant.
Carthage grew from a Phoenician colony of Tyrian traders on the North African coast into the capital of its own Punic empire, its people still writing and speaking a Canaanite tongue.
The Carthaginian general Hannibal led 38,000 troops and 38 war elephants across the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE; almost none of the elephants survived the crossing.

In January 49 BCE Caesar led his legion across the Rubicon, the river marking Italy's northern boundary -- an act forbidden to any general under arms -- igniting the civil war that ended the Republic.
When Alexander's empire fractured on his death in 323 BCE, his general Ptolemy I took Egypt and founded the Ptolemaic dynasty; Cleopatra VII, who became queen in 51 BCE, was its last ruler.
Caesar's adopted heir Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE, taking Egypt, and in 27 BCE was granted the title Augustus by the Senate -- Rome's first emperor.
Following Han envoy Zhang Qian's reports on Central Asia around 130 BCE, camel caravans carried Chinese silk as far as Rome, where the Senate tried in vain to ban it as a decadent drain of gold.

The Nubian kingdom of Kush, on the Nile south of Egypt, conquered Egypt under King Piye around 727 BCE to found its 25th Dynasty, and its later capital Meroe grew into a major ironworking center rich in ore and hardwood fuel.
Hinduism evolved over more than 3,000 years from the Vedic religion of the Indus-Ganges region and rests on scriptures such as the Vedas and Upanishads, with no single founder.

After his conversion, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka issued edicts protecting dozens of animal species from slaughter and cutting the animals killed daily for his own kitchen, putting ahimsa into imperial policy.
Mohandas Gandhi built his campaigns of nonviolent civil disobedience, which he called satyagraha, on ahimsa, the principle of nonviolence.
Buddhism traces its origin to the 6th-century-BCE teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, later gathered by his followers into scriptures such as the Pali Canon.
After the Buddha's death, his teaching was carried on by a growing community of monks and teachers, who over the centuries split into the Theravada and Mahayana traditions.
In Buddhist thought, karma is the principle that intentional actions shape future rebirths, keeping beings tied to samsara until the Buddhist path leads them out.
In Hindu philosophy, karma in the present shapes the nature and quality of a person's future lives, or samsara.
In Hinduism, dharma refers to a person's moral and religious duty appropriate to their place in life — the dharma of a farmer differs from that of a soldier.
Nirvana comes from a Sanskrit word meaning 'blown out': Buddhists describe it as the extinguishing of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion that cause suffering.
Buddhists hold that following the Noble Eightfold Path ends craving and leads to nirvana, a state of liberation the Buddha described as attainable in this life.
In Hindu belief, samsara is the beginningless cycle of death and rebirth, driven onward by karma, the residue of past actions.
Buddhism inherited the idea of samsara, an endless cycle of rebirth driven by karma, from earlier Indian religion, while denying that any fixed self passes between lives.
The Buddha's first sermon set out Four Noble Truths: dukkha (suffering), samudaya (its origin), nirodha (its ending), and magga (the path to its ending).
Buddhist tradition holds that the Buddha first taught the Four Noble Truths in a sermon called 'Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion,' delivered after his enlightenment.
The Noble Eightfold Path is the content of Buddhism's Fourth Noble Truth: eight practices of right view, speech, and action grouped into wisdom, ethical conduct, and mental discipline.
The earliest description of the Buddhist path may have been simply 'the Middle Way'; over time this short description was elaborated into the fuller Eightfold Path.
Having tried both a life of luxury and years of extreme asceticism, Siddhartha Gautama taught that a balanced Middle Way between these extremes leads to enlightenment.
In Mahayana Buddhism, a bodhisattva is a being on the path to enlightenment who, out of compassion, vows to delay or forgo their own nirvana to help all others reach it too.
Bodhisattva images are often shown holding a lotus, an ancient symbol of purity said to rise from muddy water unstained, representing the enlightened mind above worldly suffering.
Zen, called Chan in China, is a Buddhist meditation tradition traditionally traced to the monk Bodhidharma, said to have brought it from India to China around the 5th-6th century CE.
Japanese Zen gardens of carefully raked gravel or sand serve as aids to meditation, and Zen monks practice the raking itself to help their concentration.
The Dalai Lama, leading figure of Tibetan Buddhism's Gelug school, is traditionally regarded as the living incarnation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

When a Dalai Lama dies, monks search for his successor among young children and test candidates by having them identify personal belongings of their predecessor, taken as a sign of true reincarnation.
Ashoka, emperor of the Mauryan Empire, converted to Buddhism in the 3rd century BCE after a bloody war of conquest, and thereafter promoted Buddhist principles including protection of animal life.
Many of Ashoka's edicts survive carved onto rock faces and stone pillars across the Indian subcontinent, among the oldest deciphered inscriptions in Indian history.
Judaism's practice and identity are organized around a series of covenants between God and the Israelites, first with Abraham and renewed through Moses, recorded in the Torah.
A Torah scroll is handwritten entirely by a trained scribe on parchment, using a quill dipped in special ink, a task that can take about a year and a half.
According to the Torah, God inscribed the Ten Commandments onto two stone tablets and gave them to Moses on Mount Sinai.
The Ten Commandments form the core of the covenant God made with Israel at Sinai, prohibiting the worship of other gods and mandating a weekly Sabbath day of rest.
The Torah describes a covenant God made with the Israelites at Mount Sinai, promising to make them 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' if they kept his commandments.
The Torah also describes an earlier covenant with Noah after the flood, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood — a promise it says the rainbow was given to signify.
Kabbalah is a body of Jewish mystical teaching, originally transmitted orally and collected in a text called the Zohar, or 'Divine Splendor,' traditionally dated to 13th-century Spain.

The influential 16th-century kabbalist Isaac Luria taught that creation involved vessels shattering under the strain of holding divine light, scattering sparks that people gather and restore through good deeds.
In Jewish tradition, 'messiah' (Hebrew for 'anointed one') originally meant any anointed king, but came to mean a specific future ruler descended from King David who would restore Israel.
Among the traditional reasons for sounding the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, the medieval scholar Saadia Gaon listed arousing belief in the future ingathering of the exiles and the coming of the Messiah.
After Rome crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 CE and barred Jews from Jerusalem, the Jewish diaspora — communities dispersed beyond their homeland — became the center of Jewish life for centuries.

Displaced first by Babylon in the 6th century BCE and again by Rome in 70 CE, Jewish communities scattered across the Mediterranean world, forming the diaspora that would shape Jewish life for two millennia.
The 12th-century philosopher Moses Maimonides argued that God's absolute oneness means God has no parts or describable attributes, a position known as negative theology.
Early Christians adopted the ichthys, a simple two-arc fish outline, as a visual shorthand for their faith, evoking the Gospel image of the apostles as 'fishers of men.'
The doctrine of the Trinity was settled in its classic form at the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE and expanded at the Council of Constantinople in 381 CE, in the Nicene Creed.
In 325 CE the Roman emperor Constantine convened bishops from across his empire at Nicaea to agree a common statement of Christian belief, aiming to end disputes dividing the newly tolerated faith.
The Nicene Creed condemned the teaching of Arius, known as Arianism, that the Son was not co-eternal with God the Father but a distinct being of merely similar substance.
In the Eucharist, Christians reenact Jesus's Last Supper, at which he shared bread and wine with his disciples, calling the bread 'my body' and the cup 'the blood of my covenant.'

The 13th-century theologian Thomas Aquinas gave classic form to the doctrine of transubstantiation, teaching that in the Eucharist the substance of bread and wine changes into the body and blood of Christ while their outward appearance does not.

Baptism, one of Christianity's most widespread rites, marks a person's entry into the Church through ritual washing with water, following the example of Jesus's own baptism by John the Baptist in the Jordan.
Christian monasticism traces its roots to 3rd-century hermits such as Anthony of Egypt, who withdrew into the desert to live simple lives of prayer and ascetic discipline.
Medieval European monasteries became centers of learning where monks copied and illuminated manuscripts, preserving much of the West's literary heritage through the Middle Ages.

Martin Luther was angered by the Church's sale of indulgences, payments believed to reduce punishment for sin, and in 1517 wrote 95 Theses opposing the practice, helping ignite the Protestant Reformation.

The recently invented printing press let Martin Luther's 1522 German translation of the New Testament spread rapidly and cheaply, letting ordinary people read scripture for themselves and fueling the Reformation.
Metal rods are heated soft, bent into rings, and forge-welded shut before they cool, then linked together — a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
Once doors could be barred, a metal sliver shaped to match one lock's internal wards let its owner — and no one else — open it.
Prometheus fashioned the first humans from clay, then stole fire from the gods' own forge, hidden inside a hollow fennel stalk, and gave it to his creations.
For stealing fire, Zeus chained Prometheus to a rock in the Caucasus and sent an eagle to eat his liver; it regrew every night so the torment never ended, until Heracles freed him.
Prometheus's brother Epimetheus — "Afterthought" to Prometheus's "Forethought" — ignored his warning never to accept a gift from Zeus, and married Pandora anyway.
Hephaestus molded Pandora, the first woman, from clay on Zeus's orders; every god then added a gift, from beauty to a dangerously curious mind.
Hesiod's original jar (later mistranslated "box") that Pandora opened despite the warning, loosing every evil into the world — only Hope stayed trapped inside.

Punished by Zeus for leading the Titans against the Olympians, Atlas was condemned to hold up the heavens forever — a burden Heracles briefly shouldered so Atlas could fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides.
Son of Prometheus, Deucalion built a wooden chest that let him and his wife Pyrrha survive nine days of the flood Zeus sent to destroy a corrupt humanity.
Told by an oracle to throw "the bones of their mother" behind them, Deucalion and Pyrrha cast stones over their shoulders — his became men, hers became women, repopulating the earth.
Crete's exiled master craftsman built the Labyrinth to hold the Minotaur, then fashioned wings of feathers bound with beeswax so he and his son Icarus could fly free of the island.
Wearing wings his father built, Icarus ignored every warning and flew too close to the sun; the wax melted and he fell into the sea that now bears his name.
Son of the sun god Helios, Phaethon begged to drive his father's chariot for a day, lost control near the earth, and was struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt before he could burn the world.
Daedalus built this maze on Crete at King Minos's order to contain the Minotaur — its passages so winding that no one inside could find the way out unaided.
Born when Queen Pasiphaë mated with a bull sent by Poseidon, the half-man half-bull Minotaur was imprisoned by King Minos inside the Labyrinth built to contain it.
Sent as one of Athens's tribute youths to Crete, Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Labyrinth and used Ariadne's ball of thread to find his way back out.
After her ball of thread saved Theseus from the Labyrinth, Ariadne was abandoned on Naxos — where the god Dionysus found and married her.
Conceived when Zeus visited the imprisoned princess Danaë as a shower of gold, Perseus grew up to behead the Gorgon Medusa using a mirrored shield to avoid her petrifying gaze.
One of three Gorgon sisters but the only mortal one, Medusa's living snake hair and stone-turning gaze made her deadly until Perseus beheaded her with Athena's mirrored shield.
When Perseus beheaded the pregnant Medusa, the winged horse Pegasus sprang fully formed from her blood, along with his brother, the giant Chrysaor.
Chained to a sea cliff as a sacrifice to the monster Poseidon sent to punish her mother Cassiopeia's boast, Andromeda was rescued — and later married — by Perseus.
The fleece of the winged golden ram Chrysomallus, hung on an oak in a sacred grove of Colchis and guarded by a dragon that never slept.
Rightful heir to Iolcos, Jason sailed the Argo to Colchis to win the Golden Fleece for his crown — a quest only the sorceress Medea's love and magic made possible.
The Colchian sorceress helped Jason win the Golden Fleece by lulling its sleepless dragon guardian with narcotic herbs — a mortal reaching into a god of sleep's own domain.
Unlike Egypt's benevolent guardian statues, the Greek Sphinx — a woman's head on a winged lion's body — strangled every traveler at Thebes who failed her riddle.
Fated by a Delphic prophecy to kill his father and marry his mother, Oedipus fulfilled it unknowingly, then won the Theban throne by solving the Sphinx's riddle about man's three ages.
Greek mythology's greatest musician, Orpheus charmed the lord of the underworld with his lyre after his wife Eurydice died of a snakebite, winning permission to lead her back to the living.
Orpheus's bride was allowed to follow him out of the underworld on one condition — that he not look back until both reached the surface. He looked back too soon, and she was lost forever.
Mortal princess loved by Cupid (Eros), Psyche was set impossible tasks by jealous Venus, including fetching a jar of beauty from Persephone in the Underworld — which she opened despite every warning.
As thanks for kindly hosting the satyr Silenus, King Midas won a wish from Dionysus: everything he touched would turn to gold — a blessing that became a curse the moment his food and wine did too.

The nymph Echo used to distract Hera with long stories so other nymphs could escape notice while Zeus pursued them; when Hera realized the trick, she cursed Echo to only ever repeat the last words spoken to her.
The beautiful youth who spurned Echo's love fell instead for his own reflection in a woodland pool, wasted away staring at it, and was transformed into the flower that bears his name.

A Lydian weaver so skilled she claimed to surpass Athena, Arachne wove a tapestry mocking the gods' misdeeds; after the contest that followed ended in her disgrace, she was reborn as the first spider.

Described by Plato as an advanced island empire beyond the Pillars of Heracles that grew corrupt and warred on Athens, Atlantis was swallowed by the sea "in a single day and night" as divine punishment.
Roman god of doorways, gates, and transitions, Janus was shown with two faces looking in opposite directions at once; no Greek god matches him, and the month of January bears his name.
First of Kronos's children swallowed, and the last disgorged, Hestia is the Greek goddess of the hearth fire that burned at the heart of every home and city.
Vesta is Hestia's Roman counterpart, virgin goddess of the hearth; the Vestal Virgins tended her eternal flame in the Roman Forum for over a thousand years.
Twin son of the war god Mars and the priestess Rhea Silvia, Romulus was suckled by a she-wolf after being abandoned as an infant, then founded Rome in 753 BCE.
Romulus's twin, also suckled by the she-wolf as an infant; when Remus mocked the walls of his brother's new city, Romulus (or one of his supporters) killed him.
Son of the goddess Aphrodite (Venus) and the Trojan Anchises, Aeneas carried his father from burning Troy on his back and, per Virgil's Aeneid, became the legendary ancestor of Rome's founders.
Succeeding Romulus as Rome's second king, the Sabine Numa Pompilius held nightly consultations with the nymph Egeria and founded the Vestal cult, the priesthoods, and the Roman calendar.
The Anatolian "Great Mother" goddess, worshipped in Phrygia since the Bronze Age, is shown enthroned with a lion; Rome formally adopted her in 204 BCE as a black meteoric stone carried from Pessinus.

Cybele's devoted companion Attis castrated himself in a fit of madness beneath a pine tree and bled to death; the goddess mourned him into a yearly spring resurrection, and the pine became sacred to her cult.

Center of a secretive Roman mystery religion practiced in underground temples, Mithras dragged the cosmic bull into a cave and killed it with a dagger — the scene, called the tauroctony, decorated every one of his shrines.
A Cypriot sculptor carved an ivory woman so beautiful he fell in love with his own creation; when he prayed at her festival, Venus (Aphrodite) brought the statue to life.
Apollo granted the Sibyl of Cumae as many years of life as grains of dust in her hand, but not eternal youth, so she withered for centuries; she later guided Aeneas into the Underworld.
Mecca sat at the crossroads of major desert caravan routes, its trade — much of it by camel — making it the wealthiest Arabian trading town by the 6th century.
Muhammad grew up in Mecca and, before any revelation, led camel caravans on trade routes to Syria for the merchant Khadija, whom he later married.
According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad received his first revelation from the angel Gabriel in a cave near Mecca in 610, the event Muslims mark as Islam's origin.
Threatened in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers accepted an invitation from Yathrib's feuding tribes to migrate there in 622 and mediate between them — the hijra that renamed the city Medina.
After the civil war following Caliph Ali's assassination, Mu'awiyah founded the Umayyad dynasty in 661, moving the caliphate's capital from Medina to Damascus.
The Abbasid Revolution of 750 overthrew the Umayyads, the new dynasty claiming legitimacy through descent from Muhammad's uncle Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib.
Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris River in 762 as the Abbasid capital, and within a generation it had grown into a center of learning, home to the House of Wisdom.
The Seljuk chieftain Tugrul Beg took Baghdad in 1055; from then on the Abbasid caliphs kept only religious authority while the Seljuk sultans held the real power.

Around 552, Nestorian monks smuggled silkworm eggs out of Central Asia for Emperor Justinian, breaking China's monopoly and founding a silk industry that, with its stable gold solidus coin, helped fund the empire for centuries.
In 1095, Byzantine Emperor Alexius I appealed to Pope Urban II for help against Seljuk Turk advances; the Pope's call at Clermont that November launched the First Crusade toward Jerusalem.
Chinese gunsmiths cast the earliest known cannons in bronze by the 13th century — the Xanadu Gun of 1298 is the oldest confirmed survivor — before the technology reached Europe in the 1320s.
In 1453, Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II's cannons — including a Hungarian engineer's 27-foot bombard — battered gaps in Constantinople's walls after a 53-day siege, ending the Byzantine Empire.
Raised among horse-mounted nomads who lived in felt-covered gers on the steppe, Temüjin united the rival Mongol clans and, in 1206, was proclaimed Genghis Khan at an assembly on the Onon River.
Genghis Khan's conquests unified Central Asia under Mongol rule, and the resulting Pax Mongolica secured the Silk Road for merchants and travelers — Marco Polo among them.
Mongol forces besieging the Genoese trading post of Caffa in Crimea let the plague reach the Black Sea in 1346; fleeing Genoese ships carried it to Sicily by October 1347, launching it in Europe.
The bubonic plague bacterium Yersinia pestis is carried by fleas living on rats — the transmission mechanism behind the pandemic that killed between a third and half of Europe's population.
Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai pushed Mongol armies past the Great Wall frontier to conquer Song China, founding the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completing the conquest by 1279.
Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty issued jiaochao, paper banknotes that circulated nationwide — a currency so novel that Marco Polo described it to disbelieving Europeans.

Born into a poor rice-farming family, Zhu Yuanzhang joined the agrarian Red Turban Rebellion against Yuan rule in 1352 and, by 1368, had overthrown the Mongols to found the Ming as the Hongwu Emperor.

The Ming Yongle Emperor built his new Beijing palace complex from 1406 to 1420 using whole logs of precious phoebe zhennan timber hauled from southwestern China's jungles, alongside specially baked brick.
The Yongle Emperor commissioned the eunuch admiral Zheng He to lead seven treasure-fleet voyages between 1405 and 1433, reaching as far as the Swahili coast of East Africa.
With the Ming capital falling to a rebel army in 1644, Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to Manchu forces, who defeated the rebels and founded the Qing dynasty in Beijing.

As Japan's national conscript army dissolved by the late 8th century, wealthy landholding families who could afford horses, iron weapons, and years of archery training formed the mounted warrior class that became the samurai.
A katana's blade is folded and welded from steel, then differentially quenched under a layer of clay slurry to harden its edge; the Tokugawa shogunate required samurai to wear one as a mark of rank.
Minamoto no Yoritomo's samurai crushed the rival Taira clan at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185, and in 1192 he was appointed shogun, founding Japan's first military government at Kamakura.

Turkic cavalry armies carried Islam into northern India, routing Rajput defenders in 1192 under Muhammad of Ghor; after his death in 1206, his former slave-general Qutb-ud-din Aibak became the first Sultan of Delhi.
Timur styled himself the restorer of Genghis Khan's Mongol Empire, and in 1398 his armies captured and sacked Delhi, devastating the Sultanate so badly the city took nearly a century to recover.

Babur, descended from Tamerlane and Genghis Khan, used matchlock guns and field cannon behind a barricade of carts to rout the Delhi Sultanate's far larger army at Panipat in 1526, founding the Mughal Empire.
Jayavarman II founded the Khmer Empire in 802, and its wealth rested on a vast hydraulic network of canals and reservoirs that irrigated rice paddies fed by the Tonlé Sap and its rivers.
King Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between 1122 and 1150 as a temple-mountain, its central towers symbolizing the five peaks of Mount Meru, the Hindu gods' sacred mountain.

After defeating the Sosso at the Battle of Kirina around 1235, Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire, which taxed the desert caravan trade and became one of the richest sources of gold in the medieval world.
Mansa Musa's 1324-25 pilgrimage to Mecca passed through Cairo, where the chronicler al-Umari reported he gave away so much gold that its price stayed depressed there for over a decade.

The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 and grew maize on artificial chinampa islands in Lake Texcoco, while obsidian-edged weapons like the macuahuitl armed the empire they built by the 15th century.
Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and linked to the mainland by causeway-bridges whose sections could be pulled away to defend the city, while chinampas expanded the island itself.

Centered on Cuzco high in the Andes, the Inca Empire expanded explosively from 1438 under Pachacuti, growing wealthy on gold worked by skilled metalsmiths — though the Spanish would melt almost all of it down.
Inca ruler Pachacuti ordered Machu Picchu built as a royal estate on a mountain ridge around 1450, after his conquest of the Urubamba valley; it was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest.

Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with only about 500 men and 13 horses — animals unknown to the Aztecs — and, allied with the Aztecs' Tlaxcalan enemies, besieged and captured Tenochtitlan by August 1521.

With roughly 168 men and a few dozen horses, Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 during a civil war between Atahualpa and his brother, then had him executed in 1533 after his gold ransom was paid.

A smallpox epidemic, introduced by an infected member of a Spanish expedition in 1520, swept Tenochtitlan and killed the newly chosen emperor Cuitláhuac within 80 days of taking power, crippling Aztec resistance.
Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and theology professor at Wittenberg, protested the Church's sale of indulgences by nailing his 95 Theses to the church door on 31 October 1517.

Gutenberg's printing press let Luther's 95 Theses and his German Bible translation spread rapidly across Europe in the vernacular, turning a local theological protest into the continent-wide Protestant Reformation.

Sparked by Edward III's claim to the French throne, the war saw England's earliest cannons fire at Crécy in 1346, and ended in 1453 when French field artillery under Jean Bureau won at Castillon — Europe's first major battle decided by field artillery.

Claiming divine visions, Joan of Arc helped break the English siege of Orléans in 1429, reviving French fortunes in the Hundred Years' War, but was captured and burned at the stake as a heretic in 1431.

Sumerian city-states arose in southern Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates from the 4th millennium BCE, their irrigation canals and mudbrick building turning river silt into the world's first cities -- Uruk alone held over 50,000 people by 2900 BCE.

Sargon of Akkad defeated Lugal-zage-si of Umma and conquered Sumer's independent city-states around 2334 BCE, founding the first empire in world history and making Akkadian, not Sumerian, the language of government.

The Hittite kingdom, centred on Hattusa in Anatolia, fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh in 1274 BCE; the peace that followed in 1259 BCE is history's earliest surviving treaty -- its lost original on silver tablets, the Hittite copy in cuneiform on clay.

Neo-Assyrian kings pioneered large-scale cavalry and siege-warfare, and ruled through deliberate terror -- mass deportations, mutilations -- building an empire of some 1.4 million square kilometres, reaching its height with the conquest of Egypt in 671 BCE.

By around 1050 BCE Phoenician traders had reduced Near Eastern scripts like cuneiform to a 22-sign consonantal alphabet and carried it across the Mediterranean aboard their merchant ships -- the direct ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets.

Minoan Crete built its wealth on Mediterranean sea trade to Egypt, Cyprus and the Levant, and the palace of Knossos is covered in frescoes of bull-leaping acrobats -- a bull cult later Greek myth wove into the legend of the Minotaur in its labyrinth.

Mycenaean Greeks took control of Knossos around 1450 BCE, adapting the Minoans' Linear A into Linear B -- the earliest written form of Greek -- while fortifying mainland citadels at Mycenae and Tiryns with Cyclopean walls the open Minoan palaces never had.

Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath, a brick-built tank 12 by 7 metres and 2.4 metres deep, was sealed watertight with a lining of bitumen -- one of the oldest public water tanks in the ancient world, at the heart of a city built around 2500 BCE.

China's Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE) cast ritual bronze vessels for ancestor worship and cracked heated turtle shells and ox bones to divine the future, inscribing the answers in China's earliest confirmed writing -- oracle bones found since the 1920s.

The Olmecs, Mesoamerica's earliest major civilization (c. 1200-400 BCE), carved colossal basalt heads up to 55 tonnes and worked obsidian traded from Guatemala, building their religious art around 'werejaguar' beings blending human and jaguar features.

The Chavín culture (900-250 BCE) spread a shared religion of fanged jaguar deities across Peru's highlands and coast from its temple at Chavín de Huántar -- through religious authority alone, not war -- centred on a 4.53-metre carved granite shaft, the Lanzón.

Cyrus the Great defeated Croesus of Lydia in 546 BCE, and his cavalry went on to build the largest empire the world had yet seen -- some 5.5 million square kilometres stretching from the Aegean to the Indus.

Cyrus the Great's forces won at Opis on the Tigris in October 539 BCE, then took Babylon itself without a fight -- ending the Neo-Babylonian dynasty Nebuchadnezzar had built and absorbing Mesopotamia into the new Achaemenid Empire.

Darius I founded Persepolis around 515 BCE as the Achaemenid Empire's ceremonial capital, its Apadana reception hall built to hold thousands of tribute-bearers from across the empire -- until Alexander's troops burned the palace to the ground in 330 BCE.

Aristotle tutored the teenage Alexander at the Macedonian court; riding his warhorse Bucephalus, Alexander went on to shatter the last Achaemenid king Darius III at Gaugamela on 1 October 331 BCE, conquering the entire Persian Empire.

After capturing Persepolis in 330 BCE, Alexander's troops burned the Achaemenid ceremonial capital to the ground -- ancient sources blame either revenge for Athens or a drunken celebration -- a fire that symbolically ended the empire he had just conquered.

After Alexander died in 323 BCE his generals -- the Diadochi -- split his empire into rival Hellenistic kingdoms, chiefly Ptolemaic Egypt, Seleucid Syria, and Antigonid Macedon, spreading Greek temples, cities and language across the Near East for centuries.

Rome expelled its last king, Tarquinius Superbus, in 509 BCE, then after decades of plebeian pressure against patrician rule wrote its first law code, the Twelve Tables, and had it posted on bronze in the Forum in 449 BCE.

Gauls under Brennus sacked Rome around 390 BCE and, by legend, weighed out its gold ransom on rigged scales, meeting Roman protests with the taunt 'Vae victis' -- woe to the vanquished -- a humiliation Rome remembered for centuries.

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul's Celtic tribes between 58 and 51 BCE, and the wealth and battle-hardened legions it gave him let him cross the Rubicon in 49 BCE and seize control of the Republic he served; he was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.

Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BCE, opening the Second Punic War, and destroyed a Roman army of some 86,000 men at Cannae in 216 BCE before Scipio finally broke Carthage at Zama in 202 BCE.

Carthage, founded generations earlier by settlers from the eastern Mediterranean, grew into Rome's greatest rival; three Punic Wars between 264 and 146 BCE ended with Carthage stormed, sacked, and its territory annexed as the Roman province of Africa.

Caesar's assassination by knife-wielding senators on the Ides of March, 44 BCE, left his 18-year-old adopted heir Octavian to avenge him and outmanoeuvre every rival, taking the title Augustus from the Senate in 27 BCE.

Octavian's fleet crushed Antony and Cleopatra's navy at Actium in 31 BCE; when Egypt fell the next year the last independent Hellenistic kingdom was gone, and Octavian stood unchallenged as Rome's first emperor.

Huns pressing in from Central Asia forced Goths into Roman land from 376 CE; they sacked Rome in 410 -- the first time in 800 years an outside enemy had taken the city -- and in 476 CE Odoacer deposed the last emperor, ending the empire Augustus founded.
Iron Age Celtic Europe's La Tène culture, from around 450 BCE, saw iron production explode while druids held their rites in sacred oak groves and tribes sheltered in hilltop forts.

Scythian nomads of the Pontic-Caspian steppe were expert mounted archers -- their name likely derives from a root meaning 'archer' -- who buried their rulers in kurgans, earthen mounds furnished with gold objects from as early as the 8th century BCE.

Huns sweeping out of Central Asia crushed the Alans and the Sarmatians -- who had displaced the Scythians on the Pontic steppe centuries earlier -- east of the Don around 375 CE, then turned their mounted archers on the Goths and, eventually, Rome.

Chandragupta Maurya founded India's first empire around 320 BCE, and around 302 BCE struck a treaty with Seleucus I -- one of Alexander's former generals -- ceding him 500 war elephants in exchange for territory stretching toward the Hindu Kush.

Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta, conquered Kalinga around 261-260 BCE in a war his own edicts say killed or displaced hundreds of thousands, then turned to Gautama Buddha's teachings, carving edicts of dhamma onto stone pillars across his empire.

Chandragupta I built the Gupta dynasty into an empire from around 319 CE, ruling from Pataliputra -- the old Mauryan capital -- and marrying into the Licchavi line to claim 'king of great kings'; his successors presided over India's later golden age.

Qin Shi Huang conquered the last Warring State, Qi, in 221 BCE to unify China, then standardized coinage, weights and script under Legalist rule -- and in 213-212 BCE had rival texts burned and, by one tradition, some 460 scholars buried alive.

Qin Shi Huang's mausoleum was guarded underground by more than 8,000 life-sized terracotta soldiers, 130 chariots and 520 horses, each face individually finished from ten base moulds -- discovered by farmers digging a well in March 1974.

Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty in 202 BCE after Qin's collapse, and under Emperor Wudi Han campaigns against the Xiongnu opened the Silk Road through the Tarim Basin by 60 BCE -- a trade network that eventually carried Chinese silk as far as Rome.

Teotihuacan grew into the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas, its population reaching 100,000-200,000 by around 400-500 CE on the back of a monopoly over obsidian trade from the Pachuca mines, centred on the Pyramid of the Sun, completed by 100 CE.

The Zapotecs founded Monte Albán on a defensible mountaintop above Oaxaca's three valleys around 700-500 BCE, neutral ground between competing rival polities, and carved the Danzante stones there with some of Mesoamerica's earliest writing.

Classic Maya civilization (c. 250-900 CE) built city-states like Tikal and Palenque on an economy of maize, while jaguar imagery marked royal authority -- Maya kings sat enthroned on jaguar-skin cushions beneath temples like Tikal's Temple of the Great Jaguar.

Cleisthenes's reforms of 508-507 BCE organized Athenian citizens into ten tribes supplying a Council of 500 chosen by lot, and gave the Assembly the power of ostracism -- exile by a vote scratched onto broken pottery shards, ostraka.

Spartan citizens were freed for lifelong military training, the agoge starting at age seven, because a subjugated population of helots -- conquered Messenian and Laconian Greeks -- farmed their land and surrendered half the harvest to their Spartan masters.

In 480 BCE, Spartan king Leonidas and a rearguard of roughly 300 Spartans plus Thespian and Theban allies held the pass at Thermopylae against Xerxes's Achaemenid army for three days before being outflanked and wiped out -- buying Greece time to win the war.

The 27-year Peloponnesian War pitted democratic, sea-based Athens against oligarchic, land-based Sparta; it ended in 405 BCE when Sparta's fleet destroyed the Athenian navy beached at Aegospotami, and Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, tearing down its own walls.
Thales held that everything is ultimately water, the first attempt in the West to explain the cosmos through a single natural substance rather than the will of the gods.

Thales is said to have predicted a bumper olive harvest, buying up the region's olive presses cheaply and renting them out at a high price once demand peaked — proof, Aristotle said, that philosophers could be rich if they cared to.
Pythagoras has been credited since antiquity with proving that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.

According to legend, Pythagoras discovered that musical harmony follows mathematical ratios after hearing blacksmiths' hammers of different sizes ring out different, pleasing tones against their anvils.

Heraclitus taught that the cosmos is in permanent flux: step into a river, and by the time your foot touches it, different waters are already flowing past — even as we still call it one and the same river.
Heraclitus held that the world is united only through the tension of its opposites: night and day, he said, are one, each endlessly turning into the other.
Parmenides argued through logic alone that what truly exists must be a single, eternal, indivisible whole, unchanging and complete — an idea later thinkers pictured as a perfect, well-rounded unity.

Protagoras taught that 'man is the measure of all things': a person from a cold country may call the weather warm while a person from a hot country calls the very same day cold, and Protagoras held both perceptions equally true.
Democritus, developing the theory with Leucippus, held that the only true realities are atoms and the void: everything we perceive, from water to human beings, is just atoms combined in empty space.
Quoting an old verse, Mozi taught that 'when one throws to me a peach, I return to him a plum' — kindness given is kindness returned, the basis of his doctrine of impartial, universal love.

Diogenes lived by choice in a large ceramic storage jar — later Latin writers rendered it as a 'tub' or barrel — and embraced the nickname Cynic, Greek for 'dog-like', for living as shamelessly as a stray.

Zeno of Citium was a merchant shipwrecked near Athens with the loss of his entire cargo; wandering into the city, a chance find in a bookseller's shop turned him toward philosophy, and he went on to found Stoicism.
Central to the Stoicism Zeno of Citium founded is the idea that living well means living in agreement with nature, aligning one's will with the rational order of the world.

After the Oracle at Delphi called him the wisest man in Greece, Socrates treated the claim as a paradox to test, pressing people with question after question until their confident beliefs collapsed under their own contradictions.

Augustine argued that evil is not a thing God created but a privation, an absence of good, and that moral evil enters the world only because rational creatures have the free will to choose it — as Adam did in Eden.

In his Confessions, Augustine describes his conversion in a garden: hearing what sounded like a child's voice chanting 'take up and read', he picked up a book of Paul's letters and, opening it at random, read the passage that changed his life.

Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while imprisoned and awaiting execution on a charge of treason; in it, Philosophy herself is asked whether an all-knowing God's foreknowledge leaves any room for human free will.

Anselm's Ontological Argument defines God as 'that than which no greater can be conceived', then reasons that a being existing both in the mind and in reality is greater than one existing in the mind alone — so God must exist.

Averroes argued that philosophy and Islamic revelation cannot truly contradict, since both are methods of reaching the same truth; where reasoned conclusions and a literal reading of scripture appear to clash, he held that the text must be read allegorically.

Erasmus's 1509 satire In Praise of Folly is delivered as a mock speech by Folly herself, who praises naivety and simple faith over intellectual pride — a paradox that ultimately turns worldly foolishness into a figure for Christian wisdom.

In The Prince, Machiavelli advises a ruler to be 'a fox to recognize snares, and a lion to frighten off wolves' — combining an animal's cunning with another's ferocity, unconstrained by conventional morality.

In 1513 Machiavelli was arrested, tortured with the strappado, and imprisoned after being falsely implicated in a conspiracy against the Medici; released weeks later, he retired to his farm and wrote The Prince.

In 1571 Montaigne retired to the tower of his family château, inscribing its beams with maxims, to write his Essays — arguing that chasing enduring fame, the good opinion of others, only corrodes one's own tranquility.

Francis Bacon is credited with the phrase 'knowledge is power' and is called the father of empiricism, arguing that scientific knowledge must be built from careful observation and inductive reasoning rather than assumption.

According to a story recorded by his friend John Aubrey, Bacon caught his final, fatal chill on a snowy road while personally testing whether stuffing a chicken with snow would preserve the meat — dying, if the tale is true, in the course of an experiment.
Pascal's 1654 correspondence with Pierre de Fermat about gambling problems founded mathematical probability theory; his triangle of binomial coefficients still bears his name.
During a mystical experience on the night of November 23, 1654, Pascal wrote 'Fire...' and sewed the note into his coat lining, moving it to each new garment; a servant found it only after his death.
Spinoza's central claim was 'Deus sive Natura' -- God or Nature -- naming a single infinite substance, not a separate creator standing outside the world it made.
Leibniz argued the universe is built of monads: simple substances that never interact with each other directly, yet each one represents the whole universe from its own unique point of view.
Berkeley denied that matter exists independent of the mind, holding 'esse est percipi' -- to be is to be perceived; an apple no one is perceiving, he argued, simply is not there.
In 1728 Berkeley sailed for Rhode Island to found a college for the New World on a promised parliamentary grant that never arrived; he abandoned the project and returned to London in 1732.
The 1755 Lisbon earthquake convinced Voltaire that Leibniz's claim we live in 'the best of all possible worlds' was untenable; he satirized the idea in Candide (1759).
Voltaire was staggeringly prolific, writing more than 20,000 letters and 2,000 books and pamphlets, and publishing much of it under pen names -- he used at least 178 over his lifetime.
Hume argued causation is never something we perceive directly, only inferred from a 'constant conjunction' of events grown so familiar that habit, not reason, makes us expect one to follow the other.

Rousseau wrote that 'the first person who, having enclosed a plot of land, took it into his head to say this is mine... was the true founder of civil society' -- the moment private property, and inequality, began.

Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) opens with a pin factory split into about eighteen steps -- 'one man draws out the wire; another straights it; a third cuts it' -- letting ten workers turn out 48,000 pins a day.
Smith argued that a person pursuing only their own gain is 'led by an invisible hand' to promote the interest of society more effectually than if they had set out to do so directly.

Burke described society as 'a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born' -- obligations running root-deep across generations.

Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) condemned the Revolution for having 'completely pulled down to the ground' France's monarchy, church, and law; it sold 17,500 copies within a year.
Bentham arranged for his skeleton to be dressed, seated, and preserved as an 'auto-icon'; it has been kept at University College London since 1850, today in a glass display case.

Bentham designed the Panopticon, a circular prison he described as 'an iron cage, glazed,' with a central watchtower letting one guard observe every inmate without them knowing if they were being watched.
Wollstonecraft died on September 10, 1797, eleven days after giving birth to her daughter Mary, from a childbirth infection; that daughter grew up to write Frankenstein as Mary Shelley.
