Hegel wrote that 'the owl of Minerva takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering' -- philosophy, he meant, only understands a historical moment after it has already passed.

Hegel's dialectic holds that a concept's internal contradictions are resolved not by discarding it but by transforming it into a higher, more comprehensive unity -- much as carbon under pressure becomes diamond.
Schopenhauer lived largely alone in Frankfurt from 1833, keeping a succession of pet poodles he named Atman, after the Hindu concept of the self, or Butz.
Feuerbach argued 'God is nothing else than man: he is, so to speak, the outward projection of man's inward nature' -- we make gods by idealizing our own best qualities and calling the result divine.

Mill's On Liberty (1859) holds that "the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others" -- a threshold the individual's own liberty stops at.
Kierkegaard proposed to Regine Olsen in September 1840, then broke off the engagement in August 1841, writing in his journals only that his melancholy made him unsuited to marriage.
The Communist Manifesto (1848) opens 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism' and declares 'the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.'
Thoreau built a small cabin near Walden Pond for $28.12 and lived there from July 1845 to September 1847, testing whether he could live simply by 'stripping away all superfluous luxuries.'
Peirce's pragmatic maxim holds that the whole of our conception of an object lies in conceiving its practical, conceivable effects -- an idea's meaning is what it would do, not some hidden essence.
James argued that an idea's truth lies in its practical 'cash-value': 'you must bring out of each word its practical cash-value, set it at work within the stream of your experience.'

In The Gay Science (1882), Nietzsche's madman declares 'God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him' -- not a claim about a literal death, but about the collapse of the values Christianity once anchored.
In Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-85), Nietzsche argues mankind's goal must be to create something superior to itself -- a new type of human he called the Übermensch.
Saussure argued the linguistic sign is arbitrary -- 'any sensible image could in principle be paired with any concept' -- nothing in a word's sound inherently connects it to its meaning.
Martin Heidegger became Husserl's assistant at Freiburg in 1919 and succeeded him to the philosophy chair there when Husserl retired in 1928.
Bergson's Creative Evolution (1907) described an élan vital, a 'vital impetus,' driving evolution in a more dynamic and creative way than any purely mechanical process could.

Dewey argued in his essay Kant and the Philosophic Method that we only think when we are confronted with problems -- philosophy exists to work through the contradictions life presents, not to describe the world from afar.
Santayana's The Life of Reason (1905) contains his famous aphorism: 'those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.'

Unamuno's The Tragic Sense of Life (1913) grounded human existence in an awareness of death and the desire to exist rather than in pure reason; the Spanish Church placed it on its Index of banned books in 1957.
Du Bois's The Souls of Black Folk (1903) named 'the problem of the Twentieth Century' as 'the problem of the colour-line,' a phrase he first delivered at the 1900 Pan-African Conference in London.
Russell's essay In Praise of Idleness (1932) argued 'the belief in the virtue of labour causes great evils in the modern world,' and that a four-hour workday would free everyone for a fuller life.
A 12th-century monk described Slavs invoking two gods over a shared bowl at their feasts, one good and one bad -- the bad one, called Chernobog, 'the black god,' was said to arrange all misfortune.
Belobog, the 'White God,' has no genuine ancient source. Unlike Chernobog, who is named in a 12th-century chronicle, Belobog first appears in 16th-century writing, invented as his opposite.
She travels in a wooden mortar, wielding a pestle, and lives deep in the forest in a hut that stands and turns on chicken legs.
The Baltic god of the daylit sky, who walked the earth disguised as a beggar to find out who would be kind to one.
Known across Aboriginal Australia by dozens of names, the Rainbow Serpent pushed up from beneath the ground to carve mountains and gorges, and lives in the permanent waterholes it created.
The sky father who came down, shaped the rivers and mountains, and went back up.
Before creation there was only Ta'aroa, alone inside a huge cosmic shell. He broke it open and used its two halves to build the dome of the sky and the rocky foundation of the earth.
Tane, first of the gods Ta'aroa summoned forth, took charge of decorating creation -- placing the stars, sun and moon in the sky -- and became god of forests and birds.
Where his brothers failed, Tane separated his sky father and earth mother by lying on his back and pushing them apart with his legs, letting light into the cramped darkness between them.
The sky father, held in an embrace with the earth mother Papa so tight that their children grew up in the dark between them.
Papatuanuku, the Maori earth mother, is the ground itself -- held so close in sky father Rangi's embrace that their children lived for generations in total darkness between them.
The only child of Rangi and Papa who protested their separation, and answered it with an army of storms.
Tumatauenga, god of war, was the only brother who stood and fought Tawhirimatea's storm rather than flee -- afterward he turned on his siblings in turn, felling Tane's forests for the first weapons.
Maui hauled up islands of the Pacific from a canoe, tricking his brothers into paddling hard while his magic hook dragged land up from the sea floor behind them.
Days were too short to dry cloth, so Maui climbed to where the sun rises and lassoed its rays with a rope, forcing it to slow down and lengthen the day.
Makemake, creator god and chief deity of Rapa Nui's birdman cult, is carved into the island's rocks as a face with huge eyes, worshipped through the seabirds that nest on its cliffs.
Haua shared Makemake's role at the heart of Rapa Nui's birdman cult, the two gods honored together through the island's nesting seabirds.
In the Navajo Dine Bahane' creation narrative, Spider Woman and Spider Man introduced the spindle and the loom to the people.
In Hopi tradition, Spider Grandmother guided the people through the underground worlds, teaching them to weave and to make clay pots along the way.
The Haida credit this shapeshifting trickster with finding the first humans hiding inside a clam shell, and bringing them berries and salmon to eat.
Iktomi, the Lakota trickster, is the first-born son of Inyan, the Rock -- and became a spider, the meaning of his name, through his own cunning.
Nanabozho, the Ojibwe trickster and culture hero, is called Michabo -- 'the Great Hare who created the Earth' -- and is credited as the inventor of fishing.
Kiviuq is an Inuit hero said to travel eternally by kayak and sled across the Arctic regions of Canada, Alaska and Greenland, known by different names in each place.
An inua is the spirit the Inuit believe exists in every person, animal, lake, mountain and plant -- not one individual soul, but the shared life-force of an entire kind, including the whale's own.
He rose out of Lake Titicaca in darkness and made humankind by breathing into stone.
Viracocha's first people -- brainless giants -- displeased him, so he sent a flood down from the Andes to destroy them, then remade humanity, better this time, from smaller stones.
Addressed as the possessor of brightness, and said to rest on Mount Kenya — the mountain is where he is, not what he is made from.
Amma, the Dogon sky god, is said to have united with the earth goddess through a termite mound standing in her place -- only after it was cleared away could he father true offspring.
Nommo, the first living creature made by the Dogon sky god Amma, are hermaphroditic water spirits pictured with a human body and a fish's tail.

Papa Legba, intermediary between gods and humanity in Haitian Vodou, traces his origins to Yoruba and Fon traditions carried across the Atlantic by enslaved West Africans, among them the trickster Eshu.
Fearing he sought to be king, a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Caesar to death on the Ides of March, 44 BCE, shortly after he was proclaimed dictator in perpetuity.
In 27 BCE the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus, 'the revered,' making him Rome's first emperor; he later boasted he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.
In 343 BCE, King Philip II hired Aristotle to tutor his 13-year-old son at the Temple of the Nymphs at Mieza — the boy who would become Alexander the Great.
As consul in 63 BCE, Cicero exposed Catiline's conspiracy to overthrow the Republic, denouncing the plot in four famous speeches and earning the title 'father of the fatherland.'
Forced into exile in 58 BCE after his enemy Clodius passed legislation targeting him, Cicero returned to Italy in triumph on 5 August 57 BCE.
In 610 CE, at age 40, Muhammad received his first Quranic revelation from the angel Gabriel in a cave on Mount Hira, in the hills outside Mecca.
In 622 CE Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina — the Hijra, an event that marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.
In August 386 Augustine underwent a sudden conversion in a garden in Milan, hearing a child's voice say 'take up and read' before opening St. Paul's letters to a passage that ended his inner turmoil.
Augustine composed his autobiographical Confessions in 397-398, a work of unsparing self-examination often called the first Western autobiography.
On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne 'emperor of the Romans' during Mass at St. Peter's Basilica, reviving the western imperial title for the first time since 476.
In 774 Charlemagne besieged and captured Pavia, defeating the Lombard King Desiderius and adding King of the Lombards to his own titles.
In 1206, at a kurultai assembly by the Onon River, Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan, uniting the Mongol tribes into a disciplined army of mounted archers.
In 1215 the Mongols captured Zhongdu, the Jin dynasty capital near modern Beijing, a major milestone in Genghis Khan's campaign against northern China.
At the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066, William's forces defeated and killed King Harold II — later legend, shown on the Bayeux Tapestry, holds he was struck in the eye by an arrow.
In 1086 William ordered a nationwide survey of England's land and wealth for taxation, compiled as the Domesday Book.
In 1429 Joan of Arc, a 17-year-old peasant claiming divine visions, led French troops that lifted the English siege of Orléans, a turning point in the Hundred Years' War.
Convicted of heresy by a pro-English church court, Joan of Arc was tied to a stake and burned in Rouen on 30 May 1431, aged about nineteen.
Leonardo began the Mona Lisa in October 1503 using layers of translucent oil glazes, and kept reworking the portrait until his death in 1519.
Michelangelo carved his statue of David from a single block of marble, completing the Renaissance masterpiece in 1504.
From 1508 to 1512 Michelangelo worked from scaffolding to fresco the Sistine Chapel ceiling with over 300 figures, including the Creation of Adam.
On 31 October 1517 Luther is said to have nailed his Ninety-Five Theses, protesting the sale of indulgences, to the door of Wittenberg's Castle Church.
Henry VIII married six times between 1509 and 1547 — Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard, and Catherine Parr — beheading two of them.
In 1534 the Act of Supremacy made Henry VIII 'Supreme Head of the Church of England,' severing ties with the papacy after Rome refused to annul his first marriage.
On 28-29 July 1588, English fire ships scattered the anchored Spanish Armada off Gravelines, leading to a decisive battle that shattered Spain's invasion fleet.
Elizabeth I was crowned queen at Westminster Abbey on 15 January 1559, beginning a 44-year reign later remembered as the Elizabethan Age.
In 1543, the year of his death, Copernicus published De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, proposing that the Sun, not Earth, sits at the center of the universe.
In March 1610 Galileo published Sidereus Nuncius after turning his telescope on the sky, describing the Moon's cratered surface and four moons orbiting Jupiter.

Galileo's 1632 book Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, defending the Sun-centered model, led the Roman Inquisition to try him for heresy in 1633; he recanted and lived under house arrest.
Newton described how watching an apple fall started his thinking about gravity; his 1687 Principia Mathematica united that force with the mathematics of planetary motion.
During 1665-66, while Cambridge closed for the Great Plague, Newton worked out the basics of calculus, the mathematics he later used to describe planetary motion.
After Cardinal Mazarin's death in 1661, Louis XIV began his personal rule of France and later moved his court to the newly built Palace of Versailles.
In 1685 Louis XIV signed the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking a century of religious tolerance for Protestants and forcing many Huguenots to flee France or convert.
At the Battle of Naseby in 1645, Cromwell's cavalry broke the Royalist lines, a decisive victory that effectively ended the First English Civil War in Parliament's favor.
Cromwell was the third man to sign Charles I's death warrant; the king was beheaded on a scaffold outside the Banqueting House on 30 January 1649, and England briefly became a republic.
Voltaire was imprisoned in the Bastille fortress in Paris from May 1717 to April 1718 after writing a satirical verse accusing the French regent of incest.
Published anonymously in early 1759, Voltaire's Candide became his most enduring work, satirizing the Leibnizian idea that we live in 'the best of all possible worlds.'
Unanimously elected the first U.S. president, Washington voluntarily stepped down after two terms in 1797, a precedent nearly every successor followed for over a century.
Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, which the Second Continental Congress voted to adopt on 4 July 1776.
In 1803 Jefferson's administration purchased the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million, doubling the young nation's size and securing control of the Mississippi River.

In June 1752 Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm to demonstrate that lightning is an electrical phenomenon, work that led him to invent the lightning rod — a grounded wire that lets a strike pass harmlessly to earth.
In December 1804 Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame, and had his own portrait struck onto the new imperial coinage.
Defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in June 1815, Napoleon was exiled to the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.
Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto on 21 February 1848, opening with the line 'A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of Communism.'
From 1831 to 1836 Darwin sailed around the world aboard HMS Beagle, collecting specimens including finches from the Galápagos Islands that later shaped his theory of evolution.
Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, opening his case for evolution by natural selection with evidence from the artificial selection long practiced by dog and pigeon breeders.

On 30 September 1862 Bismarck told the Prussian parliament that the great questions of the age would be decided not by speeches but 'by iron and blood,' a phrase that became shorthand for his politics.
On 18 January 1871 Bismarck had Wilhelm I proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, staging German unification inside a defeated France.
In 1930 Gandhi led a 24-day, 240-mile march to the sea at Dandi to make salt from seawater in defiance of the British crown's salt tax, launching a mass civil disobedience campaign.
Gandhi was shot three times at close range by Nathuram Godse during an evening prayer meeting in Delhi on 30 January 1948.
On 29 June 1613 a theatrical cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII misfired and ignited the Globe Theatre's thatched roof, burning it to the ground within an hour.
Seven years after Shakespeare's death, his colleagues John Heminges and Henry Condell published the First Folio in 1623, a collected edition preserving 36 of his plays.
In May 1747 Bach visited the court of King Frederick the Great in Potsdam, where the king gave him a theme and challenged him to improvise a fugue on the spot, later worked into The Musical Offering.
Sun-dried mud brick and organized temple precincts let Uruk grow into the world's first true city by around 3200 BC, ringed by its own city walls.
Uruk's temple administrators needed to track livestock and grain, so around 3300 BC they began pressing a reed stylus into wet clay tablets -- the world's first writing system.
Sumerian poems about Uruk's king Gilgamesh, first written down in cuneiform around 2100 BC, grew into the world's oldest surviving narrative epic.
Sargon tore down Uruk's walls and captured its king, and went on to conquer Ur, Lagash, and Umma -- uniting Sumer into the world's first known empire around 2334 BC.
Some 5,000-6,000 bronze-fitted chariots collided at Kadesh in 1274 BC between Ramesses II's Egyptians and Muwatalli II's Hittites -- the largest chariot battle in recorded history, and a stalemate.
Fifteen years after neither side won at Kadesh, Egypt and the Hittites exchanged treaty tablets of silver in 1259 BC -- the oldest peace treaty for which both parties' own copies have survived.
Five centuries after Caesar's legions crossed the Rubicon, the Germanic king Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in AD 476, ending the Western Roman Empire.

Having conquered most of Western Europe on horseback and sponsored a revival of book-copying and learning known as the Carolingian Renaissance, Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800 AD.
William of Normandy ferried his cavalry across the Channel by ship and defeated King Harold's English army at Hastings on 14 October 1066, the last successful invasion of England.
Twenty years after conquering England at Hastings, William ordered a survey of every manor, ox, and peasant in his new kingdom, compiled by 1086 into the Domesday Book.
Facing an armed baronial revolt over taxation and abuses of royal power, King John sealed the Great Charter at Runnymede on 15 June 1215, the first document to put the English crown under the law.

The Mongol peace that Genghis Khan's empire imposed across Central Asia made the Silk Road safe enough for the young Venetian merchant Marco Polo to travel it to Kublai Khan's court, starting in 1271.

A dispute over the French crown between the English and French royal houses erupted into intermittent warfare in 1337 -- fought partly with iron-tipped English longbow volleys at battles like Crecy and Agincourt -- that dragged on until 1453.

Sultan Mehmed II's gunpowder cannons, some hurling 600-pound stone balls over a mile, breached Constantinople's ancient walls after a 53-day siege in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire nearly 1,500 years after it began.

Cinnamon bark carries caryophyllene alongside cinnamaldehyde — a sesquiterpene also found in cloves and black pepper, and one of the few plant compounds shown to directly activate a cannabinoid receptor, CB2.

What gets sold as 'cinnamon' is usually cassia bark, and cassia carries far more coumarin than true Ceylon cinnamon does — over 1mg per gram against barely a trace — which is why food regulators set separate safe limits for the two.

Anethole is what makes star anise taste of liquorice, and it measures about 13 times sweeter than table sugar on the tongue's own sweetness receptors — a compound three unrelated plant families arrived at independently.

Anise and star anise are not related plants — one is a carrot-family herb, the other a magnolia relative from China — but both concentrate the same anethole in their seeds, a case of convergent chemistry rather than shared ancestry.

Star anise pods are the commercial source of shikimic acid, the starting molecule for synthesizing the antiviral drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — a dependency real enough that a 2005 shortage of the acid tightened world Tamiflu supply during a flu scare.

Vanillin is the single dominant compound in cured vanilla pods among several hundred flavour compounds altogether, and it's cheap enough to synthesize that most vanilla-flavoured food today is flavoured with lab vanillin rather than the orchid.

Myristicin is nutmeg's own defensive chemical, a weak inhibitor of the enzyme that clears certain neurotransmitters, and a high-quality nutmeg seed can carry up to 13mg of it per gram — enough that a couple of whole seeds is a real overdose.
Mace and nutmeg come from the same fruit — mace is the seed's lacy red covering — and both carry sabinene, a woody, peppery terpene also documented in black pepper and carrot seed oil.

Mace and nutmeg both carry safrole in their oil, the same compound sassafras is named for. The US banned safrole as a food additive in 1960 after it proved to cause liver tumours in rats at high, sustained dose.

Dill seed's essential oil is dominated by carvone but also carries a real share of limonene, the same citrus terpene found in orange peel and pine resin — part of why dill reads as both spicy and bright.

Liquorice root's sweetness is almost entirely glycyrrhizin, 30 to 50 times sweeter than table sugar by weight, and shaped like a soap molecule — it drags oil and water into the same mixture rather than just adding sweetness.

Cardamom oil runs 20 to 50 percent 1,8-cineole — in Java cardamom sometimes up to 70 — the same eucalyptus-smelling compound that makes up most of eucalyptus oil itself, which is why cardamom carries a cooling, medicinal edge.

Cuminaldehyde is the molecule responsible for cumin's characteristic aroma — spicy, green, distinctly cumin — and it's why cumin doesn't smell like its close carrot-family relatives caraway, dill, and fennel.
Beneath fennel's anethole sweetness sits fenchone, a bitter, camphor-toned compound in the same chemical family as camphor itself — part of what keeps fennel from tasting like pure liquorice.
Caraway is cumin's own close cousin in the carrot family, sometimes called 'meridian fennel' or Persian cumin — the two seeds look alike enough to mix up by sight despite tasting nothing alike.
Liquorice is a legume, not an aromatic herb, and harvest means digging up the whole plant and cutting the sweet root free from three to five years of growth.
Score the bark of a Chios mastic tree and the resin oozes out, hardening into brittle tears over roughly 15 to 20 days as it dries in the open air.
Damask rose petals are hand-picked at bloom and either dried whole as a spice or steam-distilled with oil-bearing steam to make attar of roses.
Aframomum melegueta's trumpet-shaped flowers develop into 5 to 7cm pods holding numerous small reddish-brown seeds, dried and sold as grains of paradise.
Ajwain is a small annual in the parsley family, the same family as caraway, cumin and fennel, grown for its thymol-rich seed.
Asafoetida is literally dried latex — a gum oleoresin exuded from a Ferula taproot after repeated shallow cuts, collected and dried between bleeds.
Berberis vulgaris's thorny branches are difficult to harvest by hand, so the tart red berries are often knocked down and then dried for use as zereshk.
Amchoor is made from unripe green mangoes, harvested early, peeled, thinly sliced, and sun-dried before being ground into a sour powder.
Lemon myrtle's leaves are harvested year-round from the tree and dried for their intensely citral-rich oil.
Black cardamom's pods are dried over open flames for days, and that traditional smoke-drying is where the spice's campfire flavour actually comes from.
Xylopia aethiopica's dried fruits are sold as grains of Selim; in Senegal the immature pods are smoked before drying, elsewhere they are simply sun-dried.
A dried lime has simply lost its water content, spending most of its drying time out in the sun until it turns hard, dark, and musky.
Wattleseed is the roasted, milled seed of Australian Acacia species — specialised seed-grinding stones for processing it date back at least 1,000 years.
For anardana, pomegranate seeds and their fleshy pulp are separated from the bitter white membrane and dried in the sun until reddish-brown.
Germacrene D is the single most abundant compound in annatto seed's essential oil, measured at nearly 18 percent — more than caryophyllene or pinene.
Alpha-pinene is mastic gum's dominant compound; analyses of Pistacia lentiscus essential oil have measured it at up to 79 percent.
Steam-distilling damask rose petals yields rose oil, in which geraniol is one of the three major components alongside citronellol and nonadecane.

Nigella sativa seeds are dry-roasted before use in spice blends, a step that draws out thymoquinone, the phytochemical dominating the seed's own aroma profile, alongside dihydrothymoquinone and other minor compounds.
Nigellone — better known chemically as dithymoquinone — forms when sunlight photodimerises two thymoquinone molecules together during the separation and extraction of nigella oil.
(6)-Paradol gives grains of paradise its pungent, black-pepper-like heat with hints of citrus — structurally a close relative of ginger's gingerol.
Picrocrocin, saffron's bitter glucoside, makes up as much as 4 percent of the dried spice's weight after the stigmas are harvested and cured.
When saffron is dried after harvest, heat combined with enzymatic action splits picrocrocin into D-glucose and free safranal, the volatile molecule behind most of saffron's aroma.
Wikipedia credits sedanolide, alongside butylphthalide, as the main chemicals responsible for celery's aroma and taste.
1-Phenylethanethiol is named as one of the major odour compounds in curry leaves, giving them their sulphury, meaty note alongside citrusy linalool and resinous pinene.
2-Pentylfuran is identified as poppy seed's primary flavour compound.
Turmerones are a group of sesquiterpene compounds found in turmeric's steam-distilled essential oil, chemically distinct from the curcumin that gives turmeric its colour.
Terpenes including ocimene, myrcene, and limonene have been identified in the dried unripe mango used to make amchoor, alongside the citric acid behind its sourness.
Panch phoron, the Bengali five-spice blend used whole rather than ground, consists of fenugreek, cumin, nigella, black mustard, and fennel seed in equal parts.
Chaat masala typically consists of amchoor, cumin, coriander, dried ginger, black salt, black pepper, asafoetida, and chilli powder — the tangy, savoury seasoning behind Indian street-food chaat.

Bart Bok first described these small, dense, isolated clouds in 1947 — among the coldest objects in the universe, and one of the few places a collapsing pocket of a molecular cloud can be picked out from outside.
Near-infrared observations confirmed in 1990 that stars really do form inside Bok globules — usually as a double or multiple system rather than a single star.
Ultraviolet light from a nearby hot star strips material off one side of a Bok globule, leaving a bright ionized rim and a trailing dark tail — a cometary globule.
Material ejected from an accreting protostar rams into the surrounding gas at hundreds of kilometres a second, lighting up glowing shock fronts — more than a thousand of these are now catalogued.
As infall dies down and the shrouding envelope clears, a low-mass protostar becomes visible as a T Tauri star — still contracting toward the main sequence, not yet fusing hydrogen in its core.

An intermediate-mass protostar of 2 to 8 solar masses, still wrapped in its accretion disc, is a Herbig Ae/Be star — the heavier counterpart to a T Tauri star, first identified by George Herbig in 1960.

Sometimes a T Tauri star's own accretion disc dumps a burst of mass onto it all at once, brightening the star by several magnitudes for decades — the average young star erupts like this 10 to 20 times over its life.

Thousands of ATP-bound globular actin subunits polymerize head-to-tail into a helical filament with a fast-growing plus end and a slow minus end; muscle cells pack them densest, as the thin filaments of the sarcomere.

Myosin-II's two heads bind actin and hydrolyze ATP in a cycle — phosphate release powers the stroke, ADP release locks it into rigor, and fresh ATP finally lets go — walking the motor toward the filament's plus end.

Keratin is only one branch of a whole family — vimentin, desmin, lamins, neurofilaments — that all assemble into 10 nm ropes tougher and more stretchable than actin or microtubules, built for mechanical strength rather than movement.

Integrins are transmembrane heterodimers that grip the extracellular matrix outside the cell and couple, inside it, to the actin cytoskeleton through focal adhesions — signaling runs both directions across that same membrane.

Myosin heads on the thick filament repeatedly bind actin, pull, and let go, sliding the thin filaments deeper into the sarcomere without either filament changing length — the sliding filament model of muscle contraction.
Actin polymerizing at the front pushes out lamellipodia and filopodia, while integrins grip the substrate like feet and recycle from back to front, so the cell body is pulled forward.

GPCRs snake across the membrane in seven transmembrane helices; a ligand binding outside twists the whole bundle, and the new shape lets the receptor act as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor on an associated G protein inside.
A growth factor binding outside pairs up two receptors, and each one then spends ATP autophosphorylating tyrosines on its partner's cytosolic tail — the docking sites that launch the signal inward.

A GPCR's activated G protein alpha subunit diffuses along the membrane and switches on adenylyl cyclase — Earl Sutherland's Nobel-winning 1971 discovery tying a hormone outside the cell to a new enzyme inside it.

Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP directly into cyclic AMP plus pyrophosphate — one of biology's oldest and most widespread second messengers, relaying signals like adrenaline and glucagon that never cross the membrane themselves.

PKA sits locked as two regulatory and two catalytic subunits until four cAMP molecules bind the regulatory pair; the complex falls apart and the freed catalytic subunits phosphorylate target serines and threonines.
A different flavor of G protein, Gq, activates phospholipase C instead of adenylyl cyclase; PLC then cleaves the membrane lipid PIP2 into two separate second messengers in a single reaction.
Cleaving PIP2 releases IP3, the water-soluble half of the split, carrying three phosphate groups and enough charge to diffuse straight into the cytosol, where it opens calcium channels on the ER.

The other half of the same PIP2 cut, diacylglycerol is too lipophilic to leave the membrane, so it stays anchored there and waits for calcium to arrive before it can finish activating protein kinase C.

Diacylglycerol and a rise in cytosolic calcium — the second half of the same phospholipase C signal — together pull PKC to the membrane and switch it on to phosphorylate serine and threonine residues.

Docking proteins recruited to a phosphorylated RTK tail switch Ras from its GDP-bound off state to its GTP-bound on state — a binary molecular switch whose stuck-on mutants are found in 20–25% of all human tumors.

Active Ras kicks off a three-kinase relay — each one phosphorylating and activating the next using ATP — until the last kinase reaches the nucleus and phosphorylates transcription factors, changing which genes get read.

Cortisol is built from cholesterol through a chain of enzyme reactions in the adrenal cortex's zona fasciculata — as with every steroid hormone, the raw material is the same molecule that also stiffens cell membranes.

Because cortisol is small and lipophilic, it needs no surface receptor at all — it diffuses across the membrane and binds a receptor sitting inside the cell, which then acts directly on DNA as a transcription factor.

Continental crust is thicker but far less dense than oceanic crust, so it floats higher on the mantle — built from granitic rock old enough, in places, to exceed 3 billion years, since subduction rarely destroys it.

Magma constantly rises through mid-ocean ridges to add new basaltic seafloor, driving the plates apart and widening the ocean basin — the ridge system runs 65,000 km, longer than any mountain range on land.
A peninsula extends from a mainland, connected to it on only one side while mostly surrounded by water — the Peloponnese, for instance, is tied to the rest of Greece by the narrow Isthmus of Corinth.

An archipelago is a chain, cluster, or collection of islands — the Hawaiian Islands and the Azores are two well-known examples, both built up by repeated volcanic activity rather than any single eruption.

A strait is a water body connecting two seas or larger basins, with surface water flowing through in either direction — the Strait of Gibraltar does exactly that between two continents, Europe and Africa.

The Isthmus of Panama closed a seaway between the Pacific and Atlantic around 3 million years ago, as colliding plates threw up volcanoes whose gaps filled with sediment until North and South America were welded into one strip of land.
The equator is the circle of latitude at 0°, running around Earth's midpoint exactly between the poles — the line that divides the planet into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Cut along the equator and Earth divides into a Northern Hemisphere, holding about 68% of the planet's land and 90% of its population, and a Southern Hemisphere with the rest.

Latitude measures north-south position as an angle from 0° at the Equator to 90° at the poles; lines of constant latitude, called parallels, are circles running east-west, parallel to the Equator and shrinking as they near the poles.

Meridians are imaginary lines running from pole to pole, perpendicular to the circles of latitude, that measure a point's position east or west — cut across the parallels and you get the other half of the coordinate grid.

In October 1884, delegates at the International Meridian Conference chose the meridian through Greenwich, England as the common zero of longitude, from which every other line is measured east or west.

Because Earth spins once every 24 hours, the world is split into time zones, each defined by a standard offset from Coordinated Universal Time — the successor to Greenwich Mean Time, measured from the Prime Meridian.
The Tropic of Cancer, at about 23°26'N, is Earth's northernmost circle of latitude where the Sun appears directly overhead — a moment that occurs once a year, on the June solstice.
The Tropic of Capricorn, at about 23°26'S, is the southernmost latitude that contains the subsolar point — the Sun sits directly overhead there once a year, on the December solstice.

A steppe is grassland plains without closed forest, getting 250-500 mm of rain a year — too dry to support trees, not dry enough to be desert. The Eurasian Steppe, the largest, helped spread the horse, the wheel, and Indo-European languages.

Savanna is grassy woodland where the trees, like acacia, stand far enough apart that the canopy never closes; it covers about a fifth of Earth's land, with most of its 500-1,270 mm of yearly rain falling in a single season.

Political borders are imposed by human agency — war, colonization, or treaty — and often follow rivers or mountain ranges, though ones formalized recently, especially in Africa, more often run the straight lines colonial powers drew instead.
A country is a political entity or its territory, ranging from a fully sovereign state to an unrecognized state or dependent territory — a bordered piece of a continent claimed as its own.

A nation-state is where the state and the nation — a population sharing a common identity — are congruent; the model became dominant in the 19th century, after the Peace of Westphalia had already set the norm of sovereign, recognized territories.

A capital city holds primary status as a country's seat of government — not always its largest city. Brazil built Brasília, Australia built Canberra as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, and Canada chose Ottawa on the old Upper/Lower Canada boundary.

Population density is population size per unit of land area. Monaco packs in over 18,000 people per km², Singapore over 8,000 — while Mongolia, with vast arid land unable to support crops, has one of the lowest densities of any country.
A supply chain is the network of facilities that convert raw materials into finished products and distribute them onward — ports and freight wagons are two of its physical links.

Logistics is the flow of goods, services and information from origin to consumption; the English word arrived around 1846 from the French logistique, which Antoine-Henri Jomini tied to logis, 'lodgings.'

Supply chain management coordinates procurement, operations, logistics and marketing from raw material to end customer; computers made that coordination practical through EDI and ERP systems from the 1960s on.
Sales forecasting uses past sales figures to predict short- or long-term future performance and enable sound financial planning, drawing on historical sales and economic data.
Demand planning predicts future customer demand using predictive analytics; it's described as an important tool for optimizing business profitability through efficient supply chain management.

S&OP is a business management process that integrates demand forecasting with supply planning to balance demand against available resources; its modern form is credited to consultant Richard Ling of Oliver Wight in the 1980s.
A warehouse is simply a building for storing goods — used by manufacturers, importers, exporters, wholesalers and transport businesses, usually fitted with loading docks, cranes and forklifts.
Inventory is the quantity of goods and materials a business holds for the ultimate goal of resale, production or utilisation — stock on the shelf, not money in the till.

Inventory management software records and tracks stock levels, orders and deliveries; the first retail barcode scan was in 1974, and personal computers made computerized inventory records practical for smaller firms by the early 1980s.
Safety stock is a level of extra stock maintained to mitigate the risk of stockouts caused by uncertainty in demand, supply, or the accuracy of the forecast itself.
Economic order quantity is the order quantity that minimizes total holding costs and ordering costs in inventory management; Ford W. Harris derived the original formula in 1913.

The bullwhip effect is a supply-chain phenomenon where orders to suppliers show larger swings than sales to buyers, amplifying demand variability upstream; Jay Forrester first modeled it in 1961, so it's also called the Forrester effect.

Just-in-time manufacturing receives goods only as needed to reduce cost and waste; Toyota engineer Taiichi Ohno developed it after noticing American supermarkets restock shelves based on what customers actually take.

Kanban — Japanese for 'signboard' — is a scheduling system for just-in-time manufacturing in which a card authorizes production only once it's requested downstream; Taiichi Ohno modeled it on how supermarkets restock only what shoppers take.

Lean manufacturing is built on producing only what's needed when it's needed, correcting abnormalities immediately, and empowering workers to improve the process; it grew out of Toyota's postwar system and was formally named 'Lean' by John Krafcik in 1988.

Material requirements planning is a production planning, scheduling and inventory control system; Joseph Orlicky developed it in 1964, it first ran at Black and Decker that year, and roughly 700 companies had adopted it by 1975.

Enterprise resource planning is the integrated, software-mediated management of an organization's main business processes; the acronym was coined by research firm Gartner in the 1990s as a functional extension of material requirements planning.

In vendor-managed inventory, the supplier — usually the manufacturer — takes responsibility for optimizing the inventory held by a distributor, deciding order sizes itself; Walmart and Procter & Gamble are among the retailers built around the model.

Distribution requirements planning applies material-requirements-style logic to a distribution network, letting planners set inventory-control parameters such as safety stock and calculate time-phased inventory requirements across warehouses.
Chinese soldiers packed gunpowder and a slow match into a bamboo tube strapped to a spear; the earliest fire lances appeared by 950 and saw combat at the 1132 siege of De'an, ancestor of the gun.
Bronze Age bowyers glued a horn belly and sinew backing onto a wood core with animal glue; composite bows buried with Tutankhamun, who died in 1324 BC, show the design was already standard in Egypt.
The spoked wheel, far lighter than a solid wooden disk, was the invention that let horses pull a cart fast enough for war; chariots fielded by both sides decided the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BC.
The Ghaznavids fielded 1,300 iron-armored war elephants by 1023; centuries earlier Hannibal marched armored elephants over the Alps in 218 BC, and Chandragupta Maurya commanded some 9,000 of them.
Eurasian steppe cavalry paired the compact composite bow with the horse, shooting on the gallop and wheeling away before contact; Parthian horse archers annihilated a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC.

India's earliest stirrup was a rope loop for the big toe, used by the 2nd century BC; China then developed the sturdier paired stirrup, cast in bronze and iron by 415 AD, freeing riders to fight from horseback.

Devised around 672 AD by Kallinikos, a refugee engineer from Syria, Greek fire was pumped from bow-mounted siphons and helped Byzantine ships repel Arab sieges of Constantinople between 674 and 678 AD.

French gunsmith Marin le Bourgeoys built the first true flintlock for Louis XIII around 1610 to 1615, its flint-on-steel spark replacing the smoldering match cord and making loaded muskets safer to carry.

Patented by Hiram Maxim in 1883, his water-cooled gun used the energy of its own recoil to eject and reload each cartridge, sustaining 600 rounds per minute and becoming the weapon most associated with imperial conquest.

Robert Whitehead's self-propelled torpedo, presented to the Austrian navy on 21 December 1866, was driven by a compressed-air engine inside a body of polished steel or phosphor bronze — the largest models used either metal.

Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin's rigid, aluminum-framed hydrogen airship first flew in 1900; between 1915 and 1918 German Zeppelins flew 51 raids on England, dropping 5,806 bombs that killed 557 people.

Mikhail Kalashnikov's rifle, accepted by the Soviet Armed Forces in early 1949, diverts propellant gas from the barrel to drive a piston that cycles the bolt — a rugged, cheap design later carried on every continent.
Manhattan Project scientists used reactors like Hanford's B Reactor to breed plutonium-239 from uranium-238; that plutonium armed the Fat Man bomb dropped on Nagasaki in August 1945.

On 22 April 1915 German troops released 168 tons of chlorine from 5,730 cylinders along a 4-mile front at Ypres; a north-easterly breeze carried the cloud onto French lines, tearing open a 3.7-mile gap.

Voltage-gated sodium channels are transmembrane proteins embedded in the axon's membrane, permeable specifically to sodium ions; when the membrane depolarizes they open, and the resulting sodium influx constitutes the action potential's rising phase.
Voltage-gated potassium channels open during and after an action potential, and the resulting outward flow of potassium ions is what returns the depolarized membrane to its resting state.

For a short interval after firing, an axon's voltage-gated sodium channels sit inactivated rather than merely closed, so no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second action potential until they reset.

A myelin sheath doesn't cover an axon continuously; it leaves short gaps exposed to extracellular fluid, and it's exactly at those gaps that voltage-gated sodium channels cluster at high density, concentrating where the signal actually regenerates.

Because ion exchange can only happen at an axon's exposed nodes of Ranvier, the action potential appears to jump node to node rather than propagate continuously, reaching speeds up to 150 m/s versus 0.5-10 m/s in an unmyelinated axon.

Schwann cells are the principal glia of the peripheral nervous system; myelinating Schwann cells wrap around the axons of motor and sensory neurons the way oligodendrocytes do in the brain and spinal cord, but each one insulates only a single axon.

A mechanoreceptor is a sensory receptor that responds to mechanical pressure or distortion; the skin is packed with dendritic nerve endings tuned to exactly that stimulus, converting touch into an electrical signal for the nervous system.

Nociceptors are sensory neurons that respond to damaging or potentially damaging stimuli; besides the skin, they're distributed through internal tissue such as muscle, where sustained contraction cutting off blood supply is itself enough to trigger them.

The Pacinian corpuscle is a low-threshold mechanoreceptor built from 20 to 70 concentric connective-tissue lamellae wrapped around a nerve ending, situated deep in the dermis, where it rapidly adapts to detect vibration and gross pressure changes.

Muscle spindles are stretch receptors embedded within the body of a skeletal muscle, a specialized mechanoreceptor that primarily detects changes in the muscle's own length and feeds that information back to the central nervous system.

The retina and the optic nerve both originate as outgrowths of the embryonic diencephalon, so the retina is classified as part of the central nervous system, and is, developmentally, actual brain tissue rather than a peripheral sense organ.

A photoreceptor cell's membranous opsin protein pairs with the pigment retinal; in rod cells the two together are called rhodopsin, and absorbing a single photon changes the pigment's shape, the first step in converting light into a nerve signal.

The cornea is the eye's transparent front layer, and its stroma is built from roughly 200 layers of type I collagen fibrils; the fibrils are spaced so precisely that light scattered by one is cancelled by destructive interference from its neighbors.

The vertebrate eye's lens is built almost entirely from crystallin proteins, which make up over 90% of its protein content; densely packed crystallins raise the lens's refractive index while keeping it transparent.
The iris is a thin, muscular diaphragm controlling pupil size: a circular sphincter muscle contracts to narrow the pupil, while a separate set of dilator muscles pulls the iris outward to widen it.

The oculomotor nerve innervates most of the eye's own movement muscles, but it also carries parasympathetic fibers that reach the iris directly, driving the sphincter muscle that constricts the pupil and controlling the lens's focus for near objects.

Hair cells are the sensory receptors of both the auditory and vestibular systems in the inner ear, a mechanoreceptor whose named tuft of stereocilia bends in response to fluid motion, converting that mechanical deflection into an electrical signal.

The cochlea is a spiral-shaped, fluid-filled cavity of the inner ear making about 2.75 turns; running along it is the organ of Corti, whose hair cells sense the fluid's motion through their stereocilia and convert it into the electrical signal of hearing.

The eardrum is a thin, cone-shaped membrane separating the outer ear from the middle ear; it flexes with incoming sound pressure and transmits that vibration to the ossicles, the middle ear's chain of tiny bones.

The vestibular system, housed in the inner ear alongside the cochlea, is the sensory system that creates the sense of balance and spatial orientation, and its output is carried to the brain by the vestibular branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve.

The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste sensation from the posterior third of the tongue and, on its motor side, supplies parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland by way of the otic ganglion, the signal that starts salivation flowing.

Taste buds are clusters of gustatory receptor cells across the tongue, but the circumvallate papillae at the tongue's back are innervated specifically by the glossopharyngeal nerve, distinct from the facial nerve supplying taste further forward.

The olfactory epithelium is specialized tissue lining the nasal cavity whose olfactory sensory neurons carry odorant receptors on their cilia; their axons pool together and cross the skull to form the olfactory nerve directly.

A motor neuron's cell body sits in the brainstem or the spinal cord, for the alpha motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle, specifically in the spinal cord's ventral horn, with its axon projecting out to directly innervate a muscle fiber.

The knee-jerk stretch reflex is a monosynaptic reflex arc: a muscle spindle's sensory afferent, activated by a change in muscle length, synapses directly onto a spinal motor neuron, triggering a muscle contraction without any input from the brain.

The basal ganglia are a group of subcortical nuclei found within the cerebral hemispheres, gray matter buried inside the cerebrum rather than spread across its surface, that help regulate voluntary motor movement.

The substantia nigra is a basal ganglia structure whose pars compacta neurons supply the striatum with dopamine; the loss of exactly these dopamine-producing neurons is the defining pathology behind Parkinson's disease.

Adrenaline is made from noradrenaline in a single step: the enzyme phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase adds a methyl group to noradrenaline's amine, using SAMe as the methyl donor, chiefly inside the adrenal medulla's chromaffin cells.

Endorphins are endogenous opioid peptides that block the perception of pain; peripherally they bind mu-opioid receptors directly on nociceptor nerve terminals, blocking those very endings' release of the pain-signaling peptide substance P.

An electroencephalogram records electrical activity from the cortex non-invasively via scalp electrodes; the signal it picks up chiefly represents postsynaptic potentials of pyramidal neurons in the cortex, not action potentials themselves.

Alpha waves are EEG oscillations in the 8-to-13-hertz range, and the leading explanation for the rhythm's origin points to synchronous cortical activity driven by pacemaker circuitry within the thalamus.

REM sleep is driven by 'REM-on' neurons that are chiefly cholinergic, using acetylcholine much as waking brain activity does, while the noradrenaline- and serotonin-releasing 'REM-off' neurons that normally suppress them fall silent.

Wernicke's area sits in the posterior superior temporal gyrus and receives input from the auditory cortex, assigning meaning to spoken words carried in by the auditory pathway that begins at the vestibulocochlear nerve.

Broca's area, in the inferior frontal gyrus, is classically described as connected to Wernicke's area by the arcuate fasciculus, a white-matter tract carrying comprehended language forward to the region responsible for producing speech.
Norman swords grew a crossguard (quillons) by the 11th century, and in the late Middle Ages the grip was sometimes wrapped in wire for a firmer hold that was harder to knock loose.
Cross-hilt daggers reappearing in the 12th century resembled miniature swords -- a short, tapered double edge with its own crossguard and pommel -- worn suspended by a strap from the leather belt.
A long and narrow dagger, thin enough to push through the eye-slit of a visor or thrust under the arm through a gap in plate, delivering a mercy killing to a mortally wounded knight.
Against full plate, cutting and slicing became almost entirely ineffective, so the blade sharpened its point and grew a 15-30 cm grip usable with one or both hands for thrusting instead.
Layers of wool or linen padding stitched together by a quilting technique called pourpointing made a jacket that served as armor on its own for foot soldiers, or as cushioning under a mail coat.

Wire pulled thin through a draw plate was coiled into rings, and each ring was riveted shut and linked through four others -- a hauberk that stayed standard European armor from the 3rd century BC to the 16th century AD.
Early medieval round shields were built from light, non-splitting wood like linden or fir, reinforced with a leather facing and a metal boss riveted through the center to protect the hand behind it.

A round shield left a horseman's leg exposed, especially when charging with a lance, so by the 1000s Western Europe adopted an almond-shaped shield curving down to a point that covered the rider's leg.
Steel plates progressively covered the mail coat through the 14th century's 'coat of plates' stage, and by about 1420 Europe had complete suits of well-tempered steel, articulated joint by joint.

First documented in 13th-century German texts and carried by Swiss forces at Morgarten in 1315, the halberd tops a long shaft with an axe blade, a spike, and a hook on the back for grappling mounted men.

Extending a spear's shaft to as much as 7 meters and reinforcing it near the head with metal strips called langets made a pike -- dense ranks of them were nearly immune to mounted men-at-arms as long as the line held.

Emerging in the mid-14th century as a direct response to plate armor, the war hammer pairs a blunt face with a spike on the reverse: stun with the hammer side, then rotate it to punch through with the point.

Built during the 14th and 15th centuries specifically to breach plate, the poleaxe mounted an axe head or hammer head plus a spike on an ash shaft up to 180 cm long, giving several ways to find a weak point.
The flanged mace spread across Europe from the 12th century: a steel head cast with ridges to focus a blow's force into a small point, its conical socket riveted fast to a tapered wooden handle.

Descended from the two-handed farm flail used to thresh grain, the medieval military flail joins one or more iron-shod striking heads to a wooden shaft by a length of chain -- Hussite peasant armies swung both.

Mounting a bow-like prod crosswise on a wooden stock, with a trigger to release the string and loose a short bolt, gave Europe a weapon that reappeared at the 947 siege of Senlis and was common by the 12th century.

The English longbow was made specifically of yew, strung with hemp, flax or silk on horn nocks, and stood about six feet tall -- it drove back the French at Crecy in 1346 and again at Agincourt in 1415.
A heavy log capped in iron or steel was slung from ropes or chains inside a wheeled, fireproofed frame and swung by a crew against a wall or gate -- Roman armies were already using rams by 503 BC.

Builders faced a wooden tower on wheels with whatever non-flammable covering they could procure, usually iron plates or fresh animal skins, then rolled it to a wall and dropped a gangplank so troops could rush the ramparts.

Most daggers pair a metal blade with a hilt of some other material, but the katar's H-shaped, parallel-bar grip is forged from the same steel as its blade — a form tied to South India's 14th-century Vijayanagara Empire.

Javanese smiths forge-weld alternating layers of iron and nickel-rich iron, then etch the blade with acid so the nickel streaks show as the kris's pamor pattern — the finest blades used nickel from a meteorite that fell near Prambanan.

The shotel's iron blade curves far more sharply than a Persian shamshir, letting a swordsman reach around a shield to strike; its hilt is normally three pieces of rhinoceros horn with no guard at all.

Tuareg smiths build the takouba's crossguard from iron sheet or iron-framed wood and finish the pommel in brass, copper or silver, while the straight blade itself is hand-ground with three or more fuller grooves.

Tulwar blades were commonly forged from wootz crucible steel and fixed into an all-metal hilt of iron, brass or silver with lac resin; the hilt's disc-shaped pommel flange became the sword's signature.

The flyssa's hilt is a wooden grip sheathed in brass worked with repoussé and chasing, ending in a downturned animal-head pommel; the acutely pointed blade was carried by the Kabyle Iflissen confederacy of Algeria.

Shaka had Zulu smiths shorten the long throwing spear's shaft to about 24 inches and broaden its blade to 12, trading throwing range for a weapon built to stab at close quarters — named for the sound it made pulled free.

Persian smiths hilted the shamshir's crucible wootz-steel blade — its surface watered with the pattern the steel's own structure leaves — in ivory or wood, worn with the curve pointing forward for a slashing draw-cut.

Lacking a guard, the yataghan instead flares into wing-like 'ears' at the pommel — often horn on Anatolian examples — that keep the hilt from sliding out of a cutting hand; production centered on Istanbul, Foça and Prizren.

Chinese crossbow locks cast in bronze date to about 650 BC; unlike a handheld bow, the crossbow's trigger held its string drawn indefinitely, so it could be aimed at leisure and fired by far less-trained troops.

Pushing and pulling one lever on this Warring States-era Chinese design spans the bow, drops a bolt from the magazine on top, and fires it in a single motion — up to ten bolts in twenty seconds, though too weak to trouble armor.

Woven from non-elastic fiber such as wool, flax or hemp into two cords and a pouch, the sling armed Balearic mercenaries and Assyrian and Egyptian armies — and, in the biblical account, David against Goliath.

Mexica warriors glued rows of obsidian blades into the grooved edges of a flat wooden paddle; Spanish accounts describe it decapitating a horse in one stroke, though the volcanic glass chipped and dulled on impact.
Song dynasty troops used gunpowder tubes lashed to spears against the Jin as early as 1132; as shrapnel was packed in and the tube became metal, the fire lance's line led directly to the hand cannon.
Draping cloth from a horizontal crossbar lashed to a spear, rather than hoisting it up a pole, builds the vexillum -- the Roman cavalry standard that gave the study of flags its name.
Cutting a cross diagonally into an X reproduces the saltire -- the shape tradition says Saint Andrew was crucified on, and the form behind Scotland's flag.
A gilded lance carrying cloth dyed blood-red with rose madder reproduces the Oriflamme, the French royal battle standard whose name -- 'golden flame' -- described its blaze in the wind.
Flying cloth from a ship's stern to declare its nationality makes an ensign -- Britain alone keeps three colours: White for the Royal Navy, Blue for government service, Red for merchant ships.
Banding indigo-blue and madder-red either side of undyed white cloth reproduces France's tricolore, fixed in its blue-white-red order in 1794 and copied worldwide as a symbol of liberty.
England's red St George's cross joined with Scotland's white saltire on blue -- 'joyned together' by royal proclamation in 1606 -- produced the first Union Flag.

A white cross sewn onto red cloth, shifted toward the hoist, reproduces the Dannebrog -- tradition says it fell from the sky in the 1219 Battle of Lyndanisse; it is the Guinness-record oldest flag still in use.

Dyeing a dark blue cross with indigo onto the Dannebrog's pattern gives Fredrik Meltzer's 1821 design -- he chose blue for colours that, in his words, 'now denote freedom' in the French, Dutch, and American flags.
Dyeing the Nordic cross saffron-gold on blue, instead of white on red, reproduces Sweden's flag -- colours drawn from the Three Crowns coat of arms used since at least 1364.
Bleaching the Dannebrog's field to snow-white and dyeing its cross lake-blue gives the flag Finland adopted at independence in 1918.
Recolouring the Dannebrog's cross cochineal-red and fringing it white, over blue rather than red, gives Iceland's flag -- blue for mountains and sea, white for ice, red for volcanic fire.
Iron-black cloth trimmed in gold recalls the black uniforms and gold buttons of the Napoleonic-era Lützow Free Corps, whose colours the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament declared Germany's.
A white eagle set on cochineal-red cloth reproduces the tinctures of Poland's coat of arms, adopted as national colours in 1831 and as the flag itself in 1919.

A gold sun stitched onto indigo-blue and white bands reproduces Argentina's flag -- the colours from the 1810 May Revolution cockade, the Sun of May added in 1818 and linked by some historians to the Inca sun god Inti.
A gold Sun of May set in a white cotton canton above nine blue-and-white stripes -- one per original department -- reproduces the flag Joaquin Suarez designed in 1828.
White stars scattered on a blue globe over a gold rhombus reproduce Brazil's flag -- 27 stars mapping the sky over Rio de Janeiro on 15 November 1889, the day the republic was proclaimed.
A white star representing Venus, set on Andes-snow white above sky blue, reproduces Chile's flag, adopted in 1817 -- more than twenty years before Texas's similarly single-starred flag.
Weaving rainbow-dyed wool into a diagonal seven-by-seven checkerboard produces the wiphala, the Andean emblem Bolivia's 2009 constitution made an official flag alongside its tricolour.
Banding indigo-blue beneath saffron-yellow reproduces the top two bands of the tricolour Francisco de Miranda first flew on 12 March 1806 at Jacmel, Haiti.
Three volcanoes rising between the Pacific and Caribbean, ringed by seven stars for Costa Rica's seven provinces, form the coat of arms placed on the flag after its 1848 redesign.
Five volcanoes, one for each founding state of the United Provinces of Central America, set beneath a rainbow -- the biblical sign of God's covenant with Noah -- form El Salvador's 1912 coat of arms.

A blue star for the Conservative party and a red star for the Liberal party, designed by First Lady Maria de la Ossa de Amador in 1903, sit beside a coat of arms whose golden winged wheel stands for progress.
A gold saltire for the shining sun, quartering green land and black hardship, reproduces the flag Jamaica adopted at 1962 independence -- one of only two sovereign flags with no white, red, or blue.

A white Lone Star set on a cochineal-red equilateral triangle -- a Masonic symbol found across former Spanish-empire flags -- reproduces the design Narciso Lopez's rebels first raised at Cardenas in 1850.
An eagle on a cactus, devouring a serpent, recreates the Aztec omen marking where the Mexica were to found their capital, Tenochtitlan -- the emblem at the centre of Mexico's flag.
A red maple leaf on a white field flanked by red bars gives the flag Canada adopted on 15 February 1965, its eleven-point leaf chosen after wind-tunnel tests for staying sharpest in high wind.

Fifty white stars on a blue canton over thirteen red-and-white stripes reproduce the current US flag, ordered by Eisenhower in 1959 and flown from the following Independence Day after Hawaii's statehood.
Early shields paired a wood frame -- often light, split-resistant timber -- with a leather or hide facing and a metal boss for extra strength.
Bronze-fitted spoked wheels turned a simple cart into a fighting platform; some 5,000-6,000 chariots collided at Kadesh in 1274 BC between Ramesses II's Egyptians and the Hittites.
A leather pouch slung between two cords of flax or hemp, whirled overhead and released to hurl a stone; Balearic islanders, trained from childhood, served Carthage as legendary slingers.

The Achaemenid Empire Cyrus founded fielded an elite corps of 10,000 heavy infantry Herodotus called the Immortals, so named because every casualty was instantly replaced, keeping the unit's strength constant.
Greek city-state citizens armed with a large concave aspis shield and a 2.5-4.5 meter spear fought shoulder to shoulder in the tightly packed phalanx that broke the Persians at Marathon.
Philip II lengthened the Greek dory into this 5-7 meter pike so several rows of points projected past the front rank; Alexander's phalanx carried it into Persia.
Rome adopted this short iron sword from Celtiberian designs met through Carthaginian mercenaries in the Punic Wars; legionaries led with the shield and thrust with the gladius rather than slashing.
A roughly 2-meter javelin with a pyramidal iron head on a soft iron shank that bent on impact, jamming an enemy's shield; legionaries threw pila before closing with the gladius.

Overlapping iron strips were fastened into bands and buckled with leather straps over a padded cloth tunic; Roman legionaries wore it from the 1st century AD, with evidence from the Teutoburg Forest disaster of 9 AD.
Legionaries carrying gladius and shield could lock their shields into a packed formation covered on the front and top -- the 'tortoise' that shrugged off arrows and stones during a siege assault.
Cataphracts armored both rider and horse in scale or lamellar and carried heavy lances, serving as shock cavalry for the Sassanid Persians, Byzantines, Sarmatians and Parthians to break enemy lines.

Byzantine emperors recruited their elite personal guard from Northern Europe -- mainly Norse Scandinavians, later joined by Anglo-Saxons -- precisely because outsiders carried no local political ties.
The 9th-century skaldic poem Haraldskvaedi first names these Norse warriors, describing them as men clad in wolf skins who fought in a trance-like fury, complete with shield-biting and animal howls.

Housecarls were paid, professional soldiers who served kings like Cnut the Great; at Hastings in 1066, Harold Godwinson's housecarls held the center of his line around the standard until the last man fell.

Cast in bronze in Jin dynasty China around the early 4th century AD, the stirrup spread west via Central Asian nomads by the 7th-8th centuries and let a rider fight two-handed instead of just clinging on.

Medieval Europe's knight was a mounted, armored warrior granted a fief of land by a lord in exchange for military service -- often reckoned at about 40 days a year -- the reciprocal bond at feudalism's core.

Traction trebuchets, hauled by crews pulling ropes, appeared in China by the 4th century BC and spread west; medieval counterweight versions swapped human muscle for a falling weighted box to batter castle walls.

English longbows cut from yew staves drew an estimated 100-185 lbf; at Agincourt in 1415, exhausted French knights crossing muddy ground under a hail of English arrows were overwhelmed in close combat.
Small iron rings linked ring-through-ring into a flexible mesh; the earliest surviving mail comes from the 3rd century BC Celtic Carpathian Basin, and Rome adopted the technology soon after.

Shaped steel plates replaced mail piece by piece across 14th-15th century Europe, driven by thrusting poleaxes, estocs and halberds and by increasingly effective crossbows that mail alone could no longer stop.

First documented in 13th-century German texts, this two-handed polearm topped an axe blade with a spike; its hook could pull a mounted knight from the saddle, and it became the primary weapon of the early Swiss armies.
Renaissance pikes ran 3 to 7 meters long; Swiss and Landsknecht infantry massed them into dense squares that presented four or five overlapping layers of spearheads to an advancing enemy.

Once swords and axes could no longer pierce plate armor, the war hammer's blunt head -- paired with a spike or beak on the reverse -- delivered concentrated impact that dented or stunned the wearer instead.

This slender, sharply pointed two-edged thrusting sword emerged in 16th-century Spain and Italy, fashionable among nobility for civilian dueling and self-defense before giving way to the lighter small sword.

This single-edged sword, curved for a slashing draw-cut, originated among Turkic horsemen of Central Asia and spread to Persian, Arab, Ottoman and Indian cavalry, prized for being light on a galloping horse.

Founded in 1363, the Janissaries were levied as Christian boys from the Balkans and trained as the sultan's slave-soldiers; the corps that mastered the composite bow later became one of Europe's first standing infantry armed with firearms.

German pike-and-shot mercenaries of the late 15th to 16th century, Landsknechts were as famous for their flamboyant slashed-and-puffed clothing as for their pikes, winning fame at battles like Pavia in 1525.

Poland's winged hussars fought as heavy cavalry from 1503 to 1702, riding into battle with feathered wing frames on their backs; their charge helped break the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683, the largest cavalry charge in history.

This curved-blade polearm emerged in Japan's Heian period and proved especially effective at dismounting cavalry during the Genpei War; by the Edo period it had become a status weapon associated with women of the samurai class.

Parthian cavalry paired mounted archery with a signature trick: turning in the saddle to loose an arrow backward at full gallop, a tactic that helped annihilate Crassus's legions at Carrhae in 53 BCE.

At Yale in 1961, Stanley Milgram had volunteers work a fake shock generator labeled up to 450 volts, believing they shocked a 'learner' in another room after wrong answers; 65% went all the way to the maximum voltage when told to continue.

Solomon Asch seated a real subject among actors who unanimously named the wrong line length in a simple matching task; across twelve such trials, about three-quarters of subjects conformed to the wrong answer at least once.

The term entered psychiatry in 1889 when Paul Näcke and Havelock Ellis independently coined 'narcissism,' and Freud gave it a full theory in his 1914 essay 'On Narcissism' — both borrowing the name of the myth's youth who fell in love with his own reflection.

Richard Christie and Florence Geis built the trait's 1970 Mach-IV scale from statements inspired by The Prince, naming it for Machiavelli only as a source of ideas — Christie was explicit it has no real link to his own political philosophy.

Hervey Cleckley gave the condition its first influential clinical description in his 1941 book The Mask of Sanity; Robert Hare later built the Psychopathy Checklist on that base, turning low remorse and callous exploitation into a standard measure.

Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams grouped narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy together in 2002 as the 'Dark Triad' — three distinct but overlapping traits, present at ordinary, non-clinical levels in the general population.
All three Dark Triad traits share a callous, manipulative style and low agreeableness; researchers commonly score them together, as with the 27-item Short Dark Triad's nine questions per trait.

In a 2018 Psychological Review paper, Ingo Zettler, Morten Moshagen, and Benjamin Hilbig proposed a shared 'D-factor' behind dark traits: maximizing one's own utility at others' expense, backed by self-serving justifying beliefs.

In a 1959 Stanford study, Leon Festinger and James Carlsmith paid subjects $1 or $20 to call a boring task enjoyable; those paid only $1 later rated it more enjoyable, since the smaller sum gave less outside justification for the lie.

Ivan Pavlov, studying dog digestion around 1901, found that after repeatedly pairing feeding with a signal — a bell among the stimuli he tried — the dogs began salivating at the signal alone, before any food appeared.

In his 1984 book Influence, Robert Cialdini distilled research from car lots, charities, and telemarketing floors into six compliance principles, including reciprocity — the documented pull to return a favor, like an unsolicited free gift.

In a 1966 study, Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser found homeowners who'd first agreed to a small sign were far likelier — 76% versus 17% — to later accept a large 'Drive Carefully' yard sign than homeowners asked only the larger favor.

In a 1975 study, Robert Cialdini's team asked students to counsel juvenile delinquents for two years — nearly all refused — then asked a smaller favor, chaperoning a zoo trip; 50% agreed after refusing the big request, versus 17% asked cold.

Yale psychologist Irving Janis developed the concept in his 1972 book Victims of Groupthink, using the Kennedy administration's 1961 Bay of Pigs planning as his case study of suppressed dissent; the word had first appeared in a 1952 Fortune article.

Bandler and Grinder, who introduced NLP in 1975, taught that the direction a person's eyes move reveals whether they're recalling an image, a sound, or a feeling — the 'eye-accessing cues' chart from their 1979 book Frogs into Princes.

Paralyzed by polio at seventeen, Erickson regained control of his body by recalling 'body memories' of his own past muscular activity — an early exercise in the close self-observation that shaped his later indirect, permissive hypnotherapy.

A Cummins 600-horsepower diesel turns the Bradley's aluminum-armored hull into a fighting vehicle that can keep pace with the M1 Abrams it escorts, entering U.S. Army service in 1981 as an infantry carrier built to fight rather than just carry troops.
Sikorsky paired the basic helicopter with two General Electric T700 turboshaft engines instead of one, the redundancy and power the Army wanted when the UH-60 replaced the single-engine Huey in 1979.

A second main rotor, counter-rotating against the first, cancels the torque a tail rotor would otherwise have to fight — the tandem-rotor layout Boeing's Chinook has flown since entering service in 1962.

A millimeter-wave AN/APG-78 'Longbow' radar mounted above the main rotor lets the AH-64D track up to 128 targets at once and engage 16 of them — automation no pilot scanning by eye could match, fielded from 1997.

A mast-mounted sight above the rotor — a television camera, thermal imager and laser rangefinder/designator packed into a ball crews nicknamed the 'beach ball' — let the OH-58D scout and mark targets without exposing the fuselage, entering service in 1991.

Bolting the cannon onto its own tracked, diesel-driven chassis lets the 155mm howitzer displace under its own power the moment it fires, instead of waiting for a truck to tow it — the self-propelled artillery the M109 has flown since 1963.

Swapping the cannon's single barrel for twelve rocket pods on a Bradley-derived tracked chassis lets one launcher blanket a square kilometer in one salvo — British troops in the 1991 Gulf War nicknamed it the 'grid square removal system.'

Halving the MLRS's rocket load to one six-pack pod and mounting it on a wheeled truck frame instead of tracks makes the launcher light enough to fit inside a C-130 — the HIMARS variant that entered service in 2005.
An AN/MPQ-53 phased-array radar tracks both target and missile and radios corrections back — 'track-via-missile' guidance the Patriot has used since replacing Nike Hercules in 1984.

An onboard imaging-infrared seeker and tracking computer lock onto the target before the trigger is even pulled, so the missile flies itself in afterward — 'fire-and-forget' guidance that let the Javelin, in service from 1996, replace the wire-guided Dragon.

Two command wires spool out from the launcher as it flies, carrying steering corrections back to the missile all the way to the target — wire guidance the TOW has used since entering service around 1970.

A seeker in the nose homes in on reflected laser light — semi-active laser homing — so a helicopter, drone or ground team can mark a target and let the missile do the rest, the guidance the Hellfire has flown with since 1996.

An aluminum cabin bolted to a narrow steel frame, with portal-axle hubs that raise the drivetrain above the wheel centers instead of running through it, nearly doubles a normal automobile's ground clearance in the Jeep-replacement the Army fielded from 1985.

Eight driven wheels instead of tracks trade some off-road pivot-turning and armor for road speed and easy upkeep — the Stryker, fielded from 2002, later gained a slat-armor cage in 2005 to detonate RPGs before they reach the hull.

A monocoque V-shaped hull directs a mine or IED blast outward instead of straight up through the floor — a shape South Africa pioneered on the Casspir in 1979 that the Army adopted once IEDs made the flat-bottomed Humvee too costly to field.

An aluminum-alloy receiver, instead of the machined steel and walnut of the rifles before it, cut enough weight that a soldier could carry far more 5.56mm ammunition — the tradeoff behind the M16 the U.S. military adopted in 1964.

Cutting the M16A2's 20-inch barrel to 14.5 inches still leaves 80% of the parts interchangeable — the carbine the Army adopted in 1994 after 1993's Mogadishu firefight showed how unwieldy a full rifle is up close.

A welded, stamped-steel receiver -- cheaper than a machined one -- carries the FN Minimi's belt feed, so the M249 fires the M16's own 5.56mm round but keeps feeding long after a box magazine runs dry; adopted in 1984.

Firing a half-inch .50 BMG round with a tungsten penetrator in its armor-piercing loads gives the M2 the punch to down aircraft or crack light armor — Browning's design, in continuous service since 1933.
APP is a cell-surface receptor protein encoded by an 18-exon gene, concentrated in the synapses of neurons — mutations in that gene are one direct cause of early-onset familial Alzheimer's.
APP spans a neuron's membrane by a single anchor, and its gene sits on chromosome 21 — the same chromosome duplicated in every cell of someone with Down syndrome.
Beta-secretase and gamma-secretase cut APP in two places, releasing a fragment of 36 to 43 amino acids — the peptide amyloid plaques are built from.
Certain inherited mutations in critical regions of APP dramatically increase how much of this fragment gets cut loose, causing familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease.
Amyloid-beta misfolds and templates neighboring copies into the same shape, aggregating into a dense core surrounded by a corona of less tightly packed protein.
These extracellular deposits form first in the grey matter of the neocortex, then spread to deeper brain structures as Alzheimer's disease progresses.
Tau binds tubulin and stabilizes the microtubule tracks running down a neuron's axon, keeping that internal scaffolding both sturdy and flexible.
Tau is especially abundant in the cerebral cortex, where it does the same microtubule-stabilizing job it does everywhere else in the nervous system.
Excess phosphate groups hyperphosphorylate tau, making it let go of the microtubules and misfold into paired helical filaments that bundle into tangles.
Once one tau molecule misfolds, it can act as a seed that templates neighboring tau into the same shape — a prion-like spread through the brain.
Concentrated in the axon terminals of presynaptic neurons, alpha-synuclein binds synaptic vesicles and helps regulate how much neurotransmitter they release.
