Adding hydrogen across a fat's carbon-carbon double bonds — hydrogenation — removes every kink in its fatty-acid tails, letting the molecules pack tightly enough to stay solid at room temperature; palmitic acid, a common saturated fatty acid, makes up about 29% of butter's total fat.

A fatty-acid tail with even one carbon-carbon double bond gets a kink that stops it stacking neatly against its neighbors, which is why oils — triglycerides built from unsaturated fatty acids — stay liquid at room temperature while saturated fats like butter turn solid.

A steroid is built around a rigid skeleton of four fused rings of carbon atoms — three six-membered and one five-membered. Cholesterol, testosterone, and the anti-inflammatory drug cortisone all share this same core, differing only in the side groups attached to it.

A sterol is a steroid with a hydroxyl group attached to the third carbon of its ring system. Cholesterol is the animal version, wedging into cell membranes to tune their fluidity; ergosterol plays the identical structural role in fungal membranes.

Cholesterol and other fats cannot dissolve in blood plasma on their own, so the body wraps them in a shell of protein and phospholipid to make them water-soluble. LDL particles built this way carry cholesterol outward to tissues; HDL particles carry it back to the liver.

Adding a water molecule across ATP's outermost phosphate bond — hydrolysis — snaps it off as free phosphate and releases the energy that powers most cellular work, leaving adenosine diphosphate behind to be recharged back into ATP.

Heat breaks the weak hydrogen bonds and other interactions holding a protein's folded shape together, without touching the strong peptide bonds of its amino acid backbone. Egg white shows it in every kitchen: heat turns its dissolved, transparent proteins into an opaque, solid tangle.

A buffer pairs a weak acid with its conjugate base: adding extra acid shifts the equilibrium toward the base side and vice versa, so pH barely moves. The body's own carbonic-acid/bicarbonate buffer keeps blood between pH 7.35 and 7.45 — stray outside that band and acidosis or alkalosis follows.

Once Pasteur's experiments showed that life comes only from existing life, and bacteria were established as independently living organisms rather than products of decay, the idea that a specific germ causes a specific disease followed naturally — by the 1880s germ theory had displaced the older miasma theory.

Robert Koch and Friedrich Loeffler formalized germ theory into four testable criteria in 1884: the microbe must be present in every diseased case, isolated and grown in pure culture under the microscope, cause the same disease when reintroduced into a healthy host, and be recovered from it unchanged.

Pasteur's swan-neck-flask experiments helped establish germ theory, and the same principle — heating a liquid between 60 and 100°C to kill spoilage microbes without cooking it — became pasteurization, the process still used on milk today. In 1885 he also produced the first rabies vaccine.

Robert Koch identified Bacillus anthracis as the cause of anthrax in 1876 and Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the cause of tuberculosis in 1882, then formalized the criteria — his postulates — for proving any microbe causes any disease, winning the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground and polished tiny glass lenses by hand, mounting them in metal holders that magnified up to roughly 275 times. Examining a drop of rainwater in 1676, he became the first person to observe and describe bacteria and other single-celled 'animalcules.'

Starved of nutrients, a bacterium such as Bacillus or Clostridium converts itself into a dormant endospore, walling off a thick-coated core stabilized by calcium bound to dipicolinic acid — up to a fifth of the spore's dry weight — shedding everything else into a capsule resistant to boiling and decades of dormancy.

A prion is a misfolded version of a normal cellular protein; when it contacts a correctly folded copy of that same protein, it forces the copy into its own abnormal shape, and the reaction cascades — no genetic material is involved at any step. Stanley Prusiner proposed the idea in 1982 and won the 1997 Nobel Prize for it.

Helicobacter pylori survives stomach acid by producing massive amounts of the enzyme urease, which splits urea into ammonia and neutralizes the acid immediately around the cell. In 1984 Barry Marshall drank a culture of it to prove — against prevailing medical opinion — that this bacterium, not stress, causes most peptic ulcers.

A compound light microscope focuses light through two lens systems in series, objective and ocular, typically multiplying to about 1,000x total magnification. Beyond that, no extra detail resolves — visible light's own wavelength caps useful resolution at around 200 nanometers.

Firing a beam of electrons through a specimen thinner than 100 nanometers and focusing it magnetically resolves detail down to a single column of atoms, thousands of times finer than any light microscope. Max Knoll and Ernst Ruska built the first one in 1931; Ruska won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

A scanning electron microscope rasters a focused electron beam across a specimen's surface rather than through it, collecting the low-energy secondary electrons it knocks loose to build an image with striking depth of field. Because the beam needs a conductive surface, biological samples are first coated in a thin layer of metal, commonly gold.

Ordinary bright-field microscopy needs a stain to see transparent living cells, which kills them. Phase-contrast optics instead convert the tiny phase shifts light undergoes passing through a cell into visible differences in brightness, letting biologists watch a living cell divide in a drop of water. Frits Zernike invented it around 1930 and won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.

A fluorescence microscope illuminates a specimen with light of a specific wavelength, often ultraviolet, which fluorescent molecules absorb and re-emit at a longer wavelength. Only pre-labeled structures — tagged with a fluorescent antibody or dye — glow back, standing out against an otherwise dark field.

A confocal microscope scans a laser across the specimen and places a pinhole in front of the detector to block any light coming from outside the exact plane of focus. Capturing a stack of these optically clean slices at different depths lets software reconstruct a three-dimensional image.

Crystal violet dye enters every cell, then iodine binds it into a large complex too big to wash out easily. A thick peptidoglycan wall traps that complex through an alcohol rinse and stays purple; a thin one loses it and picks up the pink safranin counterstain instead. Hans Christian Gram devised the four-step method in 1884.

Mycobacterium's cell wall is packed with waxy mycolic acid that resists ordinary Gram staining. The acid-fast method drives red carbolfuchsin through that wax with heat, then rinses with acid-alcohol far harsher than a standard Gram decolorizer — the mycolic acid still holds on, staying red, while every other organism loses the dye.

Negative staining uses an acidic dye like India ink, repelled by the negatively charged surface of most cells, so it colors only the background. It's the standard way to see a bacterial capsule, which itself resists staining and shows up as a clear halo against the dark field.

An endospore's coat is tough enough to block ordinary dyes, so the Schaeffer-Fulton method steams malachite green directly onto the slide for five to seven minutes to force it through. Rinsing removes the green from every vegetative cell but not from spores, and a safranin counterstain then turns those cells pink.

Peptidoglycan is built from alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid sugar units, strung into long chains that short peptide bridges — three to five amino acids long — cross-link into a rigid mesh. It's this mesh, unique to bacteria and absent from archaea, that lets a cell wall resist the cytoplasm's own osmotic pressure.

Teichoic acids are glycerol-phosphate or ribitol-phosphate polymers found only in Gram-positive cell walls, bound either directly to peptidoglycan or anchored in the membrane below it. Their negative charge attracts cations like magnesium and calcium, giving the otherwise rigid wall some flexibility.

Lipopolysaccharide has three parts: a lipid A anchor embedded in the membrane, a short core sugar chain, and a long, highly variable O-antigen chain used to identify bacterial strains like E. coli O157:H7. Lipid A is the toxic part — released when Gram-negative bacteria die, it can trigger fever and, in large amounts, fatal septic shock.

The Gram-negative outer membrane is asymmetric: its inner leaflet is ordinary phospholipid, like any other membrane, but its outer leaflet is built from lipopolysaccharide instead — a structure found nowhere else in biology, and one reason Gram-negative bacteria resist antibiotics that work fine on Gram-positive ones.

In Gram-negative bacteria, the periplasm fills the space between the inner cytoplasmic membrane and the outer membrane — as much as 40% of total cell volume — holding enzymes for nutrient breakdown, protein folding, and transport that a Gram-positive cell has nowhere equivalent to keep.

Porins are beta-barrel proteins that puncture the outer membrane with a water-filled channel, letting small hydrophilic molecules — generally under about 600 daltons — diffuse through while blocking larger ones. Their size cutoff is one reason large antibiotic molecules struggle to reach Gram-negative bacteria at all.

Mycoplasma has no peptidoglycan wall whatsoever, only a plasma membrane reinforced with sterols borrowed from its host for enough mechanical strength to survive. Because penicillin works by blocking cell-wall construction, a bacterium with no wall to build is simply immune to it.

A coccus is a spherical bacterium, but the plane in which it divides sets its arrangement: Streptococcus divides along one axis into chains, Staphylococcus divides on random planes into grape-like clusters, and Neisseria divides into side-by-side pairs called diplococci.

Spirochetes are helically coiled bacteria whose flagella — called endoflagella — are wound inside the periplasmic space between the cell's two membranes, rather than trailing outside like other bacteria's. Rotating there, they flex the whole corkscrew-shaped cell through thick, viscous environments. Treponema pallidum and Borrelia are both spirochetes.

Pumping protons across a membrane builds up both a concentration difference and an electrical charge separation — the proton motive force. Letting those protons flow back through ATP synthase powers ATP production, but bacteria also tap the same gradient directly to run transport proteins and to spin the flagellum.

Unlike a eukaryotic flagellum's whipping microtubule core, a bacterial flagellum is a rigid protein propeller — filament, hook, and a basal-body motor — turned entirely by the proton motive force rather than ATP. The bare rotor can spin at up to 100,000 rpm, and with the filament attached it can still drive a cell forward at roughly 60 body lengths a second.

When a bacterium's flagella all rotate counterclockwise they bundle together and drive it in a straight run; switching to clockwise flings the bundle apart into a tumble that reorients it randomly. Sensing an increasing concentration of an attractant such as glucose over time simply suppresses tumbling, biasing the random walk toward the food.

A pilus is a hair-like protein filament anchored through the cell envelope, thinner and shorter than a flagellum, made of repeating pilin subunits. Fimbriae grip host cells or surfaces; type IV pili haul the cell forward by grappling-hook 'twitching motility'; and the sex pilus draws two cells together to form a mating bridge.

In bacterial conjugation, a sex pilus emerging from a donor cell grabs a recipient and draws it into direct contact, forming a mating bridge across which a single strand of plasmid DNA — often the F plasmid — passes. Both cells then synthesize a complementary strand, and the genes on that plasmid, including antibiotic resistance, are now shared.

Bacteriophage lambda, a classic example of specialized transduction, occasionally excises imprecisely from the host chromosome when it re-enters its lytic cycle, dragging a piece of adjacent bacterial DNA along with its own genome into the next capsid it builds — gene transfer with no direct cell-to-cell contact required.

The nucleoid is the region of a bacterial cell where its chromosome is packed, not enclosed by any membrane, unlike a eukaryotic nucleus. Supercoiling and DNA-binding proteins compact the DNA roughly a thousandfold, squeezing what would be a 1.5-millimeter loop of E. coli DNA into a cell only a few micrometers long.

A bacterial capsule is a distinct, well-organized layer of polysaccharide built up outside the cell wall. It shields the cell from phagocytosis — a Streptococcus pneumoniae strain stripped of its capsule is readily engulfed and killed by immune cells, while an encapsulated strain of the same species can cause invasive disease.

When carbon is plentiful but another nutrient like nitrogen or phosphorus runs short, bacteria such as Cupriavidus necator convert the surplus into internal granules of polyhydroxybutyrate as an energy reserve — the same storage strategy glycogen serves in other cells. The polymer is now manufactured commercially as a biodegradable, compostable plastic, including absorbable surgical sutures.

Peroxisomes break long fatty-acid chains down through beta-oxidation and use the enzyme catalase to convert the toxic hydrogen peroxide this generates into harmless water and oxygen. In the liver, these small organelles — just 0.1 to 1 micrometer across — also handle about a quarter of the ethanol a person drinks.

An aquaporin is a channel protein whose pore is shaped to let water molecules through in single file — around a billion per second per channel — while excluding ions and other solutes entirely, letting cells move water by osmosis far faster than plain diffusion across the bilayer would allow.
The epidermis is built from keratinocytes packed with water-retaining keratin protein — dead cells by the time they reach the surface, shed and fully replaced roughly every 48 days.

The dermis sits beneath the epidermis as dense connective tissue built from collagen and elastic fibers, laced with the blood vessels that nourish both layers and the nerve endings that give skin its sense of touch.
Skin really is these two layers doing different jobs: the epidermis as a keratin barrier on top, the dermis as collagen-rich structure and blood supply underneath.

The epidermis is the single outermost cell layer covering a plant's leaves, stems, flowers and roots — its cells carry almost no chloroplasts of their own, except the guard cells that ring each stoma.

Epidermal cell walls are built from cutin, a polymer of fatty acids, and the epidermis coats itself in a wax-infused cuticle made from the same material — the actual water-permeability barrier that keeps a leaf from drying out.

Meton of Athens, tracking the Moon over decades in the 5th century BC, found that 235 lunar months come to almost exactly 19 solar years, so the phases return to the same calendar dates. The Greek and Hebrew calendars still add a leap month in seven of those nineteen years to stay in step with the seasons.
Crystal violet gets trapped inside a Gram-positive cell's thick peptidoglycan wall; a Gram-negative cell's thin wall lets it wash out, so it takes up a pink counterstain instead.
Woese, Kandler, and Wheelis proposed splitting life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eucarya in 1990, based on differences in ribosomal RNA sequences rather than visible anatomy.
First published in 1923, Bergey's Manual remains the main reference microbiologists use to identify prokaryotes, arranging every characterized species by shared traits.
Linnaeus formalized naming every species with two italicized Latin words, genus then species, in Species Plantarum (1753) — a fix for common names that differ in every language.
Woese compared ribosomal RNA sequences across organisms and, with George Fox in 1977, showed that some 'bacteria' were different enough to form an entirely new domain: Archaea.
A phylogenetic tree's branches trace evolutionary divergence and its nodes mark a most recent common ancestor; the single branching tree diagram in On the Origin of Species is its only illustration.
Starved of carbon or nitrogen, some Gram-positive bacteria pack their DNA into a dehydrated, chemical-resistant endospore that can stay viable for decades before conditions improve.
Methanogen archaea living in a cow's rumen oxidize hydrogen gas, using carbon dioxide as their terminal electron acceptor and releasing methane — the only way they make ATP at all.
Extreme halophiles need at least 2 molar salt and often grow best in fully saturated brine around 36% salt, thriving in places like the Dead Sea and Great Salt Lake.
Hyperthermophiles thrive above 80°C in places like geysers and hydrothermal vents; the current growth-temperature record holder, Methanopyrus kandleri, keeps dividing at 122°C.
Rhizobium bacteria colonize legume root nodules, where their nitrogenase enzyme breaks apart atmospheric N2 into ammonia the plant can use — but the enzyme is destroyed almost instantly by oxygen.
Filamentous cyanobacteria like Anabaena build thick-walled heterocyst cells that drop photosystem II so no oxygen is made inside, letting oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase keep working.
Spirochetes move by rotating endoflagella hidden inside their own periplasm rather than trailing outside the cell, producing a corkscrew motion; the group includes syphilis and Lyme disease.
Mycoplasma species never build a peptidoglycan cell wall around their membrane, which is why beta-lactam antibiotics like penicillin — which target wall synthesis — have no effect on them.
Rickettsia bacteria can only grow inside a living host cell, so blood-feeding fleas, ticks, and lice inject them during a bite; flea-borne Rickettsia typhi causes murine typhus this way.
Chlamydia alternates between an infectious, spore-like elementary body and a growing reticulate body, never leaving a host cell — a life cycle unlike any other bacterium's.
Myxobacteria glide through soil and rotting organic matter in coordinated swarms nicknamed wolf packs, then starve into a fruiting body where vegetative cells become dormant, thick-walled myxospores.
Deinococcus radiodurans survives an acute dose of 5,000 grays of gamma radiation with almost no loss of viability — about a thousand times the roughly 5-gray dose that kills a human.
Thermus aquaticus was first isolated from a near-boiling Yellowstone spring in 1969; the heat-stable Taq polymerase later extracted from it made repeat-cycle PCR possible.
Bdellovibrio swims over 100 body-lengths per second to ram another Gram-negative bacterium, bores into its periplasm, and consumes it from within over the next few hours.
Clostridium species are anaerobic, endospore-forming, Gram-positive soil dwellers; different species cause tetanus, botulism, and the toxin-driven tissue death of gas gangrene.
Bacillus anthracis endospores can persist for years in soil, animal hides, or wool; inhaling, touching, or ingesting them is what causes anthrax.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis has a waxy, mycolic-acid cell wall that resists the Gram stain entirely; only an acid-fast stain reveals the bacterium as it colonizes the lungs.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is ubiquitous in water and soil, gives off a sweet grape-like odor and blue-green pigment, and is flagged by the WHO as a top antibiotic-resistance threat.

Legionella bacteria naturally live inside protozoa such as amoebae in water and soil; the genus was named after a 1976 pneumonia outbreak among attendees of an American Legion convention in Philadelphia.
Chytrids are the only fungi that make motile, flagellated zoospores. The chytrid Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, discovered in 1998, has driven amphibian species like the golden toad extinct.
Rhizopus stolonifer, black bread mold, grows bulbous sporangia packed with asexual spores, and forms a thick-walled, hardy zygospore when two mating strains fuse sexually.
Ascomycota, the sac fungi, is the largest fungal phylum at over 64,000 species; it includes Penicillium, the source of the first antibiotic, along with baker's yeast, morels, and truffles.
Apicomplexans are parasitic protists built around an apical complex — microtubules, secretory rhoptries, and polar rings — used to invade a host cell; Plasmodium causes malaria this way.
Oomycetes look fungus-like but have cellulose cell walls and diploid nuclei instead of chitin and haploid ones; Phytophthora infestans, an oomycete, caused the Irish Potato Famine.
Trypanosoma parasites move with a corkscrew motion and repeatedly swap their surface coat to dodge the immune system; Trypanosoma brucei, spread by tsetse flies, causes sleeping sickness.

Leishmania lives as a motile, flagellated promastigote in a sandfly's gut, then as a nonmotile amastigote inside human immune cells after a bite — causing leishmaniasis in about 1 million people a year.
Naegleria fowleri lives in warm freshwater, including hot springs; when inhaled up the nose it can travel to the brain and cause a primary amoebic meningoencephalitis fatal over 97% of the time.

Nematodes may be the most numerous animals on Earth by individual count, thriving in soil and compost; the roundworm C. elegans was the first animal with its whole genome sequenced and every neuron mapped.
A prion is a misfolded protein with no nucleic acid of its own; it forces normal copies of the same protein to misfold too, riddling brain tissue with holes in diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob.
During generalized transduction, a phage occasionally packages a random fragment of its old bacterial host's DNA instead of its own genome, then injects that DNA into the next cell it infects.
Every healthy cell carries proto-oncogenes, normal genes that promote controlled growth and division; a mutation or overexpression is all it takes to turn one into a cancer-driving oncogene.
Tumor suppressor genes like p53 halt the cell cycle before mitosis or trigger apoptosis in damaged cells; p53 alone is disabled in roughly 37% of cancers, removing that brake on runaway growth.
Mimivirus infects amoebae and was first mistaken for a Gram-positive bacterium under the microscope; its 1.18-million-base-pair genome, encoding nearly 1,000 proteins, rivals a small cell's.
In a plaque assay, phage-infected bacteria are grown under a soft-agar overlay; each clear plaque in the resulting lawn descends from one infectious phage particle, giving a precise viral titer.

A restriction enzyme cuts up incoming phage DNA at specific sequences, while a partner modification enzyme methylates those same sequences in the host's own DNA so it is never mistaken for an invader.

A single mutation, gene duplication, or chromosomal translocation can convert a proto-oncogene into an oncogene — an overactive growth gene, like the BCR-ABL fusion behind chronic myelogenous leukemia.
Over time, Earth's gravity locked the Moon's rotation to its orbit, so the same hemisphere always faces us — most of the far side stayed unseen until Luna 3's photographs in 1959.

Cytokines are small proteins that cells, especially white blood cells like macrophages and lymphocytes, secrete to signal one another — interleukins, interferons, chemokines and colony-stimulating factors are all members of the family.

Discovered in 1957 by Alick Isaacs and Jean Lindenmann, interferons are cytokines a virus-infected cell releases; they bind receptors on neighboring cells and prime them to resist infection before the virus ever arrives.
About 50 plasma proteins make up the complement system, circulating inactive in the blood until three separate pathways — classical, alternative, and lectin — trigger the same cascade of activation.

Dendritic cells process antigen and present it to T cells, bridging innate and adaptive immunity; Ralph Steinman coined the name in 1973, and one major type, the Langerhans cell, sits in the skin itself.

Toll-like receptors are anchored in the membranes of sentinel cells like dendritic cells, where they recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns; humans carry genes for ten working types, TLR1 through TLR10.

Natural killer cells are lymphocytes that, unlike B and T cells, carry no antigen-specific receptor; instead they recognize cells that have stopped displaying MHC class I and push those “missing-self” cells into apoptosis.

Mast cells are tissue-resident white blood cells packed with secretory granules of histamine and heparin, stationed in large numbers under mucous membranes where they stand ready to detect antigen and degranulate.

When a mast cell degranulates, the histamine it releases dilates local blood vessels and increases their permeability — the redness, heat, swelling, and pain that the Roman physician Celsus catalogued around the time of Christ.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines carried in the blood act on the hypothalamus, resetting the body's temperature set point upward; a reading above roughly 38.3°C crosses the line clinicians call a fever.

A viral surface protein is a textbook antigen — a molecule able to bind a specific antibody or T-cell receptor. The word itself is short for “antibody generator,” though not every antigen manages to provoke one.
An epitope is the specific patch of an antigen that an antibody, B cell, or T cell actually recognizes and binds — usually just a handful of amino acids out of an entire protein's surface.

B cells are the white blood cells programmed to make antibody; the name comes from the bursa of Fabricius, the organ in birds where they were first identified, even though human B cells mature in bone marrow instead.

T cells are white blood cells named for the thymus, where they mature; unlike a B cell, a T cell's receptor never binds free antigen — it only recognizes a fragment already presented on an MHC molecule.
Helper T cells carry the CD4 marker and, once activated, release cytokines that switch on B cells and macrophages — the same CD4 receptor HIV uses to target and infect this cell type.
Cytotoxic T cells carry the CD8 marker and recognize peptides on MHC class I; on finding an infected cell, they deliver perforin and granzymes directly into it, triggering apoptosis from the inside.

A plasma cell is a B cell that has fully differentiated into an antibody factory, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum and capable of secreting several thousand identical antibody molecules every second.

Memory B cells form after an infection or a vaccination and can circulate quietly in the blood for decades; when the same antigen reappears, they differentiate into plasma cells far faster than any naive B cell could.

MHC class I molecules sit on the surface of every nucleated cell, displaying peptide fragments cut from the cell's own cytoplasmic proteins — antigen, in effect — for inspection by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.

MHC class II molecules are made only by professional antigen-presenting cells — dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells — which use them to display antigen gathered from outside the cell to CD4+ helper T cells.

Frank Macfarlane Burnet's 1957 clonal selection theory holds that an antigen doesn't teach a B cell anything — it simply activates the one cell already carrying a matching receptor, which then multiplies.

IgM is normally assembled into a five-unit pentamer, the first antibody class made in a primary immune response; that bulk keeps it almost entirely confined to the bloodstream rather than the tissues.
IgG makes up roughly 75% of the antibody circulating in human serum, and it is the only immunoglobulin class equipped with a receptor that lets it cross the placenta to protect a developing fetus.

More IgA is produced in the body than every other antibody class put together, but nearly all of it is secreted straight into mucus, tears, saliva and breast milk rather than staying in the bloodstream.

IgE makes up less than 0.0001% of serum antibody — the scarcest class by far — because most of it is bound tightly by its Fc region to receptors on mast cells and basophils rather than circulating free.

The normal microbiota is the population of microorganisms that routinely colonizes a healthy body's surfaces, from skin to mucous membranes; researchers have catalogued roughly 10,000 species across all the body's habitats.

An adhesin is a bacterial surface protein that lets the cell attach to a host surface; in many pathogens it is a single minor protein riding at the very tip of a pilus, and it decides which tissue the bacterium can colonize.

An exotoxin is a protein bacteria secrete into their surroundings; some, like botulinum toxin, are among the most potent poisons known, yet heat or chemical treatment can inactivate them into safe toxoid vaccines.

Endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide built into the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria; lipid A, its toxic core, does little harm while anchored there but triggers a dangerous immune response once the cell lyses and releases it.

Virulence factors are the cellular structures and molecules — adhesins, capsules, destructive enzymes, and toxins like exotoxins and endotoxins among them — that let a pathogen actually colonize a host and cause disease.

Candida albicans is a routine part of the normal human microbiota, held in check by competition and a working immune system; let immunodeficiency shift that balance and the same organism turns into an infection.

Hypersensitivity is tissue damage caused by an otherwise protective immune response turned excessive; Philip Gell and Robin Coombs sorted every mechanism — antibody-driven and inflammatory alike — into four types in 1963.

An allergy is a hypersensitivity reaction in which IgE bound to mast cells mistakes an ordinarily harmless substance for a threat; just eight foods — milk, soy, egg, wheat, peanut, tree nut, fish and shellfish — cause 90% of food allergies.

Anaphylaxis is systemic allergy: antigen reaching the bloodstream triggers body-wide mast cell and basophil degranulation. Charles Richet coined the term in 1902, naming it the opposite of protection, and won a Nobel Prize for the work in 1913.

Type 1 diabetes is the textbook autoimmune disease: the body's own cytotoxic T cells destroy the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas, leaving the immune system's precision aimed squarely at self.
HIV targets and destroys CD4+ helper T cells; AIDS, the resulting immunodeficiency, is formally defined once a patient's CD4+ T cell count falls below 200 cells per microliter of blood.

Transplant rejection is driven mainly by T cells reading mismatched HLA — the human version of MHC class I and II — on a donor organ as foreign; matching those proteins, alongside lifelong immunosuppressants, is what keeps a graft alive.
Memory lymphocytes are the long-lived descendants of an earlier immune response; their presence, quietly waiting for years, is what a body's acquired immunity to a pathogen actually consists of.

RNA polymerase does not start transcribing just anywhere on DNA — in bacteria it is recruited, together with a sigma factor, to a promoter sequence sitting upstream of a gene, which marks where transcription begins.
A promoter is often located by an activator protein that binds its own site nearby and helps bring RNA polymerase and sigma factor to the promoter DNA to start transcription of the downstream gene.

A terminator is the nucleic-acid sequence marking the end of a gene or operon; in bacteria a GC-rich hairpin (rho-independent) or the Rho helicase riding the mRNA (rho-dependent) forces RNA polymerase to release the transcript.

An operator is a segment of DNA positioned between the promoter and the structural genes of an operon, to which a repressor protein binds and physically obstructs RNA polymerase from transcribing those genes.

A repressor is a DNA-binding protein that attaches to an operator and blocks RNA polymerase from reaching the promoter; the lac repressor loses its grip and detaches once the inducer allolactose changes its shape.

Sigma factor is the dissociable subunit that lets bacterial RNA polymerase recognize a specific promoter sequence; swapping in a different sigma factor (like E. coli's heat-stress sigma-32) redirects the polymerase to a different set of genes.

A membrane-embedded histidine kinase senses an environmental change and autophosphorylates, then transfers that phosphate to a response-regulator protein, which switches target genes on or off much like a transcription factor.

A short interfering or micro RNA is loaded into the RNA-induced silencing complex, which base-pairs with a matching messenger RNA and degrades it, silencing that gene after transcription — work honored with the 2006 Nobel Prize.

An open reading frame is the stretch of sequence between a start codon and a stop codon with no stop codon interrupting it; scanning sequenced DNA for long uninterrupted stretches like this is how software flags candidate genes.

Bioinformatics took off once protein sequences — starting with Frederick Sanger's sequencing of insulin in the early 1950s — became too numerous to compare by hand, driving tools like BLAST that now scan hundreds of billions of nucleotides.

Metagenomics extracts and sequences all the DNA directly from an environmental sample such as soil, sidestepping the need to culture each species — cultivation-based methods find less than 1% of the bacterial and archaeal species actually present.

When glucose is abundant, E. coli keeps cAMP low and its lac operon off regardless of lactose; only once glucose runs out does cAMP rise, bind the CAP protein, and let the cAMP-CAP complex switch the operon on.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae alters the surface protein it displays by recombining which pilin gene cassette sits in its expression locus, changing shape faster than point mutation alone so antibodies from the last variant miss the new one.

An invertible DNA segment carries its own promoter; flipping that segment's orientation reversibly turns a gene like E. coli's fimA pilin gene on or off, letting the population switch phenotype without any new mutation.

A mutation that knocks out a gene in a biosynthetic pathway leaves a microbe unable to make a compound, such as an amino acid, on its own — it becomes an auxotroph that can only grow once that compound is supplied in the medium.

UV photons are absorbed by two adjacent thymine bases on the same DNA strand and fuse them into a single covalent dimer within about a picosecond, distorting Watson-Crick base pairing and blocking replication and transcription past the site.

Photolyase, found in bacteria, fungi, plants and animals but not humans, absorbs visible blue/violet light and uses that energy to directly break the covalent bonds of a UV-induced thymine dimer, restoring the original DNA bases.

Nucleotide excision repair cuts out a short single-stranded DNA segment containing a lesion such as a thymine dimer; DNA polymerase then uses the intact complementary strand to resynthesize the missing sequence, and DNA ligase seals the remaining nick.

When DNA damage overwhelms normal repair, RecA triggers the bacterial SOS response, inducing error-prone polymerases like Pol V to synthesize past the damage without proofreading — survival at the cost of new mutations.

The Ames test exposes a histidine-requiring auxotrophic strain of Salmonella to a candidate chemical and counts colonies that mutate back to histidine-independence; a higher reversion rate signals a stronger mutagen.

Because most known carcinogens are also mutagens, Bruce Ames used a histidine-auxotroph Salmonella strain as a fast, cheap stand-in for animal testing, flagging likely carcinogens by their power to cause reversion mutations back to growth.

Barbara McClintock discovered transposons in the 1940s while studying maize: a mobile DNA segment jumped into a pigment gene and switched it off, producing the mottled, variegated kernel colors that first revealed 'jumping genes.'

Transposable elements, first described in maize, were later discovered in bacteria too, where a mobile DNA segment can excise itself from one site and insert into another, often inactivating whichever gene it lands in.
An F+ cell's pilus, built from genes on the F plasmid, attaches to an F- cell and draws the two together so a single strand of plasmid DNA can cross through a channel between them.
First described by Esther Lederberg, the F-plasmid (sex factor) is a specific plasmid of E. coli whose tra genes build a pilus and transfer the plasmid, converting an F- recipient into F+.

While assembling inside a host, a phage occasionally packages a stray piece of bacterial DNA into its protein coat instead of its own genome; that transducing particle then injects the bacterial DNA into the next cell it infects.

A prophage sitting in the chromosome can excise itself imprecisely, dragging along a nearby bacterial gene into the new phage particle — specialized transduction, limited to genes near the old integration site.
R factors can carry up to ten resistance genes on one plasmid, turning resistance to drugs like streptomycin into a package that spreads by conjugation between bacteria, even across species.
Resistance plasmids are frequently loaded with genes for toxic heavy metals like mercury alongside their antibiotic-resistance genes, riding together on the same mobile piece of DNA.

A block of chromosomal DNA larger than 10 kilobases with nucleotide composition unlike its surroundings marks a genomic island acquired by horizontal transfer; disease-gene-carrying ones are called pathogenicity islands.

Devised by Joshua and Esther Lederberg, the technique presses a velvet-covered stamp onto a master agar plate, then onto fresh plates in the same orientation, revealing which colonies fail on a selective medium without exposing the mutant itself.

A genomic DNA library is built by cutting an organism's chromosome into fragments with restriction enzymes, then cloning that pool into host cells so each cell carries, on average, just one fragment — together they preserve the whole genome.

Reverse transcriptase copies mature messenger RNA back into DNA. Because that mRNA has already been spliced, the resulting cDNA contains only exons and no introns, so bacteria — which cannot splice — can still read it and make a working eukaryotic protein.

Placing an antibiotic-resistance gene on a cloning vector makes it a selectable marker: on medium containing that antibiotic, only cells that actually took up and expressed the vector survive and form colonies.

Green fluorescent protein was first purified from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria and glows green when exposed to blue-to-ultraviolet light; fused to a gene of interest, it lets researchers see exactly when and where that gene switches on.

Colonies growing on an agar plate are pressed onto a membrane filter, the cells are lysed open in place, and their DNA is probed with a labeled sequence — autoradiography then reveals exactly which colonies in a library carry the gene of interest.
A short single strand of DNA, labeled radioactively or fluorescently, hybridizes only to its exact complementary sequence, so wherever the probe lights up marks the target sequence's location.

FISH detects a target sequence inside an intact cell on a slide; for identifying bacteria, probes are commonly aimed at the 16S rRNA region because each cell holds thousands of rRNA copies, giving a far stronger signal than a single-copy gene.

A DNA microarray is a solid surface spotted with as many as millions of microscopic DNA probes; fluorescently labeled cDNA from a sample hybridizes to matching spots, and the resulting signal pattern reveals which genes an organism was expressing all at once.

Plant genomes can be engineered by using Agrobacterium to deliver a gene of interest carried in T-DNA binary vectors derived from the Ti plasmid, integrating the foreign gene into the plant's own chromosome to produce a transgenic plant.

Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, makes crystal Cry proteins while forming spores that bind gut-cell receptors unique to certain insects and rupture them; the gene was engineered into cotton so the plant makes its own insect toxin, harmless to humans.

Golden Rice is rice genetically engineered to biosynthesize beta-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A, in the edible grain — developed from 1982 by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer to address vitamin A deficiency in regions where rice is the dietary staple.

Golden Rice grain was engineered to carry beta-carotene, vitamin A's biological precursor, directly in the part of the plant people actually eat, so a staple food itself can supply a nutrient its ordinary grain lacks.

The Ti plasmid occurs naturally in the soil bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens; its T-DNA region is transferred by conjugation into a wounded plant cell and integrates into the plant's chromosome, causing crown gall disease.

A brief high-voltage electric pulse destabilizes a cell's lipid bilayer, opening nanoscale pores that let plasmid DNA enter — a standard way to transform E. coli and other cells that are not naturally competent to take up DNA on their own.

S. pyogenes colonies on blood agar clear a wide zone of beta-hemolysis — complete destruction of the red blood cells around them — which is exactly how the species is told apart from the many other, gentler streptococci that share its usual haunts.

S. pyogenes typically colonizes the throat, and when the infection is there it's strep throat by name. It spreads on the respiratory droplets a cough or sneeze sends into someone else's nose and mouth.
The most common routes of entry for C. diphtheriae are the nose, tonsils, and throat — a club-shaped, palisade-forming rod that sets up in exactly the passage air takes on the way in.

Diphtheria's damage isn't the bacterium invading tissue directly — it barely does. Its toxin spreads through the blood instead, and that's what causes the life-threatening complications in the heart and kidneys, and the nerve damage that can lead to paralysis.
Streptococcus pneumoniae, cells paired up as a diplococcus, is the main cause of community-acquired pneumonia in children and the elderly — a species defined by the organ it targets.

It's the most common bacterial pneumonia found in adults. Pneumonia's own mechanism is mechanical: it fills the lung's alveoli, the tiny air sacs, with fluid, and that fluid is what hinders oxygen from crossing into the blood.

Bordetella pertussis is a tiny, encapsulated coccobacillus that attaches to the ciliated epithelial cells lining the respiratory tract using surface proteins built specifically for that job — cilia are the whole reason this species exists as a distinct thing.

Whooping cough is what Bordetella pertussis causes once it's down in the airway: paroxysms of coughing, and following a fit of coughing, a high-pitched whoop or gasp as the next breath forces its way back in.

An alveolar macrophage phagocytoses M. tuberculosis but can't kill or digest it, and the body's attempt to wall the infection off produces the caseating granulomas — tubercles — the bacterium is named for and characterized by in tissue.
Tuberculosis initially infects the lungs, though it can spread elsewhere from there. Most infections stay latent, showing no symptoms at all, for years before some ever progress to active disease.
Human rhinoviruses grow best at 33°C, noticeably colder than the body's 37°C core, which is exactly why they primarily infect nasal epithelial cells rather than settling deeper in the airway.
Rhinoviruses alone cause up to 40% of common colds, and there are more than 100 known types of just that one genus — which is why no single vaccine has ever covered the disease.

S. aureus is a usual member of the skin's own microbiota, frequently found there and in the nostrils — and it turns opportunist, becoming a common cause of skin infections, only once a barrier it normally respects gets breached.
Folliculitis is the infection and inflammation of one or more hair follicles, and most carbuncles, boils, and other cases of it are infected with exactly this species.

S. aureus's exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1, the protein holding the epidermis's granulosum and spinosum layers together — the layers sitting just beneath the fully keratinized stratum corneum — so the skin separates from itself like a scald.

Impetigo is a contagious bacterial infection of the superficial skin, and it's typically due to either Staphylococcus aureus or, as here, Streptococcus pyogenes — the same species behind strep throat, just at a different portal.
After a bite from an infected tick, R. rickettsii rides tick salivary secretions straight into the bloodstream, where it goes on to invade the endothelial cells lining the host's own blood vessels.
R. rickettsii's invasion of blood vessel walls is what produces the disease's signature rash — small spots of bleeding starting on the wrists and ankles, then working toward the trunk.

After spreading through the lymphatic system, measles virions circulate in the blood and go on to target epithelial cells in the skin and respiratory tract — the skin being exactly where the disease's signature rash comes from.
Humans are the only natural host of measles virus, and it is one of the most contagious diseases known — nine in ten non-immune people sharing a home with a case will catch it.
Rubella virus is found in the blood five to seven days after infection and spreads throughout the body from there — viremia is how this virus gets everywhere it goes, skin and placenta included.

Rubella's rash is typically pink or light red, not as bright as measles' — a lighter disease on the skin, but the virus that causes it can also cross the placenta and interrupt fetal cell development.

Dermatophytes are defined by their diet: they obtain nutrients from keratinized material, which is exactly why this whole group of fungi is restricted to skin, hair, and nails and nowhere else on the body.
Dermatophytosis, better known as ringworm or tinea, is a fungal infection of the skin producing a red, itchy, scaly, circular rash — tinea is Latin for worm, but no worm is ever actually involved.
Warts are caused by human papillomavirus, and the virus is believed to infect the host through the entrance of a skin wound — a break too small to notice is all the opening it needs.

C. tetani cannot grow in the presence of oxygen at all, and once its toxin is loose it is taken up specifically into the nervous system, blocking the inhibitory neurotransmitters that motor nerve endings need to let a contracted muscle relax.
Tetanus often begins with mild spasms in the jaw muscles — lockjaw — the direct result of the toxin blocking the nerve signal that would otherwise let those muscles relax between contractions.

C. perfringens has the shortest reported generation time of any known organism, 6.3 minutes — an anaerobic spore-former whose alpha toxin embeds in and disrupts cell membranes, muscle cells included, faster than almost anything else can react.
Gas gangrene is myonecrosis — outright muscle tissue death — with gas production alongside it, and progression to toxemia and shock is often very rapid once it starts.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa forms tenacious biofilms on catheters, contact lenses and cystic-fibrosis lungs alike, and thrives in soil, water and skin flora, essentially anywhere there is moisture.
P. aeruginosa is the most common cause of infections in burn injuries — a breach in the skin is the opening this ordinarily-environmental organism needs to become a serious opportunist.
Actinomyces israelii is a normal colonizer of the mouth — present in ordinary saliva-bathed tissue — harmless there as long as it stays confined to the small, anoxic pockets it usually occupies.

About 70% of actinomycosis cases trace to this one species, and it takes real tissue damage to get there — dental work, a broken jaw, or another trauma that lets a normal mouth commensal spread slowly through tissue it never usually reaches.
Bartonella henselae is transmitted to humans through scratches, bites, or flea vectors associated with domestic and feral cats — the cat itself is this species' whole reservoir.
Most cases of cat scratch disease trace to a scratch or bite from a kitten rather than an adult cat — the bacterium riding straight through the broken skin the scratch itself made.
Nearly all domestic and wild rats are colonized by Streptobacillus moniliformis, and most of them carry it without any symptoms of their own — a completely silent passenger until it changes hosts.
A bite or scratch from a colonized rat, gerbil, or mouse is enough to transmit it, and the resulting fever is a genuinely systemic one — high prostrating fevers, shivering, headache, and joint pain.

H. pylori's helical shape is built for progressing through the stomach's own viscous mucosa lining, and its urease neutralizes the acid immediately around it as it corkscrews through — a bacterium engineered for one specific, hostile organ.

H. pylori is one of the major causative factors of peptic ulcer disease — most people infected never experience symptoms, but a real fraction develop an actual ulcer in the stomach lining it's been living in.
Mumps virus is transmitted via contact with respiratory secretions and saliva specifically, and humans are its only natural host — a virus whose entire spread depends on exactly this fluid.
Humans are the only natural host of mumps virus, and once inside one, painful swelling of the parotid salivary glands in front of the ears is the single most common symptom the infection produces.
Hepatitis A virus is a non-enveloped RNA picornavirus that spreads primarily by the fecal-oral route, most often through water or food that's been contaminated with infected feces.
Once contracted, hepatitis A usually resolves completely and without any ongoing liver disease left behind — the acute illness runs its course and the liver recovers.
C. difficile is normally held in check by a healthy gut microbiome — if an antibiotic disrupts that microbiome, it can grow freely as its competitors die off around it.

Signs and symptoms of C. difficile infection range from mild diarrhea to severe, life-threatening inflammation of the colon, with a pseudomembrane of inflammatory cells and fibrin sometimes forming right there in the large intestine.
As few as ten norovirus virions are needed to infect a person, making it one of the most contagious viruses known — and humans are its host throughout.

Norovirus is usually spread by the fecal-oral route, through contaminated food or water, or through direct person-to-person contact — any one of which is enough given how few virions it takes to infect someone.
Cyclospora spreads fecal-orally through oocysts shed in feces, but those oocysts aren't infectious the moment they're passed — sporulation takes one to several weeks outdoors first.

Cyclospora cayetanensis causes cyclosporiasis, a diarrheal disease, once its slow-sporulating oocysts finally reach a human gut — the same weeks-long delay that makes direct person-to-person spread unlikely.
Cryptosporidium affects the distal small intestine, resulting in watery diarrhea, sometimes alongside an unexplained cough if it reaches the respiratory tract too.

Unlike the nontyphoidal Salmonella that causes ordinary food poisoning in a wide range of animal hosts, Salmonella Typhi is believed to infect and replicate only within humans — the same genus, a completely different epidemiology.
A short mucosa-lined muscular tube from bladder to skin surface — about 4 cm in women versus roughly 20 cm in men, leaving women far less distance for bacteria to travel before reaching the bladder.

The vaginal wall is a mucosa-lined muscular tube kept acidic, pH 3.8 to 4.5, by resident Lactobacillus that ferment glycogen stored in its epithelial cells into lactic acid, a barrier most pathogens can't tolerate.

Leptospira interrogans is a hook-ended spirochete that colonizes the kidneys of chronically infected rodents without making them sick, then is shed continuously in their urine to contaminate soil and water.

Gardnerella vaginalis is a small, gram-variable rod that can live in a healthy vagina without causing any problem — it becomes a marker of trouble only once Lactobacillus numbers fall and an anaerobic community grows in its place.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae attaches to non-ciliated mucosal cells using retractable pili, then reshuffles its pilin and Opa surface genes into over a hundred antigenic variants — one reason no vaccine against it exists.

Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that infects cells lining the urethra and cervix, alternating between a rigid infectious form and a dividing form that never leaves the host cell it invaded.

Treponema pallidum is a corkscrew-shaped spirochete driven by internal endoflagella, too thin to see by ordinary staining — it shows up only under dark-field microscopy, and still cannot be grown outside living tissue.

True to its genus name, Haemophilus ducreyi is 'blood-loving' — it grows only on blood-enriched chocolate agar under humid, CO2-rich conditions, and its cytolethal distending toxin helps disable nearby immune cells.

A compressed core of cotton, rayon, or a blend of the two. The most absorbent rayon blends of the late 1970s could soak up nearly 20 times their own weight in fluid, a property later tied to a rise in toxic shock syndrome.

Uropathogenic E. coli causes roughly 75% of uncomplicated bladder infections by climbing the urethra and attaching to bladder cells with fimbriae — a much shorter trip in women, whose urethra averages just 4 cm.

Left untreated, a bladder infection can climb the ureters into the kidneys, becoming pyelonephritis — a more serious infection that strikes 1 to 2 women per 1,000 each year and can leave lasting kidney scarring.

Leptospira interrogans enters through mucous membranes or broken skin after contact with water or soil fouled by infected animal urine, then spreads through the bloodstream to the kidneys, liver, and other organs.

Bacterial vaginosis develops when the vagina's normal Lactobacillus-dominated community collapses and anaerobic species, commonly signaled by Gardnerella vaginalis, overgrow in its place, raising the pH above 4.5 and producing a thin, fishy-smelling discharge.

Candida albicans already lives in the vagina of many women without causing symptoms. When something disrupts the normal microbiota — oral antibiotics trigger it in about 30% of courses — the yeast overgrows, causing itching and a thick, white discharge.

Certain Staphylococcus aureus strains growing in a blood-soaked, high-absorbency tampon release TSST-1, a superantigen that floods the bloodstream and triggers a massive cytokine release, crashing blood pressure within days.

Gonorrhea infects roughly 88 million people worldwide each year. About half of infected women have no symptoms at all, letting the infection climb silently into the fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease or infertility.

Chlamydial infection is the most frequently reported bacterial STI in the US. About 70% of infected women and half of infected men have no symptoms, so it often goes untreated long enough to scar the fallopian tubes and cause infertility.

Syphilis begins with a painless ulcer at the site of entry, then can progress through a systemic rash, a silent latent phase lasting years, and — in a minority of untreated cases — late damage to the heart, brain, and blood vessels.

Chancroid produces one or more painful, soft genital ulcers, unlike the painless hard chancre of syphilis, and often swells the lymph nodes in the groin into tender, pus-filled buboes that can rupture.

Formaldehyde crosslinks an exotoxin's structure, destroying its toxicity while leaving enough shape intact for the immune system to recognize — this is exactly how tetanus and diphtheria vaccines are made.

Clostridium tetani's toxin, tetanospasmin, blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine at synapses, so motor neurons fire unchecked and muscles can't relax, producing the rigid spasms of lockjaw.

Botulinum toxin from Clostridium botulinum blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, the opposite target from tetanus toxin — instead of rigid spasms, this produces flaccid, descending paralysis.
Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae cause most bacterial meningitis; even treated, overall mortality is roughly one in six, and higher still in newborns.
Enteroviruses and other viruses inflame the same meninges, but viral meningitis follows a far more benign course than the bacterial kind and is rarely fatal.

When Neisseria meningitidis enters the bloodstream it can release endotoxin at up to 1,000 times normal levels, hemorrhaging small vessels into the telltale petechial rash; untreated, case-fatality reaches roughly 80%.

About three-quarters of poliovirus infections cause no symptoms at all; only rarely does the virus reach and destroy motor neurons in the spinal cord, producing the disease's characteristic asymmetric, flaccid paralysis.

Arbovirus is short for arthropod-borne virus — mosquitoes, ticks, and other blood-feeding arthropods pick it up from a reservoir host whose blood carries enough virus to infect the next bite, then pass it to the next host.

West Nile virus cycles mainly between mosquitoes and birds, which is why it spread across North America within a few years of its 1999 arrival; humans rarely carry enough virus in their blood to pass it on, making them a dead-end host.

Epidemic viral encephalitis in the US is caused mainly by arboviruses like La Crosse, eastern equine, and West Nile virus — mosquito-borne infections that occasionally spread from the blood into the brain itself.

Herpes simplex virus, latent for years in a facial nerve ganglion, can reactivate and travel by the nerve into the brain instead of just the skin — herpes encephalitis is still fatal in about a third of cases even when treated.

Rabies virus rides retrograde transport backward up motor-neuron axons to reach the brain, where it triggers acute encephalitis; once that stage begins and symptoms appear, treatment is almost never effective and mortality exceeds 99%.
Y. pestis multiplies in a flea's gut until a clot of bacteria blocks its foregut; the starving flea bites repeatedly, regurgitating the blockage — and the bacteria — into the wound.
A flea bite delivers Y. pestis into the lymphatic system; it multiplies in the nearest lymph node until acute inflammation swells it into the hard, tender bubo that gives bubonic plague its name.
Rabbits and other small mammals are reservoir hosts for F. tularensis, and handling an infected one is a classic route of infection — the source of the name 'rabbit fever.'
In the most common form, a skin ulcer marks where the bacteria got in, and the regional lymph node draining that site swells and becomes tender within days.
Brucella melitensis, the species most often behind human illness, keeps mainly to goats and sheep as its natural host.
Brucella abortus is the cattle-adapted species of the genus, the counterpart to B. melitensis in goats and B. suis in pigs.
Undulant fever, its old name, for how the fever recurs in waves over weeks; most human cases trace to unpasteurized milk or cheese, or direct contact with an infected animal.

Sepsis is the body's own dysregulated response to a bloodstream infection, not the microbe's damage directly — Gram-negative bacteria releasing endotoxin is a well-studied trigger of the resulting cytokine storm.
Left uncontrolled, sepsis can progress to blood pressure so low it doesn't recover with fluids alone — septic shock, which carries a mortality rate near 40%.
Bacteria seed a thin clot that forms on a damaged heart valve and build a biofilm there — since a heart valve has no blood supply of its own, the immune system has no direct way to reach them.

Lymph nodes are strung along the vessels that drain lymph fluid from tissue and skin, and act as filters — B cells fill the outer cortex, T cells and dendritic cells the paracortex, macrophages the sinuses.
Tucked behind the stomach in the upper left abdomen, the spleen filters blood the way lymph nodes filter lymph — its red pulp clears out worn and damaged red blood cells.
Every lymphocyte — B cell, T cell, or NK cell — descends from a common progenitor born of hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow.
EBV is an enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus whose defining trick is B lymphocytes: it infects them, then persists there for life once the initial infection clears.
Nicknamed 'kissing disease' because EBV spreads mainly through saliva — weeks of fever, sore throat and swollen lymph nodes follow, with fatigue that can linger for months.
Outside cities, yellow fever virus keeps a sylvatic cycle running between forest mosquitoes and monkeys — mostly without making the monkeys sick — long before any human is bitten.
Named for the jaundice liver damage causes in severe cases — among patients who develop jaundice, the fatality rate is 20% to 50%.
Untreated, HIV floods the bloodstream in the first weeks after infection, producing a flu-like illness in most people 2 to 4 weeks after exposure — the acute retroviral syndrome.
After acute symptoms subside, HIV keeps replicating at a stable 'viral set point' for years — an asymptomatic period that, without treatment, lasts three to over twenty years, averaging about eight.
Years of continuous HIV replication gradually exhausts the CD4+ T cell supply; AIDS is diagnosed once the count falls below 200 cells per microliter or a defining opportunistic disease appears.
A single needlestick exposure to HIV-infected blood infects a health care worker about 0.3% of the time, well below the roughly 10% seroconversion risk from a hepatitis B needlestick.
Without antiretroviral treatment, HIV passes from mother to child around birth in about 20% of cases, rising to 35% with breastfeeding; treatment cuts that risk below 5%.
Human herpesvirus 8 packages a large double-stranded DNA genome and was first identified in 1994 by analyzing DNA extracted directly from Kaposi's sarcoma tumor tissue.

HHV-8 infects the endothelial cells lining blood and lymphatic vessels; up to 50% of AIDS patients developed Kaposi's sarcoma during the early epidemic, before antiretroviral therapy could suppress it.
Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus so adapted to mammalian lung tissue that every life stage occurs there, and it has never been successfully grown outside a host.
Pneumocystis colonizes most people harmlessly, but once CD4+ counts fall below 200 cells per microliter it can cause a severe pneumonia that was once the most common AIDS-defining illness in the US.
Severe immunodeficiency lets latent Toxoplasma cysts reactivate in brain tissue, causing encephalitis; treatment is recommended once CD4+ counts drop below 200 cells per microliter.
Cytomegalovirus carries roughly 235,000 base pairs of double-stranded DNA in an icosahedral capsid inside a lipid envelope — longer than the genome of any other human herpesvirus.
Reactivated cytomegalovirus infects the retina in 15% to 40% of people with AIDS, historically one of the leading causes of AIDS-related blindness before antiviral treatment.
Chronic, uncontrolled HIV infection causes cachexia — muscle and fat loss without another explanation — which presented as the first sign of AIDS in about a fifth of early cases.

Zidovudine mimics thymidine closely enough that reverse transcriptase incorporates it into the growing DNA chain, but it lacks the 3' hydroxyl group needed to add the next nucleotide, so the chain stops.

Combining antiretrovirals from different drug classes creates multiple simultaneous obstacles to replication, suppressing HIV to a low viral set point for years — though it never clears the latent provirus, so it is not a cure.

Big Bang nucleosynthesis produced the universe's first elements within minutes of its beginning — overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, the same two that still make up nearly all its ordinary matter today.

The Big Bang describes how the universe expanded from that early hot, dense state into everything it now is: all space, time, matter and energy, roughly 93 billion light-years across at its observable edge.

Bacteria and fungi are two of the domains microorganism actually spans — any organism of microscopic size, found in nearly every one of the three domains of life. (Viruses are generally excluded: not considered alive.)

Most microbes never harm a host at all. A pathogen is specifically one equipped with virulence factors — the traits that let it actually cause disease, which is exactly why the word exists separately from microbe.
Infection is the pathogen actually establishing itself and multiplying in a host -- the event itself, which can happen with or without producing any visible symptom.
The same infection can stay silent (asymptomatic carriage) or progress into disease -- the actual harm and symptoms an infection produces once it overwhelms the host's defenses.
The English word 'geyser' comes from Geysir in Iceland's Haukadalur, meaning 'gusher' in Icelandic; the island is volcanically active because it straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Norway's coast is cut by roughly 1,200 fjords — U-shaped valleys gouged by glaciers and then drowned by the sea — which stretch its coastline from about 2,500 km to about 29,000 km.
Malta is a limestone archipelago in the central Mediterranean about 80 km south of Italy, and that soft stone was quarried for its megalithic temples around 3500 BC.
Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean and was antiquity's great copper source — the Latin 'aes Cyprium', metal of Cyprus, was shortened to cuprum.
Georgia borders Türkiye to the south and holds the earliest known winemaking sites in the world, dating to around 6000 BCE.
The Kingdom of Kush ruled the Nile valley of what is now Sudan, leaving the pyramids of Meroë, and the Blue and White Niles converge at Sudan's capital Khartoum.
Rwanda's highest ground is the Virunga volcanic chain on its north-western border with the DR Congo, crowned by Mount Karisimbi at 4,507 m.
Zambia borders the DR Congo to the north, and its population and mining industry are concentrated in the Copperbelt Province along that border.
The Kalahari covers up to 70% of Botswana, and the Okavango, one of the largest inland deltas in the world, spreads into those desert sands instead of reaching the sea.
The Namib, the oldest desert in the world, runs the length of Namibia's Atlantic shore as the Skeleton Coast, making it the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa.
Angola's oil-producing province of Cabinda is an exclave cut off from the rest of the country by DR Congo territory.
Mauritius is a volcanic island in the Indian Ocean that became the British Empire's main sugar-producing colony before independence in 1968.
Seychelles is unusual in combining 42 granitic islands, including Mahé and Praslin, with far-flung coral atolls such as Aldabra.
Cabo Verde is an archipelago of ten volcanic islands in the eastern Atlantic, uninhabited until Portuguese and Genoese navigators settled it from the 1460s.
The equator crosses the country's islet of Ilhéu das Rolas, and by 1905 São Tomé was the world's largest producer of cocoa, still its most important crop.
Gabon straddles the equator in Central Africa and is 89.3% forested, with about 10% of its territory set aside in thirteen national parks.
The Republic of the Congo borders Gabon to the west and lies on the western side of the Congo River, its capital Brazzaville facing Kinshasa across the water.
Mali takes its name from the medieval Mali Empire that grew rich on trans-Saharan trade, and its northern borders reach deep into the Sahara.
The Guinea Highlands hold the sources of the Niger, Gambia and Senegal rivers, and Guinea is the world's second-largest producer of bauxite.
The ruins of Carthage, the Mediterranean power Rome destroyed in 146 BC, stand beside modern Tunis on Tunisia's northeastern Mediterranean coast.
Barbuda is a flat island built almost entirely of coral limestone, while Antigua's English Harbour held the Royal Navy's Nelson's Dockyard until Britain granted independence in 1981.
The Bahamian archipelago of some 700 islands and 2,500 cays supports a queen conch fishery that employs over 9,000 Bahamian fishers.
Belize holds Maya cities of the Mesoamerican lowlands on land and the Belize Barrier Reef, the second-longest barrier reef in the world, offshore.
The maple leaf on Canada's flag names the tree that gives the country more than 75 percent of the world's maple syrup, most of it from Quebec.
Costa Rica occupies a narrow stretch of the Central American isthmus, with the Caribbean Sea on its northeast coast and the Pacific Ocean on its southwest.
Sugarcane was central to Cuba's development and sugar remains one of its principal exports alongside tobacco and coffee.
Columbus sighted the island on Sunday 3 November 1493 and named it for dies Dominica; it is the youngest island of the Lesser Antilles volcanic arc and still volcanically active.
El Salvador is called the Land of Volcanoes for its more than twenty volcanic cones, among them Santa Ana at 2,365 m and the still-active San Miguel and Izalco.
Nutmeg introduced to Grenada in 1843 became a mainstay of its economy and earned the island the name Island of Spice.
Guatemala hosted the core of the Maya civilization, with cities such as Tikal, across highlands defined by its chain of volcanoes.
Rainforest covers over 80 percent of Guyana and contains Kaieteur Falls, one of the world's most powerful waterfalls.
Honduras holds the Maya city of Copán, and its banana trade was so dominated by fruit companies that O. Henry coined 'banana republic' about it in 1904.
Bauxite discovered in the 1940s reshaped Jamaica's economy; by 1998 it produced 10.4 percent of world bauxite, and bauxite and alumina made 55.2 percent of exports in 1999.
Mexico takes its name from Mēxihko, the Nahuatl term for the Aztec heartland, and Mexico City stands on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan.
Nicaragua is called the land of lakes and volcanoes, and Lake Nicaragua holds Ometepe, an island formed where the volcanoes Concepción and Maderas join at a low isthmus.
Panama occupies the isthmus that joined North and South America about three million years ago, cut through by the 83 km Panama Canal completed in 1914.
Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans covered the volcanic slopes of Saint Kitts until the state-owned sugar company was closed in 2005.
England and France fought fourteen times for control of Saint Lucia, whose position was so contested it was nicknamed the Helen of the West.

William Bligh's 1791 Providence expedition carried seedless breadfruit from Tahiti to Saint Vincent, where it took hold on the volcanic slopes below La Soufriere, still an active volcano — it erupted explosively in April 2021.
Suriname was Dutch until independence on 25 November 1975, and at 90.2 percent forest cover it is the most forested nation in the world.
The epidermis is dead stratified squamous keratinized epithelium — the skin's outer layer is epithelial tissue, and like all epithelium it has no blood vessels of its own.
The airways are lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium: about 200 cilia per cell beating 10 to 20 times a second to sweep mucus up toward the pharynx.
Tendon is dense connective tissue — collagen fibres laid down one way by fibroblasts in the ground substance they secrete.
Cartilage is 'special' connective tissue: sparse cells in a collagen-rich matrix, the same pattern that also covers bone and the fluid types, blood and lymph.
Muscle tissue is myocytes doing all the work — a skeletal muscle fibre is a single multinucleate cell that can run from a few millimetres to several inches long.
Actin and myosin are the contractile proteins that define muscle tissue; troponin and tropomyosin decide when the two are allowed to interact.
Nervous tissue is exactly two cell classes — neurons that carry impulses and neuroglia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells) that feed and support them.
Two tissue types in one wall is what makes an organ: the intestine lines itself with epithelium and wraps that lining in smooth muscle.
The nervous system is one of the eleven organ systems in the human body — the tier above the organ, where several organs share a single function.
Glycolysis is catabolism's opening move, splitting glucose to pyruvate and banking the energy as ATP — the currency every anabolic reaction then spends.
Metabolism is enzyme-catalysed chains of reactions, and the mitochondrion runs the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation that pay for the rest of them.
Salivary amylase breaks down about 30% of dietary starch before you swallow, and gastric juice — roughly 0.5% hydrochloric acid, pH 1 to 3 — then takes over on protein.
Digestion runs on two tracks at once: mechanical churning and peristaltic waves moving food along, while enzymes cut it into water-soluble pieces the blood can absorb.
Heart, blood vessels and blood are the three parts of the circulatory system; William Harvey published the proof in 1628 that blood goes round and round rather than being used up.
Inhalation at rest is simply the diaphragm contracting and dropping, pulling air down to 300 million alveoli and about 145 m² of gas-exchange surface.
Mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus — about nine metres of tract, the last stretch taking 30 to 40 hours over what was not absorbed.
The pancreas is an accessory digestive organ: no food passes through it, it just pipes enzymes into the small intestine downstream of the stomach.
Around 270 bones at birth fuse to about 206 in an adult, split 80 axial to 126 appendicular — support, movement, protection and blood production in one system.
The skeleton doubles as a mineral bank, storing the body's calcium and iron and releasing them on demand.
Skeletal muscles pull on bone through tendons; more than 600 of them make up roughly 40% of body mass and hold posture as well as move it.
The anterior pituitary's tropic hormones — TSH, ACTH, growth hormone — ride the bloodstream to command other glands, TSH being the order that brings thyroxine out of the thyroid.
The pancreas doubles as an endocrine organ, releasing insulin directly into the circulation rather than down a duct.
Kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra: 180 litres of filtrate a day with 99% reabsorbed, which is how blood volume, electrolytes and pH are held steady.
Roughly 800 lymph nodes plus spleen, thymus and tonsils on a network with no pump — muscle contraction alone returns about 3 litres of leaked fluid to the blood each day.
Leukocytes are the immune system's workforce: phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils engulf whatever gets in, while lymphocytes mount the response tailored to that pathogen.
Adaptive immunity's two halves — B cells raise antibodies that tag a pathogen for complement or phagocytes, T cells handle infected cells, and both leave long-lived memory cells behind.
The only organ system an individual can survive without: testicles make sperm, ovaries make ova, and every other part of the tract exists to bring the two together.
The female tract runs ovary to fallopian tube to uterus to cervix to vagina — the ovum comes down it and the sperm go up, meeting in the tube.
Skin, hair, nails, scales and claws are one system — in humans 1.5 to 2 m² of covering weighing 12 to 15% of the body.
The kidney is where a mammal does its osmoregulation — about 180 litres of filtrate a day, with fluid volume, osmolality, acid-base balance and electrolyte levels all set by how much is reabsorbed.
The liver converts ammonia into urea through the urea cycle, and the urea is carried away in the blood to be excreted in the urine.
About 80% of the body's daily cholesterol production happens in the liver and intestines, and the liver oxidises cholesterol into bile acids — the same organ that banks roughly 100 g of glycogen.
The liver makes 400 to 800 ml of bile a day; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it, then releases it when fatty food arrives, where bile salts wrap triglyceride droplets into micelles.
Peristaltic contractions of the oesophageal muscle push a swallow down to the stomach, past a lower sphincter that then closes to prevent reflux of acidic stomach contents.
The airway down to the lungs is held permanently open by 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, each 4 mm high.
The trachea divides at the carina into a main bronchus for each lung — three secondary bronchi for the right lung's three lobes, two for the left's two.

An artery's middle layer, the tunica media, packs smooth muscle with elastic tissue and collagen — far thicker than a vein's, which is how it carries blood away from the heart against the circulatory system's highest pressure.
Blood comes back at low pressure, so contracting skeletal muscle presses on the intramuscular veins to drive it toward the heart while one-way valves prevent backflow.

Capillaries convey blood from the smallest arteries, the arterioles, to the smallest veins, the venules — and that 5 to 10 micrometre gap is where water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, glucose and urea are exchanged.
The branching airway ends in about 480 million alveoli, each wrapped in capillaries across a membrane between 0.2 and 0.6 micrometres thick, giving 70 to 80 square metres of gas exchange.
The blastocyst implants in the endometrium lining the uterus, whose middle layer — the myometrium — is smooth muscle that grows to several times its size and contracts in labour.
The ovary both releases the ovum, one per menstrual cycle, and secretes oestrogen, androgen, inhibin and progestogen directly into the bloodstream.
Leydig cells sit next to the sperm-making seminiferous tubules and shuttle cholesterol into their mitochondria, where it becomes pregnenolone and eventually testosterone.
Fetal tissue builds the placenta against the uterine wall, exchanging nutrients and oxygen with no intermingling of fetal and maternal blood, and it is expelled in the third stage of labour.
Twenty-two bones make up the skull, and the mandible is the only freely-jointed one, articulating with the temporal bones at the paired temporomandibular joints.

Joints are classed by what connects the bones — dense collagen in a fibrous joint, cartilage in a cartilaginous one, and in a synovial joint no direct connection at all, just a capsule and a fluid-filled cavity.
The head of the femur sits in the acetabulum of the pelvis as the hip joint and its lower end meets tibia and patella at the knee; neck and shaft meet at roughly 130 degrees.
Twelve pairs of ribs cage the heart, lungs and great vessels, and evert on inhalation so the chest circumference expands by 3 to 5 cm.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary drives the follicle cells that concentrate iodide out of the bloodstream and build it into the colloid's thyroglobulin.
