One gland, two tissues: the outer cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone, while the medulla inside it releases roughly 80% adrenaline and 20% noradrenaline.
Glucagon from the pancreatic alpha cells drives glycogenolysis in the liver, breaking stored glycogen back down into circulating glucose.
Pituitary luteinizing hormone tells the testes' Leydig cells — the source of over 95% of a man's testosterone — to build it out of cholesterol.
One enzyme makes every estrogen: aromatase strips the C19 methyl group off testosterone and aromatizes the A ring, turning it into estradiol.
The follicle left behind once the ovum is released becomes the corpus luteum, which converts cholesterol through pregnenolone into about 30 mg of progesterone a day.
Somatotropic cells in the anterior pituitary release a 191-amino-acid chain that divides growth-plate cartilage directly, and grows bone again indirectly by making the liver secrete IGF-1.
Vitamin K — the K is for Koagulation — carboxylates prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X into Gla residues that can chelate calcium, and without it blood will not clot.
Calcium is factor IV: it bridges factors IXa and Xa onto phospholipid surfaces through their gamma-carboxy residues, and the cascade stalls without it.
The clot is only the first of four phases — fibroblasts arrive two to five days in and lay down type III collagen, later swapped for type I during remodeling.
The preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus is the body's thermostat, correcting in both directions: sweating and vasodilation above the setpoint, shivering and brown fat below it.
Rising estrogen thickens the endometrium in the proliferative half; progesterone from the corpus luteum holds it for about 14 days, and when that gland fails the lining sheds.
The hypothalamus resumes pulses of GnRH, the pituitary answers with LH and FSH, and the gonads answer with testosterone or estradiol.
Growth hormone drives the growth-plate spurt and estrogen ends it — rising estrogen in both sexes kills off the plate's chondrocytes until cartilage is replaced by bone.
Bile is cholesterol turned into detergent plus bilirubin, the pigment macrophages make from the heme of destroyed red blood cells.
Deep in the epithalamus between the two halves of the thalamus sits the gland that N-acetylates serotonin and then methylates it into melatonin.
Melanopsin ganglion cells run straight from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, resetting a clock that otherwise free-runs at about 24 hours 11 minutes.
Two enzymes do it in the dark — AANAT acetylates serotonin, ASMT methylates the result — and the pineal gland releases about 30 micrograms a day, 80% of it at night.
The ventral part of the striatum is where the ventral tegmental area's mesolimbic dopamine axons terminate, on the medium spiny neurons that are 95% of the cells there.
Struck, the fork's two tines swing apart and together and drive pressure pulses into the air — nearly a pure sine wave at the fundamental, most often A440.
Pitch lives in the listener, not the air — the ear ordering sounds high to low on a frequency-related scale, which is why it counts as a psychoacoustic attribute rather than a physical one.
Halve a vibrating string and it sounds at twice the frequency, a pitch exactly one octave higher — the 2:1 ratio demonstrated on the monochord since antiquity.
A scale is the series of notes running from one pitch up to its octave; the keyboard divides each octave into twelve equal semitones, of which a major scale selects seven.
A chord is two or more notes sounding together, most often a triad of root, third and fifth built on a scale degree — a guitar lets one hand stop all three at once.
Rhythm is sound placed in time, accented beats against unaccented ones — and an unpitched drum stroke carries almost no information except when it lands.
Tempo sets how fast the beats go by, counted in beats per minute — the same unit as a pulse, and a resting adult heart's 60–100 bpm sits inside the Andante band of 56–108.
In its most literal sense a melody is a combination of pitch and rhythm — a linear succession of tones the listener perceives as one entity.
Harmony is the vertical dimension to melody's horizontal one — pitches combined at once and chords moving in progression, the basis of Western tonal practice since about 1600.
Music is the arrangement of sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody and rhythm — melody running in sequence, harmony stacked beneath it.
Put music on a page and you get notation: neumes written above chant text in 9th-century monasteries, which Guido of Arezzo ruled onto a staff around 1000.

A full orchestra runs seventy to over a hundred players across four sections; the violins head the strings and the timpani head the percussion, which in Baroque scoring were called for whenever trumpets were.
A symphony is an extended orchestral work notated in a score holding every instrument's part, from which each player reads only their own line.

Monteverdi's L'Orfeo, premiered at Mantua on 24 February 1607, sets exactly this myth — the descent to Hades and the failed attempt to lead Eurydice back — and is the earliest opera still regularly performed.
Jazz came out of New Orleans at the turn of the 20th century on swung rhythm and improvisation; the saxophone entered its instrumentation around 1912.
The lungs are the pump: their airflow sets the vocal folds in the larynx vibrating into audible pulses, which the tongue, palate and lips then filter into speech.
The cello's top three strings, G2–D3–A3, sit exactly one octave below the violin's lowest three, G3–D4–A4, with a low C2 added underneath.
Both are strung frames, but a lyre's strings stretch from a yoke across a bridge in the plane of the sound table, while a harp's rise almost perpendicular out of the soundboard.

Human language is a structured system of grammar and vocabulary, the primary means by which humans convey meaning -- spoken, signed, or written down. The spoken form is shaped by the vocal tract, tongue included.
A phoneme is defined by perception: a set of similar speech sounds that a language's own speakers hear as a single basic sound. Those are the contrasts that let one word be told from another.
Phonemes are the smallest units that distinguish one word from another; strung together they build the words that carry meaning.
Grammar is the system of rules governing how a natural language's words combine into phrases and clauses, as its speakers and writers actually use them.

Cuneiform is one of the earliest conventional writing systems: a fixed set of symbols, plus the rules they encode, for representing a particular spoken language. Such systems first appear in the late 4th millennium BC.

Alphabetic writing starts in Egypt: the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai and Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt repurposed Egyptian hieroglyphs as signs for single sounds, and later alphabets descend from them.
A writing system is the abstract set of symbols and rules; a script is the concrete character set put on the page. They are coded separately because one script can serve many different languages.

In a dialect continuum neighbouring varieties stay mutually intelligible while distant ones do not, so the line is usually drawn politically: one variety gets codified as a state's standard language and serves as the authority for that part of the chain.
Sogdian, the Eastern Iranian language of Samarkand and Bukhara, became the most important lingua franca of Mongolia, China and Inner Asia, carried along the trade routes by Sogdian merchants.

Every family descends from a single proto-language, and the split typically happens through geographical separation: speakers move apart, their regional dialects change differently, and daughter languages result.
When two groups with no language in common have to deal with each other -- typically to trade -- they improvise a pidgin, grammatically simplified, its words pulled from both sides.

A pidgin becomes a creole once children acquire it as their first language. That is the dividing line: creoles have native speakers, systematized grammar and stable vocabularies; pidgins have none of the three.
Sign languages convey meaning through manual articulation combined with non-manual markers rather than spoken words -- a different modality for language, not a gestured version of speech.
Where languages meet, words cross. Indonesian's vocabulary has taken words from Javanese, Sundanese, Minangkabau and Balinese, and also from Arabic, Dutch, Hokkien, Portuguese, Sanskrit and English.

Literacy -- the ability to read and write -- has spread in step with the invention of writing systems and the expansion of education, and rates have risen substantially worldwide since the mid-twentieth century.

Esperanto is a constructed auxiliary language: Zamenhof designed its vocabulary and grammar deliberately and published them in 1887 as 'the International Language', intended as a neutral second language for international communication.

The Steppe theory -- the most widely accepted answer to the Proto-Indo-European homeland question -- places the proto-language on the steppe, from which the Indo-European migrations carried its daughters across Europe, Iran and northern India.

Beyond the Sinitic giants, most Sino-Tibetan languages are spoken by small communities in the Himalayas, the Southeast Asian Massif and the eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, and are poorly documented as a result.
Afroasiatic's roughly 400 languages are spoken across West Asia, North Africa, the Horn of Africa and parts of the Sahara and the Sahel, by more than 500 million native speakers.
Niger-Congo is spoken over the majority of sub-Saharan Africa and unites the Mande and Atlantic-Congo groups; Yoruba, spoken across south-west Nigeria, is one of its Atlantic-Congo languages.
Austronesian spread by sea: its languages are spoken across Taiwan, Maritime Southeast Asia, Madagascar and the islands of the Pacific, making it the fifth-largest family by number of speakers.
The Dravidian family's 250 million speakers are concentrated in South India, spilling into north India, Bangladesh, Nepal, north-east Sri Lanka and south-west Pakistan.

Proto-Turkic is thought to have been spoken in a region of East Asia spanning Mongolia and northwest China, from which the Turkic languages expanded into Central Asia and further west during the first millennium.
The Greeks took the Phoenician alphabet in the late 9th or early 8th century BC and added something no earlier script had: systematic letters for vowels alongside the consonants.
The Latin script began as the Greek alphabet in use at Cumae in Magna Graecia; the Etruscans altered it, and the Romans altered the Etruscan version in turn.
Cyrillic is a writing system used for languages across Eurasia, and the national script of Russia and of many countries in Southeastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia.
Devanagari is an Indic abugida based on the ancient Brahmi script, developed and in regular use by the 8th century CE; it is one of the official scripts of India and Nepal.
Of the four independently invented writing systems scholars accept, Chinese characters are the only one to have remained in continuous use -- a documented history spanning more than three millennia.

Korean had been written with Chinese characters, which suited the language poorly and left illiteracy high, so Joseon king Sejong the Great had a new alphabet announced in 1443-44 and published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum.
Both Japanese syllabaries descend from magana: Chinese characters used purely for their sound to transcribe Japanese, rather than for their meaning.

Ge'ez was first used to write the Ge'ez language, now the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and has since been adapted for Amharic, Tigrinya and at least 20 other languages of Ethiopia.
Latin was originally spoken by the Latins in Latium, the lower Tiber valley around Rome, and spread through the Italian peninsula with the expansion of the Roman Republic.

English is a West Germanic language that emerged in early medieval England, named after the Angles who migrated to Britain after Roman rule ended; the British Empire and then the United States made it a global lingua franca.

Mandarin is the largest branch of the Sinitic languages, stretching from Yunnan to Xinjiang to Heilongjiang; its spread is generally credited to how much easier the North China Plain is to travel than the mountainous south.
Modern Standard Hindi is an Indo-Aryan language written in the Devanagari script, an official language of the government of India and the lingua franca of most of the northern half of the country.

Spanish originated in the Kingdom of Castile in north-central Spain, evolving out of the Vulgar Latin spoken on the Iberian Peninsula, and is now one of the six official languages of the United Nations.
Castilian is what became of the Vulgar Latin spoken on the Iberian Peninsula -- the most widely spoken Romance language today.
Arabic is a Central Semitic language of the Afroasiatic family spoken primarily across the Arab world, whose varieties share a literary standard derived from Classical Arabic.

French descends from the Vulgar Latin of Roman Gaul, marked by native Celtic languages and by the Germanic Frankish of the post-Roman invaders, and over time supplanted most of France's other regional Romance varieties.
French and its closest relatives, the langues d'oil of northern France and southern Belgium, all descend from the Vulgar Latin of the Roman Empire.
Bengali, known by its endonym Bangla, is the Indo-Aryan language of the Bengal region, spoken natively across Bangladesh and eastern India.
Portuguese is a Western Romance language of the Indo-European family, written in the Latin script and official in Portugal, with approximately 267 million native speakers worldwide.

Portuguese is the official language of eight countries -- Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Sao Tome and Principe and Timor-Leste -- and the most widely spoken language of the Southern Hemisphere.
Russian is an East Slavic language of the Balto-Slavic branch, and remains a lingua franca in Ukraine, Moldova, the Caucasus and Central Asia.
Urdu is an Indo-Aryan language spoken primarily in South Asia, and is the national language and lingua franca of Pakistan.

Indonesian is a standardised variety of Malay, the Austronesian language that had served as the lingua franca of the multilingual Indonesian archipelago for centuries before it was made the national language.
German is a West Germanic language of the Indo-European family, spoken mainly in Western and Central Europe, with sizeable communities across the Americas.
Japanese is the principal language of the Japonic family, spoken by the Japanese people and by the Japanese diaspora worldwide.
Swahili, or Kiswahili, is a Bantu language of the Atlantic-Congo family, originally spoken by the Swahili people of Tanzania, Kenya and Mozambique.
Swahili's speaker estimates run from 150 to 200 million once second-language speakers are counted -- far beyond the coastal Swahili people who speak it natively.
Korean is a Koreanic language native to Korea and the official language of both North and South Korea; it is written in the Hangul alphabet.

Turkish is the most widely spoken of the Turkic languages: the national language of Turkey, one of two official languages of Cyprus, and spoken by sizeable communities in Germany, Bulgaria and the Caucasus.
Vietnamese is an Austroasiatic language of the Vietic subgroup and the official language of Vietnam, where it also serves as a second language for other ethnic groups.
Tamil is the Dravidian language of the Tamil people, concentrated in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry in India and in the Northern and Eastern Provinces of Sri Lanka.
Tamil is the Dravidian language of Tamil Nadu in South India, and one of the longest-surviving classical languages anywhere.
Persian, or Farsi, is a Western Iranian language of the Indo-European family, spoken and used officially within Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan.
Italian is a standardised form of literary Florentine Tuscan and, together with Sardinian, the Romance language least differentiated from Latin.
Thai is a Tai language of the Kra-Dai family, spoken in Central Thailand and the sole official language of the country.
Polish is a West Slavic language of the Lechitic subgroup, written in the Latin script, and the official language of Poland.
Dutch is the native language of most of the population of the Netherlands and of Flanders; it was an official language of South Africa until 1925, when Afrikaans, its daughter language, replaced it.
Greek constitutes an independent Hellenic branch of Indo-European, native to Greece, Cyprus and the eastern Mediterranean; before the alphabet it was recorded in Linear B and the Cypriot syllabary.

Hebrew was spoken natively by the Israelites, remained in regular first-language use until after 200 CE, survived as the liturgical language of Judaism, and was revived as a spoken language in the 19th century.
Amharic is an Ethio-Semitic language within the Semitic branch of Afroasiatic, spoken as a first language by the Amhara and as a common language by other city populations of Ethiopia.
Hausa is a Chadic language spoken primarily by the Hausa people of Niger and Nigeria, and used as a common language far beyond them across West Africa.
Tagalog is an Austronesian language spoken as a first language by the ethnic Tagalog people and as a second language by the majority of the Philippine population.
Yoruba is a pluricentric Atlantic-Congo language spoken across a dialect area spanning south-west Nigeria, Benin and Togo, with migrated communities in Cote d'Ivoire, Sierra Leone and the Gambia.
Punjabi is an Indo-Aryan language native to the Punjab region, which straddles Pakistan and India.
Javanese is the Austronesian language of the Javanese people of Java; Indonesian, the national language, has borrowed heavily from it.
Telugu is the Dravidian language of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, where it is the official language -- one of the few Indian languages with primary official status in more than one state.

Sanskrit is a classical Indo-Aryan language and the sacred language of Hinduism; its most archaic form, Vedic Sanskrit, is the language of the Rigveda's 1,028 hymns, composed between 1500 and 1200 BCE.
The Arabic script is the writing system used for Arabic and for several other languages of Asia and Africa -- Persian, for one, is written in a derivative of it.

An adult male lion needs about 7 kg of meat a day and takes all of it from animal tissue. Obligate carnivores like the big cats cannot get nutrients such as taurine and retinol any other way, so meat is not a preference for them but a requirement.

A cow's rumen holds no cellulase of the cow's own — the mutualistic bacteria and protozoans fermenting inside it break the grass's cross-linked cellulose down instead. That outsourcing is what lets a herbivore live on a diet no vertebrate enzyme can handle.

An omnivore takes energy and nutrients from both plant and animal matter, feeding across more than one trophic level at once — which is exactly why bears, pigs, crows and humans cannot be pinned to a single rung of any food chain.
Lions hunt medium-to-large hooved mammals — plains zebra, blue wildebeest, buffalo — killing and eating them. That is the whole definition of predation: one organism kills another and eats it.

The prey is the organism the predator kills and eats, and plains zebra are among the lion's principal prey. Prey numbers drive predator numbers in turn — the lynx and the snowshoe hare cycle together on a 10-year period across the boreal forest.

A bee working a flower picks up pollen on its body and rubs it onto the stigma of the next one. This is the biotic route, and over 87.5% of flowering plants depend on pollination of some kind to fertilise their ovules and set seed.
The pollinator is the animal doing the moving — all bee families qualify, and honey bee pollination alone adds more than $15 billion of value to United States crops each year.

The orchid Angraecum sesquipedale is pollinated by Morgan's sphinx moth and effectively nothing else. Pollination can narrow to a single species on each side, which is why losing one moth can strand a whole plant.

The tapetum lucidum is a mirror behind the retina that sends light back through it a second time — the eyeshine you get in a torch beam. It is one of the night-adapted features mammals kept from their long nocturnal past, alongside acute hearing and whiskers.

Most animals were originally diurnal and some adapted into the night; lineages have since re-evolved daytime activity, geckos about 20 separate times. The suprachiasmatic nucleus reads incoming light to set which way round an animal runs.

An Ophrys orchid's lip mimics a female bee closely enough in shape and pheromone that males attempt to mate with it — pseudocopulation — and leave carrying pollen on their head or abdomen. The flower offers no nectar at all; the whole transaction is a deception.

Venom is defined by being actively delivered into another animal through a wound — a bite, a sting, a penetrating strike — rather than passively ingested or absorbed the way a poison is. About 450 snake species carry it.

Both are skeletons; what differs is which side the soft tissue sits on. An endoskeleton of bone and cartilage grows with its owner, while an arthropod has to moult its exoskeleton repeatedly through its juvenile stages just to get bigger.
Gestation is the stretch during which an embryo, and later a fetus, develops inside a viviparous mother. The African bush elephant runs it for 22 months and ends with a calf of 100 to 120 kg.

A butterfly's egg hatches into a caterpillar, not a small butterfly. The larva has structures and organs the adult never has, a different diet, and often a different habitat — it eats to fuel the metamorphosis that will replace it.

Habitat is a species-specific term: the array of resources and biotic factors present in an area that lets that particular species survive and reproduce. Savanna grass, water and open space is what makes savanna zebra habitat rather than merely scenery.

Add the abiotic half — soil, water, climate — to the living food web occupying a habitat and you have an ecosystem: biotic and abiotic components tied together by nutrient cycles and energy flows, which is precisely the definition Tansley published in 1935.

Habitat is where a species lives; the niche is what it does there — Elton defined it in 1927 as an animal's place in the biotic environment, its relations to food and enemies. A species' habitat is the physical manifestation of the niche its adaptations fit it for.

A biome is a distinct geographical region with its own climate, vegetation and animal life. Whittaker's classification needs nothing but average annual temperature and average annual precipitation to tell one from another.

Scavengers feed on dead and decaying organic matter. The spotted hyena is a facultative one — its bone-crushing bite lets it take the parts of a carcass other carnivores abandon — while obligate scavenging is nearly a vulture monopoly, and diclofenac cutting Asia's Gyps vultures by at least 95% was followed by rises in rabies, plague and anthrax.

A bat's wing is a hand. It is built from the same ancestral tetrapod forelimb bones as a whale's flipper, a horse's foreleg and a human arm, reshaped for a different job — similarity of structure from shared ancestry, regardless of what the structure now does.

Mendel crossed round-seeded peas with wrinkled ones and got an F1 generation that was entirely round: the round allele masked the wrinkled one in every heterozygote. Self-cross that F1 and the hidden version reappears, in the characteristic 3:1 ratio.

Punnett drew the square in 1905 to make Mendel's arithmetic visible. Cross two heterozygotes and the four cells read 25% BB, 50% Bb and 25% bb — three offspring showing the dominant phenotype for every one showing the recessive.

A spontaneous mutation that happens to blunt a drug becomes an advantage the instant that drug is present. Tuberculosis regimens built on streptomycin alone selected for exactly that and failed — which is why TB is now treated with several drugs at once.

Selection pressure from overuse in medicine and agriculture does the sorting, and horizontal gene transfer spreads the result: bacteria hand resistance genes sideways between species by conjugation, transformation and transduction, so a trait selected in one lineage need not stay there.

Selection can only see reproductive success: an allele spreads when its carriers average more offspring than the alternatives, and adaptation is what accumulates from that. Spencer's 1864 phrase 'survival of the fittest' describes this arithmetic, not strength or health — a frail organism that leaves more offspring is the fitter one.

Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behaviour; Wundt made it a laboratory discipline at Leipzig, and psychologists in Germany, Denmark, Austria, England and the United States soon set up laboratories of their own.

The discipline's two founding lines: Wundt breaking mental processes into basic components in the laboratory, by analogy to chemistry, and Freud's clinical account of unconscious phenomena — psychology covers conscious and unconscious alike.
Misfolded alpha-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies inside the substantia nigra's dopamine neurons; by the time motor symptoms appear, 50-80% of those neurons have degenerated.

Autism is classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder: the differences in social communication, sensory processing and repetitive interests emerge in early childhood and usually persist for life, and twin studies show genetic factors explain most of the variation.

ADHD involves the dopamine and norepinephrine systems that modulate executive function, with the greatest volume reduction found in the left prefrontal cortex; stimulant medication works by increasing activity in exactly those two systems.

The DSM-5 diagnosis needs three things together — energy intake restricted to a low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and a disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced — and about 5% of people with it die of complications within ten years.

Nicotine activates alpha4beta2 nicotinic receptors on neurons of the ventral tegmental area, releasing dopamine along the mesolimbic pathway — the same reward circuit, projecting to the nucleus accumbens, that nearly every addictive drug ends up driving.

A sugar pill handed over as a painkiller really can reduce pain: since Levine, Gordon and Fields in 1978 it has been known that placebo analgesia depends on the release of the brain's own opioids, which the opioid blocker naloxone abolishes.

In Wason's 1960 rule-discovery task, people given the triple 2-4-6 tested only sequences their hypothesis predicted rather than ones that could falsify it; imaging of partisans reading their own candidate's contradictions shows the same one-sided handling of evidence damping down dissonance.

Wertheimer flashed light bars in alternation and saw one bar moving where nothing moved; publishing that phi phenomenon in 1912 launched a school arguing perception hands over organized structured wholes, not summed sensations.

Titchener, a student of Wundt at Leipzig, took the laboratory method home and tried to classify the structures of the mind the way chemists classify the elements, using introspection as, in his words, the final court of appeal.

Gall began lecturing in 1796 on brain organs whose size supposedly bulged the skull into readable bumps; Flourens' experiments indicated the organs were imaginary, and measuring skull contour to predict personality is discredited by empirical research.

Egas Moniz began severing most connections to and from the prefrontal cortex in 1935 and won a Nobel Prize for it in 1949; Walter Freeman sped the operation up in 1945 with a kitchen ice pick through the eye socket, and about 40,000 Americans were lobotomized before it was abandoned.

In the 1923 structural model of The Ego and the Id, the id is the organism's unconscious array of uncoordinated instinctual needs, impulses and desires — the only one of the three agencies present from the start.

Freud defined the ego as the part of the id that has been modified by the direct influence of the external world: as the infant meets reality, one region of raw drive becomes the agency that tests, delays and decides.

Freud called the super-ego 'the heir to the Oedipus complex': as the phallic-stage rivalry of roughly ages three to six resolves through identification with the same-sex parent, the family's prohibitions are internalised as conscience.

One of Gardner's eight criteria in Frames of Mind (1983) was potential isolation by brain damage — an injury knocking out one ability and sparing the rest; the theory is popular in education, though reviewers report no published studies offering evidence of its validity.

Kandel's 1970 study of habituation and dishabituation of the gill-withdrawal reflex in Aplysia traced a fading response to changes in synaptic transmission between sensory and motor neurons — the simplest form of learning, read off single identified cells.

A mnemonic re-encodes hard material as something easier to hold: 'Richard of York gave battle in vain' fixes red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet in order, the same trick as the ancient method of loci walking items through the rooms of a remembered house.
Under the crust lies 2,900 km of peridotite — olivine-rich mantle rock making up 84% of Earth's volume and 86% of its mass, kept solid by pressure despite being hotter than its own melting point.
The continents are granitic crust 25–70 km thick floating high on the mantle, while the ocean floors are basalt only 5–10 km thick — together less than 1% of the planet's volume.
New crust is made at mid-ocean spreading centres, where partial melting of the mantle underneath yields basaltic magma that freezes into fresh ocean floor.
The core begins 2,889 km down: a liquid iron outer shell ending at 5,150 km, wrapped around a solid iron-nickel inner core with a radius of about 1,221 km.
Earth's field is generated by a geodynamo — thermal and chemical convection in the liquid outer core, iron with roughly 5% nickel by weight, which shear waves cannot cross.

Weathering granite sheds quartz and feldspar grains that bury and cement into sandstone — arkose, where the feldspar survives the trip — and burying that deep enough melts it back to magma that freezes as granite again.

Moving air carries off the humid layer sitting on the surface, so laundry dries faster on a windy day — evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature, unlike boiling, which waits for vapour pressure to match the air.
Roughly 505,000 km³ evaporates each year and the same 505,000 km³ falls as precipitation, 86% of the evaporation happening over the ocean and about 9 days passing in between.
Gondwana, Euramerica and Siberia converged from about 335 million years ago, and the collision threw up the Central Pangean Mountains on the seam — a range comparable to the modern Himalayas.
Wegener's case for a former single landmass rested largely on fossils: the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus in both Brazil and South Africa, Lystrosaurus in Africa, India and Antarctica.

Drift was rejected for want of a mechanism until the ridges supplied one — new seafloor welling up along them, recorded in magnetic stripes, validated spreading in the mid-1960s and the theory was accepted.
Lateral density differences drive slow convection through the solid mantle, and the plates ride that creep at zero to about 10 cm a year.
Cold oceanic lithosphere is denser than the asthenosphere beneath it, so where plates converge it bends and sinks largely under its own weight; the trench is the surface scar of the bend.

A transform boundary is a fault at plate scale: the San Andreas is a right-lateral strike-slip fault running about 1,210 km through the crust, the Pacific plate sliding past North America at 20–35 mm a year.

Shaking destabilises slopes outright and weakens the rest for later failure — the magnitude 7.5 Hebgen Lake quake of 1959 dropped a mountainside into the Madison River and dammed it into Quake Lake overnight.
The same gravity-driven slope failure, in snow: a weak buried layer of faceted crystals gives way and the cohesive slab above it releases, most often between 35 and 45 degrees.

Water seeps slowly through the pore space between sandstone grains and is stored there; the Ogallala under eight US states holds fossil water from the last glaciation and recharges at roughly a tenth of what is pumped out.
Gas bubbles frozen into volcanic rock leave vesicles, and hydrothermal fluid seeping through deposits dissolved silica on the inside walls, growing quartz crystals inward into the hollow.
The sedimentary version: groundwater fills rounded cavities in limestone with chalcedony and banded agate instead — the classic geodes of the American Midwest.
An ice age is glaciation gone continental: at the last maximum, 26,000 to 20,000 years ago, North American ice sheets 3–4 km thick reached the 45th parallel and held sea level 110 m lower.
Andesite and dacite are silica-rich and viscous, so the lava stiffens near the vent instead of spreading — alternating with tephra it stacks into the steep layered cone of Fuji, Rainier or Vesuvius.

Hydrous minerals in the descending slab break down and release fluid that makes the mantle above partially melt, feeding an arc of volcanoes roughly 100 km above the slab — stratovolcanoes, almost all of them.

Basaltic lava is fluid enough to travel far before it freezes, so instead of a cone it builds a broad low dome sloping 2–3° at the flanks and about 10° higher up — Mauna Loa stands 4,169 m above the sea on a base over 60 miles across.
Kimberlite is an ultramafic melt of peridotite mantle from 150–450 km down, dominated by forsterite olivine and carbonate minerals, with MgO typically above 12%.

Diamonds crystallise 150–250 km down and are 1–3.5 billion years old, far older than the rock that carries them: kimberlite magma rises at 4–20 m/s by hydraulically fracturing its own path, and only that speed gets them up as diamond rather than graphite.

Magnitude is an instrument reading, not a sensation: a seismometer is a suspended mass whose lag behind the moving ground is recorded, and Richter defined magnitude in 1935 as the base-10 log of the largest trace amplitude in microns at 100 km.
Whether one deity exists or many is the oldest dividing line in the study of religion; monotheism and polytheism are two answers to the same question of what a god is.
Worship is devotion people direct toward a deity; the English word is Old English weorthscipe, 'worth-ship', the ascribing of worth to the one honoured.
A mantra is a sacred formula repeated in worship across Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism; prayer is that deliberate address to an object of worship, whether repeated, chanted or spoken.
Both are canonical religious texts, and 'scripture' is just Latin scriptura, 'writing' — the general word for the writings a tradition treats as authoritative.
Religion is defined as a social-cultural system binding together beliefs, texts, sanctified places and prescribed practices — scripture supplies the texts, worship the practices.

E. B. Tylor argued in Primitive Culture (1871) that animism, the doctrine of souls and spirits, was the earliest form of religion from which all later ones grew, and shamanism — trance dealings with those spirits — is among the most widely documented practices built on it.

Genesis presents Abraham's trust in God's promise as the ground of the covenant made with him, and Judaism, Christianity and Islam all hold him up as the model of faith — Paul argues in Romans 4 that this faith is why he was counted righteous.
Sin names a human act that transgresses divine law, and the Ten Commandments given at Sinai are the paradigm list of such laws for Judaism and Christianity alike.
The Egyptian Book of the Dead is a set of funerary spells meant to carry the deceased safely past the weighing of the heart and into the Fields of Aaru.
Heaven is Old English heofon, 'sky', and Hebrew shamayim and Arabic samāʾ mean the sky too — the blessed afterlife took its name from where it was placed.
Judaism regards Moses as its greatest prophet; Islam counts him among its five major prophets and calls Muhammad the seal — the last — of that same line.
These are the two rites nearly every Christian tradition counts as sacraments: the Catholic and Orthodox churches recognise seven, most Protestants only these two.
In the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches a priest is the person ordained to administer the sacraments — the Eucharist, confession and anointing that laypeople may not perform.

Popes were crowned with the triregnum, a three-tiered tiara, until Paul VI laid his on the altar of St Peter's in 1964 and no successor wore one again; the crown still appears on the flag of Vatican City.
The hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca that the fifth pillar of Islam asks once of every Muslim able to make it, drawing about 1.8 million people a year.
Fasting through Ramadan is the fourth pillar of Islam, and the month itself is set by the moon — it runs from one sighting of the crescent to the next.
The Kaaba is the stone cube at the centre of Mecca's Grand Mosque, with the Black Stone set into its eastern corner where pilgrims begin their seven circuits.
The fourth of the Ten Commandments orders the Sabbath day kept holy, and Exodus 31 calls the day a perpetual sign of the covenant between God and Israel.
The four gospels that open the Bible's New Testament narrate Jesus's words, deeds, death and post-resurrection appearances; Mark was written around AD 70 and John by about AD 100.
Hadith are the reports of Muhammad's words and deeds, and the majority of sharia's rules were derived from them rather than from the Quran's small number of legal verses.
John's gospel calls the turning of water into wine at the wedding in Cana the first of Jesus's signs, worked on six stone jars kept for ritual purification.
Judaism, Christianity and Islam all describe angels as heavenly messengers; the Quran gives them wings in twos, threes and fours, and Christian art has depicted them winged since late antiquity.
Jerusalem's Old City, under a single square kilometre, holds the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Al-Aqsa compound, drawing pilgrims of all three Abrahamic religions.

Rubbing amber against animal fibre leaves it able to attract dust and feathers — the effect Thales noted around 600 BCE, and the reason Gilbert built the word electricus out of elektron, Greek for amber.

Faraday's method of moving a loop of wire between the poles of a magnet is still the source: almost all commercial generation is electromagnetic induction with something mechanical spinning the generator.
Arkwright's water frame took spinning off the hand spindle and onto machinery driven by a river — Cromford, on the Derwent, was the world's first water-powered cotton spinning mill.
Spinning, weaving, iron rolling and papermaking were first driven by water; steam displaced it in the 19th century, so a mill no longer had to stand beside a river.
Coal gave a given amount of heat for far less labour than cutting wood for charcoal, and was more abundant — steam power in Britain grew from about 10,000 hp in 1800 to 210,000 hp by 1815.
Arkwright's cotton mill brought the whole production process into one powered building, turning cotton into a mechanised industry whose goods undersold the cottage spinners.
Blanc's swappable musket locks of about 1778 only worked with jigs to guide the machine tools, fixtures to hold the work and gauges to check it — precision that lives in a shop, not a hand.
Conveyor belts carried the Model T past 45 stations at Highland Park from 7 October 1913, cutting chassis assembly from 12.5 hours to 1 hour 33 minutes.
Substantial amounts of standardised product in constant flow needs both halves: parts that fit without fitting, and a line the assemblies move along.
Al-Khwarizmi worked at Baghdad's House of Wisdom around 820 and wrote On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals about 825; the 12th-century Latin translations of it Latinised his name into algoritmi.
Leibniz set out the system in his 1703 article Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire, using only the characters 1 and 0 — and argued the ancient I Ching figures were the same idea.
Boole published his algebra of logic in 1854 and Shannon's 1937 MIT thesis carried it out in relays and switches — a wire on or off standing for 1 or 0.
The rotor blades turn wind into low-speed rotation, and a gearbox steps that up to the speed the generator needs.
James Blyth installed a battery-charging wind machine at Marykirk in July 1887 to light his holiday home; Brush's automatic turbine followed in Cleveland the same year.
Transmission is more efficient at high voltage and low current, so transformers step the generating station up and local substations step it back down for customers.
The Chinese suanpan is rounded hardwood beads on rods — two above the bar, five below — and the earliest written records of it are from around the 2nd century BC.
A nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons bound electromagnetically around it — the nucleus is 2–7 femtometres wide, the whole atom about 100 picometres.
Proton count alone decides which element an atom is: one proton is hydrogen, 118 is oganesson, and changing the neutron count only changes the isotope.
Ionic bonds transfer electrons and covalent bonds share them, but both are the same electrostatic attraction between electrons and nuclei.
Two or more atoms sharing electron pairs; Lewis showed in 1916 that a pair could be shared to make a single, double or triple bond.
Atoms of more than one element held together in fixed stoichiometric proportions — that fixed ratio is exactly what separates a compound from a mixture.
Neither changes, no bonds form, the ratio is whatever you pour, and water parts them again — the components keep their own properties throughout.
Break the solute down to single molecules or ions and the mixture becomes one uniform phase — air does the same trick with oxygen dissolved in nitrogen.
Milk is the standard example: fat dispersed through water at between 1 nm and 1 µm — too big to dissolve into a solution, too small to settle, and big enough to scatter light.
HCl + NaOH gives NaCl and water, releasing 57.3 kJ for every mole of H+ neutralised — bonds break and re-form while every nucleus comes through untouched.
Platinum in a catalytic converter turns carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide and comes out unchanged; a catalyst offers a lower-energy path without being consumed.
The scale that sorts them: below 7 acidic, above 7 basic, 7 neutral for pure water at 25°C, and each unit a tenfold change in hydrogen ion activity.
Lavoisier defined it as reaction with oxygen, then chemists noticed the metal was really losing electrons — so sodium burning in chlorine is oxidation with no oxygen present.
One patch of the metal turns anode and gives up electrons while another reduces oxygen, and the metal dissolves into its environment.
Combustion is redox run hot: a fuel oxidised by atmospheric oxygen, exothermic enough that the heat it makes keeps the reaction going once started.
Carbon's four bonds chained together with hydrogen filling every spare site — the whole family, gas through wax through polymer, is only these two elements.
Water alone gives solid, liquid and gas; plasma, a gas with its electrons torn free, is the fourth and makes up roughly 99% of ordinary matter.
Na+ and Cl− alternate on a lattice that repeats in every direction, which is why a grain of salt has square corners visible to the naked eye.
Both are pure carbon: a tetrahedral cage gives the hardest natural material, stacked hexagonal sheets give a lubricant.
A mineral must be naturally formed, solid, of fairly definite composition and ordered crystal structure; a rock is simply an aggregate of one or more of them.
Brittle when solid, poor conductors, high electronegativity and acidic oxides — seventeen elements are widely counted as nonmetals.
Six elements straddle the line — boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium — usually looking like metals while behaving largely like nonmetals.
Top and bottom of group 1, both with a single ns1 electron; the heavier you go the more violent the water reaction, and caesium explodes even in cold water.
Full valence shells leave group 18 with nothing to gain or lose; argon is 0.94% of the air, and helium boils at 4.4 K, the lowest of any known substance.
Metals dissolved in each other stay metallically bonded with no fixed formula, and the mismatched atom sizes strain the lattice so defects cannot slide — bronze beats both copper and tin.
Tin amalgam backed nearly every mirror until production stopped around 1900 over mercury-vapour poisoning; an amalgam is just mercury alloyed with another metal.
Repeat one small molecule thousands of times and the properties change completely: ethylene becomes polyethylene, glucose becomes cellulose.
Most plastics are polymers built from petroleum and natural gas feedstocks, mouldable enough to earn the Greek name plastikos, 'able to be shaped'.
Fired clay and 2,072°C alumina are the two ends of one class: inorganic, non-metallic, hardened by heat, and brittle rather than ductile.
Steel in concrete and carbon fibre in resin are one idea: a stiff reinforcement carrying the load inside a matrix that stays a separate material.
Doping silicon with 0.001% arsenic donates about 10^17 free electrons and raises its conductivity by a factor of 10,000.
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it oxidises first and keeps protecting the steel underneath even where the coating has been scratched through.
Sulfur chains replace carbon–hydrogen bonds next to the double bonds and bridge one polymer strand to the next, so the rubber stops softening in heat.
Graphite is honeycomb sheets stacked only loosely; Geim and Novoselov cleaved a single one off with adhesive tape in 2004 and took the 2010 Nobel Prize for it.
Only three isotopes will sustain it — U-233, U-235 and Pu-239 — each absorbing a neutron and splitting into smaller nuclei plus more neutrons to keep the chain running.
The proton–proton chain in the Sun's core, at around 14 million kelvin, turns 620 million tonnes of hydrogen into 616 million tonnes of helium every second.
Dragons are composites almost everywhere they appear: a serpentine body given a bird's wings and hind legs and a lion's forelegs, from Mesopotamian mušḫuššu seals onward.
The Christian-era European dragon guards a cavern or castle stuffed with treasure — Fáfnir in the Völsung cycle, and Beowulf's dragon, whose fury is set off by the theft of a single cup.
Herodotus recorded an Egyptian account of a bird the size of an eagle, part red and part gold, returning once in 500 years; later authors have it die in flames and begin again.

Hesiod's centaur Chiron gives the earliest hint of the lifespan — 'the phoenix outlives nine ravens' — and the later accounts of a bird burnt down and reborn are where rising from the ashes comes from.
The recipe is literal: body, tail and back legs of a lion, head and wings of an eagle, with the eagle's talons on the front legs.
Aristeas in the 7th century BC placed gold-guarding griffins beyond the one-eyed Arimaspi, who rode out to rob them — a story Herodotus and Aeschylus both repeat.
Ctesias' Indica describes it as a fleet-footed wild ass with a single horn a cubit and a half — about 700 mm — long; the horse-shaped version is a later European habit.
Powdered 'alicorn' sold as medicine in Europe as late as 1741, though the Danish physician Ole Worm had shown in 1638 that the horns were narwhal tusks.
The comb and the mirror became the siren-mermaid's fixed attributes in medieval bestiaries, read there as emblems of vanity.
The naturalistic explanation is sightings from a distance of manatees, dugongs or seals — Columbus's own Caribbean mermaids are usually read as manatees.
European accounts make the change a matter of clothing: strip off, put on a belt of wolfskin, and Verstegan's 1628 report adds an enchanted girdle. Taking the clothes back off undoes it.
The full-moon trigger is not old folklore — in the traditional accounts it is a pelt, an ointment or a curse. The moon arrives with modern fiction and film.
The Talmud calls Adam himself a golem while he is still unformed dust — the word in Psalm 139:16 means raw, unfinished material.
Medieval mystics read the Sefer Yetzirah as working instructions for animating a shaped figure; the Prague story of Judah Loew came much later, as an early 19th-century German literary invention.
She sings the caoineadh, the keen that professional mourning women sang over the dead, and traditionally attends only certain old Irish families with Ó or Mac names.
Old Norse sources put trolls in isolated rocks, mountains and caves in small family groups; later Scandinavian folklore explains conspicuous boulders as trolls caught out by the sun.
The Prose Edda's Skáldskaparmál has the 9th-century skald Bragi Boddason meet a troll woman on the road — the oldest surviving encounter of the kind.
A recurring shape across traditions: the dead must be carried over a defining obstacle, usually a river or a lake, before they can enter at all.
The Greek dead were buried with an obol to pay Charon for the crossing of the Styx or the Acheron; without the fare there is no passage.
Homer's Odyssey calls it the seat of the gods, and it is a real summit — 2,917 m on the Thessaly–Macedonia border, with votive finds from around 400 BC on top.
Virgil's Aeneid puts a perpetual spring inside the land of the dead, lit by a sun and stars of its own, while the wicked go the other way to Tartarus.
Hesiod set the blessed heroes on islands out by Ocean's shore, where the grain-giving earth bears honey-sweet fruit three times a year.
Snorri's Gylfaginning describes it as a fortified city the gods built at the centre of the world, reached over the bridge Bifröst.
Valhöll is one of the halls inside the enclosure, alongside Iðavöllr and Odin's high seat Hliðskjálf.
The Hávamál has Odin hang on a windy tree nine full nights, wounded with a spear and given to himself, to win the runes.
Ratatoskr runs the trunk carrying messages between the eagle at the crown and Níðhöggr, the dragon gnawing the root from below.
The same role in two unrelated traditions: an intelligent boundary-crosser who breaks the ordinary rules, and whose mischief ends up rearranging the world rather than only disrupting it.
Comparative mythology files Eshu, Loki, Hermes, Coyote, Raven and Maui together — cunning, authority-testing figures who steal, lie and transform.
Clotho spins the thread of a life from her distaff onto the spindle, Lachesis measures the length with her rod, and Atropos cuts it.
It was built as a prison, not a hell: Cronus and the defeated Titans were shut in it after the war with Zeus, with the hundred-armed Hecatoncheires set as guards.
Hesiod's Theogony measures the drop with a falling bronze anvil: nine days from heaven to earth, and nine more from earth to Tartarus.
She shaped the nobility one at a time out of yellow clay, then dragged a cord through mud and flicked off the commoners — a myth that hands the social order a creation story.
In the Huainanzi she melts five-coloured stones to patch the broken sky and cuts the legs off a giant turtle to prop it up again after Gonggong shattered Mount Buzhou.
He wakes inside the cosmic egg and pushes it apart, the sky rising ten feet a day and the earth sinking ten, for 18,000 years — first written down by Xu Zheng in the 3rd century AD.
Perun's domain is sky, thunder, storm, law and the oak tree — the same pairing of thunder god with oak that turns up again in Baltic Perkūnas and Germanic Thor.
His weapons are hammers, axes and arrows, cut from stone in the older accounts and metal in the later ones; his name goes back to a root meaning 'to strike'.
The 'good god' of the Tuatha Dé Danann rules fertility, agriculture and druidry, and his harp Uaithne is said to set the seasons in their right order.
His cauldron, the coire ansic, is listed among the treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann: no company ever went away from it unsatisfied.
Chlorophyll in the chloroplast's thylakoid membranes absorbs light to split water and make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle then spends both on fixing CO2 into sugar.
A gymnosperm's seed sits naked on a scale. An angiosperm encloses its ovules in a carpel and wraps the result in fruit — that, and the flower itself, is the whole difference.
Meiosis cuts a spore down to one chromosome set, and that spore germinates into the gametophyte — the green cushion you see in a moss, but just a speck inside the plant in an angiosperm.

Two gametes from the gametophyte fuse into a zygote, and the zygote grows into the diploid sporophyte that will make spores by meiosis. In a moss it never leaves home — just a stalk and capsule fed by the green plant below.

Sporophyte makes spores by meiosis, spores make gametophytes, gametophytes make gametes by mitosis, and the gametes make a sporophyte again. Mosses foreground the first; ferns and seed plants the second.

A pollen grain germinates on the stigma and its tube delivers two sperm cells: one fuses with the egg to give the zygote, the other with the central cell's two polar nuclei to give triploid endosperm.
That second fusion makes the primary endosperm cell, which fills the seed with the starch and protein the embryo will live on — and which cereal farming exists to harvest.
Sepals are modified leaves that keep their chlorophyll: they wrap the bud shut while it develops, then hold the petals up in bloom.
Petals mark the route to the nectaries with lines and blotches, many of them ultraviolet — which cuts a bee's handling time and gets the flower pollinated faster.
The androecium sits inside the perianth and around the gynoecium: a ring of pollen-making stamens standing between the petals and the flower's centre.

A poricidal anther is sealed but for one pore at the tip and gives up nothing until a bumblebee grips it and fires its flight muscles — buzz pollination, which honeybees cannot do and which tomato and blueberry depend on.
Each Crocus sativus flower raises a three-pronged style tipped with crimson stigmas; picked and dried, those threads are saffron, at roughly 150 flowers per gram.
Every strand of corn silk is one elongated style attached to one ovary: pollen lands at the tip and the tube grows a foot in 24 hours to reach the ovule that becomes a single kernel.
Stigma on top, style below it, ovary at the base — that whole assembly is one carpel. A strawberry keeps its carpels free and separate; a tulip fuses them into a single compound pistil.
The ovary is the carpel's base, holding the ovules in chambers called locules; after fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become its seeds.
Meristem is tissue that never stops dividing: each daughter cell either differentiates into something or stays an undifferentiated stem cell, which is what gives plants indeterminate growth.

The apical bud sends auxin down the plant, and that auxin stops the lateral buds elongating. Cut the tip off and auxin falls, cytokinin rises, and the plant bushes out — the whole basis of pruning, coppicing and pollarding.
Cytokinins are made mostly in roots and ride the xylem upward; the ratio between auxin and cytokinin then decides what a lump of callus becomes — more cytokinin gives shoots, more auxin gives roots.

Researchers chasing the hormone behind cotton fruit shedding named this one for abscission, and the name stuck even though ethylene does most of that — its real work is slamming the guard cells shut when water runs short.

Starch-filled amyloplasts settle to the bottom of the root cap's columella cells, auxin carriers reorient, auxin piles up on the lower side and slows growth there — so the root curves down. Low-starch mutants barely notice gravity at all.
Same idea as bending toward light, different signal: contact opens calcium channels rather than setting up a light gradient, and the tendril curls even when auxin is spread evenly through it.
A potato tuber is storage parenchyma: thin-walled living cells with big central vacuoles, packed with starch.
The strings you pull off a celery stalk are collenchyma strands — living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls of cellulose and pectin, bracing a shoot that is still growing.
Cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin in a thick secondary wall; the cell then dies and is pure structure — long fibres like flax, or stubby sclereids like the grit in a pear.

Mesophyll is the leaf's parenchyma: palisade cells stacked upright for light under the upper epidermis, spongy cells below with air spaces wide enough that CO2 from the stomata reaches every one of them.
The wall they share is riddled with plasmodesmata, so the nucleated companion cell keeps its enucleate sieve tube element alive and loads sugar into it.
Water crosses from one dead tracheid to the next through bordered pits in the side walls — an arrangement that passes water while limiting how far an air embolism can spread.
Water evaporating from mesophyll walls and out through the stomata puts the whole xylem column under tension, and cohesion between water molecules drags the next one up behind it.
Autogamy: pollen from a flower's own anther landing on its own stigma. Tomatoes go further with cleistogamy, setting seed inside a flower that never opens.

Cross-pollination moves pollen to a genetically distinct plant of the same species, so the offspring combine two parents' alleles rather than one's — the reason most flowering plants have mechanisms to avoid pollinating themselves.
A maple's winged samara flutters off on the wind. Other seeds pay a bird with fruit, hook onto fur, float across an ocean, or get carried underground by ants.
Stomata sunk into pits, leaves reduced to spines, and CAM photosynthesis that takes CO2 in at night so the pores can stay shut through the heat of the day.
Water is banked in swollen parenchyma, most of it inside enormous vacuoles — an aloe does it in the leaf, a cactus in the stem, and about 60 unrelated families arrived at it separately.
An epiphyte uses the host purely for support, taking its water and minerals from rain, air and the debris that collects around it — unlike a parasite, it draws nothing out of the tree.

Three tactics are available: exclude the salt at the root, push it out through leaf glands, or dump it into leaves the plant then sheds. A mangrove filters most of it out at the root and offloads the rest into old leaves.
Physiological dormancy is chemical: abscisic acid blocks germination until cold, damp or fire tips the balance toward gibberellin. Physical dormancy is simpler — a coat too hard to let water in.
Cold and moisture together are what break physiological dormancy, so the seed cannot germinate in autumn into a winter it would not survive.
Cold recruits VIN3 and the VRN2 complex to shut the FLC repressor down by chromatin remodelling. Lysenko coined the term in 1928, then wrongly claimed the change was inherited.
Ethylene drives leaf senescence and shedding far harder than abscisic acid does; cytokinin pulls the other way, and keeping cytokinin synthesis switched on late will hold a leaf green.
The vascular cambium makes xylem inward and phloem outward while the cork cambium makes bark outward. Most monocots have neither — a palm thickens by enlarging parenchyma instead.
A dicot stem sets its bundles in a neat ring with cambium between the xylem and phloem; a monocot scatters them through the stem in an atactostele, with no ring left to thicken.
Pith is parenchyma at the dead centre of a eudicot stem, ringed by xylem and then phloem. Monocot stems have none — and sago palm pith is a starch staple across Melanesia.
Krupp began casting steel cannon in the 1840s, and Prussia's 1870-71 victory over France demonstrated the superiority of breech-loaded steel guns over muzzle-loaded brass.

A revolution in firepower unmatched by any advance in mobility: rapid-firing guns like the French 75 and machine guns handed the defender the advantage, and by the end of October 1914 the whole front had dug in.

Caterpillar-track tractors hauling guns in France showed what tracks could do; the commission that followed asked for a machine able to cross a four-foot trench and carry its own gun over ground swept by fire.
The design brief was written by the deadlock itself — an armoured machine that could cross a 4 ft trench, first tried at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916.
The deadlock machine guns helped create is what 167 tons of chlorine, released from 5,730 cylinders near Ypres on 22 April 1915, was meant to break; gas killed roughly 90,000 and broke nothing.
The Western Front solidified into a near-continuous line of fortified trenches from the English Channel to Switzerland, and Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele all failed to break it.
HMS Dreadnought put ten 12-inch guns on the first capital ship driven by steam turbines, reaching 21.6 knots on trials in October 1906.

The 1922 Washington Naval Treaty capped capital-ship building, so surplus battlecruiser hulls became the first large carriers — Lexington, Akagi, Kaga — and by Taranto in 1940 their aircraft had outclassed the guns.
A submersible hull whose weapon is the torpedo: U-20 sank the Lusitania on 7 May 1915, and unrestricted campaigns ran in 1915, again from February 1917, and through the whole of the next war.
Guderian ordered in 1933 that every German tank carry a radio; at the outbreak of war only the German army's tanks were all radio-equipped, which is what let armoured columns be handled as one mass.

Germany attacked Poland on 1 September 1939, the Soviet Union from the east on 17 September, and organised resistance ended on 6 October — the campaign Liddell Hart called a full demonstration of the theory.
The wartime programme spent over 80 percent of its near-$2 billion budget on the plants that enriched uranium at Oak Ridge and bred plutonium at Hanford.
In the Teller-Ulam design the fission primary's X-rays compress a secondary of deuterium fuel by radiation implosion; Ivy Mike, using liquid deuterium, gave 10.4 megatons.
The R-7, burning liquid oxygen and kerosene, threw a multi-megaton warhead 6,000 km to Kamchatka on 21 August 1957.
Castles were not communal defences but the private fortified residences of feudal lords — the men who granted land in return for the military service a mounted vassal owed.
Bonaparte was commissioned a second lieutenant in the La Fère artillery regiment in September 1785, and made his name massing guns above the harbour at Toulon in 1793.
Bamboo slips unearthed at Yinqueshan in Shandong in 1972, sealed in the tomb between 134 and 118 BC, carry an early version of the Art of War closely matching the text still read.
Compressed inert gas, usually nitrogen, drives heated oil through a hose to a pilot flame at the barrel, throwing fire 50 to 100 metres.
Iraq largely coincides with ancient Mesopotamia, where Sumer arose, and Baghdad, founded in 762 as the Abbasid capital, is its capital today.
Bahrain is an archipelago of 33 natural islands famed since antiquity for pearl fisheries considered the best in the world into the 19th century.
Oman's Dhofar is the UNESCO Land of Frankincense of the medieval incense trade, and its Musandam exclave is bounded by the Strait of Hormuz.
Archery is the national sport of Bhutan, contested regularly in most villages of this Vajrayana Buddhist kingdom.
The Tian Shan mountains cover over 80% of Kyrgyzstan, and its Lake Issyk-Kul was a stopover on the Silk Road between the Far East and Europe.
Nan Madol, on Pohnpei in Micronesia, is 92 artificial islets built of columnar basalt in a lagoon from around AD 1180.
On 25 September 2009 Palau announced the world's first shark sanctuary, protecting reef sharks across waters that include the Southern Lagoon of its Rock Islands.
Marshallese navigators invented stick charts that map ocean swell and wave patterns, letting sailors locate atolls still below the horizon.
Kiribati's 32 atolls straddle the equator and the 180th meridian, stretching from Banaba in the west to Kiritimati in the east.
Phosphate was discovered on the island of Nauru in 1900, and income from the mines made Nauruans among the richest people in the world.
The atolls of Tuvalu hold the .tv internet domain, whose royalties supplied 8.4% of government revenue by 2019.
The Tonga Trench's Horizon Deep drops 10,800 m into the hadal zone, second on Earth only to the Mariana, and the Hunga Tonga volcano erupted there in January 2022.
Mount Yasur, a near-continuously erupting volcano on Vanuatu's Tanna Island, is the sacred site of the John Frum cargo cult.
Mendana's 1568 expedition sailed west chasing Inca stories of gold, and the archipelago was named Islas Salomon when reports of it were conflated with the wealth of the biblical King Solomon.
Animals are the multicellular eukaryotes that have muscle cells, breathe oxygen, consume organic material, and develop through a blastula.
A sea squirt larva carries a notochord and a hollow dorsal nerve cord just as any vertebrate does — those, plus an endostyle, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail, define the phylum Chordata.
Vertebrates are the chordates whose vertebral column surrounds and protects the nerve cord, with a cranium around the brain.
Mammals are the vertebrates that feed their young on milk from mammary glands; around 6,640 living species have been described.
Synapsida is the amniote clade that contains all mammals and their extinct relatives; hair and mammary glands mark the surviving branch, which split from the reptile line over 300 million years ago.
Sauropsida is the amniote clade broadly equivalent to class Reptilia; reptiles are its ectothermic members, developing inside an amniotic egg.
Amphibians are the anamniotic tetrapods: four-limbed vertebrates that never gained the amniotic egg, so most begin as gilled aquatic larvae and metamorphose into air-breathing adults.
Arthropods are the invertebrates with a chitin exoskeleton, segmented bodies and paired jointed appendages — and they must moult that shell to keep growing.
In every mollusk the dorsal body wall forms a mantle, and it is the mantle that secretes the calcareous plates or shell.
Cnidaria is named for the cnidocyte, the stinging cell that fires the nematocyst, and most of its species alternate between a sessile polyp and a free-swimming medusa.
Insects are the largest group within the arthropods, marked by a three-part body, three pairs of jointed legs, one pair of antennae and compound eyes.
Primates are the mammals that adapted to life in the treetops: large brains, binocular colour vision, mobile shoulders and opposable thumbs for grasping.
Rodentia is defined by a single pair of continuously growing incisors in each of the upper and lower jaws — and it accounts for about 40% of all mammal species.
A beaver and a house mouse are both Rodentia, gnawing with the same pair of ever-growing incisors — the order is native to every major landmass except Antarctica.
Metamorphosis grows the legs, swaps gills for lungs, and draws the tadpole's tail inward as an internal urostyle — leaving an adult of Anura, 'without tail'.
Frogs make up about 87% of all amphibian species — over 7,700 of them in 59 families — and almost all start as jelly-wrapped spawn laid in water.
Speciation is the point where diverging populations can no longer interbreed; taxonomy then treats the result as the basic unit of classification, a species.
The first half of a two-part Latin name is the genus, the rank just above species and below family: Panthera leo and Panthera onca share theirs.
Arthropoda and Chordata are two of the roughly 32 phyla in the animal kingdom — the rank sitting below kingdom and above class.
Fungi and Plantae are separate kingdoms, alongside Animalia — the rank Linnaeus put at the top of his 1735 hierarchy.
Kingdoms are the rank divided into phyla: Animalia contains about 32 of them, Plantae about 14.
Woese, Kandler and Wheelis introduced domain in 1990 as a rank above kingdom, splitting all cellular life into Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
Comparing 16S ribosomal RNA in 1977, Woese found Archaea were no kind of bacterium at all — which forced a new highest rank to hold the three branches.
Aristotle's History of Animals investigates animal structure, development and the function of the parts — formal zoology is said to originate with him.
Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee waggle dance; he, Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen founded ethology, the branch of zoology studying animal behaviour, and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for it.
Homo sapiens emerged around 300,000 years ago from a big-brained heidelbergensis-grade population, then spread out of Africa and replaced the archaic humans it met.
Carl Linnaeus coined the binomial Homo sapiens in 1758 — and is himself the designated type specimen of the species he named.
A. ramidus, described in 1994 from 4.4-million-year-old deposits at Aramis, is the type species of the genus Ardipithecus; the older A. kadabba at 5.6 million years is the other.
Every known Ardipithecus fossil comes from the Afar region of Ethiopia, unearthed at Aramis and in the Middle Awash between 1992 and 1993.

Ardipithecus walked upright but kept a divergent grasping big toe for the trees; by 3.7 million years ago Australopithecus afarensis had lost it, and the Laetoli footprints record a committed two-legged stride.
Two legs have been invented over and over: all the early dinosaurs and the theropod clade that became birds, and among mammals kangaroos, hopping mice and hominins, each independently.
Gene flow carries alleles between populations and mixes their gene pools — the set of all genetic information a population holds.
A species' gene pool is the sum of its genetic diversity; a large one survives bouts of intense selection, while a small one drifts toward extinction.
With no oxygen, Saccharomyces cerevisiae takes about 2 ATP from each sugar and dumps the leftover carbon as ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Fermentation is what the ferment verb does: yeast, starved of oxygen, breaks each glucose molecule into two ethanol and two carbon dioxide molecules — the reaction behind beer, wine and a risen loaf.
Gluten is 75–85% of the total protein in bread wheat, as two storage proteins: glutenin supplying elasticity and gliadin supplying extensibility.
Kneading wet flour cross-links glutenin molecules through disulfide bonds into a submicroscopic network that gliadin attaches to.
It needs both halves — amino acids from the protein and a reducing sugar — which is exactly what separates it from caramelization, where sugar alone pyrolyses.
The TAS1R1+TAS1R3 receptor pair, identified at the University of Miami in 2000, is what reports free glutamate as a taste in its own right.
Kikunae Ikeda traced the palatability of kombu broth to glutamate in 1908 and coined the word; the symposium that accepted it as a basic taste met in Hawaii in 1985.
Two liquids that will not mix, forced into a dispersed phase inside a continuous one — it takes energy input to make, and it separates again on its own.
Lecithin is amphiphilic: one end dissolves in water, the other in oil, so it sits on the interface and lowers the tension holding the droplets apart.
Each sugar has its own threshold, and glucose starts at 150 °C — twenty degrees below sucrose. No amino acids are involved at all, which is what separates caramelization from the Maillard reaction.
Every sugar has its own threshold: fructose at 105 °C, glucose at 150 °C, sucrose at 170 °C, maltose at 180 °C.
The same class of molecule in two states: saturated chains pack tight and set solid, unsaturated ones kink and stay liquid.
Rendered pig fat and rendered beef suet are both esters of fatty acids on glycerol; how saturated those chains are decides how hard the fat sits at room temperature.
Equal proportions by weight: the fat is heated first, the flour stirred in and cooked until it loses its raw taste.
Cajun cooks use oil or lard rather than butter and take it to dark brown for gumbo; Hungarian cooks stir paprika into theirs.
Velouté is exactly this — a pale stock thickened with roux — and it is one of Escoffier's five mother sauces.
Béchamel, a butter-and-flour roux loosened with milk, was named in Vincent La Chapelle's The Modern Cook of 1733.
A leaf and a root land in the same category because cooks group by how a plant part is eaten, not by which organ it is.
One is a swollen underground stem and the other a berry, yet Nix v. Hedden (1893) taxed the tomato as a vegetable because it arrives with the main course.
Cinnamon is bark and ginger a rhizome — spices come from seed, fruit, root, bark or flower bud, never from the leaf.
Same shelf, different anatomy: herbs are the leaves, flowers and stems of a plant, spices everything else it offers.
Escoffier drew the line here: salt, acids and spices are seasonings, while onions, mustard and fats he counted as condiments.
Salt draws water out and magnifies the flavours already present; used properly the seasoning itself cannot be tasted.
Served alongside rather than stirred in during cooking — that timing is what separates a condiment from a seasoning.
The archetypes of the narrow definition: prepared compounds made in advance, added after cooking, dosed by the eater.
Carbohydrates, amino acids and fatty acids are the macronutrients an animal needs in bulk; vitamins and minerals are the trace list beside them.
An essential nutrient is one the body cannot make in sufficient quantity — 9 amino acids, 2 fatty acids, 13 vitamins, 14 minerals — so it has to arrive on the plate.
Biological leavening: Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments the dough's sugars and the carbon dioxide is caught in the starch-and-gluten matrix.
Chemical leavening: a bicarbonate salt and a dry acid that only meet once moisture arrives, so quick breads need no fermentation time.
The juices meat and vegetables run naturally during cooking, thickened with flour or cornstarch — that is the whole definition.
Drippings let down with stock: cream gravy in the American South, onion gravy in Britain, giblet gravy at Thanksgiving.
Butter holds almost no lactose because it is milk fat, while milk itself carries the most — the category spans that entire range.
Cattle were domesticated about 12,000 years ago, but the earliest evidence of milking them is seventh-millennium-BC northwestern Anatolia.
Ethanol boils at 78.1 °C, but at 95.6% by mass it forms an azeotrope with water where vapour and liquid match and ordinary distilling can go no further.
Selective boiling and condensing the vapour in a still — a physical separation, not a chemical reaction. Alexandria's alchemists were doing it by the 1st century CE.
Air, sun, wind and smoke all do one job: remove the moisture that bacteria, yeasts and mould need to grow. Jerky and prosciutto are the meat version.
Lofoten stockfish hangs unsalted on wooden racks from February to May at just above 0 °C and loses about 80% of its water.
Salt does the osmosis; nitrite breaks down to nitric oxide, binds myoglobin's heme group for the pink colour, and inhibits the bacteria that cause botulism.
Osmotic pressure pulls water out of the microbes rather than killing them, and this was the main way to keep meat and fish until the late 19th century.
Hot smoking runs 52–80 °C and cooks as it flavours; cold smoking at 20–30 °C leaves the food raw and leans entirely on the smoke's antimicrobials.
Smoke's phenols are antioxidant and antimicrobial, but it is nearly always paired with salt because smoke mainly seals the outer layer.
Lactic acid bacteria ferment at room temperature in 20–40 grams of salt per litre and generate the required acidity themselves — no sterilisation needed.
The other route: sterilised jars, vinegar and spices, holding the solution at pH 4.6 or below so enzyme activity and microbial growth both stop.
The coating fats and oils leave is a texture sensation, distinct from taste and smell, and research shows viscosity alone can shift how full you feel.
Wine tasters rate mouthfeel from first perception on the palate through chewing to aftertaste; tannin drops protein out of solution, so its grip is felt, not tasted.
The first of the WHO's five keys is keeping pathogens off food from people, pets and pests; the rest are separating raw from cooked, cooking through, storing right, and safe water.
Spoilage organisms announce themselves by smell; pathogens do not, which is why safety is governed by the 5–60 °C danger zone rather than by taste.
Malting, mashing, lautering, boiling, fermenting: the yeast only gets to work after amylase has turned the grain's starch into sugar it can eat.
Mashing steeps barley malt at 60–70 °C, where alpha- and beta-amylase cut starch into dextrins and fermentable sugars such as maltose.
The surface must pass about 150 °C to brown, and since water boils off at 100 °C it has to be dry first. The browning is Maillard, not caramelization.
Experiments from the 1930s found seared roasts lost as much moisture or more; the high heat ruptures more cells and releases extra liquid. The payoff is flavour and contrast.
A combination method — dry heat first for the browning, then moist heat in a covered pot, with less liquid and bigger cuts than a stew.
Wine, stock or beer, often with something acidic: coq au vin and osso buco work because connective tissue and collagen break down and lubricate the fibres.

Adolphe Sax put the clarinet's single-reed mouthpiece onto a conical brass body — Wikipedia calls the saxophone 'a type of single-reed woodwind instrument with a conical body, usually made of brass' whose mouthpiece is 'similar to that of the clarinet'. The saxophone's own fact says this; no recipe did.

The bassoon is the oboe's double reed on a long maple bore: a 'Double-reed woodwind instrument', 'generally made of maple', standing 1.34 m tall with a sounding length of 2.54 m because the tube doubles back on itself.

The bag is animal skin — 'the skins of local animals such as goats, dogs, sheep, and cows' — and every pipe it feeds is sounded by a reed, 'single... or double reed'. The current recipe is air plus hide and never touches the reed.
The two things that make a modern piano: 'a massive, strong, cast iron frame' to hold the string tension, and 'firm felt hammer coverings instead of layered leather or cotton' to strike the strings.

Tuning forks are 'traditional sources of standard pitch for tuning musical instruments', and 'the most common tuning fork sounds the note of A = 440 Hz, the standard concert pitch'. That is exactly how a piano gets its reference.

Pitch is made in the cochlea: hair cells 'are tuned to certain sound frequencies by way of their location in the cochlea, due to the degree of stiffness in the basilar membrane' — 'this spatial arrangement of sound reception is referred to as tonotopy'.
