Smallpox eradication was achieved by exhaustive contact tracing to find every infected person, then isolating them and immunising the surrounding community and at-risk contacts.
Snow's identification of the Broad Street pump as the source of the 1854 Soho cholera epidemic — he removed the handle and it stopped — is the field's founding example.
John Graunt's 1662 analysis of London's Bills of Mortality, just before the Great Plague, produced one of the first life tables and time trends for many diseases — counting the population came first.

A biological vector has to let the pathogen develop inside it first: Plasmodium needs 10 to 28 days in the mosquito, and a female that does not outlive that extrinsic incubation period never transmits malaria at all.
The incubation period is the time from exposure to the first sign, taken up by the organism multiplying to the threshold needed to produce a symptom at all.
Breathing, talking, coughing and sneezing all throw out a continuum of particle sizes; droplets over 100 μm usually settle within 2 metres, smaller ones stay aloft and travel farther.
Tuberculosis is the standard example of an obligate airborne infection — it spreads through aerosols and by no other route.
A shallow transparent lidded dish whose only job is to hold the agar growth medium flat and covered — the most common culture plate in biology.
Koch developed the precursor dish in his private laboratory in 1881; his assistant Julius Richard Petri modified it into today's form at Berlin University in 1887.
The streak plate drags the inoculum back and forth with a loop until single cells are separated, so each colony that grows after incubation came from one cell.
Koch made isolation in pure culture a step of his postulates and worked that way himself, isolating the cholera bacterium in pure culture on 7 January 1884.
The basic procedures are hand washing, gloves, masks and gowns, and sterilising instruments and linens by autoclaving or using disposables.
Asepsis grew out of antisepsis: Giuseppe Ruggi shifted the movement in the 1870s from killing germs already in the wound to keeping them out of the field.
Jenner coined Variolae vaccinae, "pustules of the cow", for cowpox and used it in the title of his 1798 Inquiry — vaccine and vaccination come straight from that phrase.
On 14 May 1796 he scraped pus from cowpox blisters on milkmaid Sarah Nelmes's hands into two cuts on James Phipps's arm; a July challenge with smallpox produced nothing.

Returning on 3 September 1928 he found a Penicillium contaminant on a staphylococcus plate with the colonies around it destroyed; he grew the mould in pure culture and named penicillin on 7 March 1929.
Both are his: lysozyme, found in his own nasal mucus and reported on 1 May 1922, and penicillin in 1928 — he noted in his Nobel lecture that penicillin was not his first antibiotic.
Carbolic acid is phenol; Lister dressed compound fractures with lint dipped in it from 12 August 1865, and amputation deaths in his wards fell from 16 in 35 before to 6 in 40 after.
Thomas Anderson pointed Lister to Pasteur's papers on putrefaction around 1865; from them Lister concluded wounds rot because of germs, and set out to kill them with carbolic acid.
He ordered washing in chlorinated lime — calcium hypochlorite — between the autopsy room and the delivery ward, chosen because it best removed the smell of infected cadaveric tissue.
Doctors carrying cadaveric particles from autopsies to mothers is the founding case of hospital-acquired infection: the midwives' clinic, which did no autopsies, ran at a third the death rate.
A genome is every gene an organism carries, packaged across its chromosomes — 3.1 billion base pairs on 24 distinct chromosome molecules in a human.
The nucleoid is what defines a prokaryotic cell: a single circular chromosome sitting in a bare tangle with no nuclear envelope around it.
Archaea are one of the two prokaryote domains, and like all prokaryotes they reproduce asexually by binary fission rather than mitosis.
De Bary's 1878 definition takes in the whole range of long-term interspecies living, from the commensal that costs its host nothing to the parasite that feeds on it.
Albert Bernhard Frank coined 'symbiosis' in 1877 for exactly one case: the lichen, a fungus and an alga living as a single body.
Suzanne Batra coined 'eusocial' in 1966 for halictid bees; E. O. Wilson extended it in 1971 to ants, wasps and termites, every species of which is eusocial.
The naked mole-rat was the first mammal found to be eusocial: colonies of 75 to 80 with one breeding queen and one to three breeding males, the rest sterile workers.
Hamilton's 1964 rule rB > C shows how selection can favour a sterile worker: she passes her genes on through the relatives she helps rear.
A clade is one branch cut from the tree at a node — a common ancestor plus every descendant of it, which is also what 'monophyletic' means.
Willi Hennig's cladistics carves the tree of life by shared derived traits, and the unit it produces is the clade.
A zygote gets one full set of chromosomes from each parent and the genes on them stay discrete — particulate inheritance, not the blending Darwin assumed.
Mendel's pea crosses of 1856 to 1863 turned heredity into three stateable laws and produced the 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 generation.
A recessive allele's effect on the phenotype is masked whenever a dominant copy is present; it appears only in the homozygous state.
One of each at a locus, written Rr: the dominant allele is expressed and the individual silently carries the recessive one.
A recessive trait shows only in the homozygous-recessive genotype — Mendel's wrinkled peas are the rr quarter and nothing else.
HbAS heterozygotes resist malaria because infected cells sickle and are cleared, while HbSS homozygotes get sickle-cell anaemia — balancing selection keeps both alleles.
64 codons map onto 20 amino acids plus stop, so the code is redundant but never ambiguous — each codon names exactly one amino acid.
Transcription then translation is the route Crick set out in 1957: DNA to RNA to protein, with no way back out of the protein.
Transcription factors bound at a gene's promoter switch it on or off — the first and largest of the levels at which expression is controlled.
Acetylation and methylation of histone tails change how accessible DNA is and so which genes run, and they persist through cell division without altering the sequence.
The commonest epigenetic mark is a methyl group on the C5 position of a cytosine, written by DNMT3A and DNMT3B and maintained by DNMT1.
In the pachytene stage of prophase I, homologous chromosomes break and rejoin across non-sister chromatids, reshuffling alleles so no gamete keeps a parental combination intact.
SRY, a single gene on the human Y, is the only one that directly switches an embryo onto the male developmental path.
The centromere links the sister chromatids and is where the kinetochore assembles to capture spindle microtubules — without it the chromatids never separate.
A karyotype is the genome seen as objects: chromosomes arrested at metaphase with colchicine, stained, counted and paired — 46 in a human.
Feathers evolved for heat regulation and display and were only later co-opted for flight — the example Gould and Vrba used in 1982.
Darwin's 1871 account: female choice pays for the peacock's train even though it hampers flight and draws predators, while the peahen stays brown.
The mane is a male lion's secondary sexual characteristic, a trait lionesses lack entirely.
Oxygen from cyanobacteria precipitated dissolved iron out of the sea as banded iron formations, which peak around 2.5 Ga and vanish from the record by 1.85 Ga.
Cyanobacterial oxygenic photosynthesis raised free O2 from nothing to about 10% of modern atmospheric levels between roughly 2.46 and 2.06 billion years ago.
Glacial deposits at tropical latitudes are the core evidence: ice-albedo feedback ran away twice in the Cryogenian, 717 to 660 and 650 to 635 Ma.
Volcanic outgassing under the ice is the only way out — CO2 has to build to an estimated 350 times present levels before a frozen Earth thaws.
Trilobites are the signature arthropod of Cambrian deposits like the Burgess Shale, their exoskeleton built of calcite and calcium phosphate in a chitin lattice.
Each lens of a trilobite's compound eye was a single calcite crystal — a holochroal eye held 100 to 15,000 of them under one corneal membrane.
The flood basalts of the Siberian Traps released sulfur dioxide and CO2 around 251.9 Ma, acidifying the oceans and killing 81% of marine species.
Trilobites had dwindled to five surviving genera since the Devonian, and the end-Permian took every one of them after 270 million years.
Cyanobacteria secrete adhesive compounds that cement sand and sediment into laminated carbonate mounds; living ones survive in hypersaline Shark Bay, Western Australia.
Ribozymes are the crux of the hypothesis: if RNA can store the message and catalyse reactions at once, early life needed neither DNA nor protein.
Alexander Rich argued in 1962 that the early Earth's chemistry could produce RNA molecules that went on to acquire enzymatic and self-replicating function.
Hair cells in the organ of Corti do not fire themselves — they depolarise and release neurotransmitter onto auditory nerve fibres, which carry the cochlea's frequency map to the brainstem.
A sound wave travelling through cochlear fluid vibrates the basilar membrane, and hair cells sitting on it depolarise — that is the whole conversion from pressure to signal.
The Weber and Rinne tuning-fork tests are still how a bedside examiner separates conductive loss from sensorineural loss, before any audiogram.

'Wherever communities of deaf and hard of hearing people exist, sign languages have developed' — full natural languages with their own grammar and lexicon, and not universal: British and American Sign Language are mutually unintelligible though the hearing populations share English.
Caffè latte is literally 'coffee and milk': espresso plus steamed milk, more milk than a cappuccino carries, and no thick foam cap.
The ancestor is Vienna's Kapuziner, on Habsburg coffeehouse menus by the late 1700s — dark coffee with whipped cream and spice, lightened to the colour of a Capuchin's habit.
The steam wand added to the espresso machine in 1903 is what makes the difference: texture the milk into foam and the latte becomes a cappuccino, one third of each.
Chai is brewed as a decoction and then boiled with milk — one Maharashtrian method uses equal parts water and milk, with the tea and masala going in together.
Cardamom is the commonest of the chai spices, alongside grated ginger and cinnamon, with cloves and black peppercorns behind them.
The highest peak in the Alps stands between Italy's Aosta Valley and France's Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, and ownership of the summit area has been disputed between the two for centuries.
It sits on the frontier itself: the 11.6 km Mont Blanc Tunnel, dug 1957-65, runs under it from Courmayeur in Italy to Chamonix in France.
The USSR was governed through soviet councils by the Communist Party on Marxism-Leninism, and the Russian SFSR was the largest of its union republics.
An atmosphere is a layer of gases held in place by the gravity of the object it wraps — Earth's is 78.08% nitrogen before anything else.
Small, cold and without a magnetic field, Mars had its outer air stripped by the solar wind and kept only about 0.6% of Earth's surface pressure.
Magmatic eruptions are driven by gas release under decompression: as magma rises up the vent the dissolved gas comes out of solution and pushes the melt ahead of it.
Moving magma fractures the rock around it, and the swarms of volcano-tectonic quakes that result are the warning — nearly every recorded eruption was preceded by them.
Zhang Heng's Houfeng Didong Yi of about AD 132 was a bronze vessel some 2 m across with eight dragon heads holding bronze balls; a distant quake dropped one ball into a bronze toad's mouth.
Jousting armour split off from war armour in the late 15th and 16th centuries — deliberately heavier, up to 50 kg, because the wearer only had to survive one charge, not fight all day.
The First Crusade reached the walls on 7 June 1099 and took the city on 15 July, after English and Genoese ships landed timber at Jaffa on 17 June for towers, ladders and an iron-headed ram.
Told to sleep in Athena's temple, he woke holding her golden bridle and used it to take the untamed winged horse drinking at the Pirene spring in Corinth.
Fenrir is Loki's son by the giantess Angrboða; at Ragnarök he comes with his upper jaw against the sky and his lower against the earth, kills Odin, and is killed by Odin's son Víðarr.

Three goddesses at the Well of Urðr under the world tree's root shape fate — the Norse ones, not the Greek Moirai, and Norse sources also describe many lesser norns of god, elf and dwarf descent who attend births.
Their daily task is not spinning but gardening: they carry water and clay up from the well and pack it round Yggdrasil so the tree does not rot.
The city grew on both banks of the Vltava beneath Prague Castle, and Charles IV, who made it an imperial capital, tied the two sides together with the Charles Bridge.

The clay defender of the Prague ghetto is pinned on Judah Loew ben Bezalel, who took his Prague post in 1573 and is buried in Josefov — but scholars call the tale an early-19th-century German literary invention, first printed in 1834.
A cauldron is a large pot or kettle for boiling over an open fire, and the surviving early ones are metal — the Battersea cauldron of about 800 BC, the Gundestrup cauldron of the 2nd-1st century BC.
The Dagda's coire ansic, the 'un-dry cauldron', is one of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann: 'an assembly used not to go unsatisfied from it'.
Berliner's disc, sold from the 1880s and past the cylinder by about 1912, was pressed in shellac and standardised at 78 rpm.
Columbia's 1948 LP swapped shellac for vinyl and slowed the disc to 33⅓ rpm, which is what bought it about 22 minutes a side.
Sholes' first writing machine used a piano-like keyboard in alphabetical order; five years of rearranging produced a four-row layout close to the modern one by April 1870.
The same Morse key and the same dots and dashes, but the pulses ride radio waves instead of cable — Hertz proved the waves existed in 1887 and Marconi had a working system from 1894.
The contest grew straight out of the nuclear arms race and its ICBMs; Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957 set off the 'Sputnik crisis' that produced NASA the following year.
Its two poles: the first artificial satellite in October 1957, and the Moon landing of July 1969 that met Kennedy's pledge to do it before the decade was out.
Pesto alla genovese is Genovese basil, olive oil, pine nuts, garlic and cheese — Parmesan or Grana Padano with pecorino sardo — and the cheese goes in last, after the basil is crushed.
Classic moles are built on ancho, pasilla, mulato and chipotle chillies; chocolate is a latecomer, likely added only in the early 21st century, and few if any prehispanic mole recipes contained it.
Two Mexican states claim the sauce — Puebla, whose mole poblano averages twenty ingredients, and Oaxaca, 'the land of the seven moles'.
The Italian alla marinara is tomatoes, basil, olive oil, garlic and oregano; the story that Neapolitan ship cooks made it dates it to the mid-16th century, after Spain brought the tomato to Europe.
Hemp is Cannabis sativa grown for the bast fibre in its stem and for seed, using cultivars bred below 0.3% THC rather than for resin.
Canvas takes its name from cannabis: the heavy plain-weave cloth was originally woven from hemp bast, one of the first fibres humans ever spun.
Brassica napus is an amphidiploid formed by hybridising B. oleracea (cabbage) with B. rapa (turnip); canola is its low-erucic-acid cultivar group.
Canola is a mustard-family oilseed — the world's third-largest source of vegetable oil and second-largest source of protein meal.
Clover is a Trifolium legume whose root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen; put in the rotation, it replaced the nitrogen European cities took away as food.
Chia is Salvia hispanica, a sage in the mint family grown entirely for its seed, which is hydrophilic enough to swell twelvefold in water.
A Sonoran Desert shrub whose seed is about 54% liquid wax ester, not triglyceride — which is why what it yields behaves like whale oil.
Kenaf's whole stalk — 40% bast, 60% woody core — pulps to a quality similar to hardwood, which is why it is grown for newsprint.
Kenaf was first grown in Egypt over 3,000 years ago, its bast fibre made into bags, cordage and the sails of Egyptian boats.
Jute needs standing water and 20–40 °C monsoon humidity; the cut stems are retted in it until bast strands 1–4 m long pull free.
India and Bangladesh produce nearly all the world's jute, stripped from the phloem — the 'skin' — of Corchorus stems.
Sisal is Agave sisalana, its stiff leaf fibre traditionally used for rope and twine and still the standard surface of a dartboard.
Sisal fibre is extracted by crushing the agave's sword-shaped leaves and washing the pulp away — the fibre is only about 4% of the plant by weight.
Abacá is Musa textilis, a banana whose fibre comes from the leaf sheaths wrapped into its pseudostem, not from any fruit.
Manila hemp is abacá: stronger than true hemp and naturally salt-resistant, which made it the standard rope of maritime shipping.
Boehmeria nivea has been woven in China for centuries as zhu ma; the fibre is bast from the inner bark, not the woody stem.
Ramie is stripped as a bark ribbon from fresh stems, then scraped, washed and degummed before it can be spun into cloth.
Woad is Isatis tinctoria, a Brassicaceae, and the dye its leaves give is chemically the same indigo as Indigofera's — just at lower concentration.
The hop is a female flower cone; boiled in the wort, its humulones isomerise into the iso-alpha acids that make beer bitter, which unboiled hops barely are.
The modern snap pea came from a shelling-pea mutant found in 1952 by M.C. Parker, crossed with a snow pea by Calvin Lamborn and released in 1979.
Mung beans are grown as much for sprouts as for seed: the sprout is taken 4–5 days after sowing, at the moment the seed splits.
Cellophane or glass noodles are made from mung bean starch and water — Chinese bean thread noodles are nothing else.
Broad beans are rich in levodopa, dopamine's direct precursor — enough that they must be avoided by anyone on irreversible MAO inhibitors.
Lupin seed carries alkaloids bitter enough to be toxic, so it is brined and pickled before anyone eats it.
Poppy seed is harvested from the dried capsule of Papaver somniferum — the same plant as opium, but taken after the pod ripens rather than while it is green.
Quinoa is in the amaranth family, and both are pseudocereals — seeds eaten like grain from plants that are not grasses at all.
Emmer was the main wheat of Pharaonic Egypt, stored in quantity in the chambers beneath the Step Pyramid at Saqqara.
Spelt is hexaploid, most likely a hybrid of emmer with a bread-wheat type, which is why its ear is slenderer and its grain stays hulled.
Italian farro is three hulled wheats, and spelt is the largest of them — farro grande, against emmer's farro medio and einkorn's farro piccolo.
Khorasan wheat is named for the eastern Iranian region that formed a significant part of the Silk Road, where the grain was grown and traded.
Domesticated einkorn differs from the wild plant in one decisive thing: the ear no longer shatters, so a harvester can carry the seed home.
Triticale is × Triticosecale — wheat as the female parent, rye as the pollen donor — first bred in Scotland and Germany in the late 19th century.
Fonio is a Digitaria crabgrass of the West African savanna with the smallest seeds of any millet and a root more than a metre deep against drought.
Eragrostis tef is a C4 lovegrass domesticated in the Ethiopian highlands, still the staple grain of Ethiopia and Eritrea and the flour behind injera.
Zizania is not Oryza, though both sit in the tribe Oryzeae; it grows in the shallow standing water of small lakes and slow streams, only its flowering head above the surface.
The spice is the inner bark of Cinnamomum verum, an evergreen laurel kept coppiced as a bush so its side branches can be peeled by hand.
Sri Lanka still supplies 80–90% of true cinnamon, whose flavour is essentially one compound, cinnamaldehyde, in the bark oil.
Cloves are the unopened flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum, an evergreen of the myrtle family that grows 8–12 m tall.
The clove tree is native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia, and the eugenol in its buds is what the spice trade was after.
One Maluku tree, Myristica fragrans, yields two different spices from a single fruit: nutmeg from the seed, mace from the crimson aril wrapped around it.
Myristica fragrans is a dioecious evergreen 5–15 m tall; only carpellate trees set the yellow fruit that splits to show the seed.
Curcuma longa is lifted every year — some rhizomes replanted for the next season, the rest boiled and dried into powder averaging 3.14% curcumin.
Turmeric needs 20–30 °C and high annual rainfall to thrive, which is why it is a monsoon-belt crop of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
Capsicum was domesticated in the Americas by at least 3000 BC — chilli remains turn up in pottery from Puebla and Oaxaca.
The chilli is botanically a berry on a nightshade; its name only borrows 'pepper' from black pepper, to which it has no botanical relation.
Fennel's fruits are loaded with trans-anethole, the same compound that makes anise taste as it does; the two together flavour absinthe.
Foeniculum vulgare is an Apiaceae — carrot's own family — a hollow-stemmed perennial to 2.1 m whose swollen stem base is Florence fennel.
Star anise is unrelated to anise but shares its anethole flavour; its shikimic acid was the feedstock Roche used for oseltamivir until 2012.
Illicium verum is an evergreen tree native to South China and northeast Vietnam, and those two countries are still its main producers.
Greek used one word for both plants; Latin split it into anethum for dill and anisum for anise, and Anethum is still dill's genus.
Dill is an Apiaceae, the celery family, growing 0.5–1.5 m from a taproot with hollow stems and flat yellow umbels.
Crocus sativus is a sterile triploid — three sets of eight chromosomes, 24 in all — so it sets no viable seed and survives only by hand division.
The autumn-blooming crocus is a purple flower; only its three crimson stigmas are picked and dried into the spice.
Spearmint's smell is R-carvone — the exact mirror image of the S-carvone that makes caraway smell of rye.
Mentha × piperita is the hybrid of spearmint (M. spicata) with watermint (M. aquatica), first identified in Hertfordshire and published in 1696.
Peppermint is sterile and spreads only by wide fleshy rhizomes, so a peppermint field is one plant repeated over and over.
Tea is the leaf and bud of Camellia sinensis, an evergreen of the Theaceae named for the Jesuit pharmacist Georg Kamel.
The plant is native to the highlands between southwest China, north Myanmar and northeast India, but China, India and Kenya are now the three largest growers.
Coffea is a Rubiaceae shrub or small tree, 3–3.5 m in the tropics, and it takes three to five years before it fruits at all.
The coffee cherry is a drupe that takes about nine months to ripen; 5–10% of them hold a single round bean instead of two, called a peaberry.
Honeydew and cantaloupe are both Cucumis melo; honeydew is the Inodorus group — smooth-rinded and, unlike cantaloupe, with no musky smell at all.
Actinidain was found in 1959 by A.C. Arcus, investigating why kiwifruit jellies would not set: the protease digests the gelatin.
Actinidain is a cysteine protease unique to Actinidia, sold as a meat tenderiser and denaturing at 60 °C — lower than papain or bromelain.
Dates are the drupes of Phoenix dactylifera, a dioecious palm — growers hand-pollinate the female trees rather than leave it to the wind.
The date palm is the tree of oasis agriculture, farmed across desert regions from the Gulf to North Africa since the 6th millennium BCE.

Passiflora edulis is a perennial vine native to southern Brazil through Paraguay and northern Argentina, producing usually one 5-7.5 cm flower at each node; missionaries in Brazil named it around 1700 after the Passion of Christ.
Garcinia mangostana is a tropical evergreen tree 6 to 25 m tall, native to the Malay Peninsula and Borneo, which prolonged exposure below 0 °C will kill outright.
The rind's polyphenols — xanthones and tannins — make the unripe fruit astringent enough to deter insects, fungi and animals, and the same rind has been used to tan leather in China.

The same flat corymb, 10-25 cm across, that is picked in flower for cordial sets fruit if it is left alone; unlike the flowers, the elder's other parts and even the ripe seeds hold the cyanogenic glycoside sambunigrin.

The boysenberry is a cross between European raspberry, European blackberry, American dewberry and loganberry; USDA's George Darrow and the berry grower Walter Knott tracked the surviving vines to Rudolph Boysen's abandoned Anaheim farm.

White pine blister rust needs two hosts to complete its life cycle: a Ribes and a white pine. Because the North American pines have no co-evolved resistance, currants were banned across the United States for much of the 20th century.
Gooseberries are Ribes, the same genus as currants; the French name groseille à maquereau translates as 'mackerel berries', from the sauce they were cooked into for mackerel in old French cuisine.

Kumquats are small Rutaceae trees native to southern China, the most cold-hardy of the citrus; the 2.5-5 cm fruit has a sweet pulpy skin and slightly acidic inner pulp, and the name is Cantonese gām gwāt, golden orange.

Cydonia oblonga is the only species in its genus and sits in the Malinae, the same subtribe as apple and pear; it is native to the Hyrcanian forests south of the Caspian Sea in Iran, and thrived on the Mesopotamian plain where apples would not.
The Greeks called quince the Cydonian pome, after Kydonia on Crete, and treated it as a sacred emblem of Aphrodite; a quince figures in a lost poem of Callimachus that survives only in prose summary.

Annona cherimola is a low-branched evergreen tree 5 to 9 m tall, native to the mountains of Honduras and Guatemala and long cultivated through the Andes; its short-lived flowers open female and turn male within hours.

Ziziphus jujuba is a thorny buckthorn-family tree of eastern Asia whose fruit holds a single hard kernel like an olive stone; dried it wrinkles into what is sold as the Chinese or red date, though it is unrelated to Phoenix dactylifera.

Amelanchier alnifolia is a rose-family shrub of North America bearing a small purple pome; Indigenous peoples in Canada have long eaten it fresh or dried, and it went into pemmican as flavour and preservative.

Feijoa sellowiana is a myrtle-family relative of the guava with the same gritty pulp, native to the highlands of Colombia, southern Brazil and northeast Uruguay; the cultivars grown internationally descend from a handful of 'Uruguayan type' introductions.

A natural mutation of the sweet orange whose flesh reddens with chrysanthemin, an anthocyanin, only when it develops through cold nights; the arancia rossa di Sicilia holds protected geographical status in Europe.

Citrus × meyeri is a hybrid of a citron with a mandarin/pomelo cross, rounder and less acidic than a true lemon; USDA agricultural explorer Frank N. Meyer collected it in China and introduced it to the United States in 1908.

Citrus australasica is a thorny understorey shrub of lowland subtropical rainforest on the Queensland-New South Wales border; its cylindrical 8 cm fruit holds globular juice vesicles marketed as lime caviar.

Phyllanthus emblica is a small deciduous tree of tropical and southern Asia bearing a hard fruit up to 26 mm across with six vertical furrows, high in ascorbic acid and bitter with ellagitannins such as emblicanin A.

Medlar and quince are both hard rose-family pomes that most varieties can only be eaten raw after bletting; the medlar is picked straight after a hard frost, which breaks down cell walls until the flesh softens enough to spoon out.

Asimina triloba is the custard-apple family's temperate outlier, a clonal understorey tree of North American hardwood forest; like its tropical relatives it carries the neurotoxin annonacin through most of the plant, though the ripe fruit is edible.

Vaccinium membranaceum is a wild western Vaccinium, the most commonly collected of the western huckleberries; black and grizzly bears eat its leaves, stems, roots and fruit, and the shrubs resprout vigorously from buried rhizomes after low-intensity fire.

Vaccinium vitis-idaea is the cranberry's northern relative, native to boreal forest and Arctic tundra across the Northern Hemisphere; it keeps its broad leaves all winter, is hardy to about -45 °C, and grows poorly where summers are hot.

A juniper berry is the female seed cone of a juniper: unlike the separated woody scales of a pine cone, its scales stay fleshy and merge into a single covering, a galbulus. Juniperus communis cones are what give gin its flavour.

Hippophae rhamnoides roots live in symbiosis with nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria and spread rapidly by root suckers, which is why the shrub establishes on poor ground and is planted to stabilise slopes and cut erosion.

Pastinaca sativa is an Apiaceae biennial beside carrot and parsley; its taproot is left in the ground through winter because frost converts part of the starch to sugar, and like its relatives the sap carries phototoxic furanocoumarins.
Helianthus tuberosus is a sunflower native to central North America, grown for tubers that hold 8-13% inulin and little starch; humans cannot break inulin down, so colon bacteria ferment it instead.

Sweet corn is a naturally occurring recessive mutation in the maize genes that convert sugar to starch inside the kernel's endosperm; it is picked immature at the milk stage, not dry at the dent stage, and stores poorly for the same reason.

Bok choy is a Chinese cabbage, Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, whose varieties form a loose cluster rather than a head; the name is Cantonese baak choi, white vegetable, after the lighter bulbous leaf bases.

Endive is Cichorium, an Asteraceae genus alongside dandelion, covering both C. endivia and the chicories sold as Belgian endive and radicchio; varieties are grown for bitter salad leaves, for blanched buds, and for roots roasted as a coffee substitute.

Radicchio is a cultivated leaf chicory, Cichorium intybus, the same genus as endive; the deep-red white-veined form was worked out in 1860 by the agronomist Francesco Van den Borre using imbianchimento, standing lifted plants in water in darkened sheds until chlorophyll production stops.

Chard is Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, the same species as beetroot and sugar beet, selected for its leaves and thick stalks rather than its taproot; its other names — leaf beet, spinach beet, silver beet — all say so.

Collard is Brassica oleracea var. viridis, in the same headless Acephala group as kale but with broad flat leaves borne on an upright stalk that often passes two feet and reaches six in the Portuguese cultivars.

Mustard greens are the leaves of Brassica juncea, the brown or Indian mustard whose seeds are pressed for mustard oil and ground for the condiment; the species is more pungent than kale, broccoli or collard, so it is often mixed with them.

Armoracia rusticana is a Brassicaceae root crop whose intact root has little aroma; cutting or grating it lets the plant's own enzymes digest the glucosinolate sinigrin into allyl isothiocyanate, mustard oil, which irritates the sinuses and eyes.

Yams are the tubers of Dioscorea, perennial herbaceous vines that reach 15 m in length and send tubers up to 1.5 m into the soil; in the United States the name is misapplied to orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, a different family entirely.

Taro is the starchy corm of Colocasia esculenta, toxic raw to humans and pets because of calcium oxalate and needle-shaped raphides in the plant cells; cooking, or steeping overnight in cold water, makes it edible.

Pachyrhizus erosus is a Mesoamerican vine in the pea family Fabaceae, grown for a single crisp tuberous root; the rest of the plant is very poisonous, its mature seeds, flowers and pods high in rotenone, which is used to poison insects and fish.

Kohlrabi is Brassica oleracea Gongylodes Group, a low stout cultivar of the same wild cabbage as broccoli and kale; the name is German Kohl plus Rübe, cabbage-turnip, because the swollen stem resembles one, and Gongylodes means roundish in Greek.
Florence fennel is a cultivar group of Foeniculum vulgare selected so the leaf bases inflate into a bulb-like vegetable — smaller than the wild herb, and sweeter.
A bamboo shoot is a new culm cut as it emerges from the ground; raw it contains cyanogenic glycosides, so it is boiled before any other use.
What is sold as lotus root is the rhizome of Nelumbo nucifera, matured six to nine months and dug out of drained pond or paddy soil.
Rutabaga and rapeseed are both Brassica napus, the same accidental cabbage-turnip hybrid Woo Jang-choon mapped in 1935 — rutabaga is the form bred for its swollen root rather than its oilseed.
Daikon is a winter radish bred for a long napiform taproot, and in some places is deliberately left in the ground because rotting roots loosen compacted soil and recover nutrients.
Under short days this sedge sends rhizomes downward that swell into a corm at the tip; the crop is grown in paddies kept submerged under about 10 cm of water.
Chayote is a Cucurbitaceae vine first cultivated between southern Mexico and Honduras, whose pear-shaped fruit holds a single flattened stone up to 10 cm long.
Spaghetti squash is a cultivar group of Cucurbita pepo — zucchini's own species — bred so the cooked flesh separates from the rind in ribbons and strands.
Acorn squash belongs to Cucurbita pepo, the same species as every summer squash including zucchini; leaving it to harden its rind is what makes it a winter squash instead.
A snow pea is to the pea what a green bean is to the bean — picked unripe and eaten whole, pod and seed together — with flat, thin pod walls rather than the snap pea's round thick ones.
The asparagus bean is Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis, the same cowpea species as the black-eyed pea, grown as a vigorous climbing vine for immature pods 35 to 75 cm long.
Crambe maritima is a halophyte of the cabbage family growing wild on shingle beaches above the high-tide mark, where clumps of it trap wind-blown sand and start dunes.
Salicornia is a leafless salt-marsh succulent that tolerates immersion in seawater; the jointed green stems are the whole of what is eaten.
Napa cabbage is Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis — the turnip's own species — bred to pack its leaves into a dense head weighing 1 to 3 kg instead of swelling a root.
Tatsoi is another Brassica rapa grown for greens, but as a flat rosette rather than a head: harvestable in 45 to 50 days and able to withstand −10 °C under snow.
Komatsuna is Brassica rapa var. perviridis, a leaf variety of the turnip's species cooked like spinach — hence its English name, Japanese mustard spinach.
Basella alba is no relation to spinach: it is a Basellaceae vine climbing to 10 m, cooked for its thick semi-succulent heart-shaped leaves.
Tetragonia tetragonioides is a halophyte of sandy shorelines, unrelated to spinach but cooked the same way — Cook's crew ate it pickled against scurvy and Joseph Banks carried seed back to Kew.
Chaya is a large fast-growing perennial shrub of the spurge family, cropped for leaves cooked like spinach — its English name is literally tree spinach.
Alfalfa seed soaked and rinsed germinates into 5 to 8 cm sprouts in three to five days; both seed and sprout contain L-canavanine.
Mung beans are soaked and kept dark and damp; the sprout is cut in the four-to-five-day window after the seed splits, while the root is still short and soft.
A microgreen is defined against a sprout: it is harvested by cutting above the soil line only after the cotyledon leaves have fully developed and one set of true leaves appears.
Button, cremini and portobello are one species at three ages — leave Agaricus bisporus to mature and the cap opens to 10–15 cm and turns brown.
Teak's natural oils make the timber termite-resistant, water-resistant and durable even untreated, which is why it goes into boat building and exterior construction.
Swietenia's colour, durability and workability made it the cabinet and furniture timber of 18th-century Europe and North America, and overharvesting eventually put all three species under CITES.
Juglans nigra is grown for both nuts and lumber — the USDA valued standing US walnut timber at $530 billion in 2017 — and its hulls are ground for abrasive cleansers.
Prunus serotina, the black cherry, is grown far more for timber than fruit: traded simply as 'cherry', around 560 kg/m³ dried, prized for tight grain and strong orange hues.
Ash seeds are samaras, known as keys; the genus Fraxinus sits in the olive family and has nothing to do with the ash left behind by fire.
Ceylon ebony is felled for its black heartwood alone — up to 1,200 kg/m³, twice the hardness of oak, water- and termite-resistant, and illegal to harvest in Sri Lanka.

Santalum album is the traditional source of sandalwood oil and paste, burned as incense and held sacred in Hinduism — over-exploited for it to the point that the wild population is vulnerable to extinction.
Frankincense is the tree's own sap: a shallow incision in the trunk or branches of Boswellia sacra drains a milky substance that coagulates on contact with air.
Commiphora myrrha thrives in the arid and semi-arid country of Somalia, Ethiopia and the southern Arabian Peninsula, and Somalia is the largest producer of both myrrh and frankincense.
Quercus suber is the evergreen oak cork actually comes from: past 25 years old its thick bark can be harvested every 9 to 12 years without harming a tree that may live two centuries.
Cinchona species are known as fever trees for their antimalarial bark — the only effective treatment against malaria through the height of European colonialism.
Powdered cinchona bark entered the London Pharmacopoeia in 1677 as Cortex Peruanus, and British and Dutch plantations later mass-produced quinine from it in India and Java.
Azadirachta indica is native to the Indian subcontinent, where its leaves and twigs have been used against insect pests for more than 2,000 years.
Neem seeds hold the highest concentration of azadirachtin in the tree, 0.2 to 0.8 percent by weight, an antifeedant and growth disruptor active against over 600 insect species.
Natural camphor is condensed from the vapour of roasted chips, or from steam passed through the pulverised wood, of this evergreen laurel.
The olive tree's gnarled, twisted trunk yields a hard, dense, attractively figured timber that is worked for decorative objects alongside the fruit crop.
Agarwood forms only after Aquilaria trees are infected by the mould Phaeoacremonium parasitica and flood the heartwood with defensive resin.
Aquilaria heartwood is pale and scentless until a Phaeoacremonium mould infects it; the tree floods the wound with a dark defensive resin, and that resin-soaked heartwood is agarwood.
Goats climb into argan branches to browse the fruit, and the nuts are collected after the ruminating animals spit them out, one route of the tree's seed dispersal.
The arganeraie forests of southwestern Morocco, a UNESCO biosphere reserve of about 8,280 square kilometres, are the tree's main native range.
Vitellaria paradoxa grows wild across the dry savannah belt from Senegal to the Ethiopian foothills, and it is the oil-rich seed inside the tart fruit pulp that is harvested.
Fat roasted and pressed from its kernels is shea butter; the tree's former genus name Butyrospermum literally means 'butter seed'.
Spruce is the standard tonewood for the soundboards of violins and guitars, long cut from stands such as the Paneveggio 'Violin Forest' in the Dolomites.
Spruce makes good pulpwood because its long fibres bind into strong paper, especially from trees over 60 years old.
Firs are distinguished within the pine family by needle-like leaves attached singly on a circular base, and by upright cones that disintegrate at maturity.
Bald cypress grows in standing swamp water, throwing up knees around its trunk, and its mature heartwood is valued for resisting rot.
Dense, sweet-smelling Dalbergia timber is the traditional wood for guitar fretboards, marimba bars and luxury furniture.
White mulberry leaves are the preferred feed of the silkworm Bombyx mori, and cultivating the tree for them began in China more than 4,700 years ago.
Its fibre-rich inner bark makes mulberry paper, strong and durable enough to be the preferred support for traditional Chinese painting.
Prunus dulcis bears the almond as a drupe of hull, hard shell and seed, and domestication began by selecting sweet-kernelled trees out of bitter wild stands.
Bitter almonds hydrolyse amygdalin into benzaldehyde and 4 to 9 mg of hydrogen cyanide per nut; the sweet cultivar is a mutant that cannot make it.
Carya illinoinensis is a hickory whose fruit is not a true nut but a drupe, a single stone released when the four-part husk splits.
The cashew's true fruit is a kidney-shaped drupe hanging below the swollen cashew apple, which is the expanded flower stalk rather than the fruit.
Cashew nutshell liquid carries anacardic acid and cardol, phenolic irritants related to poison ivy's urushiol, which is why cashews are never sold in the shell.
Castanea sativa, native to southern Europe and Anatolia, ripens starchy nuts inside a spiny bur that splits open on the tree.
Chestnut wood is about 13.4 percent tannin, which is what makes untreated coppiced poles durable enough for stakes and fencing in ground contact.
Corylus avellana, in the birch family, bears hazelnuts in clusters of one to five, each held in a short leafy husk it drops free of when ripe.
Alder roots host the nitrogen-fixing actinobacterium Frankia alni in nodules that may be as large as a fist, enriching the soil for the species that follow.
Fender has built electric guitar bodies from alder since the 1950s, valued for an evenly balanced tone and a plain grain that takes opaque lacquer.
Linden's fragrant flowers are a major nectar source for beekeepers, giving a pale, richly flavoured monofloral honey.
The soft inner bark of Tilia, called bast, is fibrous with high tensile strength, and gives the North American name basswood.
Sphagnum is the moss whose slow decay, protected by phenolic compounds in its cell walls and by anaerobic bog water, forms peat itself.
Sphagnum was used as a surgical wound dressing for centuries and through the First World War, after Hotson's 1918 paper in Science argued it beat cotton.
Tillandsia usneoides is a bromeliad, in the pineapple family, growing as an epiphyte that absorbs water and nutrients through its own leaves rather than roots.
Papyrus sheets were made from the pith of Cyperus papyrus, a sedge of the Nile shallows, cut into strips and laid crosswise in two layers.
The plant's highly buoyant stems were bundled into boats in ancient Egypt, which also used it for baskets, sandals, incense and fuel.
Typha rhizomes are a starch store with protein comparable to maize or rice; starch grains on European grinding stones show they were eaten 30,000 years ago.
In midsummer the mature male spikes shed pollen collected as a flour supplement, which the Maori bake into a bread called pungapunga.
Rattan canes are the stems of climbing Calamoideae palms, bent and woven into wickerwork furniture; almost all of it is still cut from wild plants.
Raffia fibre is stripped from the epidermal membrane on the underside of the leaf frond, then rolled together and dried into twine.
Coir is the fibre lying between the coconut's outer coat and its hard inner shell, freed by driving the fruit down onto a spike to dehusk it.
Austronesian voyagers lashed plank boats with coir cordage, and 11th-century Arab writers describe coir ropes and rigging on ships.
Levi Dickenson bound a broom from the tassels of the sorghum he grew for grain in 1797, and the panicle branches of this variety became the standard broom bristle.
Gum arabic is the dried exudate that runs from bark stripped off Senegalia senegal and Vachellia seyal, tapped by Sahelian pastoralists.
E414, the stabiliser in soft drinks and the binder in watercolour paint and lithography, is harvested from wild acacia trees across the Sahel.
Parthenium argentatum stores rubber in the stem tissue of a Chihuahuan Desert shrub, and the US turned to it for rubber when Japan cut off Malayan latex in the Second World War.
Guayule latex performs like Hevea but has none of the proteins that cause Type 1 latex allergy, the reaction that surged with glove demand in the 1980s.
Rumex hymenosepalus was cultivated in the southwestern United States for its roots, a good source of tannin for leather tanning.
Sweet gale was a main ingredient of gruit, the herb mixture used to bitter and flavour beer in the Low Countries before hops displaced it.
Its sweet resinous foliage is a traditional insect repellent, used by campers and marketed in Scotland against the Highland midge.

Serpentinite forms when mafic or ultramafic rock is hydrated by carbon-dioxide-deficient seawater pressed into it far below the ocean floor — at mid-ocean ridges, and in the forearc mantle above subduction zones.
Chrysotile is the only asbestos mineral in the serpentine group and comes out of serpentinite rock, which is common worldwide; the other five regulated forms are amphiboles.
Inhaled asbestos fibres lodge in the lining of the lung. The latency from exposure to diagnosis is typically twenty years, and mesothelioma often leaves less than twelve months after that.

Its armour is bone: hundreds of osteoderms grown inside the skin and fused into a shield across the back, ending in a club of fused tail vertebrae. Bone is the material, not a shell — ankylosaurs are not related to any shelled animal, and the resemblance is convergent.

Excavated from Mount Kirkpatrick in the Transantarctic Mountains in 1990-91, the first carnivorous dinosaur ever described from Antarctica. The rock is Early Jurassic, laid down when the continent sat far enough north to carry forest.
Known from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia, whose fine wind-blown sandstone preserved the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen — a Protoceratops locked together with a Velociraptor, buried mid-struggle.

From the Ischigualasto Formation in northwestern Argentina, dated to about 231 million years ago — among the oldest dinosaur-bearing rock anywhere, which is why it sits so close to the base of the family tree.

The first non-avian dinosaur ever found with feathers, described in 1996. The filaments are preserved well enough that their melanosomes survive, and their shape gives the colour: a banded, ginger-and-white tail.

Three skeletons from the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, China, all carrying filamentous feathers. At roughly 1,400 kg it is the largest dinosaur with direct evidence of them, forty times heavier than the previous record-holder.

Alberta's Hilda site is a bonebed of Centrosaurus so dense it is thought to be the largest dinosaur bonebed ever found — a herd drowned together, which is how we know the animal lived in herds at all.

The Kem Kem beds of eastern Morocco supply nearly everything now known about it; the original Egyptian specimen was destroyed in a 1944 air raid on Munich. Isotopes from the Moroccan teeth show a life spent largely in water.

Every specimen comes from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, a lagoon bed so fine it holds feather impressions. The first was found in 1861, two years after On the Origin of Species, and became the fossil that showed birds descend from dinosaurs.
Both known skeletons preserve a lizard in the gut — Bavarisaurus, swallowed whole. That is direct evidence of what it ate, which is rarer than a skeleton and is why this small theropod matters.

Genetic work has shown that Aconitum, as the genus was drawn before the 21st century, is nested inside Delphinium in the broad sense — monkshood arose from within the larkspurs rather than beside them. The genus now runs to over 250 species, chiefly through the mountains of the Northern Hemisphere in North America, Europe and Asia.

Amphipods are crustaceans that never grew a carapace, and a mature female carries her eggs in a brood pouch, the marsupium. There are no larval stages at all — the eggs hatch directly into juveniles — and over 10,700 species are now recognised, from a group thought to have originated in the Lower Carboniferous though its confirmed fossils only begin in the Lower Cretaceous.

Bos acutifrons, found in the Sivalik Hills of India in Early Pleistocene rock about 2 million years old, is considered a possible ancestor of the aurochs, though whether the species itself first arose in Asia or Africa is still argued. The oldest well-dated aurochs fossil is a skull from Tunisia, roughly 780,000 years old.

The brown bear is thought to have evolved from the Etruscan bear, Ursus etruscus, in Asia during the early Pliocene; its oldest fossils there are 500,000 to 300,000 years old. It reached Europe about 250,000 years ago, and crossed into North America over Beringia, where the founding genetic lineage dates to around 177,000 years ago.

A miner, Shawn Funk, struck it on 21 March 2011 in the Millennium oil sands mine 30 km north of Fort McMurray, Alberta, in marine rock of the Clearwater Formation laid down 110 to 112 million years ago. The 1.3-tonne block then took Mark Mitchell six years of preparation to free from the stone around it.

DNA up to 7,000 years old, read from the bones of wild and early-domesticated animals, puts the first domestication on the southeast coast of the Arabian Peninsula, and shows herders going back to wild dromedaries to breed into the domestic stock long afterwards. That wild ancestor had a narrow range and died out about 2,000 years after the first taming.

Chilopoda is one of the four living myriapod classes, and the only one to have turned its first pair of walking legs into forcipules — claws that fold forward over the mouth and carry venom glands. Every centipede is venomous, every centipede has one pair of legs per segment where a millipede has two, and the class runs back 430 million years to the Late Silurian.

Most of the 3,000-odd described cicadas spend two to five years underground as nymphs, but the periodical Magicicada of North America come up together on 13- or 17-year clocks. A prime number is hard for a predator's own cycle to lock onto: a 17-year cicada facing a predator that peaks every five years meets that peak only once in 85.

The lineage that produced the cougar, the jaguarundi and the cheetah crossed the Bering land bridge into the Americas 8 to 8.5 million years ago. The cougar now spans 110 degrees of latitude, from the Yukon to the southern Andes, and one reading of the genetics has North America repopulated from southern stock after the Pleistocene megafaunal extinction around 10,000 years ago.

Amanita phalloides is native to Europe, from southern Scandinavia to Ireland, east to Poland and western Russia and south through the Mediterranean. It travelled on roots people shipped: a 2006 review concluded the East Coast populations in North America were introduced inadvertently on imported plants such as chestnuts, and introduced oaks appear to have been the vector to Australia and South America.

The first bones came out of Marshall Felch's quarry at Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado in 1877, and Othniel Charles Marsh named the genus the following year. It belongs to the Morrison Formation, 152 to 149 million years old, which yields it from Wyoming, Utah and Montana as well; the tail alone carried about 80 caudal vertebrae.

It hatches in the Sargasso Sea as a leptocephalus — a flat, leaf-shaped larva that looks nothing like an eel — and drifts towards Europe on a migration of about 300 days. Reaching the coast it metamorphoses into a transparent glass eel, enters the estuaries, and many then work their way upstream.

A molecular study puts the ancestral origin of Amanita muscaria in the Siberian–Beringian region in the Tertiary, from which it radiated outwards across Asia, Europe and North America. Conveyed since with pine seedlings, it has reached Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and South America, where in places it behaves like the fungal equivalent of a weed.

Rubén Darío Carolini, an amateur fossil hunter, found the tibia while driving a dune buggy through the badlands near Villa El Chocón in 1993. The skeleton came out of the Candeleros Formation in Neuquén province, 111 to 106 million years old, and almost 70% of it was preserved — one of the most complete carcharodontosaurs known.

Gorillas, chimpanzees and humans all diverged from a common ancestor about 7 million years ago, and human gene sequences still differ from the matching gorilla genes by only 1.6% on average. The two gorilla species hold the equatorial forests of west central and east central Africa, their ranges separated by the Congo River and its tributaries.

A 2021 genomic study traced every modern domestic horse to one lineage, DOM2, domesticated around 2200 BCE in the Volga–Don region of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, which then expanded across Eurasia and replaced the local horse populations outright. Przewalski's horse is not the ancestor — it descends from a different regional gene pool on the eastern steppe.

The German Tendaguru Expedition found the first bones in 1909 in what is now the Lindi Region of Tanzania, and over four field seasons collected more than 1,200 of them, belonging to about fifty individuals; Edwin Hennig named the genus in 1915. The rock is Late Jurassic, roughly 152 million years old, and much of the collection was destroyed in the Second World War.

Lemon sharks are viviparous: the mother feeds the embryo directly through a yolk-sac placenta across a year of gestation, and then gives birth to as many as 18 live pups. Females are philopatric, returning to the shallow nursery water they know to drop them.

The earliest fossils recognisable as lions were found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania and are estimated at up to 2 million years old. From Africa the lion first dispersed into Eurasia around a million years ago, giving rise to the cave lion lineage; the Panthera lineage it belongs to split from the common ancestor of the cats about 10.8 million years ago.

Workmen on a highway construction site in Sichuan turned up the first skeleton in 1952, and C. C. Young named it in 1954 after a nearby crossing on the river. Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis carried 19 cervical vertebrae in a neck about 9.3 metres long — lightly built, highly pneumatic, and close to half the animal's total length.

Suricata suricatta is a small mongoose, and its genus split from the rest of that clade somewhere between 22.6 and 15.6 million years ago. It lives in southwestern Botswana, western and southern Namibia and northern and western South Africa, with the range barely reaching into southwestern Angola.

The first specimen came out of a chalk quarry near Maastricht in 1764, and the famous second skull from the same quarry in 1778. In 1808 Georges Cuvier concluded it belonged to a giant marine lizard with similarities to monitor lizards but unlike any living animal — an extinct form — and Conybeare named it in 1822 after the Meuse.

The genus holds about 170 species, mostly liana-forming plants of the Old World tropics, and the greatest diversity of them is on Borneo, Sumatra and the Philippines — thinning to two species in Madagascar, one in Sri Lanka, one in New Caledonia. With no intermediate forms known, all of them appear to have radiated from a single close ancestor that already had the pitcher.

Lophophora williamsii grows in desert scrub and limestone ground in the Chihuahuan Desert — Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas down to San Luis Potosí and Zacatecas, crossing into southern Texas — mostly between 100 and 1,500 m. In the wild it is extremely slow growing, where a cultivated plant can go from seedling to flowering in under three years.

Conium maculatum is an umbellifer, in the carrot and parsley family, native to Europe, Central Asia and the Mediterranean. It reached the United States from Europe in the 1800s as a garden ornamental sold as 'winter fern', and has since naturalised across Asia, North America, Australia and New Zealand — it is the poison that killed Socrates after his trial.

The psilocybin pathway is a cluster of five genes — a tryptophan decarboxylase, a P450 monooxygenase, a methyltransferase, a phosphotransferase and a transporter — and it has not simply descended down one family tree. The analyses support horizontal transfer of the whole cluster between divergent dung decomposers in the genera Psilocybe and Panaeolus, the first such case found in mushroom-forming fungi.

In 1989 morphological and genetic studies showed that the trout of the Pacific basin are closer to the Pacific salmon than to the Atlantic genus Salmo, and the rainbow trout was moved into Oncorhynchus. Its native range runs from Kamchatka east along the Aleutians and south to northern Mexico, and the sea-going form, the steelhead, is iteroparous — able to spawn several times instead of dying after one run.

One saguaro fruit holds around 2,000 seeds, and predation and lack of moisture leave only about 1% of them to germinate. A survivor may be 6.4 mm tall after two years and take 20 to 50 years to reach a metre; the first arm comes at 75 to 100 years, and the plant can live 150 to 200.

Zygentoma are primitive wingless insects — apterygotes, which never had wings to lose — and the order goes back to the Pennsylvanian. A silverfish is also one of the few insects that keeps moulting after it is adult: 17 to 66 times over a life of two to eight years, sometimes 30 times in one year.

Springtails are hexapods but no longer counted as insects: their mouthparts are held inside the head capsule, which is what puts Collembola with the Protura and Diplura in the Entognatha. Rhyniella praecursor, from the Rhynie chert of Scotland about 400 million years ago, is the oldest known, and soil today is estimated to hold 100,000 springtails per square metre.

Charles H. Sternberg found the holotype skull in the summer of 1913 along the Red Deer River in Alberta, about 19 km below the mouth of Berry Creek, and Lawrence Lambe named the animal that same year. The rock is the Dinosaur Park Formation, 75.5 to 74.5 million years old; the rest of the skeleton was dug out in 1935 and reunited with the skull in 1955.

Ticks are arachnids — parasitic mites of the order Ixodida within the superorder Parasitiformes, about 980 species in 37 genera. They are obligate hematophages, unable to pass from one life stage to the next without a meal of vertebrate blood, and the oldest tick fossils, around 100 million years old, come from Cretaceous amber.

Fruiting underground costs a fungus the wind and water that would otherwise carry its spores away, and fungi have arrived at it more than once, by convergent evolution in water-limited places. Instead a truffle exudes volatile compounds that draw animal vectors — deer, voles, squirrels, flying squirrels — and the spores come through digestion intact behind thick chitin walls.

Carl Limone's find of a large claw in October 1991 led to excavation at the Gaston Quarry in Grand County, Utah, and Kirkland, Gaston and Burge named the animal in June 1993. It comes from the Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, 139 to 134.6 million years old; the sickle claw measured about 24 cm, and a nine-ton sandstone block found in 2001 held at least seven individuals.

The genus Equus arose in North America — paleogenomic work puts the most recent common ancestor of all living equines at about 4.07 million years ago — and dispersed into the Old World during the Early and Middle Pleistocene. Zebras and asses split from each other around 2 million years ago, and the three zebra species live in eastern and southern Africa.

Equus is the only recognised living genus of the horse family, seven species of horse, ass and zebra, and every one of them takes its weight on a single digit — the middle one, the side toes shrinking away through the Pleistocene until the single-toed form emerged. The dentition tracks the same shift: large incisors that clip grass blades, and tall ridged molars for grinding it.

Sauropods carried a system of air sacs, as other saurischians including birds do, and it hollowed the skeleton out from the inside — some vertebrae ran to 60% air. That is what made the necks possible: the spaces cut the weight they had to hold up, and one-way airflow through stiff lungs got enough oxygen into an animal that size.

Myriapods breathe through spiracles opening into a tracheal system, and all of the roughly 13,000 species across their four classes are terrestrial — trace fossils have them on land by the Ordovician, and the oldest body fossils are about 427 million years old. They carry a single pair of antennae, simple eyes, and a long tubular heart.

Herpestidae runs to 34 living species in 14 genera, across southern Europe, Africa and Asia. Mongooses are one of at least four mammal groups carrying a mutation in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that stops snake venom's α-neurotoxin binding to it — and the only one in which the change is made by glycosylation.

A dromedary jawbone dated to 8,200 BC was found in Saudi Arabia on the southern coast of the Red Sea, thousands of years before any herder took the animal in. Nothing like it is left standing: the dromedary has not occurred naturally in the wild for nearly 2,000 years.

Lycaon is not a wolf and not a dog: a 2019 study puts the split of its lineage from Canis and Cuon at 1.7 million years ago, after which it specialised in Africa for a hypercarnivorous life. It has no dewclaws at all, the heel of its lower carnassial is a shearing blade — the trenchant heel — and its premolars are the largest relative to body size of any carnivore but the hyenas.

Linnaeus filed these plants under Datura in 1753, and it took until 1973, when T. E. Lockwood settled the question, for Brugmansia to stand unchallenged as a separate genus — woody trees and shrubs 3 to 11 m tall against Datura's herbs. All seven species are listed Extinct in the Wild; no wild plant has ever been confirmed, and the suspicion is that whatever animal once dispersed their seed is gone as well.

Colchicum autumnale is a monocot of the family Colchicaceae, in the order Liliales, growing from a bulb-like corm across mainland Europe from Portugal to Ukraine — the only member of its family native to Great Britain and Ireland. Its flowers come up long before the leaves, which is why it is called naked ladies, and the corms carry colchicine, a drug with a famously narrow therapeutic index.

Bees are descended from stinging wasps: molecular work published in 2018 recovers Ammoplanidae, predators of other insects, as their closest relatives. The switch is thought to have started with prey that were themselves flower visitors, partly covered in pollen and carried back to wasp larvae, and bees appear during the Early Cretaceous about 124 million years ago on West Gondwana.

On 4 July 1900 the field assistant Harold Menke found a humerus in the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation, in the valley of the Colorado River near Fruita, Colorado, and Elmer Riggs named Brachiosaurus altithorax from that material in 1903. The African Tendaguru skeletons long carried under the same genus were taken out in 2009, when Michael Taylor found significant divergences in every element known from both and made them Giraffatitan, leaving Brachiosaurus a North American animal.

William Harlow Reed found the first remains on 4 September 1879 in Albany County, Wyoming; Marsh named them Camptonotus that year and changed it to Camptosaurus in 1885, the first name already belonging to a cricket. It is a basal member of Ankylopollexia within Iguanodontia, standing between the small early ornithopods and the iguanodonts and hadrosaurs that came after.

Sequoia sempervirens carries six chromosome sets, 2n=66, which is unusual among conifers; Yang and colleagues argued in 2010 that it is an allopolyploid, AAAABB, formed from ancestors of the giant sequoia and the dawn redwood. Those extra copies come with the largest genome measured in any plant up to 2020, 26.5 gigabases.

The coyote's line is American throughout: Eucyon davisi in the Miocene 6 million years ago in the southwestern US and Mexico, the larger Canis lepophagus by the Pliocene, and fossils inside the range of the modern species by 0.74 to 0.85 million years ago at Hamilton Cave, West Virginia. A 2016 genome study placed the split between North American wolves and coyotes at about 51,000 years ago, and the two have never fully separated — every coyote carries some wolf ancestry and every North American wolf some coyote.

Cervidae is the mammal family that grows antlers: single structures of bone, cartilage, fibrous tissue, skin, nerve and blood vessel, shed and regrown every year and growing faster than any other mammal bone, extending at the tip as cartilage under the highly vascular skin called velvet that feeds them until the bone dies and the velvet comes off. That is the line between deer and the horned mammals — a bovid's horn is a two-part structure, bone under a keratin sheath, and it is not shed. The first antlered cervids, Dicrocerus, Euprox and Heteroprox, appear in the Eurasian Miocene, and as antlers came in the tusks of their antlerless ancestors went out.

Every donkey descends from the African wild ass, Equus africanus, by way of its Nubian and Somali subspecies, domesticated in Africa some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago — pastoralists in Nubia and Cushitic-speaking peoples of the Horn of Africa appear to have done it separately. Domestic donkey remains from the fourth millennium BC turn up at Ma'adi in Lower Egypt, while the wild ancestor is down to a few hundred animals in the deserts of Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia.

The stem group earwigs came from is the Protelytroptera, Permian insects with shell-like forewings and a large, unequal anal fan, known from North America, Europe and Australia. The earwig record itself starts on the far side of that boundary, in the Late Triassic about 208 million years ago in England and Australia, with around 70 specimens of the extinct suborder Archidermaptera — animals with veined tegmina and cerci not yet curled into the pincers of a modern earwig.

A flatfish starts as an ordinary symmetrical larva, and thyroid hormone then remakes it: one eye migrates across the top of the head to join the other, and the fish spends the rest of its life lying on its blind side. Amphistium and Heteronectes, about 50 million years old, catch the change partway — still an eye on each side, but one carried up towards the midline — and over 800 living species in 16 families descend from that reorganisation.

Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska found the largest skeleton at Tsaagan Khushuu in 1964, during the Polish and Mongolian academies' expeditions of 1963 to 1965 into the Nemegt Formation of the Gobi. Halszka Osmólska, Ewa Roniewicz and Rinchen Barsbold named Gallimimus bullatus from it in 1972 and placed it in the family Ornithomimidae, within Ornithomimosauria.

Helodermatid lizards have a long North American history: the genus Heloderma has been present since the Miocene, in H. texana, while the family's roots run back to the Cretaceous. The splits inside the genus fall in the Late Miocene around 10 million years ago and the Pliocene at about 4.4 and 3.0 million years, and Gila monster osteoderms turn up in Late Pleistocene deposits near Las Vegas dated 10,000 to 8,000 years old.

Hammerheads evolved out of the requiem sharks, Carcharhinidae, the family the bull shark belongs to, with DNA estimates putting the family's origin in the Miocene about 20 million years ago. The hammer is a sensory spread rather than a shape: distributing the ampullae of Lorenzini over a wider area lets the shark sweep for prey like a larger antenna, and the winghead, sister to all other hammerheads and owner of the widest head, suggests the first hammerheads were already broad.

Aesculus belongs to Sapindaceae, the maple, soapberry and lychee family. The conker tree now planted around the world is a Balkan relict: natively it grows only in Albania, Bulgaria, mainland Greece and North Macedonia, and Bulgaria's share is 9 hectares in the Preslav Mountain, in the valleys of the Dervishka and Lazarska rivers — enough for the IUCN to list a globally familiar tree as Vulnerable.

Koalas and wombats are the two surviving branches of Vombatiformes; the koala's lineage possibly split off around 40 million years ago in the Eocene, and Phascolarctos separated from the smaller Litokoala in the late Miocene. What the eucalypt diet has cost it since shows in the anatomy — a caecum 200 cm long and 10 cm across, and a brain 60% smaller than a typical diprotodont's, averaging 19.2 g.

Lemurs are strepsirrhine primates whose ancestors crossed from Africa on tangled mats of vegetation flushed out of rivers, over a Mozambique Channel at least 560 km wide; 60 million years ago Madagascar and Africa both sat 1,650 km further south, where the currents could have cut the trip to 30 days or less. From that founding population, dated to 62 to 65 million years ago by genetics or 50 to 55 on more conservative estimates, came about 100 living species in 15 genera and eight families.

Liverworts descend from the charophyte green algae that made the move onto land, and they sit at the base of the plants that resulted. Five different types of fossilised liverwort spore, found in Argentina in 2010, date to the Middle Ordovician around 470 million years ago; some 9,000 species live now, at least 85% of them in the leafy group.

A mantis is a cockroach's close kin: mantises, cockroaches and termites together make up Dictyoptera. The mantis line's own fossils begin with the Jurassic Lovec, reported in 2024 from the Karabastau Formation, and the earliest confidently identified mantises of the Early Cretaceous, among them the 10 mm Santanmantis axelrodi described in 2003 — from which over 2,400 species in about 460 genera and 33 families are recognised today.

The megamouth is a mackerel shark, Lamniformes, the same order as the basking shark, but its filter-feeding adaptations are thought to have evolved independently of every other living filter feeder, the basking shark included — the resemblance is convergence, not inheritance. It is the smallest of the three filter-feeding sharks and one of the least seen: as of 25 March 2025 only 296 had been caught or sighted, the first on 15 November 1976, snagged on a US Navy vessel's sea anchor at about 165 m off Kahuku, Hawaii.

A mosquito is a true fly like the housefly — one pair of wings, the hind pair reduced to halteres for balance — but from the older long-antennaed side of Diptera, in the infraorder Culicomorpha. The group diversified in the Cretaceous: Burmaculex in Burmese amber dates to about 99 million years ago, Paleoculicis minutus in Canadian amber to about 79, and a 2023 claim for Libanoculex in Lebanese amber reaches about 125 million years, though other authors read that fossil as a chaoborid instead.

Crocodylus is an Indo-Pacific genus that reached Africa secondarily, and the Nile crocodile's own lineage shows up in the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene of Kenya, in fossils dated about 7 to 5 million years old. It now ranges across 26 African countries, from the Nile tributaries of Sudan and Lake Nasser to the Cunene in Angola and the Olifants in South Africa, and the West African animals long counted with it stand separated as Crocodylus suchus on morphology, genetics and habitat alike.

Oysters are bivalves like the mussel, but where a mussel spins byssal threads that harden in seawater and tether it to rock, an oyster cements a valve down permanently. Ostreidae evolved in the Early Triassic — the genus Liostrea grew on the shells of living ammonoids — and a mature oyster filters 11 to 45 litres of water a day, up to 190 in ideal laboratory conditions.

Every pig breed but the Timor and Papua New Guinea stock descends from the wild boar, Sus scrofa, and it happened twice over: in the Tigris Basin of the Near East as early as 13,000 to 12,700 BCE, and separately in China about 8,000 years ago. Remains on Cyprus dated earlier than 11,400 BCE show domestic pigs were already being carried off the mainland by then.

Pokeweed is native to eastern North America, the Midwest, the Gulf Coast and the West Coast, and it belongs to Caryophyllales, the order of amaranth, beets and cacti, whose members colour themselves with betalains where other plants use anthocyanins — the two have never been found together in one plant. The magenta of a pokeweed stem and berry is betanin, and the same fruit that birds strip safely has killed infants who ate only a few raw berries.

Psittacosaurus is known from hundreds of individuals, most of them Chinese — the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, the Qingshan Formation of Shandong, the Jiufotang — in strata of the Aptian and Albian, roughly 125 to 100 million years ago. Osborn named the type species in 1924 from material of the 1922 Third Asiatic Expedition, and with up to 13 species it is the most species-rich non-avian dinosaur genus, an early ceratopsian standing below the horned dinosaurs that followed.

A ram is a male lamb that kept its testes. Castration, now usually done at around three or four weeks of age, takes away the gonads and the testosterone with them and produces a wether instead; left intact, a ram reaches sexual maturity at four to six months, ahead of ewes at six to eight.

Salvia divinorum is a sage of the mint family, hollow square stems and all, endemic to the Sierra Mazateca of Oaxaca and known only as a plant people keep: it reproduces vegetatively, no seed has ever been observed on a wild plant, and even in flower it sets few viable ones. Botanists have not settled whether it is a cultigen or a hybrid, and what carries it forward is cuttings 5 to 20 cm long, taken below a node, which root in plain tap water in two or three weeks.

Anatomy, molecules and genetics all place seahorses inside the pipefish family Syngnathidae — a seahorse is a highly modified pipefish, the two lineages having diverged in the Late Oligocene. The upright posture is thought to answer new shallow water raised by tectonic movement, which let seagrass beds spread and gave an upright fish cover; the oldest seahorse fossils, from the Tunjice Hills of Slovenia, are about 13 million years old and still pipefish-like.

Sloths and anteaters are the two branches of the order Pilosa, within the xenarthrans, placental mammals thought to have evolved in South America around 60 million years ago. The common ancestor of the two living sloth genera dates to about 28 million years ago, and Bradypus and Choloepus come from different, distantly related families — their shared life hanging in trees is one of the most striking cases of convergent evolution known among mammals.

Lawrence Lambe collected three partial skull domes from the Belly River Group along the Red Deer River in Alberta, two in 1898 and one in 1901, and named Stegoceras validus from them in 1902 — roof-horn, for the thickened cap. It is a basal member of Pachycephalosauridae, the family whose best-known animal is Pachycephalosaurus, and its type material comes from the Dinosaur Park and Oldman Formations, about 77.5 to 74 million years old.

Helarctos malayanus is the smallest bear, standing near 70 cm at the shoulder at 25 to 65 kg, and its line diverged from the two black bears between about 6.26 and 5.09 million years ago — the sloth bear and the sun bear were the first ursine bears to radiate away from the Ursus group. Its range is the forest belt from Northeast India through Bangladesh, mainland Southeast Asia, Brunei and Indonesia, reaching into Yunnan.

The tiger's closest living relative is the snow leopard, the two lineages splitting from each other between 2.70 and 3.70 million years ago within Panthera. Glaciation then squeezed the tiger hard: the population contracted around 115,000 years ago, every living tiger traces to a common ancestor from between 108,000 and 72,000 years ago, and modern populations spread back across Asia from a refuge in Indochina after the Last Glacial Maximum.

Tunas are the tribe Thunnini inside Scombridae, the mackerel family — 15 species in five genera, built on the same finletted, deeply forked plan. What separates them is heat: a rete mirabile, veins and arteries interwoven at the body's periphery, reclaims nearly all the metabolic warmth from venous blood, letting a bluefin hold a core of 25 to 33 °C in water as cold as 6 °C.

Peter Kaisen found the holotype skull on 11 August 1923 at the Flaming Cliffs, in the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia, and Osborn named Velociraptor mongoliensis the following year. It is a dromaeosaurid, kin to Microraptor and Deinonychus, and in 2007 Alan Turner and colleagues reported six quill knobs on an ulna spaced so that 14 were likely present — the marks a feathered forearm leaves in bone.

The zebra shark is the only living member of Stegostomatidae, and there is robust morphological support for placing it in a single clade with the whale shark and the nurse sharks among the carpet sharks — one analysis makes it the sister group to Rhincodon and Ginglymostoma together. Its name comes from the young: juveniles wear light vertical stripes on brown, which break up at 50 to 90 cm into the adult's dark spots on pale, a change so complete that the two stages were once described as separate species.

Equus arose in North America and spread quickly into the Old World, and molecular dating puts the split between the caballine horses and the non-caballine line at about 4 million years ago, within a genus whose most recent common ancestor lived some 5.6 million years back. The African wild ass, Equus africanus, sits on the non-caballine side in the subgenus Asinus — nearer kin to the zebras it shares a continent with than to any horse.

Mitochondrial studies place the origin of Sus scrofa on the islands of Southeast Asia, from which it spread onto mainland Eurasia and North Africa; the earliest fossils of the species, from Europe and Asia alike, are Early Pleistocene. Moving west it displaced Sus strozzii, a large, possibly swamp-adapted suid, by the late Villafranchian restricting that animal to insular Asia — and the sixteen or so subspecies recognised in 2005 still sort into Western, Indian, Eastern and Indonesian groups by skull height and lacrimal bone length.

Syngnathids — pipefishes, seahorses and seadragons — are fish rebuilt around one set of traits: an elongated snout with the jaws fused shut, no pelvic fins, and thick plates of bony armour in place of scales.
