Carrying the eggs falls to the male throughout the family, and the family is old, the earliest syngnathids coming from Paleocene strata of the Dakhla Formation in Egypt and the Eocene of Monte Bolca in Italy.

Scombridae holds 51 living species in 15 genera, divided into the mackerels proper, the Spanish mackerels, the bonitos and the tunas, and the family reaches back to the Danian, the first age of the Paleocene. What the branches share is the swimming gear: two dorsal fins with a row of finlets behind them, a stiff, deeply divided tail on a slender ridged base, and a spiny dorsal and pelvic fins that retract into grooves in the body.

Albertosaurus is a tyrannosaurid — the same family as Tyrannosaurus, in its own subfamily Albertosaurinae — and at 8–9 m it stayed much smaller than its famous relative. Its type skull was collected on 9 June 1884 from an outcrop of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation alongside the Red Deer River in Alberta, and a bonebed Barnum Brown found nearby on 11 August 1910 has since given up 1,128 bones from at least 12 individuals.

Ants evolved from vespoid wasp ancestors in the Cretaceous; the oldest ant fossils date to about 113–100 million years ago, and the modern subfamilies appear around 80–70 million years ago. What separates them from those wasps is the caste system — one or more reproducing queens and castes of sterile, wingless females — which is why a colony is described as a superorganism.

The axolotl is a salamander that reaches sexual maturity without ever metamorphosing, a condition called neoteny: it lacks the thyroid-stimulating hormone that would set off the thyroxine surge other amphibians use to leave the water. Dose it with thyroid hormone and it metamorphoses after all. Within Ambystomatidae its closest relative is the eastern tiger salamander, and it is native to the lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco in the Valley of Mexico.

The betel nut is the seed of Areca catechu, a palm native to the Philippines that grows straight to 20 m on a trunk only 10–15 cm across. It is not a true nut at all but the seed of a fruit classed as a berry, and the palm is grown commercially for that one seed crop.

Bracken is a fern, so like other ferns it reproduces by spores rather than seeds — but the fronds themselves come up from an underground rootstock that may travel a metre or more between them and makes up about 90% of the plant. That creeping rhizome lets a stand extend its area by 1–3% a year, which is how one pioneer plant becomes a hillside.

Toads are frogs, and this one is American: the cane toad's native range runs from the Rio Grande Valley in south Texas down to the central Amazon and southeastern Peru. Its Australian population is an import — 102 toads were collected in Hawaiʻi and released into Queensland cane fields in August 1935, and by March 1937 62,000 toadlets had been let loose.

The chanterelle you pick is the fruiting body of a mycelium living in mycorrhizal partnership with tree roots — with oaks in California, Texas and Mexico, with silver birch and Scots pine in Scotland, under beech in Fife. That dependence is also the catch: their mycorrhizal nature makes the species very difficult to cultivate, so there is no chanterelle farming to speak of.

All four cultivated cocas were domesticated from the wild shrub Erythroxylum gracilipes, and genomic analysis indicates it happened two or three separate times, by different South American groups during the Holocene. Chewing the leaf goes back at least 8,000 years — leaves and calcite turn up in house floors in Peru's Nanchoc Valley — and the plant, which is not frost-resistant, will not grow above 2,600 m.

The crab shape — broad flattened body with the tail folded underneath — has evolved independently in at least five groups of living decapod crustaceans, among the anomurans (king crabs, porcelain crabs, hairy stone crabs, some hermit crabs) as well as in the true crabs. Lancelot Borradaile named the pattern carcinisation in 1916, describing it as nature's repeated attempts to make a crab.

Deinonychus is a dromaeosaurid, a close relative of Velociraptor inside the subfamily Velociraptorinae, but its bones come from the other side of the world: the Cloverly Formation of Montana and Wyoming and the Antlers Formation of Oklahoma. John Ostrom published the name in February 1969, and the fast, bird-like animal he described led him to revive the idea that birds descend from dinosaurs — the start of the dinosaur renaissance.

Dragonflies are hemimetabolous: there is no pupa, only a run of nymphal stages, and they moult between six and 15 times depending on the species before the adult emerges. That underwater stage lasts up to five years in large species and between two months and three years in smaller ones, ending when the nymph climbs an emergent plant, splits its skin and pumps its wings out with hydraulic pressure.

Edelweiss belongs to Leontopodium, a genus of 30–41 species whose centre of diversity is the Sino-Himalayan region of south-western China, where about 15 species grow. AFLP data put the rarest genetic variation in Yunnan, pointing to a long in-situ history there; only two species are native to Europe, so the flower that stands for the Alps is an outlier from an Asian lineage.

A ewe is a female sheep old enough to breed, and that line is crossed early: ewes generally reach sexual maturity at six to eight months old. Breeds pull hard in both directions — Finnsheep ewe lambs may reach puberty at three to four months, Merinos sometimes not until 18 to 20 months.

Giant hogweed is native to the western Caucasus, at the Asian end of Eurasia, and was carried to Europe for its size: the first British record is 1817, on the seed list at Kew. It grows 2 to 5 m tall and a single flowering plant averages 20,000 seeds — between 10,000 and 50,000 — which is how one ornamental becomes a river-bank thicket.

The giraffe and the okapi are the only living members of the family Giraffidae, and a 2016 genetic study placed their common ancestor at about 11.5 million years ago. The okapi — 1.5 m at the shoulder, 200 to 350 kg, confined to forest north and east of the Congo River — shows how much of the giraffe is the derived half of that split.

The white shark's ancestor is Carcharodon hastalis, a broad-toothed shark long carried in the mako genus as Isurus hastalis. Around 8–6 million years ago a Pacific population of C. hastalis became C. hubbelli, whose teeth gained serrations over the next few million years, and the white shark itself first appears in the fossil record of the Pacific basin about 6–5 million years ago. Megalodon was not its parent — white sharks replaced it.

A housefly is holometabolous — egg, maggot, pupa, adult, with no stage resembling the next. Larvae hatch within a day and feed where they were laid, taking two weeks under optimal conditions or 30 days and more when it is cool, and the pupa finishes in two to six days at 35 °C but 20 days or more at 14 °C. Warm enough, the whole cycle runs in seven to ten days.

Monitor lizards originated in Asia and spread to Africa and Australasia, and the Komodo dragon's own fossil record starts in Australia: specimens from across Queensland run from the Early Pliocene, about 3.8 million years ago, to at latest 330,000 years ago. It only shows up on Flores around 1.4 million years ago, and its closest living relative is the Australian lace monitor.

Within Panthera the leopard's sister group is the clade holding the lion and the jaguar, and the lineages split 3.1–1.95 million years ago. The oldest unambiguous leopard fossils are eastern African, about 2 million years old; leopards only reached Eurasia between 1.2 and 0.6 million years ago, though the genus itself most likely arose in northern Central Asia.

Lizards belong to Squamata, which with over 11,991 species is the second-largest order of living vertebrates, and it parted from the other reptiles early: crown squamates probably originated in the Early Jurassic, with the oldest unambiguous squamate fossils from the Middle Jurassic. A 2018 study argued that Megachirella, from about 240 million years ago in the Middle Triassic, was a stem-squamate and so the oldest known, though a 2021 study left its position unresolved.

The mescal bean is the seed of Dermatophyllum secundiflorum, a flowering shrub of the pea family native to Texas, New Mexico and Mexico from Chihuahua and Coahuila south to Hidalgo, Puebla and Querétaro. Its 10 cm pods hold hard orange-red seeds carrying cytisine, a bicyclic alkaloid chemically related to nicotine; a single seed is enough to kill an adult.

Mosses are among the first land plants, and land plants emerged from multicellular charophytes — freshwater green algae similar to today's Klebsormidiophyceae — that invaded the land during the Ordovician. Spore microfossils from Argentina carry that step back to the Early Middle Ordovician, around 470 million years ago.

Cephalopods descended from a mollusc resembling the Monoplacophora some 530 million years ago, and most molluscs kept the external shell — the nautiloids and the extinct ammonoids among them. Octopuses did not: they arose from the Muensterelloidea within Vampyropoda in the Jurassic, and with no skeletal support left, their arms work as muscular hydrostats of longitudinal, transverse and circular muscle around a central axial nerve.

The pink frogmouth is an anglerfish — order Lophiiformes, family Chaunacidae, the sea toads — and it fishes the way the rest of the order does, with an illicium tipped by an esca that is a mop-like tuft of filaments. Where its deep-sea cousins hang in open water, this one is bathydemersal, resting on the bottom between 200 and 1,000 m.

Polar bears are brown bears that went out onto the ice: glaciation events over hundreds of thousands of years drove both the split and the later hybridisation between the two, and mass hybridisation appears to have stopped about 200,000 years ago. Estimates of the divergence still range widely — 150,000 years in a 2010 study, 600,000 in a 2012 study, over a million in a 2022 one — and the oldest known polar bear fossil is a jawbone 130,000 to 110,000 years old, found on Prince Charles Foreland, Norway, in 2004.

Pteranodon is a pterosaur, not a dinosaur, though both sit inside the clade Avemetatarsalia. Of the roughly 1,200 known specimens, most come from the Late Cretaceous Smoky Hill Chalk of western Kansas, with others from Wyoming, South Dakota and Alabama; Othniel Charles Marsh found the first in 1870 or 1871 and coined the name — 'wing without tooth' — in 1876.

The 36 rattlesnake species are native only to the Americas, from southern Canada to central Argentina, and the most probable ancestral area for the group is the Sierra Madre Occidental of Mexico — pine-oak forest, not desert. The diversity still sits there and just north of it: Arizona alone holds 13 species.

Echinopsis pachanoi is native to Ecuador and Peru, growing in the Andes at 2,000–3,000 m, and it is quick for a columnar cactus at up to 30 cm a year. Most plants in cultivation began as cuttings rather than seed, which makes them genetic clones of the parent — and the species has been used for healing and divination in the Andes for over 3,000 years.

The shaggy mane is the fruiting body a club-fungus mycelium raises out of lawns, gravel roads and waste ground, and it does not keep: the gills turn white, then pink, then black, and the cap dissolves itself within hours of shedding its spores. The same fungus is nematophagous, killing and digesting nematodes such as Panagrellus redivivus and Meloidogyne arenaria.

The snow leopard's closest relative in Panthera is the tiger; the two probably diverged between 3.7 and 2.7 million years ago, out of a genus that most likely originated in northern Central Asia. The earliest definitive record of the modern species is Late Pleistocene, from Niuyan Cave in China.

Sundews are flowering plants — at least 194 species — that took up insects to supplement the poor mineral nutrition of the soil they grow in; the pygmy species have gone so far as to lose enzymes for processing soil nitrogen. Their flowers are held far above the leaves on a long stem, commonly read as an adaptation to avoid trapping the pollinators the plant still needs.

Cultivated tobacco is not a wild species but an allotetraploid, 2n = 4x = 48: within the last 200,000 years, in the Andes, the diploid ancestors of Nicotiana sylvestris and N. tomentosiformis — 24 chromosomes each — crossed, and the hybrid kept both full genomes instead of halving them. N. sylvestris, woodland tobacco of Argentina and Bolivia, is still there to compare it against.

The domestic turkey comes from the south Mexican wild subspecies, Meleagris gallopavo gallopavo — the one subspecies that is not found in the United States or Canada — domesticated in Mexico or by Preclassic peoples in Mesoamerica. The wild bird it was taken from is no small animal: an adult tom weighs 5 to 11 kg and measures 100–125 cm, and at twilight it heads for the trees to roost well off the ground.

The snap trap evolved only once, in the common ancestor of Dionaea and the waterwheel plant Aldrovanda, and a 2009 study found it developed out of the flypaper traps of an ancestor shared with the sundews. What that ancient lineage has left in the wild is tiny: the Venus flytrap is native only to the coastal bogs of North and South Carolina, within about 100 km of Wilmington.

The dog whelk is a predatory sea snail that bores through barnacles and mussels with a modified radula, helped by an organ on the foot secreting a shell-softening chemical; a small prey animal is eaten in about a day, a mussel can take a week to digest. Its own shell records where it grew — the overall shape varies widely with how exposed to wave action the shore is.

The okapi is endemic to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, occurring north and east of the Congo River and nowhere else on Earth: about 1.5 m at the shoulder, 2.5 m long, 200 to 350 kg. The striping is a resemblance to a zebra and nothing more — it is most closely related to the giraffe, and a 2016 genetic study put their common ancestor at about 11.5 million years ago.

Pterosaurs are the earliest vertebrates known to have evolved powered flight, and they held it for most of the Mesozoic — from the Late Triassic to the end of the Cretaceous, 228 to 66 million years ago. They are archosaurs, avemetatarsalians closer to birds and other dinosaurs than to crocodiles or any other living reptile, and the oldest ones known were already fully adapted to flying.

Palms are monocots, and Areca catechu is one: a medium-sized palm native to the Philippines, growing straight to 20 m on a trunk only 10–15 cm in diameter, since a monocot has no vascular cambium to thicken a trunk the way a ring-forming tree does. It is grown across the tropics for one commercially important seed crop, the areca nut.

Erythroxylum is a genus of tropical flowering plants in the family Erythroxylaceae — Kew's Plants of the World Online listed 259 species as of 2021, and many of the roughly 200 examined carry the tropane alkaloid cocaine. Erythroxylum gracilipes is the wild South American member of that genus from which every cultivated coca was domesticated.

Nicotiana sylvestris is a wild flowering plant of the Andes, a diploid carrying the S-genome at 2n = 2x = 24. Within the last 200,000 years, in those same mountains, its ancestors crossed with the ancestors of N. tomentosiformis — another diploid at 2n = 2x = 24 — and the hybrid kept both genomes, which is where cultivated tobacco comes from.

The wild turkey is a North American bird in six subspecies, only one of which — the nominate south Mexican form — is absent from the United States and Canada. It came close to going: game managers estimate the entire US population fell as low as 30,000 by the late 1930s, against 1.3 million by 1973 and roughly 7 million today.

The bulk of Allosaurus comes out of the Morrison Formation of Utah, Wyoming and Colorado, where the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry alone preserves a minimum of 73 dinosaurs, at least 46 of them A. fragilis. Then a specimen turned up in 1988 near Andrés in Portugal's Leiria District, with further material from the Lourinhã, Bombarral and Alcobaça formations, making A. fragilis the first dinosaur species known from both Europe and North America. The two occurrences together are evidence of a land connection between the continents in the Late Jurassic.

Apatosaurus and Diplodocus are the two branches of one family, Diplodocidae, and the difference between them is build rather than plan: Apatosaurus's neck vertebrae are shorter and far more heavily constructed, its leg bones stockier though longer. The 2015 study that scored 477 morphological characters across 81 dinosaur individuals sorted the family out again, and in the process gave Brontosaurus back a genus of its own, 112 years after Elmer Riggs folded it into Apatosaurus in 1903.

Banisteriopsis caapi is a Malpighiaceae liana of the western Amazon, native to Ecuador and Peru, climbing up to 30 metres and flowering only infrequently. Its bark carries harmine at 0.31 to 8.43 percent, harmaline at 0.03 to 0.83 and tetrahydroharmine at 0.05 to 2.94 — the monoamine oxidase inhibitors that make the brew work at all.

Panellus stipticus is a gilled fungus of the Agaricales, the same order as the button mushroom, and sits in the mycenoid lineage that holds most known luminous fungi. Its glow is a strain trait rather than a species trait: collections from eastern North America light up, while those from the Pacific coast, Europe, Russia, Japan and New Zealand do not.

Jumping bristletails branch off below every other insect alive: Archaeognatha is the sister taxon to the Dicondylia, the line that leads on to the winged insects. The order appears in the Middle Devonian, at about the same time as the arachnids, and specimens closely resembling living species turn up as both body and trace fossils right through the Paleozoic. After all that time it still holds only about 600 species in two families, small animals that spring up to 30 cm into the air off their tails when disturbed.

Genetic and archaeological evidence puts the first domestication of cannabis about 12,000 years ago in East Asia, in the early Neolithic. The oldest hard traces are Chinese: hemp fibre imprints pressed into Yangshao culture pottery from the 5th millennium BC.

The cheetah's closest living relatives are not the big cats but the cougar and the jaguarundi; the three make up the Puma lineage, which diverged from the rest of the cat family 6.7 million years ago. Two later bottlenecks — one about 100,000 years ago tied to the crossing from North America into Asia, one 10,000 to 12,000 years ago in Africa — left it with roughly 0.1 to 4 percent of the genetic variation an average species carries.

Dactylopius coccus is a scale insect native to tropical and subtropical America, from South America north through Mexico and the southwestern United States, and one of the very few insects people ever took into cultivation. Indigenous growers moved it into gardens and kept the strains carrying more dye; the colour was in use by the second century BC, and codices were being painted with it by the thirteenth.

Freshwater crayfish fall into two superfamilies that divide by hemisphere: Astacoidea across Eurasia and North America, and Parastacoidea, whose single family Parastacidae has a Gondwanan spread over South America, Madagascar and Australasia. That line follows the break-up of Pangaea into Laurasia and Gondwana, and the crayfish sit with the lobsters in one infraorder, Astacidea.

Almost every domestic duck breed descends from the mallard, Anas platyrhynchos, the exceptions being a few Muscovy breeds, and whole-genome sequencing points to a single domestication event. It happened around 2000 BC in southern China among rice-paddy farmers, after which selection split the lineages sharply between meat birds and egg birds.

Hadrosaurids like Edmontosaurus sit inside Iguanodontia, the clade Iguanodon anchors — phylogenetic work makes the traditional iguanodontids a paraphyletic grade leading up to the duck-bills. That line ends in the most sophisticated chewing apparatus any non-avian dinosaur developed, worked by bulk feeders taking tough, low-value plants: E. annectens reached about 12 metres and 5.6 tonnes, with exceptional individuals near 15 metres and 15.9 tonnes. Lawrence Lambe named the genus in 1917 from two partial skeletons found along the Red Deer River in Alberta, in the rock then called the Edmonton Formation.

Fiddler crabs are ocypodid crabs, sharing that family with the ghost crabs, and more than 100 species of them fill 11 of the family's 13 genera. Until 2016 nearly all sat inside the single genus Uca; that year most of its subgenera were raised to genera in their own right, split between the subfamilies Gelasiminae and Ucinae.

Bathynomus belongs to the order Isopoda, the same order as the woodlouse under a garden log, and shows deep-sea gigantism at its most extreme: the giant species run 8 to 15 cm, the supergiants 17 to 50. They live from about 170 metres down to 2,140, with B. kensleyi recorded at 2,500.

The domestic goat descends from the bezoar ibex, Capra aegagrus, a wild goat now confined to the Zagros Mountains but formerly spread right across Anatolia. The oldest remains of domesticated goats, 10,000 years old, come from Ganj Dareh in Iran, with further early finds at Jericho, Choga Mami, Djeitun and Çayönü.

The grey reef shark is Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos, a requiem shark in the same genus as the bull shark; within that genus, vertebral counts, tooth shape and a 1992 allozyme phylogeny put it closest to the silvertip shark. It stays small for a Carcharhinus — most are under 1.88 metres, the maximum recorded 2.6 metres and 33.7 kg — and lives at least 25 years.

Every anatomically modern human fossil older than about 200,000 years is African: Jebel Irhoud in Morocco at roughly 315,000 years, Florisbad in South Africa at 259,000, Omo-Kibish in Ethiopia at 233,000. The Middle Pleistocene African populations usually filed under Homo heidelbergensis are the pool those first moderns emerged from, though which lineage is the direct ancestor is still argued.

Kerria lacca is a scale insect of the family Kerriidae, in the superfamily Coccoidea alongside the cochineal, and it is native to Asia. India alone produces around 20,000 tonnes of raw lac a year, at least half the world's supply, from insects farmed on host trees.

Molecular work makes Triakis semifasciata the most basal member of the houndshark family Triakidae, with the banded houndshark as its nearest relative. Genetics also shows how little it travels: seven discrete gene pools lie along the Californian coast between Humboldt Bay and San Diego, inside a range that runs only from Coos Bay in Oregon to Mazatlán in Mexico.

Decapods go back about 455 million years, and after the swimming prawns branched off first, the remainder split again into the swimming shrimp and the Reptantia — the crawling line that produced lobsters and crabs. The oldest known decapod body fossil, Palaeopalaemon, is Late Devonian; nearly 15,000 decapod species are alive today.

Marlins are the family Istiophoridae, between 9 and 11 species depending on the authority, and their closest relative is the swordfish, the only member of Xiphiidae; the two families together make up the billfish superfamily Xiphioidea. The Atlantic blue marlin reaches 5 metres and 820 kg, the black marlin over 5 metres and 670 kg.

The pupa inside a cocoon does not chew its way out. It releases proteolytic enzymes that dissolve a hole through the wall of raw silk — 300 to about 900 metres of one unbroken thread — and the adult moth walks out through it. In Bombyx mori that adult cannot fly: its body is too heavy for a wingspan of 3 to 5 cm, unlike the wild B. mandarina it was bred from.

Nerium oleander is the only species currently placed in its genus, a dogbane-family shrub native from Morocco and Portugal east through the Mediterranean to India and Myanmar, and cultivated around the Mediterranean basin for millennia. Every part of it carries cardenolide glycosides — oleandrin, odorosiside, adigoside — with a narrow therapeutic index: about 100 grams of leaf is enough to kill an adult horse.

Hadrosauridae divides into two subfamilies and these two sit one on each side: the lambeosaurines carry hollow crests with air chambers inside, the saurolophines a solid crest or none at all. The type specimen of P. walkeri, found in 1920 near Sand Creek on the Red Deer River in Alberta and named by William Parks in 1922, has a skull about 1.6 metres long including that crest.

Pinnipeds are caniform carnivorans — the branch of the order that also holds the bears, the weasels and the red panda — that went back to the water, diverging from their land relatives around 50 million years ago in the Eocene. Puijila, an otter-shaped Early Miocene animal from Arctic Canada, was still swimming on four legs in fresh water; Enaliarctos, 24 to 22 million years ago off California, already had flippers and a flexible spine.

A cnidarian egg hatches into a planula: a flattened, ciliated larva with no mouth and no gut, living on stored yolk while its cilia carry it through the water. When it reaches hard substrate it anchors there and grows into a polyp — and from that fixed sac a coral colony builds itself, or a jellyfish buds off.

A puffball is a gilled mushroom that gave up its gills and shut its spores inside instead. That rebuild, gasteromycetation, happened convergently in a number of independent events out of ordinary hymenomycetes, which is why puffballs are a shape rather than a single lineage. A mature giant puffball, Calvatia gigantea, holds about 7 × 10¹² spores, more than any other known organism.

The Pacific razor clam, Siliqua patula, is a bivalve mollusc of the family Pharidae whose two hinged valves are drawn out into a blade — the shape the muscular foot drives down through wet sand, valves closing to force it deeper. It runs 8 to 15 cm at the southern end of a range that reaches from Alaska to California, and up to 28 cm in Alaska itself.

Sand dollars are the order Clypeasteroida, sea urchins flattened for burrowing; they diverged from the other irregular echinoids, the cassiduloids, in the early Jurassic, and the first true sand dollar genus, Togocyamus, appears in the Paleocene. The rebuild moved the anus from the top of the test round to the back and cut the long defensive spines down to a velvet of ciliated ones.

Ovis aries descends from the Asiatic mouflon, Ovis gmelini; the European mouflon is a direct descendant of that same domestic population rather than a second wild source. Domestication ran between 11,000 and 9000 BC in Mesopotamia and reached Mehrgarh in the Indus Valley by about 7000 BC, and the FAO listed 1,229 breeds as of 2006.

The snowy owl was long given a genus of its own, Nyctea, until mtDNA cytochrome b sequences placed it inside Bubo, the horned owls, with the great horned owl as its closest living relative. What it did evolve on that branch is insulation: toe feathers averaging 33.3 mm against 13 mm in the great horned owl, the next longest of any owl.

The bulkiest of the stick insects are Malay Archipelago animals: Heteropteryx dilatata lives on the Malay Peninsula, in Thailand and Singapore, on Sumatra and in Sarawak on Borneo, and the female reaches 14 to 17 cm and 30 to 65 grams against a male's slender 9 to 13 cm. Its genus holds that one species and no other.

Acorus is the first branch off the monocot line — sister to all other monocots — and stands alone in its family, four species in the genus. The sweet flag that spread through Europe and North America is a sterile triploid, 3n = 36, probably a hybrid of the diploid and tetraploid cytotypes and probably from the Himalayan region; it sets no seed and travels only as cut rhizome, and unlike the diploid strains it carries β-asarone.

The tope is a houndshark, family Triakidae — the same family as the leopard shark, which a 2006 analysis makes the most basal member of the group — and it is the only living species in the genus Galeorhinus. Where the leopard shark barely moves, this one crosses oceans: fish tagged in the United Kingdom have been recovered in the Azores, the Canary Islands and Iceland, and Australian-tagged fish have turned up in New Zealand.

Trametes versicolor is a white-rot fungus of the Polyporales, the basidiomycete order that holds most white rotters, and it takes lignin apart with class II peroxidases — lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase, versatile peroxidase — backed by laccase. A 2012 study of 31 fungal genomes traced that enzymatic machinery to about the end of the Permian, which is where the great burial of undecayed wood as coal falls away.

The walrus is the only surviving odobenid, and its family separated from the eared seals — the sea lions and fur seals — roughly 15 to 20 million years ago, after both had split from the true seals 20 to 26 million years ago. The tusks are elongated canines carried by both sexes, reaching 1 metre and 5.4 kg.

Tremella mesenterica is not rotting the wood it sits on; it grows parasitically on the mycelium of Peniophora, the corticioid crust fungi that are. Its gelatinous lobes reach 7.5 cm across and 2.5 to 5 cm high, shrivel within a few days into a thin film, and revive with the next rain.

Geese and the mallard sit in one family, Anatidae — around 174 species in 43 genera — the geese and swans in the subfamily Anserinae, the mallard among the dabbling ducks of the Anatinae, genus Anas. Its own species boundary leaks badly: Anas platyrhynchos has hybridised with more than 40 species in the wild and 20 more in captivity, and the fertile hybrids have swamped the American black duck, the Hawaiian duck and the New Zealand grey duck.

Goats and sheep are the two large genera of one bovid subfamily, Caprinae — Capra with about ten species, Ovis with seven — separate wild lines that people took in separately. Ovis gmelini, the Asiatic mouflon, is the wild half of the sheep story, ranging across Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Iran, and a mature ram's horns curve almost a full revolution, up to 85 cm.

The aurochs and the wild goat are both bovids, but from opposite halves of the family — Bovinae for the cattle, Caprinae for the goats and sheep — and the Bovinae are thought to have diverged from the rest in the early Miocene, when bovids first appear about 20 million years ago. Of that family 143 species are alive now against 300 known extinct ones, and Capra aegagrus is the one holding the Zagros Mountains of Iran, formerly spread across Anatolia.

Guillermo Rougier found the only known skeleton in February 1984, on an expedition led by Jose Bonaparte, in the La Amarga Formation of Neuquen Province in northern Patagonia — sandstone and mudstone dropped by braided river channels, lakes and alluvial plains, and the oldest Cretaceous terrestrial rock in the Neuquen Basin at 130 to 120 million years old. Salgado and Bonaparte named it in 1991, and that one near-complete skeleton is still the whole of what is known.

Through spring and summer an aphid colony is entirely female, each mother giving live birth to clones of herself, and the daughters arrive already carrying their own developing embryos, so generations telescope one inside another. Cabbage aphids can run through as many as 41 such generations in a season, each lasting 20 to 40 days, before shortening days and falling temperatures finally bring out males and the mated females lay eggs that overwinter outside the body.

The olive baboon belongs to Papio, a genus of the Old World monkey family Cercopithecidae, and baboons are an African radiation: no species of the genus lives wild beyond Africa and a corner of the Arabian Peninsula. This one is the most wide-ranging of them all, spread across 25 equatorial African countries from Mali east to Ethiopia and Tanzania, with isolated populations holding on in mountains of the Sahara.

Bird's nest fungi belong to the Agaricales, inside the euagarics clade of mostly gilled mushrooms, but they gave up handing their spores to the wind the way most fungi do. The spores travel packed into disc-shaped peridioles sitting in the tiny cup, and a raindrop striking that cup at the right angle throws one about a metre; in some species a sticky funicular cord catches a passing twig and whips the packet around it.

The domestic water buffalo descends from Bubalus arnee, the wild water buffalo, now down to fewer than 4,000 mature animals in fragments of Assam, Nepal and mainland Southeast Asia. It was taken in twice over and independently: the river type in western India about 6,300 years ago, the swamp type in mainland Southeast Asia between 3,000 and 7,000 years ago. Their descendants now number some 208 million head across 77 countries.

Abelisaurids were the dominant predators of Late Cretaceous Gondwana, occupying the niche tyrannosaurids held on the northern continents, and Carnotaurus sits in Brachyrostra, a short-snouted branch of them restricted to South America. Its single known skeleton came out of the La Colonia Formation of Chubut Province, Argentina, in 1984, from rock 69 to 66 million years old.

Every breed of chicken traces back to the red junglefowl of South and Southeast Asian forest; a 2020 study put all domestic chickens down to a single domestication of Gallus gallus spadiceus in Southeast Asia around 9,500 years ago. One trait came in from a neighbour — the gene behind the yellow skin of domestic birds most likely originated in the closely related grey junglefowl.

A cockroach does not lay loose eggs: it wraps them in an ootheca, a case of structural proteins hardened by tanning agents, and a German cockroach packs about 30 to 40 long thin eggs into one. The female glues the case to a surface, wedges it into a protective crevice, or carries it about until just before hatching, when the young break out on the combined pressure of all of them gulping air — though some species keep the eggs inside the body instead, and the genus Diploptera is fully viviparous. One female may produce up to eight cases in her life, and in good conditions 300 to 400 offspring.

Datura is a genus of the nightshade family whose centre of origin is Mexico, where most of its nine to fourteen species are native. Populations long taken for native elsewhere — D. ferox in China, D. metel in India and Southeast Asia, D. leichhardtii in Australia — are almost certainly post-Columbian introductions carried out of Central America.

Jesse Williams, a Navajo man, found the bones in 1940 in the Kayenta Formation of northern Arizona, about 32 km north of Cameron on the Navajo Reservation, and Charles Camp's field party excavated three skeletons from the site in 1942. The Kayenta's red and brown sandstones outcrop across the Colorado Plateau and date the animal to roughly 198 to 179 million years ago; Welles called it Megalosaurus in 1954 and only gave it its own genus in 1970.

Duckweeds are flowering plants that selection has stripped almost bare — no obvious stem and no leaves, just a floating thallus a few cells thick, often pocketed with air, and in some species no roots at all. They sit inside the arum family, Araceae, so all that structure was lost from ancestors that had it. Wolffia's flower, 0.3 mm long, is the smallest known, and the plants mostly skip flowering altogether, budding daughters from a meristem at the base of the frond fast enough to double their biomass in four and a half days.

The specimen came out of a ravine in the Pierre Shale near Fort Wallace, Kansas, in 1867 — marine rock laid down in the Western Interior Seaway between about 80.6 and 77 million years ago. Cope named it in 1868 and reconstructed it with the skull on the wrong end of the vertebral column, at the tail; Marsh made sure the mistake was public. Of its 10.3 m length about 7.1 m was neck, carried on 72 vertebrae.

Salamandra salamandra is the salamander of southern and central Europe, usually found between 250 and 1,000 m of altitude and higher in Spain and the Balkans, and split into thirteen recognised subspecies. Most are ovoviviparous — the eggs develop inside the female and she deposits the hatched larvae straight into water — while fastuosa and bernardezi go further and bear live young.

The panda's line split from the common ancestor of the bears about 19 million years ago, which makes it the most basal member of Ursidae and equally distant from every other living bear. It has stayed where it began: six montane regions of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, up to 3,000 m, hold the entire wild population of roughly 1,900 animals.

The first known specimen was a 107 cm immature male caught in Sagami Bay near Yokohama; shipmaster Alan Owston passed it to Kakichi Mitsukuri at the University of Tokyo, who sent it on to David Starr Jordan, and Jordan named it Mitsukurina owstoni in 1898 for both men. It is the only surviving member of the family Mitsukurinidae, whose fossil record reaches back about 125 million years to the Aptian.

The European hedgehog belongs to the family Erinaceidae in the order Eulipotyphla, a branch of placental mammals quite separate from the rodents its habits might suggest. Its range runs from Iberia and Italy north into Scandinavia and reaches its western limit in Ireland, and a single animal carries up to 6,000 brown and white spines.

The Malheur National Forest fungus is not a population but one individual, spreading underground on black rhizomorphs — 'shoestrings' that carry nutrients between distant roots — and growing rather than breeding, so every cell of it is a copy. That single Armillaria ostoyae genet has been at it for an estimated 8,000 years, and now covers 3.5 square miles, about 2,200 acres, at a weight that may reach 35,000 tons.

A ladybird is a beetle, one of more than 6,000 species in the family Coccinellidae, and the adult is assembled out of a larva that looks nothing like it. In Adalia bipunctata the eggs hatch after four to eight days, the larva spends about three weeks growing through four stages and three moults, then hunches into a pupa for seven to ten days before the hardened forewings, the elytra, colour up over the following hours.

Leptocyon is the oldest known canine, the earliest member of the subfamily Caninae, and it lived in North America from about 34 million years ago until 10.3 million years ago. While the heavy-jawed borophagines alongside it specialised in a powerful killing bite, Leptocyon stayed small — as little as 2 kg — and built for snatching fast little prey.

No taxonomic line separates locusts from grasshoppers; what makes a locust is that the animal changes phase. Increased tactile stimulation of the hind legs raises serotonin, and several contacts a minute sustained over about four hours tips a solitary grasshopper into the gregarious form, which changes colour, eats much more and breeds much more readily — in swarms reaching 80 million insects per square kilometre.

The government surveyor Joseph Millard Orpen and his brothers dug the first bones out of a farm in the Drakensberg near Harrismith in 1853 and 1854, and Richard Owen described the animal in 1854. Most later material comes from the upper Elliot and Clarens formations of South Africa and Lesotho, rock spanning roughly 201 to 184 million years ago — the fossils are common enough that they are used to date the beds themselves.

A mussel starts as a drifting larva that spends anywhere from three weeks to six months in the plankton before finding a hard surface and settling as a young mussel about 1 mm across. Only then is it the bivalve mollusc anyone would recognise, holding its place with byssal threads that it can attach and detach to shuffle slowly into a better position.

Papaver somniferum is known only as a cultivated plant, and its wild ancestor has never been identified. Papaver setigerum, native to southwestern Europe and North Africa and long the favoured candidate, is tetraploid with n=22 while the opium poppy is diploid with n=11, so it cannot be the wild ancestral species. What is left is archaeology: small botanical remains around the Mediterranean and west of the Rhine push cultivation back beyond about 5000 BC.

Charles Hazelius Sternberg, collecting on commission for Uppsala University, recovered a skull and a rump at Meyers Creek near the Kimbetoh Wash in the San Juan Basin of New Mexico in 1921. The Kirtland Formation he dug them from is sandstone with shale, mudstone and conglomerate, alluvial deposits of old river channels and floodplains dated between 75.02 and 73.49 million years ago; Osborn named the animal Pentaceratops sternbergii after him in 1923.

Piranhas are characiform fish of the family Serrasalmidae, and they are confined to South America — the Amazon basin, the Orinoco, the rivers of the Guianas, the Paraguay-Parana and the Sao Francisco. Estimates of how many species there are run from fewer than 30 to more than 60, and the same continent produced the extinct Megapiranha of 8 to 10 million years ago, far larger than anything alive.

Boletus edulis cannot raise a fruit body alone: it is ectomycorrhizal, trading nutrients with tree roots across at least 30 host species in more than 15 genera, from pines, spruces and firs to oaks, chestnuts and beech. That partnership is also how it travels — it reached Christchurch in the mid-19th century on the roots of imported beech, birch and oak, and has been in South African pine plantations for over 50 years. The largest one recorded, from the Isle of Skye in 1995, weighed 3.2 kg with a 42 cm cap.

Douglas Lawson, then a graduate student, found a 0.91 m bone in an arroyo on the western edge of Big Bend National Park, Texas, in 1971, in the Javelina Formation, and published the name in 1975. It is a pterosaur rather than a dinosaur — an azhdarchid — and while early wingspan estimates ranged from 5.2 all the way to 25.8 m, recent work settles around 10 to 11 m.

The fox-like genus Leptocyon appears about 34 million years ago and splits 11.9 million years ago into two lines: Vulpes, the foxes, and the Canini. The red fox sits on the first of those branches, which is why it is unmistakably a member of the dog family and yet not a close relative of the wolf and the dog on the other side of that division.

Constantine Rafinesque described Carcharias taurus in 1810 from a specimen caught off Sicily, and that Mediterranean fish still fixes the species name. Very few individuals ever descend from a given female: she may begin with as many as 50 embryos, but once one reaches about 10 cm it eats every smaller embryo in its uterine horn, so two pups are born, each already about a metre long and fully independent.

Dendrobranchiate prawns hatch as a nauplius — three head segments under a single carapace, with one unpaired naupliar eye — and only take on a shrimp's shape after a long planktonic passage through the zoea stage, which carries thoracic swimming appendages and a large dorsal spine. Most other decapods brood their eggs on the female's pleopods and take the short route, with at most nine larval stages; a shrimp's post-larva has a name of its own, the parva.

Sphynx hairlessness is a recessive 'hr' allele of KRT71 that knocks the gene out completely, so a hair never forms a solid root or bulb; DNA work in 2010 showed that a different allele of the very same gene gives the Devon Rex its short curly coat. The breed was assembled from a handful of spontaneous carriers — Prune, born in Toronto in 1966 to a domestic shorthair called Elizabeth, the Minnesota kittens Epidermis and Dermis in 1975, and Toronto street kittens found in 1978 and crossed to a Devon Rex in the Netherlands.

Phallus impudicus does not hand its spores to the wind. Its sticky spore mass gives off methanethiol, hydrogen sulfide, dimethyl sulfide and dimethyl trisulfide — the chemistry of decomposing flesh — and an Austrian study found blow-flies such as Calliphora vicina and Lucilia caesar, which normally feed on dead animals, coming to the fungus instead and carrying spores away. The fruit body rises out of its egg at 10 to 15 cm an hour to meet them.

Termites are not a separate order at all: 21st-century phylogenetics places the infraorder Isoptera deep inside Blattodea, making them highly derived cockroaches whose closest living relatives are the wood-eating cockroaches of the genus Cryptocercus. The symbiosis gave it away long before the genetics did — the similarity of their symbiotic gut flagellates prompted the suggestion as early as 1925, and the two groups also share trophallaxis and social habits.

Othniel Charles Marsh named Torosaurus in 1891 from a skull John Bell Hatcher took out of the Lance Formation in Niobrara County, southeastern Wyoming, where badlands of buff-coloured sandstone and drab green shale are cut along Cow Creek beside the formation's type locality — stream deposits on a coastal plain at the edge of the Western Interior Seaway, 69 to 66 million years ago. Its largest known skull, 'Adam', is 3 m long, the longest of any land animal.

New World vultures are not close kin to the Old World ones; the bare head and the scavenging life evolved twice over, and the two groups do not form a single clade. The turkey vulture is one of seven surviving Cathartidae in five genera, spread from southern Canada to South America, and taxonomists still disagree about whether to keep them in their own order Cathartiformes or fold them into Accipitriformes.

Cicuta is a genus of four species in the carrot family, Apiaceae, native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere and mainly to North America — three of them, C. maculata, C. bulbifera and C. douglasii, are North American. All carry cicutoxin, an unsaturated aliphatic alcohol that blocks GABA receptors and lets neurons fire unchecked, and seizures can begin as soon as 15 minutes after a mouthful.

From Leptocyon the Canini branch runs on through Eucyon davisi about 6 to 5 million years ago, Canis lepophagus around 5 million, Canis etruscus about 2 million, and Canis mosbachensis in the Middle Pleistocene before Canis lupus itself. The oldest wolf tooth known comes from Old Crow in the Yukon, in sediment a million years old, and Alaskan specimens dated to 810,000 years point to an origin in eastern Beringia.

Gallus gallus is a bird of South and Southeast Asia and nowhere else: the range opens in Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh, runs east across southern China into Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam, then south through Malaysia and Singapore to the Philippines, Indonesia and Timor-Leste. Every chicken on every other continent arrived there with people, out of a single domestication in Southeast Asia around 9,500 years ago.

Bubalus arnee is a South and Southeast Asian bovid down to fewer than 4,000 mature animals, and Nepal holds one of its last strongholds in the Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, the source for recent translocations founding new herds. It has been listed as Endangered since 1986 and sits in CITES Appendix III, protected by law in Bhutan, India, Nepal and Thailand — and it is already gone from Bangladesh, Laos, Vietnam and Sri Lanka.

The suborder Caelifera has split into roughly 2,400 valid genera and about 11,000 described species, with many more undescribed in tropical wet forest. They are among the most ancient living groups of chewing herbivorous insects, reaching back to the early Triassic around 250 million years ago — and a few species in the family Acrididae keep a second identity in reserve, turning into locusts when they are crowded.

The genus Alligator has only two species left, one in the southeastern United States and one on China's Yangtze. The American one lives farther from the equator than any other crocodilian, and when its water freezes over it holds its snout up through the surface to breathe above the ice.

A farmer near Plaza Huincul in Neuquen Province found the first bone in 1987 and took it for a petrified log; Jose Bonaparte's 1989 excavation of the Huincul Formation yielded the vertebrae and sacrum that became the holotype, named in 1993. Everything known of this 30-35 m titanosaur comes from those few fragments, scaled against more complete relatives.

The bald eagle forms a species pair with the white-tailed eagle of Eurasia: one white-headed, one tan-headed, much the same size, each filling the same role on its own side of the world. The pair had split from the other sea eagles by the Early Miocene, around 10 million years ago.

Carcharhinus radiated so recently that its branches resist untangling: a 1998 allozyme analysis left the blacktip reef shark in an unresolved polytomy with ten other species of the genus, of which it is the type species. It also keeps extremely small home ranges, staying in one patch of reef for years at a time.

Every true bug carries the same piece of equipment: a beak of piercing-sucking mouthparts, the one arrangement shared across more than 80,000 species that otherwise drink sap, other insects, or blood. Hemiptera is also the largest order that never pupates, more than 95,000 named species whose nymphs hatch already resembling small wingless adults; every insect order with more species than that passes through a pupa instead.

Ricinus communis is the only species in its genus and in its subtribe, a spurge indigenous to East Africa, the southeastern Mediterranean basin and India, and spread from there through the tropics. India now grows over three-quarters of the world's roughly two million tonnes of castor seed a year.

Chimpanzees are one of the four surviving great-ape genera, and the African ones have left almost no fossils: three teeth found in Kenya in 2005 and dated to about 500,000 years ago are the only Pan fossils known. The split from the human line is placed 7 to 10 million years ago.

One of the earliest known dinosaurs, and among the best represented, because of a single place. David Baldwin collected the first bones in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico in 1881, and in June 1947 Edwin Colbert's crew struck a Chinle Formation bonebed at Ghost Ranch packed with skeletons of an animal that lived 215 to 201 million years ago.

The dingo descends from domesticated dogs whose lineage branched off early from today's breeds and can be traced back through Maritime Southeast Asia. The oldest dingo remains in Australia are 3,450 years old, and the skull has barely changed since: nobody bred it, it simply lived wild.

Dung beetles are not one branch of the family tree. Dung feeding turns up in several beetle families within the Scarabaeoidea, so the habit cannot have arisen only once; the true dung beetles alone, the subfamily Scarabaeinae, number more than 5,000 species.

The elephant order opens with Eritherium, a 3-8 kg animal from the Ouled Abdoun phosphate beds of Morocco about 60 million years ago, the oldest and most primitive proboscidean known. Elephants proper appeared in Africa around 10 million years ago, and the lineage only reached Eurasia after Afro-Arabia collided with it 18-19 million years ago.

Lampyridae are elateroid beetles, more than 2,400 described species. The light is thought to have begun as a warning that the larvae taste bad and was later taken over as a mating signal, and females of the genus Photuris now mimic the flash pattern of Photinus males in order to eat them.

The giant sequoia and the coast redwood are surviving genera of the same redwood subfamily, split between the Sierra Nevada and the coast. The Sierra tree holds its cones green and shut for as long as 20 years and it takes the heat of a fire to dry them open; bark up to 90 cm thick and full of tannic acid carries the parent through that same fire.

It lives in one stretch of the Choco rainforest on Colombia's Pacific coast, a range under 5,000 square kilometres, and nowhere else on earth; it was described in 1978 from specimens collected at Quebrada Guangui and La Brea. At about 6 cm it is the largest of the poison dart frogs.

Every known fossil comes from the Ischigualasto Formation of northwestern Argentina, where a goatherd named Victorino Herrera first noticed the bones in 1959 and Osvaldo Reig described them in 1963; the rock is about 231 million years old. Where exactly it sits has been argued ever since — basal saurischian or primitive theropod — with the near-complete skull found by Paul Sereno's team in 1988 pushing the theropod reading.

Hyenas are feliforms, the cat branch of the carnivores, closer to felines and civets than to any dog. The dog-like build, the running feet with blunt claws and the catching of prey with the teeth are convergence; the family began about 22 million years ago in Miocene Eurasia with civet-like animals such as Plioviverrops.

A sunfish native to the eastern and central United States, southeastern Canada and northern Mexico, carried far beyond that by anglers. A 2022 phylogenomic study found that Lacepede's 1802 type specimen from near Charleston was really a Florida bass, so the largemouth took Cuvier's name instead, typed on Lake Huron.

Convallaria sits in the asparagus family, Asparagaceae, having been shunted through Ruscaceae, a family of its own and the lilies before that. The species is native to Europe and northern Asia; the plants in eastern North America and East Asia, long treated as its varieties, are now split off as separate species, and a colony that is all one clone sets no seed, because the plant will not fertilise itself.

The first dinosaur eggs ever found in the Western Hemisphere came out of a Montana hillside in 1979, the year after Jack Horner and Bob Makela found the bonebed south of Choteau and named the animal 'good mother lizard'. The site held nests and juveniles as well, which is why the hill is called Egg Mountain and why this hadrosaur is Montana's state fossil.

The mayapple belongs to the barberry family, but as a herb of eastern North American and southeastern Canadian woodland rather than a shrub. It spreads by a creeping rhizome, so a whole colony can descend from one root, and it depends obligately on mycorrhizal fungi to feed itself.

The narwhal and the beluga are the only two living monodontids; a 2020 analysis puts their split about 5 million years ago, and they still meet, because a strange skull found in West Greenland around 1990 was confirmed by DNA in 2019 as a narwhal-beluga hybrid. The narwhal itself never leaves the Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland and Russia.

Orangutans are the only great apes outside Africa, the last of the subfamily Ponginae, which parted from the African hominids between 19.3 and 15.7 million years ago. In the Pleistocene they ranged across Southeast Asia and southern China; they are now down to Borneo and Sumatra, in three species, the third recognised only in 2017.

The falcon family, around 65 species of falcons and caracaras, likely originated in South America during the Paleocene. From that start the peregrine ended up with the widest natural breeding distribution of any bird, ranging from Greenland to Fiji.

Johann Friedrich Engelhardt found it in 1834 and Hermann von Meyer described it three years later, making it the fifth named dinosaur genus still considered valid — named before Owen coined the word dinosaur in 1842. Over 100 skeletons have since come out of the Late Triassic rock of Swabia, enough that Germans call it the Swabian lindworm.

The giant river prawn lives its adult life entirely in fresh water, but its larvae still depend on brackish water to develop — the mark of a lineage that came into the rivers from the sea and never fully cut the tie. It is native across the Indo-Pacific from India to Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and grows past 30 cm.

The European rabbit is the only rabbit ever domesticated, and every breed alive descends from it. It has been raised for food since at least the first century BC, out of a wild range covering only the Iberian Peninsula and southwestern France, and has since been put ashore on at least 800 islands and every continent except Antarctica.

The Indian rhinoceros is an odd-toed ungulate: it carries its weight on the third toe and digests plant cellulose in its intestines rather than in a chambered stomach, and horses and tapirs are its only living relatives. It holds on in 12 protected areas of the Indo-Gangetic plain in northern India and southern Nepal, under 20,000 square kilometres, where about 4,075 animals were counted by March 2025.

It has a cryptic sister species, Sphyrna gilberti, which differs from it in the number of vertebrae and little else. Females return to the coast where they were born to drop their own pups, which keeps the nursery populations apart generation after generation.

The breed has been selectively bred since the end of the 19th century from the Wichianmat, a colourpointed landrace of Thailand, which was called Siam until 1939. Those cats appear far earlier in the Tamra Maew manuscripts of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, 1351 to 1767; the pale body with dark points is a temperature-sensitive form of albinism.

Silk came before spiders. Attercopus, from rock about 390 million years old at Gilboa in New York, made silk from plates on an abdomen that was still segmented and carried a whip-scorpion-like tail, and it had no spinnerets at all. It belongs to the extinct order Uraraneida, thought to sit close to the origin of the spiders proper.

Synanceia is a scorpionfish, from the venom-spined family; Linnaeus described its type species in 1766 from Ambon Island in Indonesia, and a 2018 revision moved the stonefishes out into a family of their own. The venom sits in glands at the base of needle-like dorsal spines that stand up when the fish is disturbed, and it is injected in proportion to the pressure put on them.

A Mongolian field expedition turned up the first bones in the Gobi in 1948, in the Nemegt Formation, and Evgeny Maleev described them in 1954 as a giant turtle-like reptile, which is why the species is still called cheloniformis. It is now placed firmly among the theropods, as a maniraptoran, with hand claws over 50 cm long.

Ceratopsians began small and bipedal in Asia: Psittacosaurus and the other basal forms all come from northern China or Mongolia. The huge horned quadrupeds came later, on Laramidia, the island continent that is now western North America, and Triceratops prorsus was the last ceratopsian of all, gone at the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction 66 million years ago.

The shell was built belly-first. Odontochelys semitestacea, from 220-million-year-old marine rock in Guizhou, China, still had teeth in both jaws and a complete plastron underneath, but no carapace over its back at all, only broadened ribs like those of a turtle embryo before the plates ossify.

Water lilies sit near the base of the flowering plants, and genetic work confirmed the Nymphaeaceae as basal angiosperms, which is why their large, many-parted flowers were once read as the original floral plan. Comparison with their sister family Cabombaceae says otherwise: the beetle-pollinated flowers of Nymphaea and Victoria, with the most parts, are the derived kind rather than the ancestral one.

Woodlice are the isopods that finished the move onto land, one of very few crustacean lineages to manage it; molecular clocks put the crossing in the late Paleozoic, though the oldest known fossils are only about 100 million years old. They breathe through pleopods, the old swimming legs, and the female carries her eggs in a marsupium that supplies them with water, oxygen and nutrients.

Apes are the Old World primates that lost the tail, and the loss traces to a mutation in the TBXT gene. The superfamily is native to sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia and has two branches: the gibbons, and the great apes proper, four genera holding three orangutan species, two gorillas, two chimpanzees and ourselves.

The front pair of wings is hardened into cases, the elytra, folded over the flight wings and the body beneath — the character that separates a beetle from most other insects, and one that water beetles even use to trap a bubble of air for diving. About 400,000 species have been described, the largest order of anything: 40% of described arthropods and a quarter of all known animals.

A crocodilian's closest living relatives are birds: the two are the only surviving archosaurs, and everything else on that branch is gone. The crocodilian total group appeared about 250 million years ago in the Early Triassic, and the order itself 83.5 million years ago.

Theropods first appear 231.4 million years ago and supplied most of the large land carnivores from the Early Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous — and they are the one dinosaur branch that came through the extinction, because birds evolved from small feathered coelurosaurs among them. That leaves about 11,000 theropod species alive today.

Rabbits, hares and pikas were classed as a suborder of rodents until 1912, and they are the rodents' nearest kin rather than their descendants. The teeth separate them: four upper incisors instead of two, the second pair a small peg tucked behind the front ones, plus more cheek teeth and no pads on the feet.

About 17 species survive in three families — horses, rhinos and tapirs — and two things mark them off from the cloven-hoofed mammals. Weight passes through the third toe rather than being split evenly between two, and they break down plant cellulose in the intestine instead of in one or more stomach chambers.

Isopods carry seven pairs of jointed legs on the thorax and five pairs of branching abdominal appendages used for breathing. The female does not release her eggs into the water at all: she broods them in a marsupium, a pouch under her own thorax, which is what let the group reach dry land as well as the seabed.

Milky latex runs through the Euphorbioideae and Crotonoideae, poisonous in the first and harmless in the second; the rubber tree's latex is the world's main source of natural rubber, and spurge latex was once taken as a laxative. The flowers are unisexual and radially symmetrical, usually with both sexes on one plant.

Antoine Risso described the family in 1826, and it holds many of the most venomous fish alive: the sting is delivered by sharp spines coated in venomous mucus. They are spread through tropical and temperate seas and are richest in the Indo-Pacific; a 2018 revision moved several groups, the stonefishes among them, into families of their own.

Requiem sharks do not lay eggs. A blacktip reef shark's embryo lives on its yolk sac for the first months, and at about four months that sac converts into a placental connection anchored to the uterine wall; by five months the placenta is complete and the pup is 24 cm long.

The American bullfrog is an anuran native to eastern North America, found in every US state east of the Mississippi and ranging from the Canadian Maritimes west to Idaho and Texas. It has since been carried to more than 40 countries, where it usually turns invasive. Its tadpole takes anywhere from a few months in the south of that range to three years in the cold north before metamorphosis finishes.

Armadillos are xenarthrans, a mammal group that arose in South America in the Late Paleocene about 60 million years ago and diversified through the continent's long isolation, only spreading north from around 10 million years ago in the Great American Interchange. The name refers to extra vertebral joints found in no other mammal. The three-banded armadillo Tolypeutes tricinctus is confined to Brazil, and its genus is the only one whose armour closes into a sealed ball.

The basking shark is the only living member of Cetorhinidae, a lamniform in the same order as the great white, the mako and the thresher. Filter feeding arrived separately in three unrelated shark lineages, and by different means: the whale shark and the megamouth can suck or pump water across their gills, while the basking shark strains only what its own swimming pushes through — calculated at up to 450 tonnes of water an hour for a five-metre animal.

In 2007 a nine-year-old female blacktip at the Virginia Aquarium became pregnant having never been housed with a male, and genetic analysis confirmed automictic parthenogenesis: an ovum merged with a polar body to make a zygote, with no fertilisation at all. Blacktips normally breed every other year and carry four to seven pups for ten to twelve months, so the case suggested asexual reproduction runs wider among sharks than had been supposed.

Butterflies came out of the moths: they are a single clade nested inside Lepidoptera, which is why the moths left over do not form a natural group at all. From a Late Cretaceous origin, probably North American, the line fanned into roughly 18,500 species, most of that diversification falling in the Cenozoic. The oldest known fossil butterfly, Protocoeliades kristenseni, comes from Paleocene Denmark about 55 million years ago.

The small-spotted catshark is one of the oviparous sharks: the female anchors a horny capsule roughly 4 cm by 2 cm, trailing long tendrils, to the seabed, and the embryo develops inside it for five to eleven months depending on how warm the sea is. The pup that leaves the case is 9 to 10 cm long.

Chitons are Polyplacophora, about 940 living species carrying eight separate shell valves rather than one shell, with a fossil record reaching back to the Cambrian. Some of them have turned the light-sensing aesthetes under the shell surface into true eyes, each with a lens of aragonite - the shell mineral itself - grown as large, crystallographically aligned grains that scatter little light and form a clear image. The eyes are paid for out of the armour: as they grow larger and more complex the shell's mechanical performance drops, and they show up only in fossils of the last 10 million years or so, the most recent eyes known to have evolved in a mollusc.

Hadrosaurids are descendants of the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous iguanodontians and keep much the same body plan, the differences lying in their stacked dental batteries and, among lambeosaurines, the hollow crest. Barnum Brown found the first Corythosaurus in 1911 on the Red Deer River in Alberta, in Belly River Group rock laid down 77 to 75.7 million years ago. The crest's looping internal passages are modelled as producing loud, low calls, closer to a trombone than a shout.

Atropa belladonna and Datura sit in different tribes of the nightshade family and arrived at the same chemistry: atropine, hyoscyamine and scopolamine. Datura's centre of origin is Mexico, while belladonna is a plant of Europe and western Asia, growing from England east to Ukraine and the Iranian province of Gilan. Every part of it is loaded — 1.3% tropane alkaloid in the root, 1.2% in the leaf, 0.7% in the ripe berry, which is the part that tastes sweet.

Dinosaurs diverged from their archosaur relatives in the Middle to Late Triassic, roughly 20 million years after the end-Permian extinction, and the first of them were small bipedal predators on the pattern of Eoraptor. The oldest substantial dinosaur fossils come from Carnian rock in South America: the Ischigualasto Formation of Argentina at 231 to 230 million years, and the Santa Maria Formation of Brazil dated radiometrically to 233.23 million.

Spotted eagle rays belong to the Myliobatidae along with the manta ray, both of them open-water swimmers rather than bottom-dwellers. What was once treated as one ocean-spanning species has been split three ways: Aetobatus narinari is now restricted to the Atlantic, with A. ocellatus in the Indo-Pacific and A. laticeps in the eastern Pacific. Females carry their young about a year and bear at most four pups, 17 to 35 cm across.

Euoplocephalus is an earlier member of Ankylosaurini, the same tribe of armoured dinosaurs as Ankylosaurus, and differs from it in skull ornament and nostril structure. Lawrence Lambe found the first piece — part of a cranium and five scutes — on 18 August 1897 beside the Red Deer River in Alberta, in beds 76.4 to 75.6 million years old. Only the far half of its tail was stiffened by bundles of ossified tendons, so the club swung on a flexible shaft with force enough to break bone.

Fish are chordates that turned the notochord, dorsal nerve cord and pharyngeal slits into a body built around a backbone. The first vertebrates appear in the Cambrian about 518 million years ago — Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, jawless, with rudimentary vertebrae and a defined head and tail — and jawed vertebrates followed in the Late Ordovician around 445 million years ago. Ray-finned fish alone account for over 32,000 living species, roughly half of all described vertebrates.

Squid and cuttlefish are both Decapodiformes, the ten-limbed branch of cephalopods that made tentacles of arm pair IV while the octopus line lost arm pair II instead; the giant squid is an oegopsid within that branch. Its eyes reach at least 27 cm across with a 9 cm pupil, the largest of any living animal except perhaps the colossal squid — an investment that only repays in deep water, where a big eye gathers what little light, bioluminescence included, is there to be had.

Most domestic goose breeds come down from the greylag, Anser anser, domesticated at least as early as 1360 BCE, while the Chinese goose descends separately from the swan goose of eastern Asia. The oldest evidence of goose domestication is about 7,000 years old, from the Hemudu culture on the lower Yangtze, and geese were being kept in Egypt more than 4,000 years ago.

Where heterodontosaurids sit among the ornithischians is still unsettled, but one standing proposal ties them to the marginocephalians - Heterodontosauriformes is the name for the clade of heterodontosaurids plus pachycephalosaurs and ceratopsians - and a 2020 analysis went further, recovering the traditional heterodontosaurs as paraphyletic within Pachycephalosauria itself. They were fox-sized animals under 2 m long including the tail, about eight named genera across four continents, and southern Africa holds much the most diverse fauna of them; the Heterodontosaurus holotype came out of the Cape Province on the British-South African expedition of 1961-62. Its jaw carries three kinds of tooth at once - small incisor-like teeth, long canine-like tusks, and eleven tall chisel-shaped cheek teeth - which is what the name records.

Marsupials reached Australia from South America across the Antarctic land bridge in the Early Eocene, around 50 million years ago, in what looks like one dispersal of a single species. With terrestrial placentals gone from the continent early in the Cenozoic they radiated into roles filled elsewhere by placentals, large grazers included, and close to 70% of the 334 living marsupial species are Australian. The kangaroos are macropods that expanded from the Late Miocene on, as forest gave way to grassland.

'Limpet' names a shape rather than a lineage: the same low cone has been arrived at independently by patellogastropods, by vetigastropods such as the keyhole limpets, by neritimorphs and by several heterobranch groups. True limpets wander the rock at high tide and follow their own mucus trail back to a home scar worn into the stone. Their iron-mineralised teeth test at 3.0 to 6.5 GPa in tension, above spider silk.

Majungasaurus is an abelisaurid, the Gondwanan theropod family that also produced Carnotaurus; the family splits into western and eastern Gondwanan branches, and the most recent analyses put Majungasaurus with the Indian forms rather than the South American ones. It comes from the Maevarano Formation of Mahajanga Province in northwestern Madagascar, in the Maastrichtian, 70 to 66 million years ago. Bones bearing tooth marks of the same size and spacing as its own teeth make it the one non-avian dinosaur with direct evidence of cannibalism.

Moulting is most of what a mayfly does: the nymph works through anywhere between ten and fifty post-embryonic moults underwater, more numerous than in most other insect orders, over months or in some species years. Then it does the thing no other insect does - it moults once more after its wings already work, the winged subimago flying for a day or two, or in some species only a few minutes, before shedding again into the imago. Little is left of the animal afterwards: the adult females of Dolania americana live less than five minutes.

Morning glories are Ipomoea, a genus of over 600 species in the Convolvulaceae, and the sweet potato, Ipomoea batatas, is one of them — a morning glory grown for its root rather than its flower. The Mexican morning glory, Ipomoea tricolor, and its relatives carry lysergamides in their seeds, which Aztec and Zapotec specialists used in divination.

The nautilus is the only living cephalopod that still carries its shell on the outside; squid, cuttlefish and octopus all internalised or lost theirs after the lineages parted, and the nautilus has changed remarkably little since. Its fossil record runs from about 230 million years ago in the Triassic, and unlike the ammonites it came through the end-Cretaceous extinction. A hatchling starts with roughly four gas-filled chambers and an adult has thirty or more, the siphuncle drawing salt out of them to set buoyancy.

The orca is the largest member of Delphinidae, the oceanic dolphins. Its ecotypes have diverged far enough that a 2024 study argued the eastern North Pacific resident and transient forms should be raised to separate species, Orcinus ater and Orcinus rectipinnus; the Society for Marine Mammalogy has so far recognised them provisionally as subspecies instead, and the species as a whole remains listed as data deficient.

The common periwinkle is a littorinid sea snail of the higher and middle intertidal on rocky shores, native to the northeastern Atlantic — Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia. It reached North America around the middle of the 19th century, probably carried in rock ballast, and was first recorded in the Gulf of St Lawrence in 1840. A female packs 10,000 to 100,000 eggs into one horny capsule, and the animals live five to ten years, occasionally twenty.

The platypus is a monotreme, one of the egg-laying mammals, endemic to eastern Australia including Tasmania, and it split from the echidnas somewhere between 19 and 48 million years ago. The female lays two leathery eggs about 17 mm long, after roughly 28 days of internal development and ten more days of incubation outside. Its bill carries about 40,000 electroreceptors in rows, reading the currents thrown off by a prey animal's muscles while eyes, ears and nose are all shut underwater.

Henri Filhol named Proailurus in 1879 from fossils at the Saint-Gerand site in France, and it is generally taken as the first true cat and the ancestor of the whole family, giving rise to Pseudaelurus, which lived 20 to 10 million years ago and produced the major felid lineages. Proailurus itself ranged across Europe and Asia between about 30.8 and 25 million years ago; the type species weighed around 9 kg, was proportioned like a modern viverrid, and was at least partly a tree-climber.

Rafflesia is a flowering plant that has thrown away nearly everything a plant has — no stems, leaves or roots, only an absorptive organ spread through a Tetrastigma vine — and genetic work places it inside the Euphorbiaceae. Joseph Arnold found Rafflesia arnoldii at Bengkulu on Sumatra in 1818, and its blooms pass 100 cm across and 10 kg. The genus has taken up a large number of genes horizontally from its hosts, and one Philippine species appears to have lost its chloroplast genome outright.

Rhododendron and blueberry are both Ericaceae, plants of acid ground with a pH of roughly 4.5 to 5.5, feeding through fungal partners in soil high in organic matter. The genus runs to about 1,024 woody species, at their densest in the Sino-Himalayan region, southwest China and northern Burma. Some load grayanotoxin into pollen and nectar, and Xenophon recorded Greek soldiers behaving oddly after eating the honey in 401 BCE.

Scorpions are among the oldest known arachnids: the earliest found so far is Dolichophonus loudonensis, from the Silurian of what is now Scotland, about 430 million years ago. Over 2,500 species survive in 22 families, and unlike the great majority of arachnids, which lay eggs, scorpions appear to be universally viviparous, the young riding on the mother's back until their exoskeletons harden. All of them glow blue-green under ultraviolet light.

Every domestic silk moth descends from Bombyx mandarina, a wild moth ranging from inland China through Korea to Japan, whose males still fly perfectly well; the domestic stock traces to the inland Chinese population, and the earliest archaeological evidence for its keeping belongs to the Yangshao culture of northern China more than 5,000 years ago. Breeding since has cost Bombyx mori its colouring and its flight, and it does not exist in the wild; one cocoon unwinds into 300 to 900 m of raw silk, and a kilogram takes 4,000 to 7,000 of them.

Spiny lobsters are Achelata, a decapod group whose nearest relatives are the slipper lobsters rather than the clawed true lobsters: they never grew pincers on the first four pairs of walking legs, carrying long spiny antennae instead. In place of a claw they have a sound, made by dragging a soft plectrum at the antenna base across a file — a sticking and slipping like rubber on a hard surface, which keeps working even when a fresh moult has left the shell soft. They sometimes cross the sea floor in single files more than 50 animals long.

Strychnos nux-vomica is a deciduous flowering tree of the family Loganiaceae, native to India and southeast Asia. Its seeds run to about 1.5% strychnine and its dried blossoms about 1.0%, and the alkaloid is still used in baits to kill feral mammals. Most accidental human poisonings come not from eating it but from breathing the powder or taking it up through the skin.

Threshers are Alopiidae, lamniforms sitting alongside the Lamnidae of the great white and the mako, and two of the three species share that family's rare trick of regional endothermy — a counter-current heat exchanger warming a strip of red muscle along each flank. The lineage's own specialisation is the upper tail lobe, grown as long as the whole rest of the body; a 2013 study confirmed threshers swat schooling fish with it, stunning them before turning to feed. The common thresher reaches 6.1 m and over 500 kg.

Troodontids and dromaeosaurs such as Velociraptor are the two branches of Paraves closest to birds, similar enough that derived troodontids convergently evolved the dromaeosaur's enlarged second toe claw. The genus rests on a single tooth found in October 1855 in the Judith River Formation of Montana and described by Joseph Leidy in 1856; it was taken for a lizard's until 1877. Eggshell work published in 2023 found that several females laid into one nest, with reptile-like slow calcification and two working ovaries limiting how many eggs each could produce.

Tyrannosaurs started out as small theropods, and only some of them grew large in the Early Cretaceous: Yutyrannus, a basal tyrannosauroid from the 125-million-year-old Yixian Formation of Liaoning, weighed about 1,414 kg and carried filamentous feathers up to 20 cm long. Barnum Brown found the first partial Tyrannosaurus in eastern Wyoming in 1900 and a better skeleton in Montana's Hell Creek Formation in 1902, which Osborn named in 1905.
