The specimen 'Sue' is 12.3 to 12.8 m long at an estimated 8.4 to 9.2 tonnes.

Welwitschia is a gnetophyte and the only living genus of both its family and its order, a relict with nothing else beside it. It grows in the Namib of Namibia and Angola, where the coast gets almost no rain and the interior under 100 mm a year, so the plants gather along ephemeral water courses and draw on fog as well as groundwater. It never makes a third leaf: the two it starts with keep growing from the crown, up to 4 m long, on plants that may be 2,000 years old.

Several conifer lineages independently traded the woody cone for something fleshy a bird will swallow, and each built it from different parts: a juniper's galbulus is cone scales fused together, while the yew's cone is reduced to a single seed half-wrapped in a soft red aril 8 to 15 mm across. Thrushes and waxwings pass the hard seed undamaged in their droppings. The aril is the only part of a yew free of the alkaloid taxine, and the seed inside it is the dangerous piece.

Grey geese and swans sit together in Anserinae, the true goose and swan subfamily of the duck family Anatidae. Anser, the grey geese, has split into 11 living species spread right across the Holarctic, with at least one of them breeding in open wet country somewhere in the subarctic and cool temperate north. The greylag is the type species of the genus, the one Linnaeus described in 1758 as Anas anser, and at up to about 4 kg it is among the largest.

Bombyx mandarina is the wild moth from which every domesticated silkworm descends, ranging from inland China through Korea to Japan. Those populations have already drifted apart in the karyotype - Chinese specimens carry 56 chromosomes and Japanese ones 54 - and the domestic stock's affinities lie with the inland Chinese birds of the species, taken from wild stock as far back as 5,000 years ago. Unlike its descendant it is a fairly ordinary moth, the males with well-developed wings that still work.

Pangaea assembled around 335 million years ago and began breaking up by about 180. Africa is the piece that stayed: it lay near the middle of the supercontinent and has moved least since, which is why every other southern continent is described as having rifted away from it.

A rift opened between them around 190 million years ago at Falkland latitudes, and once a spreading ridge took over about 130 to 135 million years ago the two halves were being actively pushed apart. The South Atlantic was fully open by roughly 83 million years ago; the matching coastlines are what first suggested the whole idea.

Laurasia was Pangaea's northern half from about 335 to 175 million years ago, and separated from Gondwana between roughly 215 and 175 million years ago. Asia is the eastern bulk of it, assembled by collision as block after block was welded on.

The Uralian orogeny ran through the late Carboniferous into the early Triassic, roughly 300 to 250 million years ago, as Laurasia's eastern edge collided with Kazakhstania and the island arcs between them. That suture is the line Europe is conventionally divided from Asia along — the two are one landmass, and the Urals are the seam.

Laurasia came apart when the North Atlantic opened about 56 million years ago. The same event made Greenland a plate in its own right, separated from North America by the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay rift.

An annelid is an invertebrate built as a repeating series: a chain of segments called metameres, ringed externally by annuli and partitioned internally by septa, most carrying their own pair of coelomic cavities and their own set of organs. Chaetae of beta-chitin push through the skin for grip. Over 22,000 species live now, and the oldest confident fossil, Phragmochaeta from Sirius Passet, is about 518 million years old.

Development slowed or stopped short while sexual maturity arrives on time, so an animal breeds still wearing its larval body. It is not progenesis, where maturity is instead brought forward. Cold water and altitude select for it because metamorphosis is expensive, and a salamander short of iodine cannot complete it at all.

A skeleton worn on the outside: chitin laid down in layers as a cuticle, stiffened where support is needed and left flexible at the joints. It cannot grow with its owner, so anything wearing one has to shed it and expand before the new one hardens.

Not a group so much as everything left over: every animal that never evolved a vertebral column, which is about 95% of described animal species. The name records what they lack rather than anything they share, which is why it holds sponges and squid and beetles at once.

The branch of the amniotes that leads to reptiles and birds rather than to mammals — Huxley's 1864 division, with Synapsida on the other side. They excrete nitrogen as uric acid, which needs almost no water and goes out with the faeces, and their skin carries no glands of the kind mammals inherited from amphibians. That combination is what let the group hold arid ground.

Lepidoptera means scale-wing, from lepis and pteron, and the scales are the order: blade-like lamellae each on a stalk, their surface structured finely enough to make colour from interference as well as pigment. About 180,000 species have been described, 8.6% of all known living things, and all but roughly 18,000 of them are moths.

Feathers came before birds and before flight. The genes for them sit at the base of the archosaurs, around 250 million years ago, and branched feathers with barbs and barbules are preserved on theropods like Sinosauropteryx and on Anchiornis, which is older than Archaeopteryx. They are built from beta-keratin, hydrogen-bonded into pleated sheets and tougher than the alpha-keratin of hair and horn. The first ones could not have generated lift, so warmth, waterproofing and display came first.

Theropoda means beast-foot, from therion and pous. The group is diagnosed on the skeleton rather than the diet: hollow bones, three weight-bearing toes with claws, digit V lost early and digit I lifted clear of the ground, a ball-and-socket joint at the head of the neck, five or more sacral vertebrae, and a furcula. They appear about 231.4 million years ago and have not stopped — the 11,000-odd living birds are theropods, the smallest of them a bee hummingbird at 1.9 grams.

The arthropods that kept the two-branched limb: a crustacean's appendages are biramous, forking into two parts, and the second pair of antennae usually shows it plainly. What really unites a group this varied is the larva — the nauplius, with three pairs of appendages all on the head and a single eye. About 67,000 species are described, from Stygotantulus at 0.1 mm to a Japanese spider crab spanning 3.8 metres.

A gymnosperm that carries its seeds naked on the scales of a cone rather than inside a fruit. Most bear needle leaves, from 2 mm on the scale-leaved species to 600 mm on some pines, though cypresses flatten theirs to triangular scales instead. Pine cones open their scales to let winged seeds blow out; fir and cedar cones fall apart to release them. Just over 600 species survive, from a lineage in the fossil record for more than 300 million years.

Delphinium — about 300 species in the buttercup family, named for a flower whose five petal-like sepals fuse into a hollow pocket ending in a spur, which the Greeks thought looked like a dolphin. Every part of the plant carries diterpenoid alkaloids, methyllycaconitine chief among them, which block neuromuscular transmission and poison the heart; a fatal dose can act within hours. Aconitum turns out to sit inside this genus rather than beside it.

An antler is bone, and unlike a horn it is not sheathed in keratin — it is bone, cartilage, fibrous tissue, skin, nerve and blood vessel, grown fresh each year from a pedicle on the skull. It extends at the tip as cartilage that then turns to bone, fed the whole time by velvet, a highly vascular skin. It grows faster than any other mammal bone. When it is finished the velvet is shed, the bone dies, and osteoclasts eat through the base until the whole thing drops.

Eight legs on a cephalothorax, no antennae and no wings, the body in two parts — prosoma and opisthosoma — with chelicerae for feeding and pedipalps repurposed for feeding, walking or mating. Most are carnivores that cannot chew: they flood prey with enzymes and drink the pre-digested remains. Over 110,000 species are named, 51,000 of them spiders, and the true total may pass a million.

Not taming, which is one animal learning to tolerate you, but a multi-generational mutualism: the domesticator builds an environment where it manages another species' survival and breeding, and that species becomes dependent on the arrangement. It needed people to stay put. After the Last Glacial Maximum a warmer Holocene and growing populations made it possible from about 11,700 years ago — cereals in the Near East 13,000 to 11,000 years ago, livestock in the Fertile Crescent 11,000 to 10,000. Early farmers were not trying to make new species; they became entangled with them.

Fenton's reaction: iron(II) hands one electron to hydrogen peroxide and the peroxide comes apart into hydroxide and a hydroxyl radical — Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂ → Fe³⁺ + OH⁻ + •OH. Henry Fenton published it in 1894, from work on oxidising tartaric acid. The same chemistry runs inside cells wherever loose iron and peroxide meet.

Radiolysis. A gamma photon ionises water and the wreckage includes hydroxyl radicals, hydrated electrons, hydrogen atoms and peroxide. Because a cell is mostly water, this indirect route — radicals diffusing far enough to reach DNA — is the main damage mechanism for photons in radiation therapy, rather than a photon striking the DNA itself.

Homolysis: light of the right energy splits a shared pair down the middle instead of handing both electrons to one side, and each fragment leaves with one unpaired electron. It costs real energy — 435 kJ/mol to break H–H that way, 243 kJ/mol for Cl–Cl — which is why photodissociation, not gentle warmth, is a standard route to a radical.

The hydroxyl radical attacks guanine and leaves 8-oxoguanine, one of the commonest oxidative DNA lesions there is. The altered base pairs with adenine instead of cytosine, so the next round of copying writes G-to-T and C-to-A substitutions — a mutation rate above background, which is exactly what defines a mutagen. The glycosylase OGG1 cuts most of them back out first.

A mutagen turns carcinogenic when the damage lands in the genes that govern division — a proto-oncogene pushed into an oncogene, or a tumour suppressor switched off. The sets overlap without coinciding: around 90% of known carcinogens registered as mutagenic in the early Ames screens, yet sodium azide is mutagenic and has never been shown to cause cancer, and non-genotoxic carcinogens such as some hormones promote growth without binding DNA at all.

Muller showed in 1927 that X-rays raise the mutation rate in fruit flies and leave visible changes to the chromosomes themselves; the 1946 Nobel followed. Agents that break chromosomes outright are called clastogens, and a break put back wrong returns as a deletion, an inversion or a translocation rather than a single swapped base.

Gastrulation ends with three germ layers and no organs. Hox genes then fix which position along the head-to-tail axis is which, and the layers build to match: ectoderm into epidermis and neurons, mesoderm into heart, kidney and red cells, endoderm into lung, thyroid, pancreas and gut. In humans that work runs from about week three to week eight after fertilisation.

Two conditions make an agent a teratogen, and they are Wilson's fourth and second principles: it has to get across the placenta, and it has to arrive while the part it will damage is being built. Thalidomide is the whole argument in one drug — day 20 of gestation took the brain, day 21 the eyes, day 22 the ears and face, day 24 the arms, and after day 42 the same dose did nothing to the fetus.

A mutagen that reaches an embryo while the organs are forming can act as a teratogen too, damaging the cells doing the building. The categories overlap and are not the same: thalidomide alters no base at all — it works by making the cereblon ubiquitin ligase destroy developmental transcription factors — and what it caused was never inherited, which is what non-heritable means in the definition.

Wilson's fifth principle lists the four ways development can deviate: death, malformation, growth retardation, functional defect. Which one, and where, is set by the week — rubella between weeks five and ten damages eyes and ears, a cleft palate is decided between weeks four and seven. About 3% of US newborns have a birth defect, and around 65% of those have no cause anyone can name.

CYP2E1 in the liver oxidises vinyl chloride into chloroethylene oxide, an alkylating epoxide that binds DNA and disturbs proto-oncogene and tumour-suppressor expression — which is why the tumour turns up in the liver and not the lung that breathed the gas in. Dr John Creech found three cases of hepatic angiosarcoma among workers at B.F. Goodrich's Louisville PVC plant and reported them to NIOSH on 22 January 1974.

A flame short of oxygen builds rings instead of burning them. In the hydrogen-abstraction/acetylene-addition cycle an aromatic loses a hydrogen, the radical left behind adds a molecule of acetylene, and the sequence repeats until a new ring closes onto the old one. HACA is the route that assembles naphthalene both in flames and in the envelopes of carbon-rich stars.

Naphthalene is the most abundant single component of coal tar — typical tar is about 10% naphthalene by weight — and it melts at 80 °C, so it drops out of the distilled middle oil as pale crystals as that oil cools. Alexander Garden reported crystallising a silvery, camphor-like solid from coal-tar distillate in 1819; John Kidd named it in 1821 after the naphtha it came out of.

Coal tar is only about 1.5% anthracene, and it comes over late, in the heavy cut still called anthracene oil. Jean-Baptiste Dumas and Auguste Laurent crystallised it from that fraction in 1832; Laurent first took it for an isomer of naphthalene and called it paranaphthalene before renaming it from anthrax, the Greek for coal. Industry kept distilling for it because oxidising anthracene gives anthraquinone, and anthraquinone gives the red dye alizarin.

The same acetylene-addition cycle that closed naphthalene's second ring can close a third onto it, and the third ring goes on at an angle far more often than in line. The proof is in the tar: phenanthrene, the bent isomer, makes up around 4–6% of coke-oven coal tar, where anthracene, the straight one with the identical formula, manages about 1.5%. Fittig with Ostermayer, and Graebe independently, both pulled it out of coal tar in 1872.

A fourth ring fused onto the side of anthracene's three, which is exactly what the name records. Flames grow PAHs by adding whole rings as well as by adding acetylene: a phenyl radical adds to an aromatic and then cyclises onto it, the phenyl-addition/dehydrocyclization route, which runs efficiently at high temperatures and reaches structures that acetylene addition alone finds hard to build. The fusion leaves a bay region — the crowded inner pocket that makes four-ring PAHs easy prey for the enzymes that turn them into mutagens.

One more benzo ring fused on and the count reaches five: dibenz[a,h]anthracene, C22H14, first synthesised in 1918. It is barely volatile and barely soluble, so it travels stuck to particles in polluted air, soil and sediment, and it is genotoxic in both bacterial and mammalian cells — it slides between the base pairs of DNA and causes mutations there.

Fat dripping onto hot coals does not burn cleanly; benzo[a]pyrene is what incomplete combustion of organic matter yields between 300 and 600 °C, and the smoke carries it back up onto the meat. A 2001 National Cancer Institute study found levels far higher in food cooked well-done on a barbecue; cooked meat products have been measured at up to 4 ng/g, fried chicken at 5.5 ng/g and overcooked charcoal-barbecued beef at 62.6 ng/g.

A soot particle begins when two PAH molecules collide and stay together. Dimers held by nothing but attraction come apart again; when the pair goes on to form a covalent bond it survives, and putting that step into a flame simulation raises the predicted soot concentration by four orders of magnitude, matching what laser-induced incandescence measures. Trimers account for under 3% of the nuclei formed, so a bonded pair is essentially the whole of nucleation.

The definition the IPCC adopted turns on cooling: soot is what forms during the "quenching of gases at the outer edge of flames" of organic vapours — mostly carbon, with a little oxygen and hydrogen, in an imperfect graphitic structure. What settles on a flue wall is that: clumps of 6 to 30 nm particles, mixed with mineral matter and sometimes coated in sulfuric acid. Enough of it collecting in a chimney is what makes a chimney fire possible.

The burning cone reaches 700–950 °C during a puff, but hardly any of the smoke is made there. Just behind the fire sits an oxygen-starved distillation zone where the temperature falls from about 600 °C to 200 °C, and it is below roughly 350 °C, in that zone, that the majority of the toxicants are generated — which is the point heated tobacco products were designed around.

In 1775 Percivall Pott traced the scrotal cancer common among London's chimney sweeps to soot lodging in the skin — the first occupational cancer anyone described, and the first time a chemical mixture was tied to cancer at all. The sweeps had been in contact with soot since early childhood; one review puts the median age at first symptoms at 37.7 years, with cases in boys as young as 8. In 1922 R. D. Passey raised malignant skin tumours in mice using an extract of soot, which showed the cause was carried in the soot itself.

Benzo[a]pyrene is a procarcinogen: it does nothing until the body's own cytochrome P450 1A1 and epoxide hydrolase convert it, in three steps, into the diol epoxide BPDE. That electrophile is attacked by guanine, leaving a bulky adduct that distorts the double helix. Nucleotide excision repair clears most of them; the ones it misses produce G-to-T transversions, clustered in hotspots of the tumour-suppressor gene p53.

Chlorine substitutes into an alkane under ultraviolet light, or adds straight across the double bond of an alkene to give a di- or tetrachloro compound. Nothing in the chemistry stops at one chlorine, so controlling how far the reaction goes is the hard part. The largest single product is vinyl chloride — 13 million tonnes a year by 1985, nearly all of it polymerised into PVC.

Acetic acid dehydrated thermally gives ketene, and ketene attacks an aldehyde to close a four-membered beta-lactone — with formaldehyde, over an aluminium or zinc chloride catalyst, that lactone is beta-propiolactone. Ketene only does this under Lewis acid catalysis or against an electron-poor carbonyl, which formaldehyde is.

Ammonia opens the strained oxygen ring of ethylene oxide to give aminoethanol, and the aminoethanol is then closed back up around nitrogen — dehydrated over an oxide catalyst in the Nippon Shokubai process, or converted to a sulfate ester and eliminated in the older Wenker synthesis. Older routes aminated 1,2-dichloroethane or cyclised 2-chloroethylamine instead.

Proline's nitrogen sits inside its ring, which makes it a secondary amine, and nitrous acid from acidified nitrite nitrosates secondary amines directly. Ohshima and Bartsch turned that into a measurement in 1981: 300 mg of nitrate and 500 mg of proline by mouth, then N-nitrosoproline counted in 24 hours of urine, to see how much nitrosation is going on inside a living stomach.

Nitrosating nicotine and its relative nornicotine during tobacco curing produces the tobacco-specific nitrosamines NNN and NNK. IARC evaluated the pair in 2009 and placed both in Group 1, carcinogenic to humans. American dip snuff carries markedly more of them than Swedish snus.

Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus are ordinary weedy moulds, and on maize held warm and damp they make aflatoxin B1 as they grow. A contaminated maize harvest in Kenya in 2004 caused an acute outbreak with 125 confirmed deaths. FDA action levels for aflatoxin in food and feed run from 20 to 300 ppb depending on what it is for.

Phthalic anhydride condenses with L-glutamine, with triethylamine and acetic anhydride, at around 110 °C; the modern version of the route gives 85–93% yield at 99% purity. The molecule is a single ring system joined to a glutarimide, and that glutarimide end is the part that binds cereblon.

Mercury becomes methylmercury only when a microbe methylates it, and three groups do: sulfate-reducing bacteria, iron-reducing bacteria and methanogens, all working where oxygen has run out. From there it climbs — in top aquatic predators the concentration can reach a million times the level in the surrounding water.

Sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic sediment are the main methylators of mercury in most waters, which is what turned an industrial discharge into a poisoning. Chisso's factory at Minamata used a mercury catalyst to make acetaldehyde — 210 tonnes in 1932, 45,245 at the 1960 peak — and released waste into the bay from 1951 to 1968. Sediment at the mouth of the wastewater canal measured 2 kg of mercury per tonne.

Partial oxidation of toluene with oxygen, over cobalt or manganese naphthenate catalysts, turns the methyl group into a carboxylic acid. Abundant feedstock, high yield, and it is how nearly all of it is made now. The older route was dry distillation of gum benzoin, first described in 1556.

The precursor is 4-methoxyphenol, which is hydroquinone with one of its two hydroxyls methylated. Alkylating it with isobutylene — the branched four-carbon alkene from the same refinery cut that yields butane — hangs a tert-butyl group on the ring. It lands in two positions, and BHA is sold as the mixture of 2-tert-butyl and 3-tert-butyl-4-hydroxyanisole.

BHT is a cresol wearing two tert-butyl groups. p-Cresol — toluene with a hydroxyl on the far corner of the ring — is alkylated with isobutylene over sulfuric acid, and the two bulky groups settle either side of that hydroxyl. Isobutylene is the branched four-carbon alkene from the same refinery cut that yields butane.

A fresh cheese made from cream holds more water than its curd can keep, and whey weeps out on the shelf. Carob galactomannan binds that loose water at a fraction of a percent, which is why industrial cream cheese lists carob bean gum.

The emulsifier crowds milk protein off the fat globules, so fat part-coalesces into a network as the mix freezes. That network is what lets soft serve stand up dry at −4 °C holding 33 to 45% air, where ice cream needs −15 °C to keep shape.

Gluten's cross-linked network is what traps the carbon dioxide yeast makes; without it a batter cannot hold a bubble. Xanthan gum, used at 0.5% or less, supplies the stickiness gluten would have given, so the loaf rises and sets.

Kappa carrageenan forms strong rigid gels with potassium ions and binds hard to dairy protein, so it sets milk rather than merely thickening it. Boiling the whole red weed in milk is the old version; E407 is that extract, purified.

About 0.5 g of alginate per 100 g of juice, dripped into a bath of 0.5 g calcium chloride per 100 g of water. Calcium cross-links the alginate on contact, so a skin sets in seconds while the middle is still juice.

Milled oat solids settle out of water. Gellan sets a network too weak to taste but strong enough to hold plant particles suspended for the life of the carton, at about half the concentration agar would need to gel.

The fluid runs about 90% water, 9.5% sand and 0.5% chemicals, and thin water drops its sand at the wellbore. Guar gel, cross-linked by borate above pH 9, carries grains into the fracture; a breaker or pH 3–4 thins it for flowback.

Calcium is what holds the casein network together, and heating that network gives strings and free oil. Sodium citrate takes the calcium, so the freed protein emulsifies the fat into a sauce — Gerber and Stettler's 1911 Swiss trick.

Casein precipitates at pH 4.6 and coffee is acid enough to take it there — the white flecks called feathering. Dipotassium phosphate buffers the creamer, holding the mix off that point so the protein stays dissolved in the cup.

Curcumin is turmeric's yellow, sold on its own as E100, and it is what makes American mustard that colour rather than the dull tan of ground seed and vinegar. It is poorly soluble in water, so it is carried as a suspension rather than dissolved.

Betanin is beetroot red, E162. Light, heat and oxygen all break it down, which confines it to chilled or short-lived foods like yoghurt, and at yoghurt's pH of 4 to 5 it reads bright bluish-red. As a food additive it raises no safety concern.

The brown of a cola is caramel colour. Soft drinks take Class IV, E150d, sugar cooked with both ammonia and sulfite, which gives a dark colour and almost no flavour of its own; JECFA sets its acceptable intake at 200 mg per kg of body weight a day.

Gelatin sets clear, so a red jelly is a coloured one. Ponceau 4R, E124, is a synthetic azo red permitted across Europe, Asia and Australia at a European acceptable intake of 0.7 mg per kg of body weight; the US FDA has never approved it.

Sorbate is fungistatic, not lethal: surviving yeast cannot multiply, so the sugar stays in the bottle. Up to 200 mg a litre is allowed in wine above 5 g/L of residual sugar, always alongside sulfur dioxide — lactobacilli left to eat sorbate turn it geranium.

Benzoate only preserves acid drinks. Benzoic acid's pKa is 4.2 and only the undissociated molecule crosses into a microbe; once inside, an internal pH of 5 or lower cuts its fermentation of glucose by 95%. Food use runs 0.05 to 0.1%.

Six percent benzoic acid with three percent salicylic acid makes one fungistatic and keratolytic ointment: the second sheds the infected outer skin, the first holds back the dermatophyte in it. It is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines.

Sulfite blocks the browning reactions that darken fruit as it dries. The EU allows dried apricots up to 2,000 mg of sulfur dioxide per kg and sulphured fruit typically carries 200 to 2,000, so the 10 mg/kg declaration threshold is always crossed.

Nitrite in the brine is what leaves cured beef pink rather than grey, and it holds back Clostridium botulinum. Since 9 October 2025 the EU has capped what may be added to a meat product at 80 mg per kg, down from 150, to limit the nitrosamines that follow.

A saturated solution of calcium acetate poured into ethanol leaves a semisolid flammable gel that burns for around twenty minutes — the Sterno trick. The same salt is E263 in confectionery and a phosphate binder for failing kidneys.

Airfields spray potassium acetate solution instead of chloride salts because it is far less corrosive and easier on soils. It freezes near -60 °C, and it is fully biodegraded within about twenty days at an oxygen demand of 0.3 g per gram.

Washed fish mince will not set into a gel again once it has been frozen: the actomyosin denatures in storage and the gel strength goes with it. Sorbitol is blended in before freezing to hold that structure. A 2018 trial on freshwater fish ran four cryoprotectant blends and the strongest gel came from the highest of them — 4% sucrose, 4% sorbitol and 0.3% sodium tripolyphosphate.

Streptococcus mutans ferments sugar into the acid that dissolves enamel, and xylitol inhibits that species specifically — about three times as effectively as sorbitol does. Gum is mostly sweetener to begin with, 40 to 50% sugar alcohol by weight, so the swap is nearly the whole product. Dose matters: below 3.44 grams of xylitol a day there is no effect, and above 10.32 grams no further one.

Aspartame is about 200 times as sweet as sucrose, so the sugar in a soft drink is replaced by very little of it: a 12-fl-oz (350 ml) can of diet soda contains 0.18 grams. The FDA approved aspartame for carbonated beverages in 1983, which is what made the category possible; the acceptable daily intake is 50 mg per kg of body weight in the US and 40 mg/kg in the EU.

Sucralose is about 600 times as sweet as sucrose, so a spoonful of the pure compound is not a thing anyone could measure. The tabletop product is almost entirely carrier: Splenda granular is roughly 1.1% sucralose spread over dextrose and maltodextrin, which is what lets it be spooned against sugar one for one. A one-gram packet carries 3.36 kcal, under the 5 kcal per serving below which US labelling permits a zero-calorie claim.

Dried potato has to keep for a year in a cardboard box, and the fat left in the flake is what turns first — BHA is an antioxidant used in fat-containing foods to stop that rancidification. US regulation names the use and the amount: 21 CFR 172.110 permits 50 parts per million of BHA in potato flakes and in dehydrated potato shreds, and 10 ppm in potato granules.

Hydrogenation sets liquid oil solid, and shortening was sold from the start as a fat that needed no refrigeration — which leaves it a year of slow oxidation to survive. BHT is generally recognised as safe for that job as long as total antioxidants stay under 0.02% of the food's fat or oil content, and 21 CFR 172.115 separately allows 200 ppm in emulsion stabilisers for shortenings.

Nobody mines indium. It rides in sphalerite at trace level, and in the roast-leach-electrowin route to zinc it accumulates in the iron-rich residues left behind; from those it is leached out and finished pure by electrolysis.

Thallium is a trace passenger in iron pyrite. Roast the pyrite to make sulfuric acid and the thallium goes up the flue; it is leached back out of the flue dust with alkali or acid. Crookes first caught it there in 1861, by its green line.
209Bi + 70Zn → 278Nh + n — Riken began firing zinc-70 at a bismuth target in September 2003, took one atom in July 2004, a second in 2005, and a third after 450 more days of beam in 2012.
244Pu + 48Ca → 289Fl + 3n. Calcium-48 is both neutron-rich and doubly magic, so a fused nucleus made with it survives long enough to be seen — the hot-fusion trick that got Dubna elements 114 to 118.
243Am + 48Ca → 288Mc + 3n — Dubna and Livermore bombarded an americium-243 target with calcium-48 in August 2003 and got four atoms, each alpha-decaying on to element 113 in about 100 milliseconds.
248Cm + 48Ca → 293Lv + 3n — Dubna fired calcium-48 at a curium-248 target on 19 July 2000 and caught a single atom, identified by the flerovium it alpha-decayed into.

Didymium was never an element. Von Welsbach split it in 1885 into neodymium and a green-salted twin, and fractional crystallisation of the ammonium nitrate double salts is still how high-purity praseodymium is parted from its neighbours.

The richest terbium going is not an ore body but weathered granite. In South China's regolith the heavy rare earths cling as loose cations to kaolinite, and 0.3M ammonium sulfate pumped through the clay swaps NH4+ in and washes them straight out.

Boisbaudran worked on holmium oxide in Paris in 1886, dissolving it in acid and dropping the hydroxide back out with ammonia. He had to run the cycle more than thirty times before a new oxide separated, and named it 'hard to get at'.

Erbia was not one earth either. Cleve ran Mosander's nitrate method on erbium oxide, stripping out everything already known, and two new materials were left — one brown, one green. Soret had already seen the brown one's lines and called it element X.

Most erbium now comes from the ion-adsorption clays of southern China. Yttrium is about two thirds of the rare earth in that concentrate and erbia 4–5% of it; dissolved in acid, the erbium ion gives the pink colour Mosander saw at Ytterby.

Thulia was the green half of what Cleve took out of erbia in 1879, and nobody had enough to see the colour. Charles James got there in 1911 by fractional crystallisation of the bromate — 15,000 operations before the material came out homogeneous.

Ytterbium has europium's back door. Treat a buffered solution of the trivalent rare earths with molten sodium amalgam and only Yb3+ is reduced and pulled into the alloy, leaving the rest behind. Marignac found the earth inside erbia in 1878.

Marignac's ytterbia was two elements. Urbain split it in 1907, publishing 44 days ahead of von Welsbach, and lutetium — 0.0001% of monazite — still comes out last, crystallised as an ammonium nitrate double salt and finished by ion exchange.

Actinium-227 mostly beta-decays, but about one atom in a hundred goes by alpha instead, and what is left behind is francium-223 — long called actinium K. Perey caught it that way in 1939, and it is why uranium ore carries a trace of francium.

Ivy Mike, 1 November 1952: uranium-238 in the device swallowed fifteen neutrons inside a microsecond, then beta-decayed seven times over. Aircraft flew filter papers through the cloud, and Ghiorso's team found element 99 on them that December.

Element 100 was an order of magnitude scarcer in the debris than element 99, so filter papers were not enough: contaminated coral from Enewetak Atoll was shipped to Berkeley, and 255Fm — uranium-238 plus seventeen neutrons — came out of it.

253Es + 4He → 256Md + n. The target was a billion einsteinium atoms, and the arithmetic promised about one atom of element 101 per run; Berkeley's 60-inch cyclotron made seventeen in all, one at a time.

248Cm + 12C → 255No + 5n. Element 102 was claimed by four countries before Dubna's 1966 report settled it, and carbon-12 fired at a curium or californium target is still how the working isotope is made.

On 14 February 1961 Ghiorso's team fired boron-10 and boron-11 from Berkeley's heavy-ion linear accelerator at a three-milligram target of mixed californium isotopes. They reported 257Lr; later work showed they had actually made 258Lr.

Metal in the ground is an oxide or a sulfide — its atoms have already handed their outer electrons to oxygen or sulfur. Carbon monoxide off burning coke takes those away again, and the freed atoms pool their electrons into the sea that makes a metal.

Every gastropod does this as a larva: the visceral mass, mantle and shell rotate 180° anti-clockwise against the head and foot, carrying the mantle cavity and the anus forward over the head. The first 90° can take minutes.

Torsion is the gastropod synapomorphy: it happens in all of them during larval development and in no other mollusk. Snail, slug, limpet, whelk and nudibranch are one class of 65,000-plus species, second only to the insects.

Cephalopods are the only molluscs with a closed circulatory system: blood stays inside vessels the whole way round, driven by two branchial hearts at the gills plus one systemic heart for the rest of the body.

One shell split into left and right valves, joined by an organic ligament that works against the adductor muscles: the muscles pull the shell shut, the ligament springs it open. The head and the radula are gone entirely.

Clam is not a taxon but a way of living: the bivalves that spend life half-buried in the sand of a sea floor or riverbed, digging with a powerful foot and attached to nothing — unlike an oyster or a mussel.

The squid did not so much lose the ancestral mollusc shell as swallow it. What is left is the gladius, or pen: a feather-shaped chitinous blade in the functionally dorsal mantle, stiffening the body and anchoring muscle.

A jellyfish is a life stage, not a species. In strobilation the sessile polyp reabsorbs its tentacles and narrows into a stack of discs; each ephyra detaches, swims off, and grows into the bell-shaped medusa.

Worm names a shape, not a clade — the old taxon Vermes is paraphyletic and abandoned. Flatworms, roundworms and annelids are separate phyla; what they share is a long limbless tube of muscle, usually with no eyes.

Acoelomate, with no circulatory or respiratory organs, so oxygen has to diffuse in through the body surface and out again the same way. That only works if no cell is far from the skin — hence flat, ribbon-like, or microscopic.

Once Animalia, Plantae and Fungi had been carved out of the eukaryotes, everything left over was filed as Protista. It is a definition by exclusion: a paraphyletic group with no unique trait that unites all of them.

Carl Sagan's formulation, adopted as NASA's working definition: a self-sustaining chemical system capable of undergoing Darwinian evolution. Metabolism is the self-sustaining half, and heredity supplies the rest.
Life is a property; an organism is one packet of it — any living thing that functions as an individual, built of a single cell or of many. Where one individual stops is still genuinely argued over.
The gastropods that kept a coiled calcium-carbonate shell big enough to withdraw into. Slugs are the ones that lost it, or reduced it to an internal remnant, in several separate lineages.

An oyster reef builds itself out of oysters. Larvae need hard substrate, so spat settle and cement onto the shells of older and dead oysters, and each generation adds its shells to the structure under it.
A hen deposits gram amounts of calcium carbonate in about 20 hours: 95 to 97% of the finished shell, stabilised by a protein matrix without which the calcite would be too brittle to keep its form.

A turtle's spine and expanded ribs fuse by ossification to dermal plates under the skin, making one bony box, and scutes of keratin much like horn or nail overlay it. The ribs are in the shell, so it cannot be left behind.
Take enough heat out of anything and its particles stop sliding and lock into fixed positions. A solid keeps both its shape and its volume, and the atoms can do nothing but vibrate where they stand.
Put enough heat in and the pull between particles stops mattering. A gas keeps neither shape nor volume: it spreads until the container runs out, and it is the only common state you can squeeze.
A solid taken past its melting point is a liquid: the lattice is gone but the particles still touch. It keeps its volume and gives up its shape, and it is nearly impossible to compress.

The other way in. Cool a gas to its saturation point and it condenses to the middle state. Liquids need a narrow band of temperature and pressure, which makes them the rarest of the four in the universe.
Solid to liquid. At the melting point the ordered arrangement breaks down, and the temperature stops climbing while the latent heat of fusion goes entirely into taking the lattice apart.
Liquid to solid, and exothermic: the latent heat has to come back out. Without something to nucleate on, pure water will supercool to −40°C and still refuse to start.

Liquid to gas, by two different routes. Below the boiling point it happens only at the surface and is called evaporation; once the vapour pressure beats the air, bubbles form inside and it is boiling.
Gas back to liquid, the reverse of vaporisation. It starts when a vapour is cooled to its saturation limit — the dew point — which is every cloud, every fogged window and half of the water cycle.
Some solids never bother with the liquid step. Leave dry ice out and it goes straight to gas at −78.5°C; leave naphthalene mothballs out and they simply shrink away, never wetting the shelf.
Sublimation run backwards: vapour to solid with no liquid in between, giving out heat where sublimation takes it in. Frost on a cold window is deposition, and so is soot laid down on a chimney wall.

Heat a gas far enough and collisions start knocking electrons clean off the atoms. What is left is charged and mobile: it conducts electricity and bends to magnetic fields as a neutral gas never does.
Ionise a gas and you have the fourth state. The classical four run solid, liquid, gas, plasma, and the transition between the last two is exactly this one.
Cut the universe into what it actually contains. Under 5% of it is matter — anything with mass that takes up space. The other 95% is dark matter and dark energy, and nobody can pick either up.

Every particle has a twin of the same mass and opposite charge. Dirac's equation demanded them in 1928, and they only ever appear in pairs: a gamma ray above 1.022 MeV can become one particle and one anti.

Send silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field and the beam splits in two rather than smearing out. That is Stern and Gerlach in 1922: angular momentum that is intrinsic, and quantised in halves of ħ.
Half-integer spin makes a fermion, and fermions are what matter is built from. The Standard Model has twenty-four: six quarks, six leptons, and an antiparticle for each one.

Push two identical fermions into the same quantum state and they refuse. Pauli wrote the rule in 1925; it fills electron shells in order, gives the periodic table its shape, and holds up a white dwarf.

Spin sorts every particle into two camps. Half-integer and you are a fermion, one to a state. Whole-integer and you are a boson, and any number can pile into the same state — which is what a laser is.

Every force is a boson passed between matter particles: the photon for electromagnetism, gluons for the strong force, W and Z for the weak. Gravity is the fourth, and the one this scheme still cannot fit.
The force gluons carry. At a femtometre it is about 100 times electromagnetism and 10^38 times gravity, and unlike either it does not weaken with distance — which is why no quark ever gets out.

The force the W and Z carry, and the only one that can change a quark's flavour — so it is the force behind beta decay and behind hydrogen fusing at all. It also violates parity, which no other force does.

The force the photon carries: second strongest of the four and unlimited in range, though its two signs of charge cancel out at large scales. Every chemical bond and every push on a solid object is this.

Cut into a proton and it is not three quarks sitting quietly. Most of what is in there is the field between them: eight kinds of massless gluon, which carry colour charge themselves and so pull on each other.

The half of matter that feels the strong force, so gluons never let one go: colour confinement means no quark has ever been seen alone. They are also the only particles whose charge is not a whole multiple of e.
The other half of matter: the fermions that do not feel the strong force, so they travel alone instead of being locked inside a hadron. Six of them — electron, muon, tau, and a neutrino for each.
Quarks bound by the strong force, and always colourless: three quarks, or a quark with an antiquark. The free proton is the only stable hadron; a free neutron half-lives in about 611 seconds.
Three quarks means an odd number of half-spins, so every baryon is a fermion. Protons and neutrons are baryons, and they are very nearly all of the mass of everything you can pick up.

A quark with an antiquark means an even number of half-spins, so a meson is a boson. Yukawa predicted them in 1935 as the glue between nucleons; every one is unstable, the best lasting a fraction of a nanosecond.
The second-generation copy of the down quark: same −1/3 charge, about twenty times the mass. It got its name from the oddly long-lived 'strange particles' spotted in cosmic rays in 1947.

The second-generation copy of the up quark: same +2/3 charge, 1.27 GeV instead of a few MeV. Brookhaven and SLAC announced the J/psi on the same day in November 1974, and it is a charm-anticharm pair.
One generation further up the same −1/3 column: 4.18 GeV. Lederman's group found it at Fermilab in 1977 inside the upsilon. It decays reluctantly, which is what lets detectors tag b-jets today.
One generation further up the +2/3 column, and a staggering jump: about 173 GeV, heavier than an atom of gold. CDF and DØ found it at Fermilab in 1995. It decays too fast to form a hadron at all.
A cosmic-ray proton hits a nucleus high in the air, makes pions, and the pions decay to muons. Around 10,000 land on every square metre of ground a minute — only time dilation gets them down.

Perl's group found it at SLAC's SPEAR ring between 1974 and 1977, as events that made no sense any other way. At 1777 MeV it outweighs a proton, and it is the only lepton heavy enough to decay into hadrons.
Pauli invented it in 1930 to save the books: when a neutron becomes a proton and an electron, the energy does not add up unless something neutral leaves too. It took until 1956 to catch one.
The first-generation neutrino, paired with the electron. Cowan and Reines caught it beside a reactor in 1956. About 65 billion of them from the Sun cross every square centimetre of you each second.
Lederman, Schwartz and Steinberger aimed a neutrino beam at a detector at Brookhaven in 1962 and got only muons, never electrons. That proved neutrinos come in more than one kind. Nobel Prize, 1988.
The third-generation neutrino, and the last Standard Model fermion to be seen directly: DONUT at Fermilab announced it in July 2000, a quarter of a century after the tau itself turned up.
A neutron decays because one of its down quarks emits a W− and turns into an up quark. That is beta decay, and the W is the thing that does it. At 80.4 GeV it is heavier than a whole silver atom.
The neutral weak carrier, 91.19 GeV. The proof came in 1973, when a neutrino was seen bouncing off matter and staying a neutrino — a neutral current. CERN made real W and Z in 1983 with UA1 and UA2.

ATLAS and CMS announced it on 4 July 2012 at about 125 GeV, after a forty-year search. It has zero spin — the first elementary scalar ever found — and its field is what gives the W, the Z and the fermions mass.

Twelve matter fermions, five bosons, and three of the four forces. Settled in the mid-1970s, it has survived every test since — and still says nothing about gravity, dark matter, or the matter-antimatter imbalance.
A muon lasts 2.2 microseconds and then always ends the same way: an electron, a muon neutrino and an electron antineutrino. There is nothing lighter and charged for it to become.

Beta decay, drawn properly. A down quark of charge −1/3 emits a virtual W− and is left an up quark of +2/3; the W then becomes an electron and an antineutrino. Only the weak force can change a flavour like this.
Any compound with oxygen bonded to another element, oxygen sitting at oxidation state −2. Most of the Earth's crust is oxides, and even a sheet of aluminium foil is wearing a skin of Al2O3.
Heat a metal in air and its surface turns. Zinc powder burns outright: 2 Zn + O2 makes 2 ZnO. Gold and platinum are prized precisely because they refuse to do it.
Mendeleev laid the elements out by weight in 1869 and left gaps for what he could not find. Moseley showed in 1913 that the real order is the proton count. 118 now, of which 94 occur on Earth.
Not shared between two atoms and not handed over, but pooled: positive ions sitting in a sea of electrons that belongs to all of them at once. That sea is the conduction, the lustre, and the bend.

IUPAC's test is an atom with a partly filled d sub-shell — groups 3 to 12. That half-empty shell gives several oxidation states a step apart, which is why their salts are coloured and why so many catalysts are these.
Group 2, with two electrons filling the outer s orbital. They are named for their oxides: quicklime, magnesia and baryta were 'earths' — fireproof and water-insoluble — and they turn water alkaline.

The fifteen from lanthanum to lutetium, filling the 4f shell. Because 4f hides beneath the outer electrons they behave almost identically, so the table floats them out below and separating them needs solvent extraction.

The second floated row: actinium to lawrencium, filling 5f as the lanthanides fill 4f. Seaborg proposed the family in 1944. Every single one is radioactive, and only thorium and uranium are left on Earth in quantity.

Every raindrop is an acid before it lands. Carbon dioxide dissolves into it and becomes carbonic acid, which is why clean rain sits above pH 5 and below 7 instead of neutral. No acid went in; one came out.
Quicklime is an oxide, not a base: no hydroxide in it. Slake it and CaO plus water becomes calcium hydroxide, and a saturated solution of that sits at pH 12.4, caustic enough to burn skin.

Berzelius called them salt-formers, and a salt is where you get one back. Drive a current through sodium chloride and chloride ions surrender an electron at the anode: 2Cl- becomes Cl2, chlorine gas, 97 million tonnes of it a year.

A spiral is a galaxy whose gas settled into one flat disc where everything orbits the same way. The disc turns at different speeds by radius, so the arms cannot be fixed strings of stars: they are density waves that material drifts into and out of.
The nearest large barred spiral to us, 2.54 million light-years off, named for the patch of sky it sits in: the constellation Andromeda, itself named for the princess chained to the sea cliff.

Two suns circling a common centre every 79.8 years, swinging from 11.2 AU apart to 35.6, with a red dwarf bound to the pair 13,000 AU further out. That third star, Proxima, is the closest star to the Sun and still too faint to see.

A requiem shark that rewires its own salt balance. Entering fresh water it throttles the rectal gland back to hold on to sodium and chloride, the gills take ions up from the river, and the kidneys pour out dilute urine while reabsorbing solutes.

An antennariid frogfish, so an anglerfish. Its pink and white fingerprint stripes echo the hermatypic corals it lives among, and when it leaves the bottom it balls up until it reads as a piece of debris bouncing along rather than a fish.

The echinoderm that grew a jaw. Five calcium-carbonate teeth hang in a muscular frame Aristotle compared to a lantern, and they grasp, scrape, pull and tear well enough to cut a kelp holdfast or bore into rock.

The echinoderm that eats outside itself. It pulls a shell apart until the gap is a fraction of a millimetre, pushes its cardiac stomach through, digests the animal inside its own shell, then hauls the stomach back on ligaments in the arms.

An invertebrate built out of calcite. Its skeleton sits in the dermis as plates called ossicles, each a porous mesh named stereom, laced together by collagen fibres. Nothing outside this phylum makes a skeleton that way.

The annelid that eats the ground. Soil goes into a muscular gizzard where grit grinds it, and comes out as casts. Darwin put 53,000 of them in an acre of arable land and doubted many animals had done more to the surface of the world.

A sea star under a coat of thorn-like spines that drive saponin-bearing tissue into whatever presses on them, causing a sharp stinging pain. It eats what almost nothing else will: living hard coral, up to 6 square metres of reef a year.

Chiroptera means hand-wing. Five elongated digits radiate from the wrist and frame the patagium, a skin membrane running from arm and fingers to the flank and hind limbs — the only mammal capable of true sustained flight.

The pinniped that went without the eared seal's kit: ear holes rather than flaps, hind flippers that will not rotate forward, so on land it galumphs on its belly. It regulates heat by diverting blood into a smooth layer of blubber under the skin.

Build a chamber round the fire instead of standing the ware in it. A kiln is a thermally insulated chamber — a type of oven — and charcoal inside one reaches temperatures an open wood fire never will.
The masonry oven is a kiln you bake in: a chamber of fireproof brick, fired with wood, then swept of ash so the bread meets the heat the brick has stored. Same chamber, lower temperature.
Cast iron replaced masonry and the range shrank to fit a kitchen. A modern stove has an oven in it — an enclosed box beside the fire, for baking rather than direct heat.
A stovetop kettle is a metal pot built for one job, taking its heat from the hob below. Lid, spout and handle; stainless steel now, copper and cast iron in the 1800s.
The electric kettle moved the element off the hob and put it inside the water. Nothing heats but the water itself, which is why it beats a pan on a stove.

A toaster is heating elements with slots between them. It waited on nichrome, patented by Albert Marsh in 1906 — the oldest resistance heating alloy, and the first wire that would sit at red heat in open air day after day.
A freezer is a specialised refrigerator: the same vapour-compression loop pushed below the freezing point of water, about -18 °C. Home freezer compartments arrived in 1940.
A stationary blender is a container with a rotating blade at the bottom, powered by an electric motor in the base. The jar is only there to keep the food against the blade.
The tinsmith John Landis Mason patented the pattern in 1858: a glass jar with a thread moulded into its neck, and a metal band that screws down to press a flat lid against the rim.
A tin can is not tin. It is a steel can with a thin tin coating, and the coating is the whole point — it stops the contents rusting the steel they sit against.
Withies crossed over and under each other until they hold their own shape. Willow was the material of choice for its flexibility and for how easily it can be grown and cut.
A sink is a bowl-shaped plumbing fixture. The basin is the old part; what makes it a sink is the pipework — water arriving under pressure and a drain taking it away.
A tap is a screw with a washer on the end of it, wound down onto a seat to shut off the flow. The first screw-down mechanism was patented by the Rotherham brass founders Guest and Chrimes in 1845.
A broad, mainly flat vessel with a lip, thrown on the potter's wheel and fired hard enough for daily use. Give it a rounder, deeper profile and you have made a bowl instead.
A mug is a type of cup: one with a handle, straight-sided, holding 250 to 350 ml. Thick stoneware walls are what let you hold it while the drink inside stays hot.
Brickwork is masonry made of bricks and mortar. The mortar is not glue so much as bedding: a uniform 10 mm joint that lets units that are never quite identical stack true.
Thatching lays bundles of straw so each course sheds water onto the one below, fixed down with horizontal sways and hairpin spars of twisted hazel. The packed straw traps air and insulates as well.
Solid floors are planks milled from single pieces of timber and laid at right angles across the joists. They were structural first — the floor was the thing holding you up, not a surface.
A room is any enclosed space in a structure, bounded by walls, which you can enter only through a door or similar dividing structure. Without the door it is not a room, only a cavity.
Walls and a roofing system to keep the rain out of the dwelling space — everything else a house has is added to that. The social unit living inside it is called a household.

Masonry built to carry the smoke of a fire out past the living space, kept as near vertical as possible so the gases draw themselves up. Domestic chimneys appear in northern Europe in the 12th century; England's oldest survivor is at Conisbrough, 1185.
Locks have been in use over 6,000 years. The Egyptian wooden pin lock was a bolt, a door fixture and a key that lifted the pins clear — and the modern Yale is a developed version of exactly that.
A shelf is a flat horizontal plane fixed to a wall or other vertical surface. The board is nothing on its own; the wall is what turns it into storage.
It was a cup board: open shelved tiers for displaying plates, cups and saucers. Put doors on the front and the display becomes storage, which is what the word now means.
A woven carpet comes off a loom much like woven cloth; a knotted pile carpet adds a supplementary weft that rises at right angles from the weave. Rug meant a coarse coverlet until about 1808.
Teeth cut into the edge of a steel strip, then bent alternately left and right. That set is the whole trick: the cut ends up wider than the blade, so the blade never binds in its own kerf.
A hand drill's crank was replaced by an electric motor geared down for torque — patented in Melbourne in 1889 by Arnot and Brain, and made portable by the Fein brothers of Stuttgart in 1895.

A helical thread cut round a shank, so a twist becomes a pull. Every wood screw was filed by hand until Job and William Wyatt patented a screw machine in 1760; by the 1780s the works made 16,000 a day with 30 people.
The tool exists only because the fastener does. A screwdriver is classified entirely by its tip, because the tip has to match the driving surfaces cut into the screw head.
The other way to turn a threaded fastener: grip its flats from outside instead of a slot in its head. A wrench gives grip and mechanical advantage in applying torque to nuts and bolts.

A stone head lashed to a wooden haft — birch tar and rawhide held the blade on. Hafted axes date back at least 46,000 years in northern Australia; the unhafted hand axe is a million years older still.
A broad blade of sheet steel, its back folded into a socket, on a hardwood handle chosen for a wood that will not snap. The blade digs; the handle is the lever.

Two long stiles with rungs let into them. Rigid ladders were wood until aluminium took over in the 20th century — and one is painted on a wall of the Spider Caves in Valencia at least 10,000 years ago.
A table becomes a workbench when it gains a way to fix the workpiece to the surface, so the work can be attacked with both hands. Roubo drew the standard pattern in 1769.

Tailors used unmarked cloth tapes, notched by hand. James Chesterman's 1821 retractable design was a spring-loaded cloth strip with markings, in a compact case; he later repurposed surplus pannier-dress wire for the first steel tape.
A gear is a toothed wheel, and nothing more: cut teeth into the rim and its rotation can be handed to another wheel instead of slipping against it. Two meshed gears are a gear train.
Woven cloth cut to the shape of a body and sewn. The world's oldest preserved garment is a linen shirt from a First Dynasty tomb at Tarkhan in Egypt, and it is already sophisticatedly cut.

Trousers came from riding. The oldest known pair, from the Yanghai cemetery at Turpan and dated between the 13th and 10th centuries BC, is wool with straight legs and a wide crotch, and was likely made for horseback.
Wallets were developed after paper currency reached the West in the 1600s. Before that people carried drawstring leather coin purses — a pouch, not a flat folded case sized to a note.
Sheet metal cut and worked to one thin edge, kept only for hair. Excavations in Egypt have turned up solid gold and copper razors in tombs from the 4th millennium BC.
A printed promise standing in for metal. Banknotes were first issued by commercial banks, legally required to redeem them for coin on demand at the chief cashier's counter.
The quill pen is a flight feather cut to a nib, holding a bead of ink in its hollow shaft. It replaced the reed pen from about the 7th century, because it wrote finer on skin.
A graphite core in a wooden case that stops it snapping and keeps it off your hand. Red cedar was the favoured timber because it is aromatic and does not splinter when sharpened.

The eraser exists because the pencil does — and the material is named after the job. Edward Nairne sold natural rubber cubes for lifting pencil marks off paper from 1770, at three shillings a half inch.

Two blades joined at a pivot so their sharpened edges slide past each other. Roman pivoted shears survive from the 2nd century AD, but they were not made in numbers until Hinchliffe of Sheffield, 1761.

Printing gives you copies; the wire gives you news worth printing today. Few papers could afford foreign bureaus, so they bought telegraphed copy from agencies — Havas from 1835, the Associated Press from 1846.

A portolan chart is drawn from compass observations: a web of windrose lines showing constant bearings, coastlines, and place names written perpendicular to the shore. No latitude, no longitude at all.
A road is a prepared surface. Asphalt concrete is mineral aggregate bound with bitumen, laid in layers and compacted — the stone carries the load and the bitumen keeps it from scattering.
A street is a public thoroughfare lined with buildings on one or both sides. A road's job is transport; a street's job is the people beside it — which is why the buildings are what make one.
A market is a place people gather regularly to buy and sell — a souk, a bazaar, a mercado, a tianguis, a palengke. It needs somewhere public to stand and a coin everyone will take.
A shop is a market stall that stopped packing up. Retail shops grew over centuries from little more than rude booths into permanent premises, selling to the person who will use the goods.

What makes a town rather than a village is the market: it supplies goods and services to the countryside around it. Domesday listed 50 markets in England in 1086, and some 2,000 more were founded between 1200 and 1349.

A school is the institution and, for in-person learning, the building: a place designed to hold learners under a teacher's direction. Many early public schools were literally one room and one teacher taking seven grades.

The word means a place of hospitality, and that is what these were first: somewhere to lie down. Historically hospitals were founded and funded by Christian religious orders, and staffed by their members rather than physicians.

The chain is what made the bicycle safe. Running it from frame-mounted cranks to the rear wheel let both wheels shrink to the same size and the seat drop — the safety bicycle, about 1885, barely changed since.
A goods wagon that stopped needing to be pulled. Gottlieb Daimler built the Motor-Lastwagen in 1896; trucks still use body-on-frame construction, with the cab independent of the load behind it.

Four fixed propellers cannot be flown by hand — control comes only from varying each rotor's speed, thousands of times a second. Cheap lightweight flight controllers and accelerometers arrived around 2005-2010, and the quadcopter arrived with them.
Every adult fluke carries two cup-shaped muscular suckers, an oral and a ventral one, and a tapeworm's scolex carries four. A parasite with no legs still has to hold on.

why: The anterior end of a tapeworm is a knob under 2 mm across carrying four radially arranged acetabula, and in armed species a hooked rostellum between them. It is not a head: it has no mouth.

why: The rostellum is a fleshy protuberance in the middle of the four suckers, retractable in some species and armed in others. Taenia solium's carries two rows of 22 to 32 spiny hooks.

why: Segments bud from germinal tissue behind the scolex and are pushed backwards as newer ones form. Each is hermaphroditic; the gravid ones at the far end break off and leave in the feces.

why: An adult tapeworm has no mouth, no digestive tract and no blood vessels. Its outer surface is metabolically active, releasing enzymes from microtriches and taking everything in through the skin.

why: A gravid proglottid is a uterus packed with eggs, and inside each egg sits a hexacanth embryo — an oncosphere carrying six hooklets it uses to bore through the intermediate host's intestinal wall.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

why: Once through the gut wall the oncosphere settles in tissue and becomes a cysticercus: a small fluid-filled bladder with the scolex inverted inside it. The bladder worm is the stage that infects the next host.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

why: An Echinococcus oncosphere that reaches the liver grows slowly into a hydatid cyst, its brood capsules budding scolices into the fluid. Rupture spills that fluid, and can cause anaphylactic shock.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

why: Flukes are hermaphrodites with one exception: the blood flukes have separate sexes. The male's body curls up at its edges into a long channel, and the larger female lies inside it for their whole adult lives.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

why: A fluke egg hatches in fresh water into a ciliated, free-swimming miracidium. It must penetrate the right species of snail to go any further, and it is specific to that one species.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

why: Inside the snail the miracidium multiplies asexually through sporocysts and rediae, so hundreds of cercariae leave for every one larva that entered. Each has a swimming tail; the blood flukes' is forked.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

why: The cercariae of the gut, liver and lung flukes never pierce skin. They shed the tail, secrete a thick wall and encyst on water plants or inside a fish or a crab, and wait there to be swallowed.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

why: The exterior surface of a roundworm is a collagen-rich cuticle tough enough to resist a host's digestive enzymes. Because it cannot stretch far, the growing larva has to moult out of it four times over.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 10

why: The anterior end of a roundworm may carry hooks, teeth or cutting plates inside a hardened mouth cavity, used to grip. Ancylostoma's holds two pairs of teeth; Necator's holds a pair of cutting plates instead.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 10

why: Trichuris eggs are barrel-shaped and brown with a transparent protuberance at each pole. The two plugs are the whole identification, and the egg needs two to three weeks in soil before it can infect anyone.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: A Trichinella larva enters a striated muscle cell and reprograms it: the cell stops being muscle and becomes a collagen-walled capsule around the worm. Stomach acid is what releases the larva in the next host.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: Adult filariae in the tissues do not lay eggs; they release live embryos, microfilariae, into blood or skin. Wuchereria's peak in peripheral blood at night, matched to when the mosquito that carries them feeds.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 27

why: The Mastigophora are the protists that move by lashing flagella rather than by pseudopodia or by cilia — the group that holds Giardia, Trichomonas, the trypanosomes and Leishmania.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

why: The ventral surface of Giardia is dished into a rigid concavity built on a spiral of microtubules. It grips the intestinal epithelium, which is why the parasite is shed into the stool only intermittently.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 83

why: In Trichomonas and in the trypanosomes a flagellum runs backwards attached to the body wall instead of trailing free, and its beat sends a visible ripple down the membrane it is fastened to.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

why: Trichomonas has four flagella at the front and a fifth behind, all joined to an undulating membrane, and a barb-like rod of microtubules projecting opposite them. The axostyle is thought to anchor the cell and to do some of the tissue damage.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

why: A network of interlocked circular DNA packed inside a single mitochondrion, holding many copies of the mitochondrial genome. Only one class of flagellates carries one, and it is named after it: the Kinetoplastida.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

why: Nearly every apicomplexan is a parasite, and this is the machine that makes it one: a polar ring of microtubules with secretory rhoptries and micronemes behind it, used to force entry into a host cell.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 70

why: A blood-feeding parasite that digests haemoglobin releases free heme, which would kill it. Plasmodium crystallises the heme instead into hemozoin — inert, iron-rich, and dark enough to see down a microscope.
A roundworm named for its shape: a slender anterior three-fifths threaded into the mucosa of the large intestine, with a thicker handle behind. It feeds on tissue secretions rather than on blood.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: The parasitic females reproduce parthenogenetically, with no male anywhere in the cycle. Their eggs hatch inside the gut wall, so it is larvae that appear in the stool, and those larvae can reinfect the same host.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: The gravid female is close to a metre long and almost entirely uterus — a bag of larvae. About a year after infection she raises a burning blister in a limb, and cold water on it makes her expel them in a milky cloud.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 26

why: Adult pairs live for years coiled in fibrous nodules the host builds around them, called onchocercomas. Those adults do little harm; it is the microfilariae they release, wandering the skin and the eye, that blind people.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 27

why: The adult is tiny — 3 to 6 mm, three or four proglottids — and lives in a dog's intestine. Nearly all the animal's mass is on the other side of its cycle, in a hydatid cyst growing for years in a sheep or a person.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 46

why: A pseudophyllid tapeworm whose scolex grips with two slit-like grooves rather than four suckers. It competes for dietary vitamin B12 directly, and in about 1% of infections that causes a macrocytic anaemia.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 45

why: Its cercariae never touch skin. They encyst as metacercariae on raw water vegetation such as watercress, and whatever grazes or eats that plant swallows them; the young flukes then bore to the bile ducts.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

why: A thick, spined-tegument fluke that settles in pairs inside cysts in the lung and lays eggs that leave in sputum. The chronic bloody cough it produces is routinely mistaken for tuberculosis.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

why: A ciliate alveolate rowed along by a full coat of cilia — the only member of the phylum Ciliophora known to be pathogenic to humans. Its main reservoir is domestic and wild pigs, not people.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 96

why: Unlike most protozoan parasites it never enters a cell; it swims free in blood and lymph, driven by a flagellum bound along its side into an undulating membrane, and swaps its surface coat to stay ahead of the immune system.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 110

why: A kinetoplastid: its single mitochondrion holds a disc of interlocked DNA circles so large it is visible under a light microscope. In a blood smear the parasite takes a characteristic C shape.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 111

why: Glossina is a true fly like the housefly, but an obligate parasite: both sexes feed only on vertebrate blood, and the crop stretches enough to take a meal equal to the fly's own weight.
Phlebotomine sandflies are small — a body around 3 mm — and densely hairy, which helps them escape notice. Only the female takes blood, and she is the vector of every form of leishmaniasis.

Simulium lays its eggs in running water and the larvae hold onto submerged rocks with hooks. That is the whole reason river blindness is called river blindness: the vector cannot breed away from a fast stream.
A blood-feeding bug that bites at night, usually on the face. The parasite passes in the insect's feces, not its saliva — unusual among bloodsucking vectors — and enters when the bite is scratched.
It makes the worm's membranes permeable to calcium ions; the influx locks the muscles in contraction. It also disrupts the tegument, exposing the parasite's own antigens to the host's immune system.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 172

why: It binds the worm's beta-tubulin so microtubules cannot assemble, and glucose uptake fails with them. The parasite is forced onto its glycogen stores and dies when the ATP runs out.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 172

why: It binds the colchicine site of beta-tubulin, blocking tubulin from polymerising in the parasite's intestinal cells. The worm is immobilised gradually rather than killed outright, and passes out.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

why: Omura's soil Streptomyces yielded the avermectins, and Campbell's screen showed they paralysed nematodes. The drug binds glutamate-gated chloride channels found in invertebrate nerve and muscle, and not in ours.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 178

why: A nitroimidazole that only becomes toxic once its nitro group is reduced, which happens in anaerobic metabolism. One drug therefore covers Giardia, Trichomonas, Entamoeba and the anaerobic bacteria, and spares aerobes.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 173

why: It uncouples the worm's oxidative phosphorylation and blocks its glucose uptake, so the scolex loses its grip and is digested. It is not taken up from the gut, which is why it reaches worms in the lumen and nothing else.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

why: It inhibits arachidonic acid metabolism in microfilariae, which leaves them open to innate immune attack rather than killing them directly. The adult worms in the tissues survive it.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 173

why: A depolarising neuromuscular blocker: the roundworm contracts suddenly and is then paralysed, so it loses its grip on the intestinal wall and is passed out rather than killed in place.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

why: It interferes with pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase, an electron-transfer enzyme essential to anaerobic energy metabolism and absent from us. It is first-line for Cryptosporidium and for Giardia.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

why: Powdered cinchona bark was the only thing that worked against malaria for three centuries. Pelletier and Caventou pulled the alkaloid out of the bark in 1820, and quinine is still the fallback where chloroquine has failed.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 178

why: A person becomes the definitive host by eating undercooked pork carrying cysticerci. The bladder everts in the small intestine, the scolex hooks into the wall, and the worm buds segments behind it for years.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 39

why: The same disease from the other animal: Cysticercus bovis in raw or undercooked beef. Humans are the only known definitive host of either species, and usually carry just the one worm.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

why: Swallowing Taenia solium eggs, rather than larvae in pork, puts a person in the pig's place: the oncospheres hatch, cross the gut wall and form cysticerci in muscle, skin, eye or brain. Contaminated vegetables are a main source.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

why: Around 60% of people with cysticercosis have larvae in the brain. Seizures are the commonest symptom, and in developing countries this is one of the leading causes of them; the disease is called the great imitator.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

why: Eggs pass out in feces and need two to three weeks in warm, moist soil before they can infect anyone; then they persist there for ten years or more. Swallowed, they hatch, and the larvae set off through liver and lungs.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: Eggs in feces hatch in warm damp soil and the filariform larvae penetrate skin directly — walking barefoot is the risk factor. Chronic blood loss from the attached adults makes it a leading cause of anaemia.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: Whipworm eggs pass in feces, embryonate in soil for two to three weeks, and are swallowed on unwashed vegetables or from hands. Heavy loads cause bloody diarrhoea, growth faltering and rectal prolapse.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: The gravid female crawls out at night and lays on the perianal skin; the eggs are infective within hours. Scratching moves them to the mouth, and they are light enough to go airborne in bedding and house dust.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13
