why: Larvae penetrate skin from soil, but the disease is unusual because larvae in the gut can become infective before they leave. That autoinfective cycle has kept infections alive in people for decades.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: Simulium black flies pass the larvae on, usually over many bites. The damage comes from the microfilariae the adults release, wandering the skin and every structure of the eye, and from the allergy to them.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 29

why: The larvae travel inside copepods in drinking water; stomach acid digests the copepod and frees the worm. Filtering water through cloth breaks the cycle, which is why the disease has almost been eradicated.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 26

why: The adult worm lives in dogs and other canines; sheep are the usual intermediate host. A person who swallows eggs from close contact with an infected dog takes the sheep's place, and grows a hydatid cyst instead.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 40

why: A plant-borne trematode zoonosis: metacercariae encysted on raw watercress and other water vegetation are swallowed whole. The young flukes bore out of the gut to the liver and settle in the bile ducts.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

why: The metacercariae sit in the flesh of freshwater fish, so raw or undercooked fish is the route in. The adults live in the bile ducts for up to thirty years, and long infection is a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

why: The metacercariae are in raw or undercooked freshwater crabs and crayfish. The young flukes cross the diaphragm into the lungs, and the chronic fibrotic cough that follows is easily mistaken for tuberculosis.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

why: The plerocercoid larva waits in the flesh of freshwater fish, salmon and pike among them, so sashimi and ceviche have carried it well outside its old range. Vitamin B12 deficiency follows in about 1% of cases.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 45

why: Female phlebotomine sandflies inject metacyclic promastigotes while feeding. Where the parasite settles decides the disease: skin for the cutaneous form, mucous membranes for the mucocutaneous, spleen and liver for the visceral.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 94

why: An infected tsetse fly injects the parasite while feeding. It multiplies in blood and lymph first, then crosses into the central nervous system, and untreated it is generally fatal.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 110

why: The kissing bug defecates as it feeds and the parasite enters through the scratched bite, not the bite itself. Decades later, chronic infection damages the heart in up to a third of cases, and can enlarge the gut.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 111

why: Pigs are the main reservoir, and human infection is commonest where people and pigs live close together. Cysts pass in feces and are swallowed in contaminated food or water; fewer than 1% of people carry it.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 111

why: Spread by direct sexual contact — the parasite forms no cyst and cannot survive a trip through the environment. Women get the symptoms; men are usually asymptomatic carriers, which is how it keeps circulating.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 86

why: Undercooked pork and wild game are how the encysted larvae get in; stomach acid frees them from their nurse cells. Migration into muscle a week later brings the muscle pain and the swollen face.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: The vehicle is fresh water, but the engine is the snail: one miracidium multiplies inside it into hundreds of cercariae, and those are what pierce the skin of anyone wading. No snail, no transmission.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

why: Cysts shed in feces contaminate water and survive nearly three months in cold water. Swallowing a handful is enough, which is why the disease turns up in hikers, in nurseries and in whole water supplies at once.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 83

why: A hermaphroditic fluke holding on with an oral sucker and a ventral one, living in the common bile duct and the gall bladder and feeding on bile. It can survive thirty years in one host.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

why: Four anterior flagella, a fifth at the back, all joined to an undulating membrane, and a barb-like axostyle projecting opposite them. It never makes a cyst, which is why only direct contact passes it on.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

why: The blood flukes are the ones whose cercariae pierce skin instead of encysting: a fork-tailed larva leaves the snail, burrows into a foot or a leg on contact with fresh water, and sheds its tail to become a schistosomule.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

why: The apicomplexan genus that does its growing inside red blood cells: it digests their haemoglobin and dumps the leftover heme as hemozoin, the dark malaria pigment pathologists find in the tissues afterwards.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 100

why: A tapeworm is a flatworm of the class Cestoda, and the scolex is what makes it one: a holdfast under 2 mm long with four suckers, gripping the gut wall while the segmented body streams behind it.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 39

why: The armed tapeworm. Its scolex carries a rostellum between the four suckers, ringed with two rows of 22 to 32 spiny hooks, and that crown is exactly what separates it from the beef tapeworm.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

why: The unarmed tapeworm: four suckers on the scolex and no hooks and no rostellum at all. That absence is the identifying feature against the other Taenia, and it can still exceed twenty metres.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

why: A roundworm whose head bends back into a hook, holding the gut wall with a hardened mouth cavity — two pairs of teeth in the Old World species, a pair of cutting plates in the New World one. Feeding that way is what makes it a cause of anaemia.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 10

why: Alone among the flukes the blood flukes have separate sexes, and the male's body curls into a long channel that holds the larger female for the whole of their adult lives, in the veins of the gut or bladder.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

why: The large intestinal roundworm: a female runs 22 to 35 cm and lays as many as 200,000 eggs a day. A thick, digestion-resistant cuticle is what lets an animal that size sit in a small intestine undigested.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: It does not simply hide in muscle: the larva enters a striated muscle cell and reprograms it into a collagen-walled nurse cell, then lives inside the thing it made. Nothing else among the roundworms does this.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

why: A flagellate with four pairs of flagella and a rigid dished underside built on microtubules. That ventral disc clamps it to the lining of the small intestine, and it never invades any further than that.
srcBook: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 83

why: Break the wire and the current stops; close it again and it flows. A switch is a deliberate, repeatable gap, and it has exactly two states. Every digital machine in this chain rests on that fact.
Put the switch's contacts next to an electromagnet instead of a finger. A small current through the coil pulls them closed, switching a much larger circuit. One circuit can now command another.

Aristotle pulled the form of an argument away from its content. All A are B, all B are C, so all A are C — that holds whatever A, B and C stand for. Validity became a property of structure, like grammar.

Al-Khwarizmi, at Baghdad's House of Wisdom around 820, wrote out rules for restoring and balancing equations. Let letters stand for the unknown quantities and a single line states a method, not one sum.
Boole's Laws of Thought, 1854, gave logic the form of an algebra: the variables hold true and false instead of numbers, and the operations are and, or and not. Reasoning turned into calculation.
A Boolean operation has finitely many cases, so you can simply list them: write every combination the inputs can take, one per row, and fill in the output. The table is the complete definition.
Shannon's 1937 master's thesis proved Boolean algebra describes relay arrangements exactly: contacts in series behave as and, in parallel as or. An equation and a circuit became the same object.
Diodes pass a signal but cannot reverse one, so diode logic alone is incomplete. A transistor can: wire it to pull the output low whenever the input is high and you have negation in a circuit.

Point two diodes into a shared resistor. Current arriving at either input reaches the output, and neither input can push back through the other diode into its neighbour. That is disjunction, in parts.
De Morgan's law: A and B is exactly not(not A or not B). Invert both inputs, OR them, invert the result — conjunction assembled from the two gates already on the bench, with no new part.
Put an inverter after an AND: the output is false only when both inputs are true. This is Sheffer's stroke, and it is functionally complete — every Boolean function whatsoever can be written with it.
OR is true when either input is true, including both. Subtract the both case — OR and not AND — and what is left is true only when the inputs disagree: exclusive or.

Invert the select line so exactly one branch is enabled, gate each input against its own branch, and merge the two. A handful of NANDs and an inverter let a control signal choose which input gets through.
Cross-couple two NAND gates so each feeds the other's input. The pair has two stable states and sits in whichever one you last pushed it to. Gates could only react; this one remembers.
Add two bits and there are two answers to produce. XOR gives the sum digit (1+1 is 0), AND gives the carry into the next column. Two gates, and arithmetic has come out of pure logic.
A half adder ignores the carry coming in from the column below. Chain two of them and OR the two carries out, and you have a stage that can be stacked as wide as the numbers you want to add.
Run the adder and the bitwise AND, OR and NOT circuits all at once on the same operands, then let a multiplexer choose which result leaves. The code that steers the multiplexer is the opcode.

A switch has exactly two states, so knowing which one it is in answers exactly one yes-or-no question. That answer is the unit of information — Tukey contracted 'binary digit' to bit, Shannon made it a measure.
One bit cannot hold a letter. Group as many as it takes to encode a single character and you have a byte: eight, once IBM settled the matter, and the smallest piece of memory with its own address.
Split a byte down the middle. Four bits have sixteen possible values, so give each one symbol: 0 to 9, then A to F. Now any byte is two characters instead of eight, and the grouping is exact.
Telegraph and teleprinter codes had numbered the alphabet for decades. ASCII fixed 128 of those code points in seven bits, so any machine receiving the number 65 produces the same letter A.

128 slots hold English and almost nothing else. Unicode set out to give every script on Earth one number per character; version 17 defines 159,801 characters across 172 scripts, ASCII first among them.
Stand eight flip-flops side by side and wire them to one control line: they load or hold a whole byte together. Nothing is closer to the arithmetic, so nothing is quicker to read.

Charge on a microscopic capacitor is the 1; a transistor beside it gates access. Two parts per bit packs densely — but the charge drains in milliseconds, so every cell is read and written back over and over. That is what 'dynamic' means.
Lay out a grid and put a diode at every crossing that should read 1, leaving the rest empty. The diode matrix is decided at manufacture, so the contents cannot be altered — and cannot be forgotten.

Registers are instant but tiny; main memory is vast but tens to hundreds of times slower. Put a small fast memory between them holding copies of recently used locations and most requests never travel.

A quartz crystal is piezoelectric and flexes at one precise frequency. Build an oscillator around it and the chip gets a steady beat, so every flip-flop in the machine changes state at the same instant.
A private wire between every pair of registers grows as the square of their number. Run one shared bundle of traces instead and arbitrate who may drive it, and any component can send to any other.
The ALU already takes an opcode saying which operation to perform. Store that code as a number in memory and it stops being a setting on a wire and becomes a command the machine can be handed.
Write the whole program as those numbers, one after another: load a word into a register, run an ALU operation, jump elsewhere. No translation happens; the processor's own wiring decodes it.
Add a control unit that fetches the next instruction, points the ALU at the right operands, files the result and moves on. Fetch and execute, over and over — that loop is the whole processor.
Nobody can write raw opcodes all day. Give each instruction a short mnemonic and each address a label, then let a program do the substitution. Kathleen Booth co-wrote the first one in the late 1940s.

Assembly still names the machine's own instructions, one for one. Write the method in a language of its own and have a program translate it down instead — so the algorithm outlives the machine it ran on.

A compiler can only translate what it can parse, so the language needs a formal grammar — every legal program spelled out by rules. Fix the grammar and people write readably while the machine still gets its numbers.

When every job needs loading, compiling and running by hand, the operator is the slowest part. GM-NAA I/O, built for the IBM 704 in 1956, read the next job in and ran it itself — software minding the machine.
A reel of tape is just bytes in a row, found by counting. Give a run of them a name and a length and it becomes a thing you can ask for, without knowing where on the reel it actually sits.
One name is easy to keep track of; ten thousand are not. The operating system keeps a table of names against the blocks holding them, and hands out files while nobody else thinks about the disk.

Files hold bytes; they answer no questions. Codd's relational model holds data as relations and defines an algebra of operations over them, so you state what you want and the system works out how to fetch it.
Bouchon in 1725 and Falcon in 1728 drove a loom from punched paper: a hole or no hole at each fixed position, read by a row of pins. Information became a physical pattern you could hand to a machine.
Jacquard's 1804 machine laced the cards into a continuous chain, one complete card per row of the pattern. The design now lived on the cards, so new cloth meant new cards, not a new loom.
Hollerith punched facts about people onto cards instead of patterns for cloth. A pin dropping through a hole closes a circuit and steps a counter, so a whole census could be summed electrically.
Turing stripped an algorithm down to the least a machine could possibly need: a strip of tape, one symbol under the head, and a finite table of rules. Anything computable at all is computable on it.

Simply wait. Gordon Moore noticed in 1965 that components per integrated circuit kept doubling, and later revised the interval to about two years. It describes an industry's learning curve, not physics.
A photosite's charge becomes a number, and that number is one sample of light at one point. Arrange the samples in a grid and the picture is addressable: any point can be named and changed.
Set aside a block of memory with one number per pixel and wire it to be read out continuously to a screen. Whatever is written there appears: the picture and the memory become the same object.
Movable type held each letter as a shape cast on a slug of metal. A digital font holds the same glyphs as data — a grid of pixels, or outlines to fill — so one file replaces a whole case of sorts.
Cut the image into 8x8 blocks and express each as cosine frequencies (Ahmed's 1972 transform). Keep the coarse ones, throw away the fine, and the file shrinks about tenfold. Standardised in 1992.

Divide a register's bits into three fields: sign, exponent and significand. The point floats with the exponent, so the same 32 bits reach the enormous and the minute. IEEE 754 fixed the layout in 1985.

Add the bytes of a block together and send the total alongside them. Recompute it at the far end: if the two disagree, something was corrupted in transit or in storage, and the block is not to be trusted.

A checksum only says that something broke. Hamming, in 1950, spread check bits over overlapping subsets of the message, so the pattern of failing checks spells out the number of the wrong bit — flip it back.
Lease telephone lines between computers, give each machine an address, and data can move without a person carrying it. ARPANET, built this way, was the first wide-area packet-switched network.

Do not hold a line open for a whole file. Cut it into short pieces, each with a header giving source and destination, and let them find their own way independently — Baran at RAND and Davies at the NPL, in the 1960s.
Packets are useless unless both ends agree where the address sits, what each field means, when to speak and what to do when one goes missing. That whole agreement, written down, is the protocol.
A packet needs somewhere to go. Give every network interface a number: IPv4 uses 32 bits, which is four bytes — which is why they are written as four numbers separated by dots.
IP delivers a packet to an address and promises nothing else. TCP numbers the bytes, checksums them, and asks again for whatever never arrived — so the application sees one reliable ordered stream.
Nobody remembers a four-number address. DNS lets machines be named in words instead, and a hierarchy of servers — one level per dot — translates the name into the address before the packet leaves.
Combine three things in one string: which protocol to speak, which machine to ask for by name, and the path to the file on it. Now any document anywhere can be pointed at from anywhere else.

A URL says what you want; HTTP is the protocol for asking. The client opens a connection, sends a request naming the resource, and the server returns one response. Simple enough that anything can serve.
Keep the document as plain characters and put the structure in the same stream: mark this a heading, that a paragraph, this other a link to another document. Text and its wiring travel as one file.
One program that speaks HTTP to fetch whatever a URL names, parses the HTML for its structure, and draws the result. Every document on every server, through a single window.
Put a computer on the network whose only work is answering requests from others for data, resources or computation. The machines that ask become clients, and one server can serve many of them.

Give every station one shared cable rather than a link to each neighbour. A station listens first, transmits, and if it hears a collision it stops and retries after a random wait. Standardised as IEEE 802.3.
A telephone line carries sound, not bits. Modulate the bits onto audio tones to send and demodulate them at the far end — AT&T's Bell 103, 1963, managed 300 bits per second over an ordinary line.
Fix a rule for replacing each letter, and a key that decides which replacement. The rule can be published; only the key needs guarding — which is what makes a cipher different from a secret alphabet.
Once the message is bits, enciphering becomes arithmetic: combine each bit with a bit of key. Vernam did exactly this in 1917, and with a truly random key as long as the message it cannot be broken.
Write out the counting numbers, then strike out every multiple of two, of three, of five, and so on. What survives has no smaller factors. Eratosthenes' sieve is among the oldest algorithms there is.

Multiplying two large primes is easy; recovering them from the product is not. That one-way gap lets you hand out a key for locking while keeping the key that unlocks. Diffie and Hellman 1976, RSA 1977.

A checksum catches accidents but not liars. Harden the same idea so that reversing it, or finding two inputs that agree, is infeasible, and a short fingerprint becomes evidence about the data behind it.

Hash the document, then encrypt the hash with your private key. Anyone can decrypt it with your public key and hash the document themselves: matching hashes prove both the author and that nothing changed.
Keep the typewriter's key arrangement but put an electrical switch under each key instead of a lever and a typebar. Which switch closed becomes a number, and the number is the character.

How much can a noisy line carry? Nyquist and Hartley asked it of telegraphy in the 1920s; Shannon answered in the 1940s, in bits per second, and proved every channel has a hard capacity you cannot exceed.

A halophyte is defined by tolerance, not by address: a plant that can grow in soil or water of high salinity. Only about 2% of plant species manage it — everything else is a glycophyte and dies there.
Resin is a stem secretion, mostly terpenes, that a conifer pushes into a wound. Cut the bark and it bleeds. Sap and latex are different fluids doing different jobs; only resin sets hard.
A thorn is a whole shoot that gave up on being a branch: it arises from a bud, keeps vascular tissue inside, and lignifies to a point. A spine is a modified leaf; a prickle is only epidermis.
In a berry the whole fruit wall ripens into fleshy parenchyma with the seeds embedded in it. The endocarp is what separates it from a drupe: a drupe hardens that inner layer into a stone.
A berry comes from a single flower with one ovary, whose wall becomes flesh rather than stone. Grapes, tomatoes, bananas, kiwifruit and persimmons all qualify; strawberries and raspberries do not.
Aerenchyma is parenchyma turned to sponge: gas-filled channels that give oxygen a low-resistance path from shoot to submerged root. Some of it leaks out of the root pores into the mud around them.
Take the oxygen away and the plant builds its own airway. Low oxygen makes it produce ethylene, and cortical parenchyma cells then die and lyse on purpose, leaving lysigenous cavities behind.

Isoprene comes off a sunlit leaf, and emission climbs steeply with leaf temperature to a peak near 40 °C. Oaks and poplars are the great emitters: in a deciduous forest isoprene is about 80% of the hydrocarbons in the air.
Industrially it is a byproduct of thermally cracking petroleum naphtha — about 800,000 tonnes recovered a year, and 95% of that goes straight back into making cis-1,4-polyisoprene.
Polyisoprene is what isoprene becomes when it is polymerised — anionically with n-butyllithium, or by coordination over a Ziegler–Natta catalyst.
The monomer chains to itself, thousands of units long. Natural rubber is that same chain in the cis-1,4 arrangement, and it is about 99.99% of what comes out of the tree.
Rubber is the polymer cis-1,4-polyisoprene, whether a tree made it or a reactor did, and sulfur cross-links the chains the same way either way — around 10% by weight at the optimum.

The category, not any one member: an artificial elastomer polymerised from petroleum monomers rather than tapped from a tree. Fritz Hofmann made the first in 1909; two thirds of US rubber is now synthetic.

Carbon black is made on purpose: petroleum feedstock — fuel oil, cracking tar — burned in a deliberately limited supply of air. Unlike soot it has a huge surface area and negligible polycyclic aromatics.
Coal tar is the other classic feedstock. Burn it in too little air and what you collect is near-pure carbon: world consumption was 13.2 million tonnes in 2015.
Carbon black is the reinforcing filler in tire rubber, and 70% of all carbon black made goes into tires. It is also the reason every tire is black.

The tire is forced onto the wheel, bead into the channel between the rims. Most of the rubber is synthetic — styrene-butadiene copolymer alone is about half of it — alongside natural rubber, fabric and wire.
Hevea brasiliensis, a eudicot of the spurge family. Its latex vessels spiral up the bark in a right-handed helix; harvesters cut across them just deep enough to bleed the tree without harming it.

Mangrove is not a taxon but a habit: salt-tolerant trees that convergent evolution produced separately in several unrelated families — 35 true species in 5 families. The salt tolerance is the definition, not the shore.
Adansonia is a stem succulent the size of a tree: the swollen trunk is water-storing tissue holding up to 120,000 litres, which is how it crosses a drought that would kill an ordinary tree.
Pinus is the conifer the world taps: turpentine and rosin are both got from its resin. Its needles grow bundled in fascicles, one to seven per sheath and usually two to five.
Salix, twice over: it flowers as catkins, male and female on separate trees, and it roots so readily that almost any cutting — or a broken branch left lying on wet ground — becomes a new tree.

Illicium verum is the anethole tree. Aniseed and fennel are herbs that converged on the same molecule from unrelated families; only this one is an evergreen tree, and the spice is its whorl of six to eight boat-shaped follicles.

Durio is named for its armour — Malay duri, thorn, plus -an — and the rind carries thorns sharp enough to draw blood on a fruit 30 cm long and up to 3 kg. The smell is separate chemistry: diethyl disulfide and relatives.

Diospyros kaki is botanically a berry — one fleshy fruit from the ovary of a single flower — and its defining property is soluble tannin: astringent enough to pucker the mouth until ripening turns that tannin insoluble.
Actinidia is dioecious: a vine is male or female and never both, so no female sets fruit unless pollen is carried in from a male. Orchards plant one male for every three to eight females.
Olea europaea's drupe stores oil in its flesh where other fruit store sugar, which is why it is pressed rather than eaten — and why it is inedibly bitter with oleuropein until it is cured.
Vitis: botanically a berry, borne in clusters on a deciduous woody vine. Wine grapes are picked at about 24% sugar by weight, against roughly 15% for the table grapes juice is pressed from.
Oryza sativa survives flooding on plumbing, not luck: lysigenous aerenchyma forms in its roots even in air and increases when oxygen runs short, piping oxygen from shoot down to a drowned root tip.
Saccharum is a tall perennial grass that banks its sugar in the stalk instead of the seed: 12–16% of a mature cane stalk is soluble sugars, stored in the internodes, on C4 photosynthesis.
Agave is a monocot built for drought rather than merely found in it: large succulent, xerophytic rosettes of fibre-packed leaves, each rosette flowering once and then dying.

An empire is a state that keeps ruling what it conquers. Rome, the Mongols and the Ottomans all worked the same way: permanent troops annexed the neighbours, who were then governed from the centre as subjects rather than as fellow citizens.

War ends in writing. The oldest surviving international treaty, between Ramesses II and Hattusili III around 1259 BCE, survives in Egyptian hieroglyphs at Karnak and in Akkadian cuneiform on clay tablets found at Hattusa.

The treaties of Osnabrück and Münster, signed 24 October 1648, ended the Thirty Years' War. By convention they begin the system of states answerable to no higher authority — though historians argue over how much the texts actually say so.

Self-determination is the principle; independence is a people exercising it and taking sovereignty. Four waves carried it: the Americas from the 1770s, Europe after 1918, decolonisation after 1945, and the Soviet collapse of the early 1990s.

Not a coup and not a riot. A revolution is a rapid, fundamental remaking of a state's institutions, and it needs two things a palace plot does not: mass mobilisation, and action outside the institutions — demonstrations, strikes or force.

The document the winners put in place of the government they removed. The United States wrote its constitution in 1787 and it is still the oldest codified one in force; France wrote its first in 1791.
A state whose head of state is not born to the job, its powers written down instead of inherited. Europe held 55 monarchies and 9 republics in 1815; by 2015 it held 12 monarchies and 35 republics.
The same voting machinery, asked a question instead of asked to pick a representative. Switzerland has run almost 600 national votes since 1848; Italy, the next most frequent user, has run 78.
What separates a colonial empire from a land empire is the sea between the ruler and the ruled. European powers held roughly 35% of the world's land in 1800 and about 84% of it by 1914.

UN General Assembly Resolution 1514, passed in 1960, declared that colonial rule violated human rights and that independence should be immediate. In the two centuries after 1783, 165 colonies became sovereign states.

Ireland in 1920, British India in 1947, Korea, Vietnam, Cyprus: one territory cut in two, so that the new border and the new states arrive on the same day. Brendan O'Leary distinguishes it from secession, which works within existing units.

Fichte's argument was that those who speak one language are already bound together; the Grimms collected folk tales to prove it. Twenty-five German states were proclaimed one empire on 18 January 1871 on that reasoning.

Uruk, Athens, Venice and the eighty-odd free imperial cities: a walled city that was the whole of its own country and answered to nobody above it. Three sovereign city-states survive — Vatican City, Monaco and Singapore.
In 1278 Peter III of Aragon mediated a paréage — a feudal treaty splitting a disputed lordship — between the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix. Andorra has had two heads of state ever since.

By 1920 it covered 35.5 million km², about 24% of the Earth's land, and in 1913 it ruled some 412 million people, 23% of humanity — the largest empire in history, held together by control of the oceans.

Beaten by Prussia in 1866 and close to bankruptcy, Franz Joseph bought Hungarian consent. The Compromise ratified on 29 May 1867 gave one monarch two separate states, each with its own parliament, sharing only foreign affairs, defence and their funding.

Masaryk, Beneš and Štefánik argued the Czechoslovak case to the Allies as one of self-determination and won recognition for their National Council; the state was proclaimed on 28 October 1918 as Austria-Hungary collapsed.

On 1 December 1918 the South Slav lands of the collapsed Austria-Hungary joined the Kingdom of Serbia as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. King Alexander renamed it Yugoslavia on 3 October 1929.

Andorra had two co-princes for 715 years and no constitution. The one approved by referendum on 14 March 1993, with 74.2% in favour, made it a sovereign parliamentary co-principality; it joined the UN the same year.

Latvia did not write a new constitution. On 4 May 1990 its Supreme Council readopted articles of the 1922 Satversme, holding that the 1940 annexation was unlawful and the pre-war republic had never ended; restoration completed 21 August 1991.

The Treaty of London of 19 April 1839 cut the Grand Duchy in two: the French-speaking part became Belgium's Province of Luxembourg, and the remainder became an independent grand duchy. Its personal union with the Dutch crown lapsed in 1890.

Hans-Adam I bought Schellenberg in 1699 and Vaduz in 1712 because they owed no lord but the emperor; on 23 January 1719 Charles VI merged them into an imperial principality. The prince owed no suzerain once the Holy Roman Empire dissolved in 1806.

The 1830 rising in Brussels broke the United Kingdom of the Netherlands apart. The Treaty of London of 19 April 1839 recognised Belgium and had five great powers guarantee its neutrality — the guarantee invoked in 1914.

Constitutional Act 542, passed on 25 November 1992, agreed the federation's end. Czechoslovakia ceased to exist at midnight on 31 December 1992 and two sovereign states existed from 1 January 1993. No referendum was ever held.

The push came from the Slovak side: on 17 July 1992 the Slovak National Council adopted a declaration of the sovereignty of the Slovak nation, and six days earlier Klaus and Mečiar had agreed to split the state.
The Treaty of Trianon, signed 4 June 1920, fixed the borders of an independent Hungary after Austria-Hungary dissolved. It left about 28% of the old kingdom's territory and 36% of its people.

Yugoslavia's last remnant was renamed the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro on 4 February 2003. When Montenegro left, Serbia's parliament declared the Republic of Serbia its legal successor on 5 June 2006.

A referendum on 19 May 1991 authorised the declaration made on 25 June 1991, the same day as Slovenia's. The European Community recognised Croatia on 15 January 1992; the war that followed ran to 1995.
In the plebiscite of 23 December 1990, 88.5% of the electorate voted to leave. Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991 and secured it in the Ten-Day War.

Recognised on 6 April 1992 after a referendum, then fought over for three and a half years. The agreement negotiated at Dayton, Ohio in November 1995 carries the country's constitution as its Annex 4, still in force.
On 21 May 2006, 55.5% voted to leave the state union on an 86.5% turnout — just over the 55% threshold the EU had set. Parliament declared independence on 3 June 2006.

It voted to leave Yugoslavia on 8 September 1991 and left without fighting. The Prespa Agreement with Greece, signed 17 June 2018, settled the naming dispute; the name North Macedonia took effect on 12 February 2019.

Forty delegates under Ismail Kemal declared independence at Vlorë on 28 November 1912, as Ottoman rule collapsed in the First Balkan War. The London Conference of Ambassadors recognised Albania de facto on 17 December 1912.

The Treaty of Berlin of 1878 made Bulgaria an autonomous principality still under Ottoman suzerainty. Prince Ferdinand declared full independence at Tarnovo on 5 October 1908; the powers recognised it by spring 1909.

Moldavia and Wallachia exploited a drafting gap and elected the same prince, Alexandru Ioan Cuza, in 1859; on 3 February 1862 they merged as Romania. The Congress of Berlin recognised independence from the Ottomans in 1878.

On 11 March 1990 the Supreme Council voted 124 to 0, with six abstentions, that the sovereign powers abolished in 1940 were re-established. Lithuania was the first of the fifteen Soviet republics to declare independence.

On 16 November 1988 Estonia declared its own laws supreme over Soviet law and claimed its resources — the first union republic to declare state sovereignty. Full independence was restored on 20 August 1991.
On 1 December 1991, 92.3% of voters backed the independence act on an 84.2% turnout. A week later Ukraine, Russia and Belarus signed the accords declaring the USSR had ceased to exist.
The Belovezha Accords were signed on 8 December 1991 at Viskuli, a hunting lodge in the Belovezhskaya Pushcha in Belarus. Shushkevich, Yeltsin and Kravchuk declared the USSR was ceasing to exist.

The independence movement began with a language law: on 31 August 1989 the republic made Moldovan in the Latin script its state language and declared it identical with Romanian. Independence was declared on 27 August 1991.
The last of the fifteen union republics to declare independence, on 16 December 1991. Five days later Alma-Ata hosted the protocol at which eleven republics jointly declared the USSR at an end.

Menton and Roquebrune were about 95% of Monaco's territory and wanted out. Charles III ceded them to France for compensation, and the Franco-Monégasque Treaty of 1861 recognised his sovereignty over the 2 km² that remained.

A commune on Monte Titano that never joined Italy. Its Statutes of 1600 are the earliest written governing documents still in force, and a treaty of friendship with the new Kingdom of Italy in 1862 confirmed its independence.
The only state founded by a successful revolt of the enslaved. The insurrection that began in 1791 destroyed French Saint-Domingue, and Dessalines declared independence on 1 January 1804.

Duarte's Trinitaria seized the Puerta del Conde in Santo Domingo on 27 February 1844, ending 22 years of Haitian rule over the whole island. Spain re-annexed the country in 1861 and the Restoration War won it back by 1865.
The Indian Independence Act received royal assent on 18 July 1947 and India became a sovereign dominion on 15 August. It replaced the Act with its own constitution on 26 January 1950.
The same 1947 Act partitioned British India into two dominions and cut Bengal and Punjab in half to do it. Pakistan's independence day is 14 August 1947; its eastern wing became Bangladesh in 1971.
East Pakistan declared independence on 26 March 1971; Pakistani forces surrendered at Dhaka on 16 December after nine months of war. Pakistan itself recognised Bangladesh in 1974.
The Soulbury constitution gave Ceylon dominion status and independence was proclaimed on 4 February 1948, six months after India's. It became a republic and took the name Sri Lanka in 1972.
The Federation of Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957. On 16 September 1963 it merged with three British colonies — Singapore, Sarawak and North Borneo — to form Malaysia.
Two years after joining, Singapore left. The Malaysian parliament passed the separation bill 126 votes to nil on 9 August 1965, and Singapore became a sovereign state that day.

A Portuguese colony until 1975 and then under Indonesian rule. In a UN-run popular consultation on 30 August 1999, 78.5% chose independence on a 98.9% turnout; sovereignty was restored on 20 May 2002.

A monocot germinates with a single seed leaf. Parallel veins, vascular bundles scattered through the stem rather than set in a ring, flower parts in threes — over 70,000 species, some 25,000 of them orchids.
The eudicots were called tricolpates first, for pollen grains with three furrows where every other seed plant has one. Two seed leaves, netted veins, and over 70% of all flowering-plant species.

The first plants to wrap an embryo in a seed instead of casting a spore. The ovule sits naked on a scale or a leaf with no ovary around it — over 1,000 living species, nearly all of them conifers and cycads.

Club fungi are named for the basidium, which buds its spores on the outside rather than shutting them in a sac — 31,515 described species: mushrooms, boletes, puffballs, brackets, and the rusts and smuts.

Ophiuroidea, not a sea star: the disc is sharply cut off from the arms and no organ reaches into them. It hides under rocks, rows along on snake-like arms, and sheds one to a predator rather than be held.

Holothuroidea: an echinoderm gone long and leathery, grubbing through seabed mud on tube feet. Some reef species fire sticky Cuvierian tubules out of the anus to snare a predator, and regrow them within weeks.

Crinoidea is the oldest echinoderm class, back about 480 million years, and only some 700 species survive. A feather star grips the reef with claw-like cirri and strains plankton from the current with feathered arms.

Pycnogonida is not a spider and not even an arachnid — its own chelicerate class, over 1,300 species. The trunk is too small to hold the animal, so gut and gonads branch into the legs, which absorb oxygen straight through the cuticle.

One of about 116 species of Sepiida, cousin to octopus and squid. It trims the gas-to-liquid ratio inside the chambered cuttlebone to hold almost any depth, and its W-shaped pupil reads polarised light rather than colour.
Every fern frond comes up tightly coiled — circinate vernation — and is cut at that stage or not at all. Ostrich fern is the one usually eaten; bracken fiddleheads carry ptaquiloside, a carcinogen.

Ceratosaurus is 'horn lizard': a blade of fused nasal bone about 13 cm long, sheathed in keratin and grooved for blood vessels. Marsh named it in 1884 from a Morrison Formation skeleton dug at Garden Park, Colorado.
Peel a mushroom gill and its whole surface is basidia — club-shaped cells, each budding four spores on slender horns called sterigmata and flicking them away with a bead of fluid.

The sharks are the elasmobranchs that stayed torpedo-shaped with gill slits on the flank, and they carry the group's teeth to its extreme — rows of replacements lying flat behind the working row, rotating forward as teeth are lost, for thousands over a lifetime.

The shortfin mako is a lamnid, one of the few sharks that keeps its swimming muscle warmer than the sea using a rete mirabile — a countercurrent mesh of blood vessels that traps muscle heat instead of losing it at the gills. Warm muscle contracts faster, and the mako is the fastest shark measured.
A lamnid shark of the subarctic North Pacific that holds its core 8 to 11 degrees Celsius above the water around it — the widest gap of any shark — which is what lets it hunt in seas near freezing.
Named for the dark vertical bars along its flanks, strongest in young animals and fading with age, which break up its outline against dappled water.

A shark of the open ocean rather than the coast, ranging the warm surface layer far from land on very long, rounded, white-tipped pectoral fins that let it glide slowly over huge distances between meals.

Named for its skin. Shark scales are dermal denticles, tooth-like and normally rough enough to abrade; the silky shark's are unusually small, flat and tightly packed, so the hide feels smooth to the hand.

A slender reef shark that spends the day resting in caves and under coral ledges — unusual among sharks, most of which must keep moving to pass water over the gills — and hunts through the reef at night.
A bottom-dwelling shark with a pair of fleshy barbels hanging beside the nostrils, used to taste and feel for prey buried in sand, which it then draws out by expanding its throat into a suction pump.
The largest fish alive, and a filter feeder. It swims with its mouth open or pumps water through it, straining plankton and small fish on twenty pads of fine mesh across the throat.

A ray that left the sea floor for open water, flying on its disc rather than resting on it, and feeds by funnelling plankton into its mouth with two unrolled head fins and straining it through mesh plates in the gills.
The largest bony fish on coral reefs, reaching about 2.7 metres. It hunts by opening its very large mouth fast enough that the drop in pressure pulls prey in whole.

A lionfish is a scorpionfish, and carries the family's grooved venomous spines — thirteen dorsal, three anal, two pelvic. What sets it apart from its relatives is that it does not lie camouflaged on the bottom: it hovers in the open over the reef, fins spread, and herds small fish with them.
A South American river fish with a single row of triangular blade-like teeth that interlock when the jaw closes, so the bite shears rather than grips.
A bottom-feeding freshwater fish with two pairs of barbels at the mouth, the longer pair at the corners, which it uses to find food by touch and taste in water too silty to see through.
Europe's largest freshwater fish, and scaleless — the skin is bare and heavily coated in mucus, which is where the slipperiness of a catfish comes from.

A large predatory fish of the Nile and the rivers and lakes of tropical Africa, reaching about two metres. Introduced to Lake Victoria in the 1950s, where it drove much of the lake's cichlid fauna to extinction.

It lives among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone, which kill other small fish. A mucus coat lets it move through them unstung; it gets shelter, and the anemone gets a defender and its waste as fertiliser.

The only known cephalopod that does not hunt living prey. It lives in the oxygen minimum zone and streams out a long sticky filament to gather marine snow — sinking flakes of dead plankton and faecal matter — which it wipes off and eats.

A wolf-sized four-legged mammal from Eocene Pakistan that lived beside fresh water and is counted the earliest known whale — not from its shape but from its ear, whose thickened involucrum bone is found in whales and in nothing else.

A large plant-eating dinosaur that cropped with a horny beak at the front of the jaw and ground with packed rows of cheek teeth behind it. It also carried a conical spike in place of a thumb, which Mantell's first reconstruction put on the nose as a horn.

A wingless insect flattened side to side so it can run between the hairs of a mammal, with hind legs that store energy in a pad of resilin and release it to jump many times its own length, and mouthparts that pierce skin to drink blood.

Sharks, rays and skates are the vertebrates whose skeleton never turns to bone. It stays cartilage for life, stiffened at the jaws and spine with a crust of mineral prisms rather than replaced, which is lighter than bone and helps hold a body heavier than water off the bottom.

The rays are the elasmobranchs that went flat to live on the bottom: the body is pressed dorsoventrally, the pectoral fins have grown forward and fused to the head into a disc, and the gill slits have moved to the underside.

A thyreophoran dinosaur carrying two staggered rows of tall bony plates down its back. They were not armour — thin, and threaded with blood vessels — so they are read as display or heat exchange, with the defence left to four tail spikes.
A dinosaur whose skull roof thickened into a dome of solid bone up to 25 centimetres deep, ringed with knobs and short spikes, over a body otherwise built like any other two-legged plant-eater.

The myriapods that gave up hunting for leaf litter. Their trunk segments are fused in pairs, so each apparent segment carries two pairs of legs rather than one — many short legs pushing a body built to burrow rather than to chase.

A vascular plant that never evolved seeds. It scatters spores from the underside of its fronds, and those grow into a separate tiny plant that makes the egg and sperm, so the fern alternates between two independent generations.
The oldest surviving lineage of vascular plants. Despite the name it is not a moss: it has xylem to carry water up a stem, true roots, and small single-veined leaves, all of which the mosses lack.
The largest nematode of poultry, reaching about 12 centimetres in the small intestine of a chicken. Birds pick it up by swallowing eggs that have matured in the litter.

The pinworm, and the commonest human worm in temperate countries. Humans are its only host. The female leaves the gut at night to lay her eggs on the skin around the anus, which is what makes the infection itch and how it spreads.
A thread-thin nematode whose adults live in the lymphatic vessels. Its larvae circulate in the blood mostly at night, timed to when the mosquito that carries them between people is biting.
A wingless insect found on no animal but us, with claws curved to exactly the diameter of a human hair so it can grip the shaft, and mouthparts that pierce the scalp to drink blood.

The same species as the head louse, living in the seams of clothing and moving onto the skin only to feed. Because it cannot exist without clothes, dating the split between the two gives an estimate of when people began wearing them.

A mite under half a millimetre long. The female tunnels into the outer layer of the skin and lays her eggs along the burrow; the itch is an allergic reaction to the mite and its waste, and takes weeks to begin.
A true bug, flattened side to side and about the size of an apple pip, which spends the day in seams and crevices near where people sleep and feeds on blood at night.
A barnacle that settles on nothing but whale skin, growing its plates down into it so it cannot be shed. It never has to search for food: the whale swims, and the water brings it.
The parasitic flukes. Almost every one of them passes through a snail first, where a single larva multiplies into many before moving on to its next host.
A marine mammal with no blubber at all. It stays warm on fur alone, the densest of any animal at up to a million hairs per square inch, which traps a layer of air against the skin.
A theropod with a long narrow crocodile-like snout and conical unserrated teeth, unlike the blades of other big predators. The first skeleton found had scales of the fish Scheenstia in its gut.

Known for fifty years from nothing but a pair of arms 2.4 metres long, which is how it got its name, the horrible hand. Skeletons described in 2014 showed a large humped ornithomimosaur with a duck-like bill.

Named the egg seizer from a skeleton found lying on a nest, assumed to have been raiding it. An embryo found inside the same kind of egg in the 1990s showed the eggs were its own and it had been sitting on them.
A small feathered dinosaur with long asymmetric flight feathers on its hind limbs as well as its arms, giving it four wing surfaces rather than two.
A bird that fishes with a throat pouch of bare skin slung under a long bill, using it as a net; it drains the water out at the surface before swallowing.
An ash-grey bird found wild only in the forests of New Caledonia. It has wings large enough to display but not to fly, and nasal flaps covering its nostrils that no other bird has.

An amphibian that gave up its legs for burrowing. It drives a bone-reinforced skull through soil, its eyes are covered by skin or bone, and it finds its way with a chemical-sensing tentacle between eye and nostril.
One of the few mammals that lays eggs, and covered in spines that are not a separate structure at all but single hairs thickened with keratin.
The only mammal with true scales: overlapping plates of keratin, the same material as a fingernail, covering everything but the belly. It rolls into a ball that a lion cannot open.

An American marsupial whose blood carries a protein that neutralises snake venom, letting it survive bites that would kill an animal its size. It is also the animal that plays dead, an involuntary collapse rather than a decision.

A marsupial that eats nothing but termites, up to twenty thousand a day, gathered on a tongue longer than its own head. Unusually for an Australian marsupial it is active only by day, because that is when termites are near the surface.
An insect with a waist so narrow the abdomen hangs from a stalk, and a sting that is a modified egg-laying tube — which is why only females have one.

A small African mammal with a long flexible snout it swings to sniff out insects. Despite looking like a shrew it belongs with elephants and aardvarks, and it keeps a network of cleared trails it can sprint along.
A tall yellow-flowered daisy grown for its thick root, which stores its carbohydrate as inulin rather than starch — the substance was first isolated from this plant, and is named after it.

A Swedish province for six centuries, then an autonomous Grand Duchy under the Russian tsar from 1809. It declared independence in December 1917, weeks after the Russian empire it belonged to collapsed.

One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, drawn together on the Jutland peninsula and the islands east of it during the Viking age. The Jelling stone raised by Harald Bluetooth about 965 is the first thing to call the place Denmark.

The first state in the world to adopt Christianity, in 301. Absorbed by the Russian empire and then the Soviet Union, and independent again in 1991. Ararat, the mountain on its coat of arms, has stood over the border in Turkey since 1921.
Baku was pumping about half the world's oil by 1900, which is why the Soviet Union held the region so tightly and why the German army drove for it in 1942. Independent in 1991.
The newest country in the world. After two long civil wars, a 2011 referendum in the south of Sudan returned 98.8 per cent for separation, and it became independent that July.
An Italian colony, then federated to Ethiopia and annexed by it. Thirty years of war ended in a 1993 referendum in which almost everyone voted to leave, taking Ethiopia's entire coastline with them.
French Somaliland until 1977, held for its position on the Bab-el-Mandeb, the strait every ship between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean must pass through.
Made in 1960 by joining two colonies that became independent five days apart: British Somaliland in the north and Italian Somaliland, which Italy had continued to administer under a UN trusteeship.
A British protectorate from 1894 to 1962, assembled around the kingdom of Buganda and around Lake Victoria, where the White Nile begins.
Half of Ruanda-Urundi, a German colony taken by Belgium after the First World War and split in two at independence in 1962. It sits on the western branch of the Great Rift Valley.
The British protectorate of Nyasaland until 1964, named for the lake that fills the southern end of the rift and takes up a fifth of the country.

Southern Rhodesia, run from London and then by a white settler government that declared its own independence in 1965; majority rule came in 1980. It takes its name from Great Zimbabwe, a dry-stone city built without mortar.
Portuguese East Africa for nearly five centuries, a base on the sea route to India, until a ten-year war and the 1974 revolution in Lisbon ended the empire.
A kingdom that survived colonisation as a British protectorate and came out of it in 1968 still a monarchy. It changed its name from Swaziland in 2018.
Basutoland, which asked for British protection in 1868 to avoid being swallowed by its neighbour, and is now the only country lying entirely above 1,000 metres.
A French colony until 1975, and a chain of volcanic islands; Karthala on the largest is one of the most active volcanoes in the world.
Spanish Guinea until 1968, and the only sovereign African state where Spanish is official. Its capital stands not on the mainland but on a volcanic island 200 kilometres offshore.
German Kamerun, divided between France and Britain after the First World War and reunited at independence in 1960. Mount Cameroon, an active volcano, is the highest point in West Africa.
Ubangi-Shari, a French territory of savanna between the Sahel and the rainforest, independent in 1960.
A French territory until 1960, stretching from the deep Sahara in the north to the lake in the south that gives it its name — a lake that has lost most of its area since the 1960s.
French until 1960, named for the river that clips its south-western corner. Uranium found at Arlit in the 1960s became most of what it sells abroad.
Upper Volta under France, named for the three rivers that rise in it, until it renamed itself in 1984 Burkina Faso — the land of upright people.
German Togoland, split between Britain and France after the First World War; the French part became Togo in 1960. Phosphate rock is its main export.
Dahomey under France, and before that a kingdom powerful enough to field a regiment of women soldiers. It took the name Benin in 1975 from the bight it faces.
French until 1960, and named for the Mauri, the Berber people of the Roman province of Mauretania. Its iron ore leaves on a train more than two kilometres long.
A British colony until 1965, and barely a country at all in shape: a strip of land following the Gambia river inland, nowhere much wider than the valley itself.
Portuguese Guinea, which won its independence in 1974 after a war that helped bring down the government in Lisbon. Its coast is a maze of mangrove and tidal creeks.
A British colony from 1808, founded as a settlement for freed slaves. The name is Portuguese, Serra Leoa, the lion mountains — for the hills behind Freetown, or the thunder over them.
Settled from 1822 by free-born and formerly enslaved Black Americans, and a republic from 1847 — the only country in Africa never brought under European colonial rule.
An Italian colony from 1911, then under British and French administration, and in 1951 the first country to become independent through the United Nations. Nine-tenths of it is desert.
English from 1627 and British until 1966, and the island where the plantation and its slave code were worked out before being carried across the Caribbean.
Spanish, then British from 1797, and independent in 1962. Its Pitch Lake is the largest natural asphalt deposit on earth, and oil and gas still pay for the country.
Thirteen British colonies that declared independence in 1776 and won it by 1783.
Under Ottoman rule for four centuries, then a French mandate from 1920, and independent in 1946. Damascus had been the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, which ruled from Spain to the Indus.
Transjordan, carved out of the British mandate east of the river in 1921 and independent in 1946. Four-fifths of it is desert.
A British protectorate from 1899 to 1961, and one of the first Gulf states where oil was found in commercial quantity, at Burgan in 1938.
A peninsula under British protection until 1971, and the holder of a third of the world's proven natural gas after the North Field was found offshore in 1971.
Seven emirates known as the Trucial States, for the truces they signed with Britain in the nineteenth century to end raiding at sea. They federated as one country in 1971 when Britain withdrew.
Contested by the Ottomans for centuries, and the country that first cultivated coffee for export — the drink is named for Mocha, the Yemeni port it shipped from.
Burma, annexed to British India in three wars and independent in 1948, renamed Myanmar in 1989. The Mogok valley has produced most of the world's finest rubies.
A Soviet republic until 1991, and the most mountainous country in central Asia; the Fedchenko glacier in the Pamirs is the longest outside the polar regions.
A Soviet republic until 1991. The Karakum desert covers about four-fifths of it, and a gas crater at Darvaza has been alight since Soviet geologists set it burning.
A French colony from 1897 to 1960. It broke from Africa about 88 million years ago and its wildlife evolved alone: most of what lives there lives nowhere else.
Sawing a log lengthways rather than splitting it along the grain is what gives a flat board of even thickness, and it is the step that turns a tree into a building material.
A blade is not cast to shape. Steel is worked flat and then ground away on one or both sides until the edge is a few thousandths of a millimetre thick, which is what lets it wedge material apart.
Cut and shaped from a plank so the grain runs the length of it — across the grain and it snaps at the first hard pull, which is why an axe handle is split along the wood rather than sawn across it.

A modern pole is steel tube rather than solid bar: a hollow section resists bending almost as well as a solid one of the same outside width while using a fraction of the metal, and it is galvanised so the inside does not rust out of sight.

Ground from coloured rock and earth — ochre, malachite, cinnabar. A pigment is insoluble, so unlike a dye it sits in the film rather than staining the fibre, and the grinding is what makes the particles small enough to hold an even colour.

Pigment alone is a powder that brushes off. Suspended in a drying oil it can be spread thin, and the oil then hardens by taking up oxygen from the air rather than by evaporating, leaving the colour bound in a tough film.

Bare wire can only be strung through air on insulators. Sheathing it in rubber lets conductors run side by side, be buried, and be handled — which is the difference between a telegraph line and wiring a building.

Metal squeezed between rollers or beaten flat comes out far thinner than it can be cast, and the working hardens it as it goes. A folded edge then makes it far stiffer than the flat sheet — which is why almost everything made from it has a lip.
Wire mesh is genuinely woven, on a loom built for metal rather than thread — warp wires held under tension while weft wires are driven across them.
A road sheds water sideways because it is built with a camber, and the drain is where that water leaves. Below it sits a trap holding a plug of water, so the sewer's air cannot come back up.

A pavement is the road's surface repeated at a different level: the same made ground, laid in slabs or poured, but held above the carriageway so that water, and traffic, run past rather than across it.

A kerb is a retaining wall a hand's width tall. It stops the made-up pavement spreading sideways under load, and its face forms one side of the channel that carries surface water to the nearest drain.

The first was set outside the Palace of Westminster in 1868, gas-lit and worked by a policeman with a lever; it exploded within a month. The colours were taken from railway signalling, which had already settled on red for stop.

Lighting the street rather than the doorway is what a pole buys: raising the lamp spreads its light over a long stretch of road instead of a pool at the foot of a wall, so far fewer are needed to light a whole street.
It works by being immovable rather than by being seen: most of a bollard is below ground, set in a concrete foundation deep enough that a vehicle striking it stops rather than pushes it over.

The stripes are the whole mechanism: nothing is built, only painted, and the pattern reads at a distance and at a glance from a moving vehicle. Britain's striped version was trialled in 1949 and named the zebra.

Shape carries meaning before the words do — a triangle warns, a circle orders, a rectangle informs — so a sign can be understood at speed, in a language the driver may not read. The 1968 Vienna Convention settled much of it internationally.

The cover is cast iron and heavy on purpose: weight alone holds it down under traffic without a fastening, so it can still be lifted by one person with a bar. Round is the shape that cannot fall through its own hole.
Public bins are often open mesh rather than solid, so that what is inside can be seen at a glance — a precaution against concealment adopted widely after bombings in British and Irish cities.

It only works once postage is paid by the sender. Before the stamp, letters were paid for on delivery and had to be handed to someone; a box that anyone can post into unattended is what the prepaid stamp made possible, in Britain from 1852.

The body is pressed from a single disc of sheet metal so there is no seam to fail, and the handle is set out on a thin stalk — the narrower the bridge, the less heat crosses it, which is why a pan handle can be held while the pan is boiling.

The holes are punched rather than drilled, so each one leaves a slightly raised rim on the outside; that is also why a colander stands on a foot, keeping the holes clear of whatever has just drained through them.
A sieve sorts purely by size, which is why the same tool sifts flour, strains stock and grades sand. Mesh is counted in wires per inch, so a higher number means a finer sieve.
The wires do not mix so much as tear the liquid apart and drag air in behind them. More loops means more edges doing that at once, which is why a balloon whisk beats egg white faster than a fork.

Each hole is punched and its lip left standing proud, so the sheet carries hundreds of tiny raised cutting edges. The sharpest modern kind came from a woodworking rasp: a photo-etched blade a cook borrowed from a hardware shop.
The slot is what makes it a peeler rather than a knife: the blade floats and follows the surface, so the cut stays the same thin depth over a curve instead of digging in.
Wood closes back around a cut, which both spares the edge and gives bacteria less to sit in than a scored plastic surface. It is oiled rather than varnished so it takes up oil instead of water.

The helix does not bite into the cork so much as thread through it, spreading the pull along its whole length so the cork comes out in one piece. Samuel Henshall patented the first improvement in 1795, a disc that stops the worm going too deep.
The bowl is set at an angle to the handle so it stays level as the arm swings, and the handle is long enough to reach the bottom of a stockpot without putting a hand over the steam.
Flexibility is the whole point: the blade bends to the shape of the pan or bowl so it can get under something without breaking it, or clear the sides of a bowl in one pass.

Weight does the work rather than force, which is why it is solid wood. The French kind has no handles at all: rolling with the palms on the pin itself gives more feel for where the dough is still thick.

A mainspring stores the energy and a train of gears steps it down, but neither keeps time. The escapement does: it lets the train advance by exactly one tooth per swing of the oscillator, which is also what makes the ticking.

The flutes are the whole trick. Standing on edge between two liners they act as a row of tiny arches, so the board resists a load far out of proportion to its weight — and collapses at once if the flutes are crushed.

It does two unrelated jobs at once: the straight edge guides a pen, and the graduations measure. Only the first needs it to be straight, which is why a bent ruler still measures correctly and still draws badly.

The fold is what fastens it, not the puncture. A small anvil under the paper turns the legs inward as they come through, so the staple closes on itself; turn the anvil round and it clinches outward instead, for a staple meant to be pulled out again.

Nothing is fastened and nothing is pierced: the wire is sprung slightly open by the paper and the grip is it trying to close again. The familiar double-oval shape is the Gem pattern, made in Britain from the 1890s.
Sheets are folded into sections and sewn through the fold, section to section. A sewn book opens flat because nothing crosses the spine but thread — which is exactly what a glued one cannot do.

It is relief printing at hand scale: only the raised parts take ink, so the design must be cut in reverse. Rubber rather than metal because it gives slightly, and so prints evenly onto a surface that is not quite flat.

Ordinary ink covers. Highlighter ink is a fluorescent dye in a see-through carrier, so the words read straight through it, and the dye throws back more visible light than falls on it — which is why the colour looks brighter than the paper.
The simplest possible container: one fold, no fastening. It works because paper slides out of a stack but not out of a crease, and because the folded edge tells you which way up the contents go.

Punched holes and openable rings make the order of the pages a thing you can change afterwards, which a sewn or glued book cannot do. Friedrich Soennecken patented both the ring binder and the hole punch for it, in 1886.

The rivet is the whole machine. Because the handles are several times longer than the jaws, the hand's grip arrives at the jaws multiplied by that ratio — which is why a small pair can hold what fingers cannot.

Every grain is a tiny cutting edge presented at a random angle, and the grit number is the mesh that graded them — a count of wires per inch of the sieve the grains just fit through, which is why a higher number means finer.

The spirit it is named for is ethanol: thin enough to let the bubble move quickly and not liable to freeze. The vial is very slightly curved, so the bubble — being the lightest thing in there — always sits at the highest point of the curve, and reads centre only when the tool is level.
It exists because glue needs pressure and time at once. The screw converts a turn into a squeeze and, being a screw, does not undo itself when let go — so the joint can be left overnight.
Fixing it to the bench is the difference: a clamp holds two things to each other, a vice holds one thing to the world. That is what lets you file, saw or hammer against it without the work moving.
The bend is the point of it. It puts a fulcrum right beside the wedge, so the long bar swings on the short end and the force arriving at the joint is many times what the arm applied.

A shelf is only usable at its front edge. Pulling the box out instead turns the whole depth into the front, which is the entire reason for a drawer and why the handle is the only part of it you ever touch.
A table becomes a desk when the storage arrives at the sitter rather than the room: drawers under the top put paper, pens and ink within reach of a seated arm.
Hanging rather than folding is what the height buys. A folded coat creases along the fold and takes the shape of the pile; hung from the shoulders it keeps the shape it was cut to.

Springs under a soft layer do what neither does alone: the springs push back in proportion to how far each is pressed, so a heavy part of the body sinks further and a light part less, and the whole line of the spine stays supported.
Lying on one side leaves the head unsupported by the width of a shoulder. The pillow fills exactly that gap, which is why a side sleeper wants a thicker one than someone lying on their back.

The pole is the whole invention: it puts the cloth on the floor and the hands at waist height. Strands rather than a sheet because loose ends reach into corners and hold far more water for their weight.
A tower is not a tall house. It is built to see from, be seen from, or drop something down, and the stairs are what make the height usable — which is why the stair is often the whole interior.
The battery is what makes it a laptop rather than a small desktop: it cuts the last cable, so the machine can be used anywhere rather than merely moved between places with sockets.

It turns a grid of numbers back into a physical mark. An inkjet does it by firing droplets a few picolitres at a time, steered to a spot far smaller than the eye resolves, which is why the page looks continuous rather than dotted.

The whole image is a grid of pixels, each one three subpixels of red, green and blue lit to different amounts. There is no yellow in the screen: yellow is red and green next to each other, too close for the eye to separate.

A coil of wire sits in the field of a permanent magnet and is glued to a paper cone. Current through the coil pushes it along the magnet, the cone moves with it, and the air in front is pressed and released — which is what sound is.

Being at the ear rather than across a room changes what is needed: microwatts instead of watts, and each ear hears only its own channel, with none of the crossover that makes a room's stereo image collapse when you move.

It is not simply a supply. It must force current backwards through the cell against its own voltage, then taper off as the cell fills — charge too fast at the end and lithium plates out as metal on the anode, which is what ruins a battery.

Rails in the road are what separate it from a bus: steel on steel has a fraction of the rolling resistance of rubber on asphalt, so far less power moves the same load, and the vehicle cannot wander from its line.
Everything follows from putting a box where the back seats were: a flat floor, a high roof, doors at the side and rear, and windows only where the driver needs them.

It began as exactly that — Daimler's 1885 Reitwagen was a wooden bicycle with a petrol engine — but power meant heavier frames, real brakes and wider tyres, because a machine that can reach speed must also be able to stop and to hold the road.
Standing rather than sitting is the whole design: one foot stays on the board and the other pushes, so the rider can step off at any moment, which is why it needs no gears, no chain and no seat.
It exists because some work has no material to be near. Once the product is paper or numbers rather than cloth or steel, the workplace can be anywhere, and what it is built around is the desk.

The building is the easy part. What makes a library is the ordering: without an agreed scheme, a million books and no book are the same thing, which is why every library is really a catalogue with shelves attached.
Gaps between the boards are deliberate. They save weight and wood, let the contents be seen and let air through, and the strength comes from the corners rather than the faces.
It has to shut. A pocket holds what is put in it only while you are upright; a purse has a fastening, which is what makes it safe to carry loose coins at all.

The buttons are what make it outerwear. A coat has to be put on and taken off over other clothes and closed against wind, so it opens all the way down the front — unlike anything worn next to the skin.
Stopping at the hip is what it is for: the leg swings freely, so it can be worn to work in rather than only to travel in, and the zip closes it in one movement with one hand.

A day is one rotation of the Earth relative to the Sun — which is about four minutes longer than one rotation relative to the stars, because the Earth has also moved along its orbit and must turn a little further to face the Sun again.

The Moon takes 27.3 days to go round the Earth, but 29.5 days to return to the same phase — because the Earth has moved along its own orbit meanwhile, so the Moon must travel further to line up with the Sun again.
The mismatch is the whole problem. Twelve months fall eleven days short, so lunar calendars drift through the seasons and lunisolar ones insert a whole extra month every few years to catch up.

It is a reconciliation, not a measurement. The Julian year overshot by 11 minutes, which by the 1500s had moved the equinox ten days; the Gregorian reform of 1582 dropped those ten days and changed the leap rule for century years.

The oldest known accounting is Mesopotamian clay tokens — one small shape per sheep or per measure of grain, sealed inside a clay envelope. Counting begins as a record of goods owed, not as mathematics.

It was invented for accounts before literature. The pressed marks on Sumerian clay begin as pictures of the goods being counted and become, over centuries, signs for the sounds of words instead of the things.
The step is abstraction: once the mark for five sheep can be split into a mark for five and a mark for sheep, five can be added to anything. That separation is what makes arithmetic possible at all.

Used as a placeholder in several places, but treated as a number in its own right — one you can add, subtract and calculate with — by Brahmagupta in India in 628, who also set down the rules for negative numbers.

The name means earth-measuring, and Herodotus says that is literally what it was: the Nile flood erased field boundaries every year, and Egyptian surveyors had to re-establish who owned what, which meant measuring land.

It is not simply farming but the surplus farming makes: one family growing more than one family eats is what allows anyone at all to do something other than get food, which is where every other trade comes from.

That is the definition and the consequence together: once people are fed by others, they can specialise, and the density that follows makes trade, writing, law and disease all far more likely than they were in a village.

Writing is what changes a custom into a law. Hammurabi's code was cut into a stone pillar and set in public around 1750 BC — the point of which is not the rules but that everyone can see them and they cannot quietly change.

It is stored as change rather than as a copy: synapses that fire together strengthen, so a memory is a pattern of connections made easier to re-run. The hippocampus builds new ones; damage it and old memories survive while new ones stop forming.

The line between history and prehistory is writing, and it is drawn there because it is the point where the past can say something about itself rather than being inferred from what it left. Everything before is archaeology.
It is both at once, and neither description alone works. It arrives as countable photons and it interferes with itself like a wave, and which one you see depends only on what you set up to catch it.

Mass is what resists being accelerated, and mass is also what produces and responds to gravity. There is no obvious reason those should be the same number — they are, to about one part in a thousand trillion, and general relativity says that is because they are the same thing.

Mass and energy are the same quantity in different units, and c squared is the exchange rate between them. Because c is so large, a very small amount of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy — which is the whole of nuclear power and the whole of why the Sun shines.

Since 1967 the second has not been a fraction of a day. It is defined as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the radiation from a caesium-133 atom — because atoms are identical everywhere and the Earth's rotation is not even constant.

Since 1983 the metre has been defined as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That means the speed of light is no longer measured at all: it is fixed by definition, and measuring it now measures the metre.

It is always relative to something. There is no experiment that reveals absolute speed — which is why nothing feels different in a smoothly flying aircraft, and why the speed of light being the same for every observer forced everything else to bend instead.

It is what you actually feel. Constant speed feels like standing still; only a change in it presses you into the seat, which is why acceleration and gravity are indistinguishable from inside a closed box.
