Interior diameter and height to the oculus are the same 43.3 m, so a sphere would fit exactly.

Almost no line in it is straight. The stylobate bulges upward by 10.3 cm over 70 m, the columns swell and taper, and both columns and walls lean inward — refinements measured in the 19th century and made in Pentelic marble in the 15 years from 447 BC, cut to size in the quarry before it ever reached the hill.

It is lit from above. Light wells bring daylight and air down to rooms too deep in the building to reach a wall, which is what lets it be dense and multi-storey at once, with drains, water channels and timber-reinforced masonry running through. That plan is probably where the Greeks got the Labyrinth from — the palace came first and the story second.

Sandstone and conglomerate laid down in a delta, lifted into a plateau about 60 million years ago and cut along vertical faults until only pillars were left. Twenty-four monasteries went up on top of them from the second half of the 14th century, and until the 1600s everything and everyone arrived by rope, basket or a ladder that could be pulled up.

Four to six metres of ash and pumice set around the dead, and the bodies rotted away inside it, leaving voids. Giuseppe Fiorelli worked out that the void was the cast: fill it with plaster and the person comes back. The method is still used, with resin now, because it does not destroy the bones inside.

A stratovolcano is built out of its own eruptions, so its height is a running total rather than a fact: 3,403 m in September 2024, and different after the next summit eruption. Diodorus Siculus reports one around 1400 BCE, sixteen happened in 2001 alone, and the 1669 flows destroyed at least ten villages before reaching Catania.

An octagon 60 m across and 36 m high, with a wooden dome about 20 m in diameter carried on a drum standing on sixteen supports — four piers and twelve columns — and an inner arcade of twenty-four more around the rock itself. Completed in 72 AH, 691–2 CE, for Abd al-Malik; the original dome fell in 1015 and was rebuilt in 1022–3.

A plateau 550 by 270 m standing over 400 m above the desert has no water on it, so Herod put the water in: cisterns of about 40,000 m³ filled from runoff. That is the fortress. The Romans answered it with a ramp 114 m high and breached the wall on 16 April; Yadin's excavation found at most 28 bodies, against Josephus's 960.

Thick ash deposits from Erciyes, Hasan and Göllüdağ, with harder layers on top of softer ones. The hard cap shelters the column beneath it while everything unprotected around it washes away, which leaves standing towers of rock soft enough to be dug out with hand tools — so the houses, the churches and the underground cities are all subtraction.

Uplift did half of it. Raising the Colorado Plateau steepened the river without moving it, and when the Gulf of California opened 5.3 million years ago the base level dropped again — so the river cut down instead of wandering. It has reached the Vishnu Schist, two billion years old, with 270-million-year-old Kaibab Limestone still on the rim.

A closed basin at 3,656 m with nowhere for water to leave except upward. Lake Minchin, then Tauca 140 m deep, then Coipasa 11,500 to 13,400 years ago, each evaporating and leaving its salt: eight metres of crust whose elevation varies by less than a metre across 10,582 km², over brine about 0.3% lithium.

A stave church stands on upright posts rather than on horizontal sills, which keeps the timber out of the wet ground and is why any of them survive at all. Dendrochronology puts this one at about 1132, and the north portal is carved in the Urnes style — the last of the Viking animal ornament, on a Christian building.

Flat-roofed brick houses on a semi-orthogonal plan with drainage running through it, holding as many as 23,500 people over about 150 hectares in the Mature Harappan phase, 2600–1900 BC. The bricks were good enough that in about 1857 the Lahore–Multan railway dug the site up and used them for track ballast.

An arch-gravity dam only works in a canyon: the curve throws the water's push sideways into the rock walls, so the wall can be thick at the bottom and thin at the top. Curing was the harder problem — 2,480,000 m³ poured as one mass would have taken 125 years to cool and cracked, so it went in as columns threaded with 937 km of pipe carrying first river water and then refrigerated water.

A canal that crosses a watershed has to climb, and the summit in the Shandong foothills is 42 m up. Qiao Weiyue invented the pound lock for it in 984 — a gated chamber a boat waits in while the level changes — and the Ming dug four reservoirs and dammed the Wen to send 60% of its water north to keep the top of it wet.

Star-fort geometry exists so that every stretch of wall is covered by fire from another stretch, and that geometry assumes flat ground you can lay it out on. Ehrensvärd began in 1748 bending it instead onto eight islands, six of them fortified, each carrying its own works. It surrendered on 3 May 1808 after two months.

A 500-tonne bronze Buddha nearly 15 m tall needs a roof, and the roof became the argument: until 1998 the Daibutsuden was the largest wooden building in the world. The statue took much of Japan's bronze and all of its gold imported; the present hall, finished in 1709, is 30% smaller than its predecessor — 7 bays instead of 11, for want of funds.

About 40,000 km of road across what are now six countries, with no wheeled vehicle on any of it and no draught animal bigger than a llama — so it can climb stairs, and it does. Where it meets a gorge it crosses on cable spun from ichu grass, which rots: the bridges had to be rebuilt about every two years, and that maintenance was a tax.

Begun 15 August 1248, halted around 1560, resumed 1842 and finished 15 October 1880 — 632 years, with a gap of about 282 in the middle. It could be finished at all because the medieval plans and drawings survived it; the 19th century built to them and used iron roof girders to do it. Fourteen aerial bomb hits, and it was still standing in a flattened city.

The buttresses take the roof's weight entirely outside the building — the 14th-century ones reach fifteen metres from wall to counter-support — so the wall stops being structure and can become window. Inside that shell sat the oak roof frame called the forest, and when it and the flèche burned on 15 April 2019 the flèche brought down 750 tonnes of stone and lead, while the walls, towers, buttresses and glass survived.

A geyser needs a heat source shallow enough to boil groundwater, and here that is a caldera 72 by 45 km left by an eruption 640,000 years ago that threw out over 1,000 km³. At least 1,283 geysers have erupted in the park and about 465 are active in a year, out of at least 10,000 hydrothermal features. Protected as the first national park on 1 March 1872.

Three layers of basalt of the Serra Geral formation, and the falls step down them twice: hard rock over softer, so the lip holds while what is beneath it is cut away. About 275 drops across 2.7 km, the longest 82 m, and roughly half the river goes into the Devil's Throat, 80–90 m wide.

A tepui is a table mountain with a vertical edge, so a river on top does not descend — it leaves. 979 m in total with an uninterrupted plunge of 807 m, then about 400 m of cascade and a final 30 m drop. Jimmie Angel first flew over it on 16 November 1933 looking for ore, and in 1937 landed on the top and could not take off again.

A dome cut from granite blocks and held together by stone rivets, with no mortar anywhere. The gaps that leaves are the ventilation: the grotto breathed, and stayed dry, until an early 20th-century restoration cased it in concrete and sealed it — after which humidity, leaks and erosion of the sculptures followed. Begun 751 and completed by the Silla court in 774.

The geography does the guarding. A peninsula joined to the rest of Tasmania by a neck 30 m wide needs only that neck fenced, guarded, trapped and lined with dogs, and everything else is water. Running from 1830 to 1877; the Separate Prison of 1853 then moved the punishment inside the head instead, hooding prisoners and enforcing silence.

Iron-rich earth on sandstone under an overhang: pigment that does not fade and rock that does not get rained on. More than 5,000 recorded sites, some paintings up to 20,000 years old, on ground where the archaeology shows occupation for at least 40,000 years and possibly 65,000.

Thirty-one square rooms, each carried up to a dome on squinches and lit only through a hole at its top — rubble stone on clay mortar with gypsum sealing the joints, at 3,200 m where there is no timber to roof anything with. A caravanserai has to shelter strangers and their animals at the pass, and stone vaulting is what is available to do it.

Adobe cannot span or carry much, so the walls are thickened into twelve conical buttresses and threaded with horizontal timbers that both reinforce them and give the replasterers something to stand on. A 1970s repair rendered it in sand and cement, which trapped moisture in the mud behind and started it rotting; the 2023 work went back to adobe.

Fifty-eight oil-pressing complexes have been excavated in one town of about 42 hectares — mills, decantation basins and presses — which is what a Roman city on the far edge of the empire was for: it exported oil. About 20,000 people at its late-2nd-century peak; wrecked by the 1755 earthquake and then quarried for stone to build Meknes.

The site is an island because a river meander was closed off by a canal on the eastern side, which turns a bend in the water into a moat around the whole city — a defence that costs one cut instead of a circuit. It held until a fourteen-month Burmese siege took it on 7 April 1767.

The limit of the technique is on show, because it was reached. The largest block known from the ancient world was uncovered in 2014 in the quarry above the site — about 19.6 by 6 by 5.5 m and an estimated 1,650 tonnes — cut free and then left there. Everything at Baalbek that did get moved is the answer to the question that stone asks.

Nothing was done to the lake. In the early 1960s the Amu Darya and Syr Darya were diverted to irrigate desert for cotton, and a lake with no outlet loses whatever its rivers stop bringing: 60% of the surface and 80% of the volume gone by 1998, a tenth of the original size by 2007, salinity from 10 g/L to about 30, and a fishery employing 40,000 down to nothing by 1987.

Gaudí worked out his structure by hanging weighted strings from a ceiling and photographing the result upside down: a chain hanging free takes pure tension, so inverted it stands in pure compression and needs no buttress at all. Begun 19 March 1882, less than a quarter done when he died in 1926, and the 172.5 m central tower now makes it the tallest church in the world.

Brick instead of stone alone, and pulleys and cranes instead of numbers — both from the Silhak argument that a state should build with what works rather than with what is customary. 5.74 km of wall in two years, 1794 to 1796, on 700,000 person-hours of paid labour, and the whole thing written up in the ten volumes of the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe down to the wages.

Delta mud is anoxic, so a tree standing in it cannot get oxygen through its roots — pneumatophores grow upward out of the mud to breathe instead. That single adaptation is what allows 10,277 km² of forest on the Ganges delta, and the forest is what stands between the cyclones and millions of people behind it.

A bone tube, pigment blown through it, and a hand held against the rock: the image is the gap. Over 2,000 hands, 829 left against 31 right, because the pipe goes in the hand you are better with and the other one gets stencilled. Iron oxides for red, natrojarosite yellow, pyrolusite black, and gypsum to make them stick; from about 7,300 BC.

The Otulum ran through the middle of where they wanted a plaza, so they put it underneath one: a masonry conduit over 100 m long roofed with a corbel vault 3 m high. A corbel vault needs a great deal of mass for a small opening, which is why Maya buildings have narrow rooms and thick walls — and why running one under a square is a serious piece of work rather than a drain.

One spring, Efqa, in the middle of the Syrian desert, 215 km from Damascus. A caravan crossing that desert has to stop where the water is, and a city that owns the only stop can charge for it: Palmyrene merchants ran colonies along the Silk Road, and the place held more than 200,000 people under Zenobia before Aurelian levelled it in 273.

A domed octagonal room 14.46 m across, begun about 796 and consecrated in 805, carrying columns brought from St Gereon in Cologne and further spolia shipped from Rome and Ravenna. The building is an argument made out of salvage: a new empire assembled physically from the parts of the old one. Thirty German kings were crowned in it between 936 and 1531.

Oak under Ivan Kalita in 1339, white limestone under Dmitri Donskoi in 1366–68, and then brick: Italian masters under Ivan III between 1485 and 1495 built 2,235 m of wall enclosing about 275,000 m², 5 to 19 m high and 3.5 to 6.5 m thick, with towers that are nearly all square. Brick is what let the wall follow the ground instead of the quarry.

A shield volcano is broad and gentle, so its summit is a plateau rather than a peak — and this one reaches 4,207 m, above the inversion layer that traps cloud below it. Dry, dark, still air on flat ground you can build on: thirteen observation facilities sit there, on a summit Hawaiian tradition treats as the region of the gods and once allowed only high-ranking aliʻi to enter.

Building from 1661; Hardouin-Mansart's Hall of Mirrors 1678–86, and mirror glass was then a Venetian monopoly expensive enough that a room of it was a statement about what France could now make. 2,143 windows, 1,252 chimneys, 67 staircases and about 2,300 rooms — the point of which was that the entire nobility lived where the king could see them.

It is the most informative object in Egyptian quarrying precisely because it failed. Cut directly out of the bedrock at Aswan with dolerite pounders, it would have stood about 41.75 m and weighed nearly 1,090 tonnes — a third larger than any obelisk actually raised — and then the granite cracked and the work stopped, leaving the tool marks and the ochre working lines where they were.

Hollow and coil-built rather than solid, slipped and burnished to a gloss, then fired under a heap of grass, twigs and leaves for several hours. Hollow is the whole trick: a solid clay head that size would blow itself apart as the water inside turned to steam, and the pierced eyes vent it. From about 1500 BCE, with iron smelting in the same culture between 750 and 550 BCE.

Lost wax: model the object in wax, case it in clay, melt the wax out and pour metal into the space it leaves. The mould is destroyed to get the casting out, so every piece is unique — and the Igbo-Ukwu founders of the 9th to 12th centuries were using it for surfaces so fine that the alloys were chosen piece by piece, copper, bronze and leaded bronze rather than one recipe.

A free-standing mountain rising straight off a plain to 5,895 m carries an ice cap that nothing feeds but the mountain itself, which makes it a gauge. Almost 85% of that cover went between October 1912 and June 2011 — from 11.40 km² to under 1 km² — and the projection is that the rest goes by 2040.

Hard caprock over a soft bed. The Lockport limestone and dolomite resist the water; the Rochester shale beneath does not, so the falls undercut themselves until the unsupported cap breaks off and the whole thing moves upstream. It averaged 1 to 1.5 m a year for 560 years, and diversion for hydroelectricity has brought it down to about 30 cm.

Red fired brick, with the ornament carved into the brick after laying rather than applied to it — and chemical tests have found no trace of any organic substance between the courses, which is why the jointing is still argued over. Seventy-one temples were recorded in 1899; the site was bombed in August 1969.

The art is the evidence for the climate. Antelope, crocodile and herds of cattle are engraved and painted across eroded sandstone that now stands in desert — 15,000 engravings identified, most from the ninth and tenth millennia BP, when the Sahara was habitable savanna. The traditions run Archaic, Round Head, Pastoral, Horse and finally Camel, which is the drying recorded in what people drew.

An oracle of Amun far out in the Libyan desert, with inscriptions from the 4th century BCE, on the rock of Aghurmi in an oasis fed by about 200 springs. Alexander reached it in 331 BC and his court historians said it confirmed him as divine and as the legitimate pharaoh — which is what an oracle that far from anywhere was worth going to for.

Cuicul was laid out in the 1st century AD to the standard plan — forum in the middle, cardo and decumanus crossing — on a narrow triangular plateau 900 m up. The grid does not fit, and the town is interesting because of where it gave way: the theatre had to be built outside the walls, which is exceptional.

It began as a Swedish trading fort in 1653, named Carolusborg, and changed hands to Denmark, the Dutch and then the English within eleven years — because the coast was worth that much. By about 1682 the dungeons were cut into the rock beneath the parade ground: vaulted cellars able to hold a thousand people, under the floor the garrison drilled on.

The British demanded the Golden Stool, the Asante refused, and the war that followed ended with the Aban palace demolished and Prempeh I exiled to the Seychelles. When they brought him back they built him this in 1925 and offered it to him — and he would not take it until he had paid the full cost of the building himself.

The escarpment is hard basalt over the soft Clarens sandstone beneath it, and the sandstone weathers into overhangs the basalt then keeps dry. Between 35,000 and 40,000 San works survive in them, the largest collection of parietal art in the world; 20,000 have been recorded across 500 sites, and Sebaayeni Cave alone holds 1,146.

A Swahili town is built out of what the coast provides: coral rag quarried from the reef for the walls, mangrove poles from the creeks for the floors and roofs — which is why room widths across the whole coast are the length of a mangrove pole. Founded 1370, the oldest continuously inhabited town in Kenya, with 23 mosques and about 3,000 donkeys doing the haulage.

Rainforest hides everything in it. But African forest elephants come out into one clearing, Dzanga Bai, to eat mineral-rich soil — so the salt is what makes the animals countable, and most of what is known about forest elephant behaviour was learned by sitting at that one hole in the canopy. 6,865.54 km² of reserve, established 1990.

It was a trading state before it was a slaving one: Loango exported copper from the mines at Mindouli and was a major producer and exporter of cloth, and its Vili merchants went inland to find both. The Atlantic trade came later and in quantity. The kingdom ran from about 1550 to about 1883, at its height reaching from Cape St Catherine nearly to the mouth of the Congo.

Four quartzite hills standing out of flat Kalahari sand, which makes them visible for a long way and worth walking to. Over 4,500 paintings across some 500 archaeological sites, the oldest evidence of occupation reaching back about 24,000 years — though the paintings themselves span everything from a red giraffe no older than AD 400 to white horses that cannot predate the 1800s.

Cap Diamant does half the work and the walls do the rest, which is why this is the only walled city left north of Mexico. Champlain put a fort on top of the cliff and a habitation at the bottom of it in 1608, and the town has been two towns ever since — 1,400 buildings over 1.42 km², with a funicular between them.

The longest known Maya text is a flight of stairs: 62 steps carrying 2,200 glyphs, 21 m long, begun in AD 710 and extended in 755. Sixteen rulers from AD 426 to about 822, all of them shown on Altar Q. The Copán river then ate 300 m of the acropolis to a height of 37 m before the Carnegie Institution diverted it south in the 1930s.

The Nahr-i-Bihisht, the River of Paradise, is cut through the palaces themselves and feeds the marble pools in them, so the cooling is structural rather than added — which is what red sandstone walls 2.41 km round and up to 33 m high are enclosing. Commissioned by Shah Jahan on 12 May 1639 and finished 6 April 1648; Nadir Shah took the Peacock Throne out of it in 1739.

A stupa is solid — a dome over a relic with no interior at all — so its size is limited only by how much brick you can stack and how well the ground under it holds. Anuradhapura built several of the largest structures in the ancient world that way, and stayed the capital of Sri Lanka from 377 BCE to 1017 CE before the Chola invasion emptied it after 993.

Everything entering or leaving the Baltic passes Helsingør, and there the Sound is only 4 km wide — inside gun range from one shore. Eric VII built Krogen there in the 1420s to make ships pay the Sound Dues, and Frederick II rebuilt it as a Renaissance castle between 1574 and 1585. It burned on the night of 24–25 September 1629; only the chapel survived, saved by its vaults.

Ice cuts a U-shaped valley and cuts it below sea level, because a glacier is not a river and does not stop at the shoreline; when the ice goes the sea comes in. Fifteen kilometres long and at most 1.5 wide, with the Seven Sisters falling down one wall and abandoned farms — Skageflå, Knivsflå, Blomberg — on ledges reached by paths bolted to the rock.

It is a 19th-century building in medieval dress, and the dress is the only old thing about it: battery-powered servants' bells and telephone lines, central heating by calorifère, hot running water and automatically flushing lavatories. Begun 5 September 1869 and stopped at Ludwig's death in 1886 with about fifteen of a planned two hundred rooms finished, at 6.2 million gold marks of his own money.

Water flows in and leaves only as vapour, so everything dissolved in it stays and concentrates: 342 g/kg, about 9.6 times the ocean. The surface sits 439.78 m below sea level, the deepest hypersaline lake at 298 m, and it is going — from 395 m below sea level in 1970 to 418 by 2006, and from 1,050 km² in 1930 to 605 in 2016.

Founded in 1585 by Abtai Sain Khan after he met the 3rd Dalai Lama, and built out of stone carried from the ruins of Karakorum a few kilometres away — the Mongol imperial capital recycled into a monastery wall. That wall was meant to carry 108 stupas, 108 being the sacred number, though it probably never did. Choibalsan had the place destroyed in 1939.

Vauban's geometry, imported: angled bastions so that every stretch of wall is covered by fire from the next, with a moat fed from the Hương river. Begun under Gia Long in 1803 and finished under Minh Mạng in 1832 — nearly 10 km round, 6.6 m high and 21 m thick, with three nested enclosures. Ten of its 160 buildings survived the fighting in 1968.

Two things make the place: the traphang, ponds cut through the city to hold the wet season against the dry, and the inscription of 1292 — which did not invent Thai letters so much as settle them, writing the vowels on the line and dropping the tone marks. A city needs water stored and a state needs records, and Sukhothai is where both are visible at once.

It is the largest ancient castle in the world at almost 70,000 m² because it is not one building but a walled quarter with a cathedral inside it. St Vitus was begun under Charles IV in the 14th century and finished on 28 September 1929 — six centuries, which is what it costs to keep a cathedral inside a fortress that is also a seat of government.

Signed on 6 February 1840 in a marquee put up on the lawn of James Busby's house — a founding document with no building of its own, which is why the ground rather than a hall is what is preserved. Te Whare Rūnanga was carved beside it and opened on the treaty's centenary, 6 February 1940, so the site now holds both parties' architecture facing each other.

A trilithon on an island whose only rock is reef: three coral limestone slabs, 5.2 m high and 5.8 m long, the uprights 30 to 40 tonnes each, raised about 1200 AD under Tuʻitātui. The V cut into the top of the lintel has been read since 1967 as a solstice sight, and argued against on the grounds that at 10 cm it is too short to aim with.

A city on the Silk Road is a place caravans must stop, which is why Otrar was rich and why what happened there mattered so much: in 1218 its governor Inalchuq arrested a Mongol trade caravan of about 450 men as spies and had them all executed. Genghis Khan besieged it for five months in 1219, breached it and killed the inhabitants. Timur died there in February 1405; by 1800 forty families were left.

Newar building is brick and timber in tiered storeys, and the Kathmandu valley shakes: the square was heavily damaged in April 2015, as it had been before. Most of what stands is 17th century, from the reigns of Siddhi Narsingh Malla and his son — the Krishna Mandir of 1667 in stone, with 21 golden pinnacles, among 55 major temples and 136 courtyards.

Founded as a Greek colony called Tragurion in the 3rd century BC on a small island between the mainland and Čiovo — and the orthogonal street plan they laid out is still the plan, under Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque building. An island town cannot spread, so it rebuilds on its own lines instead.

Wall mosaic in glass tesserae by Byzantine masters, floor mosaic by local ones — a division of labour visible in the building itself. Built from 553 under Bishop Euphrasius on the site of a dilapidated older basilica, which stood on one older still, so the 5th-century floor and a fish mosaic from an earlier oratory survive underneath.

The wall was divided among the crafts and each tower was built and manned by the guild it is named for — Tinsmiths, Butchers, Tailors, Furriers. That is a defence organised the way the economy already was, and it is why the towers are hollow and fitted with lifts and galleries: they were working buildings as well as fighting ones. The Clock Tower is 64 m.

Named "the place of greenstone" for the nephrite in it, which the glaciers are what deliver: ice grinds the source rock out of the mountains and the rivers carry the boulders down to where they can be found. 2,600,000 hectares along 450 km of coast, from sea level to 3,724 m, and the best surviving example anywhere of the biota of Gondwana.

The rail spur is the point of the site, and it is why the place is preserved rather than cleared: the camp was built where the lines already met so that people could be brought to it from across occupied Europe and killed on arrival. 1.1 million people died there, 960,000 of them Jews. It has been a museum since 2 July 1947 and is inscribed by UNESCO under its full name, "Auschwitz Birkenau German Nazi Concentration and Extermination Camp (1940–1945)".

212 sculptures by one hand, in Iddefjord granite and bronze, on a site the city of Oslo gave him to fill. The Monolith is the argument: 14.12 m and 121 figures, and it is a true monolith — one block, brought from a Halden quarry in autumn 1927, raised in 1928 and cut by three masons over fourteen years from 1929, first shown at Christmas 1944.

An atoll is a ring of reef around a lagoon, and this one came up out of the sea: Rennell is the largest raised coral atoll in the world, so the lagoon is now Lake Tegano, brackish and sitting at sea level on land that used to be underwater. Isolation did the rest — 21 of the 50 recorded bird species are endemic, with one endemic bat and seven endemic land snails.

The wall does not keep anyone out. It marks where the law stops: someone who had broken a kapu and reached the ground inside it could be absolved by a priest and walk away, and defeated warriors and non-combatants could shelter there during a battle. The Hale o Keawe beside it was built about 1650 for the bones of Keaweʻīkekahialiʻiokamoku and held 23 remains.

The Boiling Lake is a fumarole with water standing in it: 82 to 92 °C at the edge and hotter in the middle, kept boiling by gas coming up through the floor rather than by anything the water is doing. Around it the Valley of Desolation has boiling mud ponds and small geysers, on an island still being built by the volcano under it.

A limestone reef gone to karst: rainwater slightly acid from the air dissolves the rock along its joints and leaves passages, and 800 m of them run 25 m below the surface here. The Taíno painted 472 figures on those walls and cut about ten more, in the dark, where nothing weathers.

Staling is not the bread drying out — it is the starch recrystallising, moisture migrating out of the granules and the molecules realigning. That happens fastest just above freezing, so a refrigerator makes bread stale faster than a counter does while freezing stops it outright. Heating to 60 °C reverses some of it, briefly.

A raw olive is inedible: 72 to 82 mg per 100 g of oleuropein and its aglycone in black ones, 56 to 59 in green. Curing removes it — days with lye, months in brine or salt — and in brine the lactic acid bacteria doing the work acidify the olives as they go, which is what allows them to be kept without refrigeration. One process solves the taste and the keeping at once.

The butter has to stay solid, so the work is done near 16 °C: roll, fold, rest and chill, and the fat stays in sheets instead of blending into the dough. Folding twice, four times over, gives 81 layers. In the oven the water in that butter turns to steam and forces the layers apart — the pastry has no other leavening at all.

Smoke preserves meat, and this is the part of it that does the work: condense and distil the wood tar and about half of what comes over between 200 and 225 °C is guaiacol and creosol. Carl Reichenbach isolated it in 1832 and found it would keep meat without putrefaction on its own — the smokehouse in a bottle, which is what liquid smoke still is.

It is a wound response. Cut the bark of Acacia senegal or seyal and the tree seals the injury with a hardening exudate; tapping is deliberate injury repeated, and the gum is collected weeks later. That is why the supply follows drought and damage rather than good growing years.

Cut into the cliff rather than built against it, and aligned so that on 22 October and 22 February the sun reaches the back wall of the sanctuary — leaving Ptah, god of the underworld, in the dark. Begun about 1264 BC under Ramesses II, with four colossi 20 m high; sawn into 1,036 blocks in the 1960s and moved 208 m inland and 65 m higher, for $41.7 million.

It is the southern end of a trans-Saharan route, and the trade is a swap: salt slabs came down from Taoudenni, 664 km north, and gold went up. That profit bought scholarship — the Djinguereber mosque was built in 1327 under Mansa Musa, three madrasahs took 25,000 students, and about 350,000 manuscripts have since been carried out of the city to keep them.

Coral stone is what the town is made of and what gives it its colour, and cloves and slaves are what paid for it. The Anglican cathedral stands on the site of the largest slave market on Zanzibar, and the altar is on the spot where the whipping post stood — a building put deliberately on top of what it is about.

Adobe walls several feet thick, stacked five or six storeys and rebuilt in place for about a thousand years — the oldest continuously inhabited settlement in the United States, and the only World Heritage site there that people still live in. Electricity, running water and indoor plumbing are prohibited in the old village.

Puuc building translates a house into stone: smooth low walls under ornate friezes that quote a Maya hut, with columns standing for bundles of reeds and trapezoids for a thatched roof. The Pyramid of the Magician is odd for another reason — its layers are oval rather than rectangular, which almost no other Maya structure is. Built around 700 AD and abandoned in the 13th century.

Twenty square kilometres of mud brick stands because the coast almost never gets rain, and the same dryness is why the city needed wells 15 m deep and canals cut from the Moche river to farm at all. The Inca took Chimor in 1470 and cut the canals. What the desert preserved for a thousand years is now going to El Niño storms and salt.

A stone roof cannot span far, so a big stone room is mostly columns: 134 of them in 5,000 m², 122 at 10 m and twelve at 21 m with diameters over 3 m, carrying architraves estimated at 70 tonnes. Raising the central rows above the rest is what makes a clerestory possible, and that is the only way to get daylight into the middle of it. Built and rebuilt over about 1,900 years.

Height is the point. The Tellem cut caves into a sandstone face rising about 500 m so that their dead and their grain sat above the flash floods, and the Dogon who arrived in the 14th century kept using the shelf. 150 km of cliff, and the buildings are on it rather than under it because the flat ground floods.

Mountain gorillas live on volcanoes because the altitude gives them the vegetation and the isolation, and the park exists around that: 7,800 km², created in 1925 as Africa's first national park. It has been on the List of World Heritage in Danger since 1994, and 175 rangers were killed there up to April 2018.

A delta is normally where a river meets the sea; this one meets a tectonic trough and stops. About 11 km³ arrives a year from rain that fell in Angola in January and February, travels some 1,200 km in about a month, and then spreads across the delta over four more — so the flood peaks between June and August, in the middle of Botswana's dry winter, and the delta swells to three times its permanent size.

Two metals that corrode each other, kept apart on purpose. The skin is repoussé copper 2.4 mm thick — hammered, not cast — hung on an iron truss Eiffel deliberately built loose, on flat bars and springs, so the statue can move in the harbour wind; the joints were insulated with shellacked asbestos against galvanic corrosion. It arrived in crates on 17 June 1885, was dedicated 28 October 1886, and went green within twenty years.

The 1650 earthquake destroyed almost every colonial building in the city and the Inca walls under them held; in 1950 more than a third of the city was damaged and the Inca masonry stood again, which is how the stonework of the Qorikancha came back into view from under the Dominican monastery built on it. Mortarless joints that fit exactly can shift and settle back; mortared ones crack.

Over a thousand feet of limestone with soft marl and shale through it, and the shale is the problem: it swells when it gets wet and forces the surrounding stone apart. Flash floods pour debris into open tombs and then work on the rock itself. 65 tombs and chambers, cut between about 1539 and 1075 BC, hidden rather than raised — and guarded by tomb police, which a pyramid cannot be.

By the 1950s the shrines were neglected and the priests had gone. The Austrian artist Susanne Wenger formed the New Sacred Art movement, rebuilt the shrines as monumental sculpture, and fought off land speculators and poachers for the rest of her life — so the grove survives as art made to keep a religious site standing rather than as a preserved ruin. 75 ha, and a festival with more than 700 years behind it.

A lake with no outlet in a desert loses water only by evaporation, which concentrates it — the largest permanent desert lake and the largest alkaline lake there is. The same rift basin has been filling with sediment for millions of years, and that is why Koobi Fora produced Skull 1470 and the Turkana Boy. The Omo brings 90% of the inflow, and a dam upstream now controls it.

The colour is engineering. Irving Morrow chose international orange because it stands out in the fog that fills the strait, over the Navy's proposal of black and yellow stripes. The span is 1,280 m — the longest in the world until 1964 — on towers 227 m above water, each cable 27,572 strands, across a mile of strait 113 m deep with strong tides and stronger winds. Opened 27 May 1937.

Structure 2 stands over 45 m on a base 120 m square, in a city of about 1,000 structures over 2 km² with 6,250 more mapped in the 20 km² around it — and all of it under canopy, which is why the Snake Kingdom was found late despite leaving 117 stelae, more than anywhere else in the region, and despite dominating the Classic period alongside Tikal.

A Miocene laccolith pushed into Cretaceous sedimentary rock and froze there without ever reaching the surface. The soft rock over it has since gone entirely — weathered off, then scoured by ice — and what is left standing is the harder granite that was underneath, in towers reaching 2,500 m.

Lava poured out between about 40 and 25 million years ago and stacked 3,000 to 3,500 m of basalt into a shield. Everything since has been subtraction: erosion cut the pile back into precipitous cliffs and deep gorges with a 2,000 m escarpment, and left Ras Dejen at 4,550 m — high enough that it snows there, which almost nowhere in tropical Africa does.

A river cuts a V and a glacier fills it and widens it into a U, which is why the walls stand 3,000 to 3,500 feet above a flat floor at 4,000 feet, and why the side streams are left hanging — Yosemite Falls drops 2,425 feet because its valley was never deepened to match the main one. The most recent glaciation only reached as far as Bridalveil Fall.

Karst leaves towers where the rock resisted and flat floor where it dissolved, and the floor is the farm: 132 km² of valley with mogotes up to 300 m standing out of tobacco grown by hand and ox. The same landform appears in Thailand, Laos and Vietnam and almost nowhere between, because it needs thick limestone and a lot of rain.

Khiva was the last stop before the desert crossing to Iran, and it is built out of the desert: mud-brick walls 8 to 10 m high, 5 to 6 m thick and 6,250 m round, with watchtowers every 30 m. The Juma mosque's hypostyle hall stands on 112 columns taken from older buildings, and the Kalta Minor minaret was left unfinished.

It has plumbing. Hidden gutters and channels run through the hair, the collar, the chest and holes behind the ears, taking water off the stone, and they have kept a 71 m carving from eroding for 1,200 years. It was begun in 722 by the monk Hai Tong to calm a dangerous confluence — and it did, because so much spoil went into the river that the current changed.

The site is a field of granite boulders and the city is made of them — including 56 carved stone beams in the Vittala hall that ring at different pitches when struck, and a shrine cut as a stone chariot. Hampi-Vijayanagara was probably the second-largest city in the world in 1500; after the defeat at Talikota in 1565 it was looted and burned for six months and never came back.

The Pythia sat on a tripod over a chasm in the rock, and ancient writers said a sweet-smelling pneuma came out of it — a claim that has been argued since as ethylene or another hydrocarbon rising along the faults under the site, and disputed on the grounds that the geology is limestone. Whatever it was, the treasuries along the Sacred Way are cities paying for the answers, and the Athenian one commemorates Marathon in 490 BC.

Cyclopean walls of blocks well over 20 tonnes, some possibly near 100 — big enough that later Greeks assumed the Cyclopes had built them — and the same mass problem solved twice over. The Lion Gate carries a relieving triangle above the lintel so the wall does not rest its weight on it, and the Treasury of Atreus is corbelled: each course laid a little further in until it closes, with no arch anywhere.

Calcarenite is soft enough to dig a house out of and porous enough that the same digging gives you a cistern, which is the only way to live on a waterless ravine — so every dwelling is paired with a tank, and the streets run over the roofs of the houses below. Occupied since about 7000 BC, and evacuated in the 1950s as an affront to the new republic.

The Magdeburg charter of 1257 laid out the largest medieval market square in Europe, and the walls that closed it were taken down in the 19th century and the moat filled and planted — so the Planty is the fortification, in outline, as a park. The ring survives by being converted rather than kept.

It was preserved by its own failure. The weavers of Bruges were reckoned the best in the world and the town reached at least 46,000 people around 1350; then from about 1500 the Zwin — the inlet that made all of it possible — silted up, and the trade went elsewhere. A city that stops making money stops rebuilding, which is why the medieval fabric is still there.

Draining peat makes the ground sink, and the river bed rises with its own sand, so the gap you are pumping across gets worse every year you pump. By about 1740 the answer here was nineteen mills working in stages: one set lifts water into a reservoir at an intermediate level, another empties that into the river whenever the tide and season let it.

The tumulus is the security. Loose rock 49 m high and 152 m across cannot be tunnelled, because anything you dig fills in behind you — so Antiochus I of Commagene put his tomb under a heap in 62 BC and flanked it with seated figures 8 to 9 m tall on terraces east and west. The heads have all come off and lie among the statues they belong to.

Over 6 km of wall in two skins about 3 m thick with 2 m between them, and inside it an archive: roughly 30,000 clay tablets, which are the main corpus of Hittite literature. Clay written on and then left is fragile; clay written on and then burned in the destruction of 1200 BC is fired, which is why the archive of a city that ended survived and the city did not.

Everything here was built for a harbour that is no longer there. The Library of Celsus of about AD 125 held nearly 12,000 scrolls in roughly 180 m², and the Great Theatre seated an estimated 25,000 — and the Cayster filled the bay in behind them, so the Mediterranean is now 3 to 4 km away and the port city sits inland.

The land is still rebounding from the weight of the ice, so a panel cut at the waterline keeps rising. That makes height a clock: the higher a carving sits above the sea now, the older it is. More than 6,000 of them have been found since 1973 — reindeer above all, with elk, bear, fish, boats, and hunting and fishing scenes.

Northern Europe has no good building stone and a great deal of clay, so Gothic had to be rebuilt in brick to get there — and this is one of the earliest in Scandinavia to do it, begun about 1170 with the choir consecrated in 1225. It then kept going: burial chapels for Christian I in the 1460s, Christian IV to 1641, Frederick V to 1825, Christian IX to 1924, eight centuries of styles in one church.

Begun 1030 under Conrad II and consecrated 1061, and rebuilt about 1090 under Henry IV with a groin vault of square bays over the nave — a stone roof over a wide span, which is the whole Romanesque problem solved. The crypt beneath, consecrated 1041, is the largest Romanesque columned hall crypt in Europe at 850 m², and holds eight rulers of three dynasties.

411 m long, 6.7 to 7.3 m wide and mostly under a metre high — which means it cannot be read from the ground at all. Radiocarbon work in 2014 and 2019 put its construction at about 300 BCE with rebuilding around 1100 CE, and whose it is has been argued ever since. The head aligns to the summer solstice sunset and the coiled tail to the winter solstice sunrise, and nobody is buried in it.

A city on a slope is a city of steps: 169 terraces cut into the mountainside, tiled roads between them and 1,200 stone stairs to get up at all. Built around 800 CE by the Tairona, six and a half centuries before Machu Picchu, for somewhere between 2,000 and 8,000 people — and found again only in 1972, by looters.

Walls of 1370 enclosing 2.25 km², 12 m high and 6,163 m round with 72 watchtowers, and inside them the Rishengchang draft bank — the first and largest in China, moving silver as paper rather than as metal, and controlling nearly half the country's silver trade under the late Qing before it went bankrupt in 1914. About 4,000 shops and houses of the 17th to 19th centuries still stand in it.

Two rivers meeting make a peninsula, and a peninsula makes a town that cannot spread sideways — so over thirty Buddhist temples, Lao vernacular houses and French colonial buildings are packed onto the same strip between the Mekong and the Nam Khan, and the monks collecting alms at sunrise walk the same street every day because there is only the one.

It is sited on a storm. In September 1723 a hurricane damaged 35 ships in other Antiguan anchorages and left the ones inside English Harbour untouched, and the Royal Navy built there from 1725 — a capstan house for careening, a stone storehouse, and later a sail loft. Nelson was stationed there from 1784 to 1787; the Navy left in 1889 and it is the only Georgian dockyard still working.

Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka are three supergiants at quite different distances that happen to fall on one line as seen from here. That is what an asterism is — a coincidence of viewpoint rather than a group of stars — and it is why the belt would be nothing in particular from anywhere else.

Cut the helix into the wall of a hole instead of onto the outside of a bar and you have the other half of the pair. A screw bites into the work and holds by that; a nut holds against a bolt that touches nothing, so the joint is a clamp rather than a bite.

A bar becomes a shaft when something holds it so that turning is the only thing it can do: the bearings define the axis and take everything that is not rotation. After that, everything keyed to the bar turns at exactly one speed — which is the constraint gears, belts and clutches all exist to get around.

Akbar founded it in 1571 and it was the Mughal capital for fourteen years, built massively in red sandstone with post-and-lintel construction throughout. Then the water supply failed and the whole thing was left. A city can be built anywhere; it can only stay where there is water, and this is what that sentence looks like at full size.

72.5 m of red and grey sandstone tapering from 14.3 m across at the base to 2.7 m at the top, with a fourth storey rebuilt in white marble after lightning struck it in 1369 — and repaired again after the 1803 earthquake. A tower that slender only stands because it narrows: the taper is what keeps the weight inside the base.

A 55 m tower built entirely in brick in the Gupta period, and one of the oldest brick structures surviving in eastern India — put up beside a tree, because the tree is the point. The one growing there now is a direct descendant of the one the Buddha sat under, and the site has been venerated since Ashoka, about 250 BCE.

Built in 1405 and laid out to the ground rather than over it — buildings fitted to the topography with the native tree cover kept, which is the opposite of the axial plan a palace usually imposes. The rear garden holds over 160 species and more than 70 trees over 300 years old, and was used for politics, drills and examinations as well as leisure. Burned in 1592 and rebuilt on the same footprints.

Over 2,100 sandstone jars between 1 and 3 m tall, some of 14 tonnes, and zircon dating shows the ones at Site 1 were brought from a quarry eight kilometres off — another quarry is about 100 km away. Put in place as early as 1240 to 660 BC, and used for secondary burial into the 13th century CE. About 80 million cluster bomblets in the ground around them failed to go off.

Three times a year, at the change of the seasons, the king personally changes the gold garments on the Emerald Buddha. That single ceremony says what the temple is: the state's shrine, where coronations, royal ordinations and the investiture of the supreme patriarch happen. Begun 1783; the image installed in early 1785, and it is about 66 cm tall.

A fringing reef grows straight off the shore instead of standing out beyond a lagoon, and this is the only large one that does — 260 km of it, less than 500 m from the beach in places. That is why the whale sharks that gather from March to August can be reached by swimming out, and why 200,000 people a year do.

Te Heuheu Tūkino IV of Ngāti Tūwharetoa gave the peaks of Tongariro, Ngauruhoe and part of Ruapehu to the Crown on 23 September 1887 on condition they were protected — the sixth national park in the world, established that October. In 1993 it became the first place anywhere listed as a cultural landscape for its spiritual significance rather than only its rocks.

The seagrass is what makes the salt. Meadows over 4,000 km² restrict the tidal flow so ocean water cannot dilute the bay, and in a hot dry climate evaporation does the rest: the water runs one and a half to two times saltier than the sea. Almost nothing grazes at that salinity, which is why Hamelin Pool still has living stromatolites building mats the way they did for two billion years.

Between 250 and 300 limestone islands undercut at the waterline — not by waves but by grazing: sponges, chitons, snails and urchins working the intertidal band eat the rock back into a notch, so each island stands on a stalk. Inside them are marine lakes cut off from the sea, including one holding stingless jellyfish found nowhere else.

Basalt runny enough to run for miles builds a shield rather than a cone, and it can keep doing it: the eruption that began on 3 January 1983 ran until September 2018, one of the longest documented anywhere, producing 4.4 km³ of lava and covering 144 km² by the end of 2016. In 2018 the lava lake in Halemaʻumaʻu — Pele's home — drained and the summit collapsed.

A barrier reef sits offshore with water behind it, and this is the longest continuous one there is: 1,500 km enclosing 24,000 km² of lagoon averaging 25 m deep. That shelter holds 2,328 fish species in 248 families, 146 recognised reef structures, the third-largest dugong population and a major green turtle nesting ground.

A lunette is a dune built on the eastern shore of a lake by the prevailing wind, out of what the lake bed gives up as it dries — and the Chibnalwood lunette is the largest clay one in the world. Those layers hold the record: three major sediment layers, full lakes between 50,000 and 19,000 years ago, at least 40,000 years of continuous occupation, and the oldest known cremation anywhere.

Groundwater dissolves limestone from below until the roof gives way, and what opens is a hole in flat ground with no rim — a trap that nothing can climb out of and that keeps working for a million years. The silt at the bottom of Victoria Cave is up to 20 m thick and holds the largest Pleistocene vertebrate deposit in Australia, including Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion.

A dome 68 m high and 18.3 m across, framed in cast iron and timber, put up in 1879–80 for the Melbourne International Exhibition — a building made for a temporary event and then used for the permanent one: the first Parliament of Australia opened under it on 9 May 1901.

A hotspot chain gets older to the north-west: islands subside, become atolls, and then drown as seamounts — so the monument is one process caught at every stage, ten islands and atolls plus more than thirty submerged banks and seamounts across 1.5 million km². Isolation did the rest: a quarter of its 7,000 marine species live nowhere else.

The slabs were not cut to shape so much as collected: the sea compacts coral sand into layers 10 to 20 cm thick over centuries, and those beds were quarried along the coast of Tongatapu and the smaller islands and brought to Lapaha to face artificial hills in three or more tiers. At least two dozen langi still stand there.

A hotspot makes islands one after another, so the chain has an age gradient — 0.05 million years for Fernandina in the west, 3.2 for San Cristóbal in the east — and each is colonised separately from 898 km away. That is a natural experiment: the same arriving lineage, isolated repeatedly under different conditions, which is what Darwin was looking at in the 1830s.

The high-grade ore was gone by 1565, and what kept Cerro Rico producing was the patio process: mercury amalgamation, which works on ore too poor to smelt. One mountain then supplied an estimated 60% of the world's silver in the second half of the 16th century, on the mita — 13,000 men conscripted a year, about one in seven adult indigenous males, carrying 100 to 300 lb loads up ladders by candlelight at 4,067 m.

Dolomite dissolves into caves with openings that are traps, and what falls in gets buried in sediment and cemented into breccia — a rock that holds bone rather than crushing it. Sterkfontein alone produced more than a third of all early hominin fossils found before 2010, including Mrs Ples at 2.3 million years and Little Foot; the Rising Star chamber has yielded over 1,500 Homo naledi specimens from at least 15 individuals.

The cold Benguela current meeting warm air offshore makes fog more than 180 days a year, and inland that fog is the only water there is — so the ecosystem drinks the air. The sand is not local either: the Orange river carried it to the sea, the current moved it north and the wind brought it back inland, which is why the sand sea has been called the wind-displaced delta of a river. Dunes over 300 m.

It is a port, and the evidence is what arrived: obsidian from Ixtepeque in Guatemala, nearly 700 km away, in high densities. The site sits on a 12 m cliff behind a wall 3 to 5 m high and 8 m thick with five narrow gates, and the shrine on top of El Castillo appears to have worked as a beacon for canoes, marking the one natural break in the reef opposite.

The rocks are the mountains. A Suzhou garden builds a whole landscape — hills, water, distance — inside a walled courtyard, using weathered stone at the scale of a boulder to stand for a range, and borrowing what is outside the wall to finish the view. Nine gardens are inscribed out of 69 surviving; there were as many as 200 in the late Ming.

Built in 1482 as Castelo de São Jorge da Mina — the mine, meaning gold — and it is the oldest European building still standing in sub-Saharan Africa. The Dutch West India Company failed to take it in 1596 and succeeded in 1637, and by 1642 held the whole Portuguese Gold Coast. The dungeons and the door out of them are what it is remembered for now.

Trajan founded it about 100 AD as a colony of veterans on open ground, so the grid could be perfect — and it was, for about 15,000 people. Then the city outgrew it and spread outward in no order at all, which is why the plan reads as an argument between two ideas of a town. The library is a rectangle 25 m by 23 m and would have held some 3,000 scrolls.

About 300 hectares of city with no cars in it, because the streets predate them and are too narrow — so goods still move by donkey, and the tanneries at Chouara and Sidi Moussa are worked the way they were. Founded as the Idrisid capital between 789 and 808, with al-Qarawiyyin, founded by Fatima al-Fihri in 859, still teaching.

Coral stone and lime mortar, single storey throughout, with sumps for storm water, lavatories in the main houses and wells at the mosques for washing before prayer. Occupied from the 11th or 12th century, richest in the 15th and 16th, and abandoned by the middle of the 17th — for reasons still argued: the Portuguese, a falling water table shown by the deepening of the well, the Wazimba raid of 1589, Oromo raids from the north.

Twenty-six kilometres of canyon that is green rather than bare, which is what makes it unlike the Grand or the Fish River. And the Kadishi falls do the opposite of erosion: water picking up calcium from dolomite lays it back down as tufa on the way over, building 200 m of rock instead of cutting it — the second tallest tufa waterfall on Earth.

Sandstone over a Precambrian granite base, weathered into towers, pillars, bridges and arches across about 60,000 km² of Sahara — and in a gorge inside it the Guelta d'Archei holds water all year. West African crocodiles cut off there have gone dwarf, which is what isolation does to a big animal in a small place. Over 86% of the rock art is painted rather than engraved, and cattle are nearly 69% of it.

Depth is what makes it volatile: 0.5 to 2 m in the southern basin and 0 to 1.8 m in the northern, so a shift in rainfall moves the shoreline enormously. Open water fell from 25,000 km² in 1960 to about 2,000 in 1980, and the lake is down about 95% since the 1960s. What has held the region together is underneath — an unconfined aquifer of roughly 500,000 km² across Chad, Niger, Nigeria and Cameroon.

Rough coral set in lime mortar, which is what the Swahili coast builds with because it is what the reef gives — and here it was used to lay out a whole town at once: six mosques, four cemeteries, two dozen house blocks and three enclosed open spaces, occupied from the 14th to the 16th century and then left.

Succulent tissue can be 90 to 95% water, which is a way of banking a wet morning against a dry month — and the mornings here are fog rather than rain, called Ihuries or Malmokkies locally. That is the whole ecology: 4,849 plant species with about 40% endemic, the only arid biodiversity hotspot on Earth, still grazed by Nama herders moving with the season and living in portable mat houses.

A tree 120 m tall cannot lift water to its own top from the roots alone, and it does not have to: coastal fog supplies about 40% of a coast redwood's annual water, taken in through the crown, and summer fog matters more to the trees' health than the rain does. Hyperion, found in 2006, is 380 feet. About 96% of the world's old-growth coast redwood has been logged.

Laterite hardens on exposure, so a wall cut from the ground stands — six metres of it here, around about 11,000 m², at least a thousand years old. It stands where it does because of the trans-Saharan gold trade, prospering between the 14th and 17th centuries between the terminals at Timbuktu and Gao, and it is the best preserved of ten such fortifications in the region.

36,000 km² and no roads: most of Africa's largest tropical rainforest reserve can only be reached by river, and some of it has never been surveyed. That inaccessibility is the protection and the problem at once — bonobos do well around the Iyaelima settlements inside it, and the park was on the Danger list from 1999 until 2021.

Sandstone can be quarried in one piece at a size limestone cannot, and Quiriguá used that: Stela F of 761 was the tallest monument the Maya had ever raised at 7.3 m, and Stela E beat it ten years later at 10.6 m and about 65 tonnes — possibly the largest free-standing worked monolith in the New World. The building programme follows the capture and public beheading of Copán's king on 3 May 738.

A natural cave was modified into an instrument. A shaft was cut through the roof with a slight slope, so between 30 April and 15 August the sun projects onto the cave floor — and at the zenith passages, around 14–15 May and 28–29 July, it comes straight down. Founded about 650 AD on an artificially levelled hilltop with terraces down the slopes, and burned around 900.

Dutch gable fronts built for a northern city, put on a Caribbean harbour and then painted — an architecture designed for grey light and cold, adapted by colour rather than by form. The Handelskade faces Sint Anna Bay, the inlet into the deep natural harbour of the Schottegat, which is the reason the town is there at all.

Around 70 sugar mills worked the Valle de los Ingenios behind the town, and Alejo Iznaga Borrell put up a 45 m tower there in 1816 to watch them — a building whose purpose is supervising the people doing the work. When the sugar trade failed, so did the money to rebuild anything, which is exactly why the 18th and 19th-century town is still standing. Founded 23 December 1514.

Steep wet forest is hard to farm, hard to march through and hard to see into — which is why the Windward Maroons could hold it, and why species stay put in it. 495.2 km², 4.5% of Jamaica, holding one of only two known habitats of the giant swallowtail, the largest butterfly in the Western Hemisphere, along with the Jamaican blackbird, boa and hutia. Listed on 3 July 2015 for both halves of that at once.

Kakezukuri: rather than cut the hillside back, the building is thrown out over it on tall pillars, so the floor stays level and the slope stays as it was. The whole frame is joined and pegged, with no nails anywhere in it — which is also what lets it move. The present main hall was rebuilt in 1633 after a fire, and the drop from the stage is about 13 m.

The five-storey pagoda solves earthquakes by not being connected: its central pillar hangs from chains rather than resting on the ground, so the storeys can shift against it instead of shearing. 42 structures in all, built from 1617 for Tokugawa Ieyasu, with the Yōmeimon gate carved in deep relief and painted — including Hidari Jingorō's sleeping cat.

Ögedei walled it and built a fixed palace in 1235, and in the middle of it Guillaume Boucher — a Parisian goldsmith taken in war — made a silver tree with four gold serpents braided up the trunk and a mechanical angel that raised a trumpet, at which the serpents poured four different drinks. Razed by the Ming in 1380, and its stone taken to build Erdene Zuu around 1585.

The lakes are dammed by their own water. Groundwater arriving saturated with calcium carbonate loses its carbon dioxide at the surface and deposits travertine, which builds the barriers between the pools and keeps building them — so the valley is a staircase that made itself. Elevations run from about 2,000 to 4,500 m; the 2017 earthquake broke several of those natural dams.

A bahay na bato is three traditions in one house: stone or brick below against damp and earthquake, timber above because timber moves, and windows glazed in flattened capiz shell because glass had to come by ship and shell did not. Laid out by Juan de Salcedo in 1572 on the Intramuros grid — 233 historic buildings along 25 streets.

Island gigantism, and the reverse of what happened to the Ennedi crocodiles: on islands with no larger predator and no competition, a monitor lizard can become the largest thing there. Males reach 3 m and 136 kg. About 5,100 of them live across five islands of volcanic origin, in the driest part of Indonesia at 800 to 1,000 mm of rain a year.

Timur commissioned it in 1389 and work stopped when he died in 1405, so the main facade still carries the timber scaffolding that was left in it — the building is a cross-section of its own construction. Its brick dome, 18.2 m across, is the largest in Central Asia, and the double-dome and vault experiments tried here became the pattern for Samarkand and Herat.

Nothing is left of the Ak-Saray but the way in: two gate-towers 65 m high in blue, white and gold mosaic, begun in 1380 by craftsmen deported from conquered Khwarezm, with "If you challenge our power — look at our buildings" written across it. A portal that survives its own palace makes the point better than the palace would.

A Parthian capital of mud brick, founded traditionally by Arsaces I and totally destroyed by an earthquake in the first decade BC — which is what sealed it. What came out of the ruins is Hellenistic: a large number of carved ivory rhytons, made for a court that had beaten the Greeks and then drank like them.

Begun under Sarki Gijimasu in the late 11th century, completed in the mid-14th under Zamnagawa and extended in the 16th — clay, because the Sahel has clay and no stone, which is also why they need constant remaking to stand. Heinrich Barth recorded them in 1851 as ten miles round and thirty feet high.

Measure one baseline precisely, then measure angles, and trigonometry gives you every other distance without pacing it out — so a chain of 258 triangles can span 2,820 km from Hammerfest to the Black Sea. Struve ran it from 1816 to 1855 to find the Earth's flattening and got 1/294.26; satellites now say 1/298.257.

A dome 44 m across needs a wooden frame to hold the masonry until it closes, and no forest could supply one that size — so Brunelleschi built without it. A double shell to save weight, and herringbone brickwork that carries each freshly laid course sideways onto the nearest vertical rib instead of letting it slide. Begun 1420, closed 1436; the lantern finished by Michelozzo in 1461.

Alder trunks driven close together through mud and sand into hard clay, with Istrian limestone plates on top of them — and the timber survives because it is below the water table, where there is no oxygen for the fungi that would rot it. 126 islands and hundreds of bridges on that. The city is still sinking 1–2 mm a year, and St Mark's sits 64 cm above sea level.

The columns were taken from Roman and Visigothic buildings and were not tall enough for the ceiling height wanted, so the answer was to stack: horseshoe arches below carrying a second tier of semicircular ones above, which buys the height from the arches rather than from the shafts. About 850 columns of jasper, onyx, marble, granite and porphyry, in a building 180 by 130 m — with a Renaissance cathedral cut into the middle of it from 1523.

Ash preserves plaster, and plaster is what the paintings are on — so the frescoes here are in better condition than anything known from Knossos or the rest of Crete. Three-storey buildings with advanced drainage, buried by the Theran eruption most probably between 1620 and 1530 BC. One gold object hidden under a floor, and no unburied human remains at all: they had time to leave.

A timber wharf burns, and Bryggen has burned repeatedly — 1702 and again in 1955 among them. Each time it was rebuilt on the same sites, so what is old about it is the plan rather than the boards: about a quarter of the buildings postdate 1702 and the rest are younger still, standing on a layout laid down when the Hanseatic Kontor was established around 1350.

It grew outward instead of being replaced. William's White Tower of 1078 — the earliest stone keep in England, 36 by 32 m and 27 m high, in Kentish ragstone with Caen stone for the detail — was later wrapped in two concentric rings of wall, and Edward I dug a 50 m moat around the lot between 1275 and 1285. Almost 12 acres in all.

Sandstone on a hidden granite foundation, cut into mortise-and-tenon joints and held together by gravity alone — no mortar. That is why the carving can be as deep as it is: every block is a structural member and a sculpture at once, and the Kandariya Mahadeva alone carries over 870 statues. Built between 885 and about 1030 CE; 85 temples once, about 25 left.

A brick basin 215 by 35 m with a 7 m inlet and a one-metre sluice in the south wall, beside a warehouse of sixty-four cubical blocks 3.6 m square on a raised platform. Whether it is a dock has been argued for decades — the inlet may be too small for sea-going ships — but marine microfossils and gypsum in the silt say seawater stood in it. Begun about 2300 BCE.

A drip ledge was cut along the overhang so that rain running down the rock falls clear of the opening instead of into it — and that one groove is why 2,100 m² of painted plaster is still on the ceilings. Five caves under a rock 160 m above the plain, holding 153 Buddha statues; founded by Valagamba in the first century BCE, gilded and extended by Nissanka Malla in 1190.

Two tiers of roof in copper under gold, on a square base, with four silver-plated doors — and 518 small temples around it over 246 hectares. It stands on the Bagmati because the river is where the dead are burned, so the temple and the ghats are one institution. Recorded as early as 400 CE; in 2015 the outer buildings were damaged and the sanctum was not.

Water dissolves limestone along its joints, and given a tropical rainfall and enough time it takes out chambers: the Sarawak Chamber is 600 m long, 415 m wide and at least 80 m high, about 12 million m³. Deer Cave has the largest cave passage in the world at 120 to 150 m across, and about three million wrinkle-lipped bats leave it every evening. 295 km of passage explored.

Built into black basalt in the 2nd century and then, from 1076, walled inside a Seljuk fortress with eight external towers added between 1202 and 1253 — so the fortification preserved what it enclosed. It is the only Roman theatre of its type whose upper gallery, a covered portico, survives complete.

The hill is not natural — it is the accumulated remains of everything built there before, and the defence works by making that slope unclimbable: a glacis faced in large blocks of gleaming limestone, 50 m from the moat to the top, with a moat 22 m deep and 30 m wide from the 12th century. Most of what stands is Ayyubid, 1193–1215; badly damaged from August 2012 and again by the 2023 earthquake.

Building tall in earth is the hard case, and 6,500 houses here do it — several storeys with flat roofs, inside clay walls 9 to 14 m high, alongside more than 100 mosques and 12 hammams. A tower of unfired earth has to thicken downward and be renewed constantly, which is why the city looks the way it does and why it cannot be left alone.

The threat was inland. The landward wall went up first, in the 1270s and 1280s, and the sea side came later — a Hanseatic town on Gotland feared the countryside more than the Baltic. Local limestone with rubble fill and lime and clay mortar; first 5 to 6 m high, raised another 3 to 4 in the 1350s. 3.44 km of the original 3.6 still stands, with 27 of 29 large towers.

Ice moving east met a plug of hard volcanic rock, scoured the soft ground away on either side and left a tail of it in the lee — so the castle sits on the crag and the whole town runs down the tail behind it. That ridge is the only buildable ground, with marsh to the south and the man-made Nor Loch to the north, which is why the closes run steeply off it and why people built upward instead of outward.

It was a marshy lake where the water off the surrounding hills collected, and the Tarquins drained it with the Cloaca Maxima — so the forum exists because of a sewer. Then the same hills kept eroding into it: excavated paving levels show the ground rising through the Republic, and the deepest dug level is 3.60 m above sea level. By the Imperial period the buildings had squeezed the open square to about 130 by 50 m.

The Sintra hills are close enough to the Atlantic that they make their own weather, and the temperate humidity was used deliberately: about 5,000 hectares planted with Atlantic and Mediterranean species around buildings placed to be seen through it. Pena was built for Ferdinand II over a 16th-century Hieronymite monastery, keeping its church and cloister, in Neo-Gothic, Neo-Manueline, Neo-Islamic and Neo-Renaissance at once.

Birch bark peels off in papery sheets, takes a scratched letter and costs nothing — so people wrote on it about ordinary things, and about a thousand of those letters have come out of the ground from the 11th to 15th centuries, most of them by laypeople in the local dialect. They survive because the soil is waterlogged and organic material does not rot without oxygen. One estimate puts about 20% of urban men literate by the mid-13th century.

A delta is a river putting down what it can no longer carry, and this one is still doing it — probably 40% of it built in the last thousand years. That new ground is marsh and floating reed island rather than farmland, which is why over 320 bird species use it and more than a million birds winter there. About 5,165 km² with the Razim–Sinoe lagoons, the second largest delta in Europe and the best preserved.

Fresco is pigment laid into wet lime plaster, so the colour becomes part of the wall as it sets rather than sitting on it — which is the only reason painting the OUTSIDE of a church was worth attempting at all. Eight churches in Suceava county carry complete cycles across their external walls, from Pătrăuți in 1487 to Sucevița in 1581.

A meander of the Răut has cut limestone cliffs on three sides, which makes a neck of land defended by the river and a soft rock face you can dig into. Everyone who arrived used both: a Geto-Dacian fortress from the 6th to 1st centuries BC, a Golden Horde town called Shehr al-Jedid in the 14th, then Moldavian works — and a cave monastery in the cliff, still in use, with inscriptions from the 1690s.

The Gloriette is the point of the garden: a building on a 60 m hill put there since 1775 to close the view from the palace, so the landscape has an edge that belongs to the house. 1,441 rooms behind it, mostly from Maria Theresa's work in the 1740s and 1750s, a Roman Ruin built new in 1778, and a menagerie that claims to be the oldest zoo in the world.

The hill is worth more than the building on it. Béla IV built the first royal residence between 1247 and 1265; the medieval castle was destroyed in the great siege of 1686, a Baroque palace went up between 1749 and 1769, that was wrecked in the siege of Budapest between 29 December 1944 and 13 February 1945, and it was rebuilt again in simplified Baroque. 4.73 km² on the southern tip of Castle Hill.

A city in the Khwarezm desert lives on its canals, and in 1221 the Mongols destroyed both the city and the irrigation, turning the country round it to marsh. The Kutlug Timur minaret is still there, 60 m high and tapering from 12 m across at the base to 2 at the top; so is the interior dome of the Turabek Khanum mausoleum, mosaicked in flowers and stars, though the outer dome fell long ago. Then the Amu Darya changed course, and that finished it.

Snow that never melts compacts into ice and flows, and the Aletsch is the biggest result of that in the Alps: 23 km long and up to 900 m thick, in 35,000 hectares of continuous ice. Nine summits over 4,000 m stand around it, Finsteraarhorn highest at 4,270 — and the Jungfrau railway, built between 1870 and 1912, climbs from 2,061 m to 3,454 to put people on it.

A relic makes a route, and a route makes a building: Vézelay held the bones said to be Mary Magdalene's, and the church built between 1120 and 1150 is sized for the people who came. Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade from it before Louis VII at Easter 1146. Wrecked in the Revolution and restored by Viollet-le-Duc between 1840 and 1861.

Sand buries things and then moves off them again, which is why the same dunes hold pottery more than 2,600 years old and one of the largest burial grounds in the Pacific, and why shards, stone tools and human remains keep appearing at the surface. 650 hectares of dune 20 to 60 m tall at the mouth of the Sigatoka river; Fiji's first national park, July 1989.

The oldest cemetery known in the Pacific, found in late 2003: 26 inhumations of 36 individuals, roughly 3,110 to 2,710 years old, with red Lapita pottery of intricate design in the graves — and the skulls removed after the flesh had gone and replaced with cone shell rings. Genetic work says the people came straight from Taiwan or the northern Philippines rather than mixing on the way.

Volcanic stone lying on the ground, stacked: a base platform of basalt 65 by 60 m carrying three more platforms with vertical or slightly sloping walls, about 12 m high on the south edge and 7 on the north, with the top paved in rounded stream stones. Built probably between 1100 and 1400 AD and out of use by 1700–1800; the largest ancient structure in Samoa.

The same answer as Nan Madol, on the next island: basalt that cooled into columns splits into ready-made beams, and a town inside a fringing reef can be built out of them. Leluh ran from about 1250 to 1850 AD, held about 1,500 people over some 27 hectares, and had burial pyramids for its nobility.

The trade calls this fermentation and it is a misnomer: nothing microbial happens. Breaking the leaf lets its own polyphenol oxidase reach the polyphenols, and the leaf oxidises itself. How far that is allowed to go is the whole difference — fully oxidised is black tea, barely oxidised is green — and the oxidised leaf then keeps its flavour for years where green tea loses it inside one.

The flavour is not in the seed; it is made afterwards. Heaped in their own pulp for several days, the beans sweat — the thick pulp liquefies as it ferments — and the heat that builds turns them from purple to brown. Underdone, the seed still tastes of raw potato and goes mouldy. Chocolate begins in a pile of wet fruit.

Not every plum can be dried. A prune is a Prunus domestica variety whose soluble solids are high enough that it does not ferment while it dries — and a freestone, so the pit comes out. About 31% water is left at the end and 64% of the rest is carbohydrate; the sorbitol in it, with the fibre, is why prunes do what they are known for.

A wool fibre is covered in scales like a hair. Heat and moisture make the scales stand open, agitation drives the fibres past each other, and the open scales catch — so the mat is one piece and cannot be taken apart again. Plant and synthetic fibres have no scales and will not do it at all.

Anything more than a light breeze moves snow onto the sheltered side of a ridge, and it lands packed. The slab forms faster than the weaker snow beneath it can adjust to the new load, so a cohesive sheet ends up sitting on something that cannot hold it. Slab avalanches account for around 90% of avalanche deaths, and cross-loaded slabs on a lee slope are usually the ones nobody can see.

Sugar plus heat plus acid makes hydroxymethylfurfural, and honey supplies all three the moment it is warmed — which turns it into a thermometer with a memory. Fresh honey holds under 15 mg/kg; the Codex Alimentarius allows 40, or 80 for tropical honeys, and above that the honey has been heated in processing.

A hole at each end and breath through one of them empties a shell without breaking it, which is the only way to keep the object and lose the contents. What is left is the arch working in three dimensions: a shell about 0.3 mm thick that a hand cannot crush end-on because the load runs round the curve.

Wind carries no message, so a plant using it must give up on advertising and buy lottery tickets instead: no scent, no showy petals, little nectar, and enormous numbers of grains 20 to 60 micrometres across, smooth and light and not sticky. About 12% of plants do it, including rice, maize, wheat and barley — and the pollen is low in protein, which is why it is worth nothing to an insect.

Cold is what sets honey, and not evenly: seed crystals nucleate fastest between 5 and 8 °C while they grow fastest between 13 and 17, so a cold larder sets a jar quicker than a fridge does. What comes out is glucose only — honey holds more of it than the water can really dissolve — and the fructose stays liquid around the granules. Warming to 40–50 °C undoes it.

It is the same mechanism as stale bread, and here it is useful. Cooking dissolves the starch granules; cooling lets the loose glucose chains reassociate into small crystals — amylose fast, amylopectin slowly — and those crystals are the wrong shape for the digestive enzymes. Boiled potatoes cooled overnight at 4 °C were found to carry 2.8 times the resistant starch.

Cocoa butter can crystallise in several forms and tempering puts it into form V on purpose, because form V is glossy and snaps. Temperature swings let it move on toward the more stable form VI, which comes to the surface as a pale film — fat bloom, slick to the touch and gone under gentle warming. Sugar bloom is the other one: condensation dissolves surface sugar and it dries back as dust. Both are still safe to eat.
